In a related thread of work, researchers have looked at
the idea of explainable agents. As agents are supposed
to represent human behavior, works in this area mainly
focus on behavior explanations generation so that agents
could explain the reasons behind their actions. Significant
earlier works proposed approaches for self-explaining virtual agents in scenario-based training systems [173], [174].
Recent works have investigated the possibilities of explainability of advanced autonomous agents like socially interactive robots [175]–[178].
E. ECONOMIC PERSPECTIVE

There are significant benefits to gain from being on the
front foot and investing in explainability today. Indeed, due
to the social and ethical pressure, XAI could turn into a
competitive differentiator and drives a real business value.
Moreover, the technical challenge of explainability involving
the tradeoff between accuracy and interpretability, affects
significantly the cost of XAI products. Curiously, in literature
economical perspective of XAI is an area of less research yet
no less important. Encouraging economic interpretations is
essential to address several issues such as explainability cost
estimation and variation, algorithm propriety, revealing trade
secrets and predicting XAI market evolution.
Amongst few works found in literature, Akyol et al. [179]
proposed a first attempt to quantitatively analyze the cost
of transparency (PoT) in ML algorithms. The work of
Igami [180] about the connections between machine learning
and econometrics, proposed the perspective of ‘‘Structural
Econometrics for Explainable AI’’. He noted that ‘‘relaxing
the implicit econometric assumptions would make the results
economically interpretable’’.
The discussed outlooks are by no means exhaustive, but
give a few leads for further exploration from different perspectives based on our compilation of existent studies in literature. We hope that the proposed directions will inspire new
research that can improve the current state of the art in XAI.
V. CONCLUSION

Matter-of-factly, XAI is a vital interdisciplinary research field
in the AI ecosystem. In the spirit of holism, we presented in
this paper a comprehensive background regarding this field.
Taking inspiration from how we assimilate and familiarize
ourselves with new topics, we focused on the Five W’s and
How (What, Who, When, Why, Where, and How) to cover all
aspects related to XAI. Moreover, in the interest of mapping
the broad landscape around XAI research, this survey has
thoroughly reviewed a portfolio of explainability approaches
and organized them from different perspectives.
Findings showed that XAI is not just a labcoat research
field, its impact is spanning in a large range of application
domains. However, we have seen evidence throughout this
work for the lack of formalism in terms of problem formulation and clear unambiguous definitions. Furthermore, it has
been noted that the human’s role is not sufficiently studied
in existing explainability approaches. In essence, attention is
52156

devoted to interpreting ML models letting other promising
AI system explainability under-explored. It has then been
concluded that considerable effort will be required in the
future to tackle the challenges and open issues with XAI.

Background: The integration of Machine Learning and Deep Learning with IoT-enabled devices for
real-time health monitoring has significantly revolutionized healthcare. These technologies
facilitate the analysis of intricate medical datasets, yielding actionable insights that promote
evidence-based clinical decision-making. Although significant advancements have been made,
there is still an absence of a thorough synthesis regarding current applications, primary challenges, and prospective research directions. This review aims to synthesize recent applications,
identify significant gaps, and propose clear direction for future research.
Methodology: A comprehensive narrative review was performed where a systematic literature
search was conducted in PubMed and Scopus for studies published between 2020 and 2025. A
total of 300 pertinent papers on ML and IoT’s applications in healthcare were selected and
analyzed to synthesize technological advancements, trade-offs, practical implications, challenges,
and potential directions for future research.
Key findings: Neural network models, such as CNNs and ANNs, along with ensemble methods like
Random Forest and XGBoost, often attain predictive accuracies ranging from 85 % to 95 %.
Advanced technique, like generative imaging models, reinforcement learning, and transformerbased architectures, improve diagnostics, chronic disease management, robotic-assisted surgery, and predictive analytics, while explainable AI promotes clinical trust. Cloud-edge integration utilizing lightweight machine learning models enables real-time, energy-efficient
applications, enhancing diagnosis, decision support, personalization, and cost-effectiveness,
notwithstanding current challenges.
Conclusion: To conclude, the integration of ML and IoT is transforming healthcare through
enhanced monitoring, improved predictive capabilities, and tailored treatment approaches.
Addressing persistent limitations is crucial for fully realizing its potential and directing future
research in this evolving field.

1. Introduction
There is a significant demand for the digitalization of healthcare industries, particularly due to advancements in wireless technologies and electronic equipment. Healthcare 5.0 is the most recent paradigm in healthcare systems, integrating technologies such as
Internet of Things (IoT) with machine learning.1,2 The prevalence of chronic diseases has significantly risen as a result of global
economic transformations. The primary threat to human health arises from chronic diseases. Furthermore, if a disease outbreaks, it
results in an inflow of patients to hospitals, straining the ability of medical facilities to provide care for all individuals. The worldwide
spreading of COVID-19 has exerted pressure on health care facilities globally. Moreover, numerous outpatient departments encounter
the issue of congestion in their waiting areas. Patients visiting hospitals present with many diseases, some necessitating urgent medical
intervention. The dilemma is further worse when patients requiring emergency care must endure an extended wait in line. The issue is
exacerbated in developing nations with inadequately staffed hospitals. A significant number of patients frequently leave without
receiving medical care due to hospital overpopulation. The enhancement and maintenance of health is only achievable through the
diagnosis and prompt prevention of ailments. Consequently, it is essential to alleviate the strain on healthcare systems while maintaining the quality and standards of healthcare facilities.3
Machine learning and IoT offer potential solutions to alleviate the pressure on healthcare systems. For example, physicians can
readily monitor patients’ heart impulses using IoT based healthcare monitoring systems and predict heart diseases with Machine
learning, hence facilitating accurate diagnoses.4 To provide consistent wireless data transfer, numerous wearable devices have been
created. The IoT application enables hospitals to monitor the vital signs of patients with chronic diseases. The IoT has ushered in a new
era for the healthcare sector, facilitating proactive connections between experts and patients. ML-driven diagnostics can deliver precise
and prompt diagnoses, enhancing treatment outcomes. The IoT is anticipated to further proliferate due to developments in sensor
technology, networking, and data analytics. With the passage of time, an increased number of medical equipment will be interconnected Through IoT, facilitating real-time monitoring, remote patient management, and the early identification of health concerns.
Real-time data transmission enables prompt action, hence diminishing problems and hospital re-admissions. Although transformative
changes on ML-IoT healthcare applications are observed in recent times, there are still some shortcomings in the overall synthesis
which needs the attention of researchers.
This paper offers comprehensive insights and synthesis into the latest technological advancements and role of machine learning and
IoT in health care applications. Researchers can benefit from acquiring a thorough awareness of the recent trends of machine learning
& IoT. Adopting these technologies and concepts can result in superior patient care, optimized healthcare operations, and innovative
research that may transform the future of healthcare delivery. Another contribution is addressing the challenges related to the
implementation of machine learning and IoT in healthcare. This knowledge can enable the researchers to link their studies with the
urgent demands and issues in healthcare. This paper also highlights future directions and research prospects, as it assists researchers in
pinpointing pertinent, effective topics of study that correspond with the dynamic requirements of the healthcare sector.
The remainder of the work is structured as follows. Section 2 presents the methodology. Section 3 highlights the State-of-the-Art
Developments and case Studies in Healthcare ML-IoT Systems. Section 4 emphasizes on the impact of integrated ML–IoT systems in
healthcare applications while addressing its role in improving outcomes in healthcare sectors and key benefits in various applications.
Section 5 discusses the result section providing analytical findings derived from the study. Section 6 presents the discussion, outlining
the challenges and limitations of this integrated technology, while highlighting future directions and research opportunities for
emerging researchers. Section 7 concludes the paper.
2. Materials & method
This review was developed as a narrative review and critical analysis of the literature on machine learning and IoT applications in
healthcare. Although it’s a narrative review, it has followed a structured process to ensure transparency of the paper. The strategy
details are shared below.
2.1. Literature search strategy
Relevant publications were identified mainly via academic databases such as Scopus, PubMed, Web of Science, ScienceDirect, and
Google Scholar, ensuring thorough coverage of recent research. The search incorporates combined keywords and phrases including
“machine learning,” “deep learning,” “artificial intelligence,” “Internet of Things,” “IoMT,” “smart healthcare,” “healthcare 5.0,”
“remote patient monitoring,” “predictive analytics,” “clinical decision support,” “wearable sensors,” and “personalized medicine.”
Boolean operators (AND/OR) were used to find intersections among machine learning techniques, Internet of Things technologies, and
healthcare applications. The search was limited to articles published within the past five years to incorporate recent and relevant
studies. Furthermore, reference lists from significant review papers, systematic reviews, and reports were examined manually to
identify additional relevant sources. The literature review encompassed various study types, such as observational studies, clinical
trials, case studies, and computational experiments, to encompass a broad range of applications, benefits, challenges, and future directions of ML-IoT in healthcare.

2.2. Inclusion criteria
The following outlines the inclusion criteria:
• Articles from peer-reviewed journals, conference proceedings, and book chapters that focus on ML and the IoT applications, and
current trends in healthcare.
• Studies published between 2020 and 2025 will be included to ensure coverage of recent advancements.
• Research articles presenting empirical findings, case studies, or thorough analyses of ML-IoT systems across various healthcare
applications
• Research published in English and indexed in Scopus or PubMed.
2.3. Exclusion criteria
The exclusion criteria are given below:
• Articles not directly related to healthcare applications of ML or IoT, such as general AI or IoT studies in other industries.
• Studies without sufficient methodological details or empirical evidence
• Publications older than the past five years.
• Non-English articles or those not indexed in reputable databases (Scopus, PubMed)
• Duplicate studies or redundant reports with overlapping data.
2.4. Scope
This review indicates recent research on the integration of machine learning (ML) and Internet of Things (IoT) technologies in
healthcare, emphasizing applications, emerging trends, and practical implementations. The research studies selected were examined
to both summarize recent advancements and to identify trade-offs, challenges, and limitations related to ML–IoT systems. The review
offers essential insights into the effectiveness and feasibility of ML–IoT solutions by analyzing various approaches, highlighting best
practices, and examining real-world applications. Additionally, it highlights gaps in existing research and suggests potential directions
for future studies, with the objective of guiding both scholarly inquiry and evidence-based implementation in clinical environments.
3. State-of-the-Art Developments and case Studies in Healthcare ML-IoT systems
Machine Learning (ML) is revolutionizing healthcare sectors by the application of methods including supervised learning, reinforcement learning, and deep learning. Supervised learning is mostly used for diagnostics, while reinforcement learning is important
for personalized treatment plans and robotics-assisted surgery. Deep learning is employed in image recognition and natural language
processing to analyze medical data and perform predictive analytics. The integration of IoT technology in healthcare, including the use
of wearable devices and smart sensors, enhances the real-time collection and analysis of data.5–7Machine Learning (ML) and the
Internet of Things (IoT) have significantly advanced healthcare through enhancements in predictive analysis, disease forecasting, and
diagnostics, among other areas8–19. Fig. 1 shows some of the applications of ML and IoT in the health-care system.

3.1. Machine learning algorithms in healthcare
Machine learning algorithms have improved the capabilities of doctors and analysts by finding complex patterns in medical data.
This has made diagnoses more accurate and made it easier to make decisions based on evidence.20–28 As a result, these algorithms also
make it easier for predictive models in early disease detection, how it will progress, and how to group patients by risk, which helps with
personalized treatment plans and proactive healthcare management.29–35 Machine learning-based techniques have been applied in
large medical centers to increase efficiency in medical imaging and monitoring to identify irregularities in blood samples, organs,
bones, robot-assisted surgeries etc..36–41 ML makes it possible to analyze the massive amounts of heterogeneous data that are produced
every day in the healthcare sector originating from multiple sources. The data include medical records, medical images, data from
wearable devices, clinical trial data, data from open sources, genomic data, data from health surveys, and cloud platform. By analyzing
such data, ML can uncover patterns, predict disease risks, personalize treatment plans, optimize hospital operations, and support
timely clinical decision-making. Fig. 2 illustrates the sources of heterogeneous data analyzed by ML.
As the healthcare industry expands into the modern technological era, numerous innovations are made. The advancement of the
discipline depends on methods and applications based on machine learning, which has led to faster, more accurate, and simpler
diagnosis & prediction processes.42–47 The next subsection outlines the various types of algorithms and their specific applications along
with recent trends in healthcare.
3.1.1. Supervised learning for disease diagnosis and prediction
Supervised learning is a machine learning algorithm that uses labeled data to acquire knowledge. The algorithm can be classified
into classification and regression algorithms, such as Logistic Regression, Decision Trees, Random Forest, Support Vector Machines
(SVM), K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), and Naive Bayes. These methods are applied when the output variable has a continuous value.
Supervised Learning algorithms are used in diagnosis and prediction of different types of diseases including breast cancer, heart
diseases, liver disease, thyroid, Alzheimer’s disease, lung cancer, prostate cancer, brain cancer, hepatitis, Covid 19, influenza etc.
Breast cancer, the second most diagnosed cancer in women, often relies on mammography, which is only 70 % accurate, leading to
potential misdiagnosis. Researchers have applied machine learning for predicting breast cancer by carefully choosing the most
effective characteristics, using six supervised learning classifiers: support vector machine, random forest, gradient boosting machine,
multilayer perceptron, logistic regression, and K-nearest neighbors (KNN). KNN outperforms all other classifiers on the 20-feature
dataset using SVD and achieves a perfect accuracy score of 100 % when employing a PCA with the 15 most significant features,

for unsupervised segmentation of brain tumors in MR images. Their study examined methods for synthesizing more realistic brain

create shape and intensity models to produce synthetic brain tumors for the purpose of model training. In the subsequent stage, an

Anomaly detection in medical imaging has proven to be crucial in medical image analysis. The Unsupervised Anomaly Detection
(UAD) method aims to differentiate anomalous tissue from normal anatomy by learning from healthy structures. Generative models
are frequently employed to generate counterfactual healthy samples from diseased images, facilitating anomaly detection without the
need for pixel-level annotations.87 The use of such models removes the necessity for extensive manual labeling, which can present
difficulties. Additionally, it enables the detection of unseen or rare anomaly cases that are underrepresented in the dataset for fully
supervised models. However, the inability of these models to reconstruct unhealthy structures results in reconstruction errors that
signify anomalies. Nonetheless, a considerable challenge lies in achieving a balance between the precise reconstruction of healthy
anatomy and the inadvertent replication of abnormal structures. In recent times, diffusion models have been proven to demonstrate
potential for detailed and accurate reconstructions. Some researchers suggested conditioning the denoising process of diffusion models
using supplementary information obtained from a latent representation of the input image.88 Other researchers have proposed an
unsupervised anomaly detection model specifically for medical images. The Synomaly noise function was applied to improve the
efficacy of anomaly detection. This noise is introduced to healthy training images to replicate the characteristics of actual anomalous
tissues following the noising process. A multi-stage diffusion process was proposed for the inference phase. Extensive validation was
conducted across various medical imaging modalities, including brain MRI, liver CT, and carotid ultrasound (US) datasets. The
findings from the three predominant medical imaging modalities (ultrasound, computed tomography, and magnetic resonance imaging) illustrate the applicability of the proposed method across various contexts. Although unsupervised anomaly detection offers
benefits, its effectiveness is significantly influenced by the generative model’s capacity to maintain healthy structures and precisely
reconstruct pathological regions as their healthy equivalents. This highlights the necessity for additional investigation into advanced
generative models to improve performance.89
Unsupervised learning has become a critical tool for medical imaging, particularly in tumor segmentation, anomaly detection, and
biomedical image clustering, as it mitigates the dependency on costly and time-consuming manual annotations. By minimizing the
domain gap between synthetic and real data can enhance unsupervised segmentation performance. Furthermore, leveraging diffusion
models or hybrid generative frameworks can ensure more accurate reconstruction of healthy anatomy and precise anomaly detection.
Further development of explainable metrics can be carried out to quantify how well models separate normal and pathological tissue.
Also, more focus on realistic data synthesis, multi-modal learning, and clinically interpretable generative models to maximize impact.
Also, training the model to selectively identify specific types of anomalies while ignoring others can facilitate selective segmentation.
These advancements would enable the model to detect and classify anomalies, thereby enhancing its value in clinical decision-making.
3.1.3. Reinforcement learning in personalized treatment plans & robotics-assisted surgery
Providing personalized recommendations has become crucial in the medical field for lessening the impact of overloaded information. The biomedical sector has yet to fully explore proper recommendations. The health care industry typically addresses chronic
or enduring concerns. When it comes to tackling health behaviors and chronic diseases, the capacity of individuals to manage their
programs is of the utmost importance. Participating in physical activities, adhering to prescribed medications, and following eating
plans are all examples of common self-management behaviors. To assist in such endeavors, it is essential to take into account the
distinct lifestyles and priorities of individuals, as well as their psychological and psychosocial circumstances, and environmental influences.90 Conventional recommended systems do not take into account the long-term consequences, thereby failing to capture the
changing emotions of individuals. When compared to non-individualized treatments, some studies have shown that providing
personalized self-management support for common health conditions or chronic diseases yields better results.91,92 The majority of
current recommended systems have not fully addressed the problems of data sparsity and non-linear user-item connections. Reinforcement learning systems have the potential to alter recommendation techniques.93 Reinforcement learning is an approach for
guiding agent behavior within an environment to optimize cumulative rewards. Recent studies have focused on various disease
treatment recommendation systems utilizing reinforcement learning. Some researchers sought to create a reinforcement
learning-based treatment recommendation model utilizing the health records of South Korean citizens to support physicians. This

3.1.4. Deep learning in image recognition, natural language processing & predictive analytics
The unique challenges of medical records when compared to general domain text include the following: the heavy use of acronyms
and unusual clinical terms by healthcare providers; inconsistent document organization and structure etc. The rapid growth and
availability of unorganized data since the inception of the Internet have had a significant role in the establishment of natural language
processing (NLP) as an essential technology for tackling complex and knowledge-based tasks. Some of the steps involved in Natural
Language Processing (NLP) include morphological analysis, syntactic analysis, semantic analysis, discourse processing etc..103,104
Conventional machine learning approaches have been extensively employed in medical natural language processing tasks. While
these methods necessitate considerable manual effort and continue to exhibit limitations in accuracy, deep learning (DL) based
methods have demonstrated substantial advancements.105 Deep learning is a subfield of machine learning that builds hierarchical
representations of input using multi-layer neural network designs.106 Deep learning is mostly used in the healthcare sector to apply
advanced computer vision methods as well as image processing to medical scans to diagnose disorders. Image analysis and Electronic
Medical Records (EMR) natural language processing are two clinical applications where deep learning has shown significant promise.
The utilization of Natural Language Processing (NLP) in analyzing free-text inside Electronic Medical Records (EMR) holds great
potential due to the comprehensive nature of EMRs. These records encompass clinical assessments, overall background, diagnostic test
summaries and research, as well as longitudinal monitoring of the patient’s progress. Several deep learning architectures have
employed adult electronic medical records (EMRs) to extract features and perform natural language processing (NLP)107–111.
Some researchers have applied deep learning-based natural language processing methods to detect colonoscopic information. The
study compared long short-term memory (LSTM) and BioBERT models to identify the one exhibiting superior performance for colonoscopy reports, ultimately determining that the bidirectional LSTM with conditional random fields was the most effective. The NLP
model utilizing pre-trained word embeddings outperformed the one employing one-hot encoding across the majority of labels. The
method employed in this study yielded promising results, indicating its applicability to diverse practical applications.112 Others sought
to predict the progression of glaucoma necessitating surgery through deep learning techniques applied to electronic health records.
This analysis incorporated features derived from both structured clinical data and natural language processing of unstructured clinical
text.113 Another study was conducted to design and validate large language models (LLMs) for the purpose of automatic clinical

In order to provide ongoing patient monitoring and intelligent care delivery, smart hospital ecosystems are increasingly based on
wearable IoT devices, seamless integration with electronic health records (EHRs), and real-time cloud connectivity. An AI-enabled
wearable IoMT architecture for long-term care settings was presented by the researchers. It combined intelligent upstream processing with edge-based physiological signal collecting. Vital signs and behavioral data are sent by wearable sensors to edge nodes, which
conduct instantaneous analytics before sending processed insights and organized EHR data via secure cloud pipelines. By utilizing
wearable data and connected, high-fidelity digital patient files, this architecture enables tailored care coordination, minimizes
needless hospital stays, and enables real-time clinician warnings.123
3.2.2. Integration of smart IoT sensors in medical devices
Every health care system that utilizes Internet of Things (IoT) technology incorporates a layer of sensors. These sensors gather data
from users/patients by detecting their vital signs and other essential signals. The data is subsequently transformed into a form that can
be analyzed and tracked. This layer may consist of a variety of sensors capable of utilizing sensors to identify and track physical
movement and observe essential health indicators, and other distinct signals that may suggest an irregularity. Multiple prototypes have
been constructed utilizing various types of sensors.124
These sensors are primarily intended to be worn, as users must be able to perform their usual activities with no disturbance. Several
of these systems employ Body Area Networks (BAN) or Wireless Sensor Networks (WSN) for networking through IoT cloud. Fig. 4
shows the commonly used architecture of remote monitoring and WBAN communication through IoT cloud.
As illustrated in Fig. 4, the WBAN is capable of diagnosing many human ailments and monitoring various user attributes, such as
body temperature, heart rate, and blood pressure. The smart phone can then get the data from the wireless sensors once the anomalous
state has been determined. After that, this information is sent to doctors or any other assistance desk so they can take the appropriate
action. As seen in Fig. 4, the data can be delivered from the gateway to the destination over the Internet or a cellular network. WBANs
are also utilized for remote monitoring and preventative health actions. Furthermore, the field also encompasses microcontrollers such
as Arduino, STM32 Microcontroller, Intel Galileo, Raspberry Pi etc..125–127 The communication protocols utilized were MQTT, LoRaWAN, GSM, ZigBee, BLE, and GPRS.128–130 In order to facilitate disease prediction and risk stratification, wearable and bedside
sensors transmit data to IoT clouds for preprocessing, feature extraction, and model training. Home monitoring data is streamed,
cleaned, processed, classifiers are trained, and doctors are given predictions for post-discharge risk monitoring by one cloud-based
machine learning platform.131 IoT/IoMT-ML pipelines enhance cardiovascular care predictability and continuous monitoring,
including event prediction, heart failure, and arrhythmia.132 The smart IoT sensors include respiratory sensor,133,134 heart Beat
Monitoring Sensor,135–139 activity detection sensors,140–144 accelerometer sensor,145 blood pressure sensor,146,147 blood glucose
monitoring sensor,148 body temperature sensor,149,150 EMG sensor151,152 etc.
3.2.3. Remote monitoring systems
Remote patient monitoring, also known as telemonitoring, focuses on specific sub-groups of patients, including those with chronic
illnesses, mobility challenges, disabilities, post-surgery patients, neonates, and elderly patients. It is advisable to continuously monitor
all patients with these types of illnesses. Most research adheres to the principle of offering patients the ability to move and engage in
activities in their own homes or personal environments, which is more advantageous than being confined to an expensive hospital
room. People in their elder age no longer require constant supervision from a caregiver because of cutting-edge remote health
monitoring software. Patients who have suffered accidents or sudden injuries may only be monitored remotely while they are being
taken to the hospital in an ambulance. Nevertheless, the main emphasis has been on guaranteeing a secure journey to the hospital,
while remote monitoring assists in delivering timely medical interventions for highly critical patients. The doctors can see and track
the decline or preservation of the patient’s condition, while also providing guidance to the paramedics who stay with the patients, if
needed.153

3.2.4. Inter-operability for seamless data transfer
The potential advantages of cutting-edge disciplines like machine learning and big data analytics are limited by this underutilization. Although 36 % of American individuals used wearable technology, according to a recent cross-sectional survey, only roughly
25 % shared their data with healthcare professionals, even though over 78 % said they would be ready to do so. This suggests that there
are gaps in workflow alignment and integration.158 Critical obstacles to using patient-generated health data (PGHD) for preventive
healthcare were also highlighted by another study that interviewed clinicians managing ischemic heart disease and discovered that
interoperability, clinical workload, and data reliability issues hindered effective use of PGHD.159
A significant barrier to interoperability, according to researchers, is the lack of commonly accepted, uniform standards for gathering and sharing clinical and patient-generated data; even in cases where frameworks such as FHIR are in place, heterogeneous
vocabularies, inconsistent metadata, and compartmentalized system architectures continue to obstruct smooth data sharing.160
Additionally, a large portion of wearable and remote monitoring data is underutilized in decision-making due to limited integration
into clinician workflows and EHRs.161 Similar to the layered approach in the OSI model, the architecture of contemporary IoT
healthcare implementations frequently extends from physical sensors to edge gateways and cloud services. But the computational,
memory, and energy limitations of resource-constrained devices, particularly sensor nodes, make it difficult for them to preprocess,
store, or perform important logic on-site.162 According to a study on smart healthcare networks, raw sensing is still lightweight and
only generates data, and such limited devices must rely on edge or fog intermediaries to carry out real-time analytics, security tasks,
and communication protocol translation.163 This layered design reinforces the hybrid hierarchy common in IoT systems by highlighting the need to transfer complex activities to more capable infrastructure.
Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR) Standard is an extensively used standard in healthcare. Standardized language,
standards, and protocols independent of vendor platforms are advocated for by the International Healthcare Technology Standards
Developing Organization (IHTSDO). As an example, one format used for sharing information across versions is Health Level Seven
(HL7). Clinical Document Architecture (CDA) and other prior HL7 standards were integrated to form FHIR. HTTP, RESTful, XML, and
JSON are some of the most popular web protocols that FHIR incorporates these features with.164,165 Moreover, Ambient Assisted Living
(UniversAAL) is another standard. The well-being and autonomy of older individuals have been greatly enhanced by recent developments in Ambient Assisted Living (AAL).166–168
The incorporation of IoT and wearable devices in healthcare facilitates continuous remote patient monitoring, real-time data
collection, and personalized care via WBANs and IoT-ML pipelines that enhance predictive analytics and risk stratification. Remote
monitoring systems improve patient autonomy, decrease hospital visits, and enable prompt interventions. However, some challenges
exist, including limited interoperability among diverse devices and electronic health record systems, computational limitations on
resource-constrained IoT devices, concerns regarding data privacy and security, and inadequate integration of wearable data into
clinical workflows. Researchers need to focus on the development of standardized frameworks for the integration of devices and
electronic health records, the implementation of edge-AI for real-time analytics, the adoption of privacy-preserving machine learning
methods like federated learning, the design of patient-centered devices focused on usability and feedback, and the utilization of AIdriven insights to facilitate predictive and preventive healthcare interventions.

3.3. Case studies on integrated ML-IoT in healthcare
This section provides an overview of the recent research works focusing on employing different diagnosis use cases that have been
proposed or implemented using machine learning (ML) and the Internet of Things (IoT) platforms. A diagnosis is established by
examining the patient’s symptoms, which are monitored by sensors to identify the kind of disease they are currently dealing with.
3.3.1. Case studies on predictive analytics for diabetes management
Doctors can leverage IoT-enabled cloud systems with AI and ML to monitor patients’ physical activity and analyze data from
wearable sensors for continuous glucose monitoring (CGM), and lifestyle inputs. These systems integrate real-time glucose levels,
activity, meals, insulin doses, and sleep patterns to predict blood glucose trends and support timely clinical interventions. For type 1
diabetes, CGM systems combined with edge-based ML allow near-real-time glycemic predictions up to 45 min in advance, aiding
insulin adjustments and hypoglycemia prevention without relying solely on the cloud.169 Meta-analyses show Random Forest offers
the most accurate forecasts over 15–60 min, with rising RMSE values but still within therapeutic use.170 Frameworks like SmartEdge
further improve latency and prediction accuracy by about 5 % compared to cloud-only solutions.171 Hybrid systems increasingly
incorporate blockchain to ensure secure, inter-institutional data sharing. AI-driven models enhance diabetes risk prediction by 4–6 %
compared to baseline approaches, highlighting the growing role of AI, ML, and IoT in delivering personalized, predictive diabetes
care.172,173
For longer prediction horizons and up to 10 % higher accuracy than LSTM baselines are supported by models such as AttenGluco,
which use transformer architectures to fuse wearable sensor data with CGM measurements.174,175 Similarly, with RMSE as low as
5.9–11.3 mg/dL, large-scale ANN models trained on millions of minutes of T1D data perform better than traditional meters. However,
they struggle with rapid glucose changes because of CGM latency.176,177 Additionally, IoT integration makes non-invasive monitoring
possible through NIRS devices, which gather glucose data every half hour, transmit it to the cloud, set off alarms for hypoglycemia (less
than 4 mmol/L) or hyperglycemia (more than 11 mmol/L), and enable remote monitoring via SMS alerts, enhancing safety, particularly at night.178–182
Meanwhile, other body fluids including saliva, sweat, tears, or skin are being used to develop non-invasive glucose monitoring
technologies like Raman spectroscopy, NIRS, mid-infrared, fluorescence, and bioimpedance.183 Prediction accuracy has increased
through developments that combine wearable optical and electrochemical sensors with AI and ML models (CNNs, Random Forest,
XGBoost). A study, found that XGBoost with multimodal physiological sensors decreased errors (RMSE ~11.9 mg/dL, MARD ~7.1
%),184 while CNN and Random Forest with SWIR spectroscopy produced great precision (MAPE 4.82 %, 100 % Clarke Zone-A).185
Predictive features for upcoming hyperglycemia events are still absent from the majority of systems, though.186
3.3.2. Case studies on remote patient monitoring for heart disease
Since cardiovascular disease is still one of the top causes of death, wearable sensors, cloud/fog computing, and artificial intelligence
(AI) are being used in IoT-enabled remote patient monitoring (RPM) systems to provide real-time cardiac care. While ML classifiers
(Random Forest, CNN, k-NN) with ECG sensors demonstrated 94 % accuracy for premature ventricular contractions and 97 % accuracy
for normal beats, advanced models like ensemble CNN–LSTM have achieved 97.23 % accuracy in detecting abnormalities in multiple
vital signs of heart failure patients, guaranteeing prompt alerts to doctors.187,188 These systems enable low-latency, high-fidelity
monitoring, even in resource-limited settings, reducing rehospitalization rates and supporting predictive cardiac care. Wireless Sensor

3.3.3. Case studies on personalized cancer treatment
When it comes to the number of fatalities, the most common type is lung cancer. The process of diagnosing cancer can be greatly
accelerated by using computer-aided diagnostic (CAD).202 Because of this, machine learning is becoming more and more important in
the detection and treatment of different forms of cancer. AI in cancer is expected to speed up the procedures of diagnosis and treatment
planning.203 Oncology uses ML for medication synthesis at the point of care, treatment planning, medical image analysis, and patient
survival prediction.204 Prognostic prediction for patients has already been enhanced by the ML model over conventional staging
techniques. The implementation of ML could also have a significant positive impact on the synthesis done directly of the required
medicinal compounds when receiving treatment.
Planning a course of treatment for cancer is extremely complicated and requires interdisciplinary cooperation from radiologists,
surgeons, oncologists, data scientists, and rehabilitation experts. Personalized oncology care is being revolutionized by recent developments in AI, DL, and ML, which are frequently combined with IoT-connected high-resolution imaging, sensor devices, and omics
platforms. The types of cancer treatments that facilitate treatment planning and help prevent cancer recurrences are depicted in Fig. 6.
While ML–IoT systems with wearable sensors and ensemble models (Random Forest, XGBoost) support real-time monitoring,
adaptive treatment adjustments, and early relapse detection, methods such as DRL have demonstrated strong potential in automated
radiation planning, including prostate cancer IMRT and HDR brachytherapy.205–207 In order to improve tailored alternatives like
immunotherapies and targeted medications, advanced ML/DL models (CNNs, autoencoders, transformers) use clinical, imaging, and
multi-omics data to predict therapy response and survival with >90 % accuracy.208 Gleason grading, lesion segmentation, recurrence
prediction, tumor classification, and the identification of treatments with fewer adverse effects are all further improved by AI-powered
MRI, pathology, and genomic methods.209,210 Notwithstanding these developments, computational modeling still faces difficulties
since ML needs to address deeper biological causality than supervised imaging classification and single-source omics.211,212 However,
by automating repetitive processes and improving clinical decision-making, ML–IoT healthcare systems trained on huge datasets can
promote precision oncology, decrease human error, improve efficiency, and assist risk assessment and treatment planning.213–217
Based on the recent studies, together with IoT data, machine learning, deep learning models, ensemble models, multi-omics
analysis, and AI-enhanced imaging can provide precise, tailored, and adaptive medical interventions. Thus, patient outcomes are
improved, and complications and readmission rates are lowered as well. To guarantee accurate, useful insights, non-invasive monitoring methods and multi-modal IoT data must be standardized and have strong interoperability. Personalized care needs to be
supported by the expansion of patient-specific, adaptive technologies, such as digital twins and automated treatment planners, which
will also optimize clinical decision-making and resource allocation.
4. Impact of integrated ML–IoT systems in healthcare applications
By enabling strong predictive analytics, improving the dependability of medical equipment through predictive maintenance, and
developing personalized and precision medicine, including pharmacogenomics to customize treatments for every patient, integrated
ML and IoT systems are revolutionizing the healthcare industry and improving healthcare outcome. While data-driven orchestration of
workflows, patient management, resource allocation, scheduling, and supply chains increases operational efficiency and results across
care settings, continuous, remote patient monitoring enhances surgical recovery and the management of chronic diseases.218–222
4.1. The role of ML-IoT in improving outcomes in healthcare sectors
Machine learning enables Predictive maintenance (PdM) frameworks to evaluate equipment conditions and predict issues for
reducing downtime and expenses.223–227 IoT sensors provide high-frequency device and patient data into cloud or edge pipelines on
the infrastructure side, where machine learning algorithms identify risks, predict failures, and initiate prompt actions. According to a
study, an SVM-plus-IoT vibration framework for immunoassay analyzers reduces diagnostic/repair costs by up to 25 % with ~1-year
payback, while analyses of 1350 ventilators reveal ensemble learners (e.g., Random Forest, XGBoost) achieve ~0.993 predictive
accuracy and K-Nearest Neighbors approaching perfect performance.228,229 These findings show that combining powerful machine
learning algorithms with real-time telemetry proactively surfaces anomalies and enhances safety, dependability, and
cost-effectiveness.

Integrated Machine Learning (ML) and IoT-based systems have significantly advanced healthcare by enabling predictive maintenance of medical equipment, personalized medicine, pharmacogenomics, and operational efficiency. ML models such as Random

Researchers should further focus on expanding patient-centered and adaptive digital twin systems, and integrating predictive analytics with hospital resource and care management to optimize treatment outcomes and healthcare delivery.
4.2. Key benefits of ML-IoT in healthcare applications
The Internet of Things (IoT) and machine learning (ML) work together to create a strong, data-driven healthcare facility that increases access, enhances clinical results, reduces costs, and facilitates prompt, individualized decisions in a variety of contexts.
Continuous physiologic and operational signal acquisition is made possible by the widespread connectivity of medical sensors,
wearables, and smart equipment. Machine learning models subsequently convert these high-velocity streams into useful information
for remote monitoring, early diagnosis, treatment selection, and recovery support.250,251 Clinicians may forecast illness risk and recovery windows, customize treatment routes, and act earlier as their understanding of symptoms and trajectories develops. These
abilities rely on interpreting the massive real-time datasets generated by IoT devices.252–254
In order to speed up the identification of mutations, biomarkers, and therapeutic targets that guide precision diagnosis and therapy
design, machine learning (ML) first identifies patterns in vast, heterogeneous biomedical corpora, such as literature, registries, hospital
electronic medical records, and sensor streams.255–265 Second, algorithms that automate repetitive processes, minimize data entry and
triage errors, and direct limited clinical care to the most vulnerable patients result in cost and resource efficiencies. CNNs, for instance,
are experts at quick, precise interpretation in imaging-centric use cases, and IoT-enabled research workflows improve clinical trial
operations by reducing data-based errors, unified electronic records, and real-time participant monitoring, all of which reduce costs
and timelines.266–270 For that, Table 3 shows the three different classes of machine learning and their cost effectiveness.

compromising data fidelity by using adaptive sampling, filtering, and on-device preprocessing, enhancing patient engagement, safety,

When Machine Learning (ML) is employed in an Internet of Things (IoT) enabled healthcare system for decision-making, the system
can make decisions regarding that particular person through collecting and evaluating information relevant to an individual’s
health.286 Based on the data, the system will then make recommendations for the most appropriate course of action to take in order to
maintain or improve that person’s health. The system must learn the problem’s context and the quality of the supplied data in order to

experiences gained from completing a single, repeating activity, the algorithm gets stronger. It’s also important to keep in mind that
when talking about utilizing computers to make decisions in the healthcare sector, the topic encompasses much more than just

I. In ML-IoT-based healthcare systems, supervised learning has demonstrated significant efficacy in diagnosing and predicting a
range of diseases, such as cancer, cardiovascular disorders, diabetes, kidney disease, liver disease, hepatitis, thyroid conditions,
and infectious diseases. The literature studies shows that ensemble models and deep learning have enhanced diagnostic and
predictive performance of various diseases. Neural networks, which include CNNs and ANNs, and ensemble methods like
Random Forest and XGBoost, continuously enhance latency and achieve high predictive accuracy, typically between 85 % and
95 %.
II. Recent advancements, including two-stage synthetic tumor creation and diffusion-based anomaly detection models, exhibit
improved segmentation accuracy and the capability to identify unusual or previously unobserved anomalies across many imaging modalities (MRI, CT, US). These methods emphasize that reducing the domain disparity between synthetic and real data,
utilizing multi-modal generative frameworks, and integrating clinically interpretable metrics can substantially enhance model
reliability, robustness, and applicability in real-world healthcare environments, providing a viable approach for more automated and scalable diagnostic systems.
III. In chronic disease management, reinforcement learning frameworks enhance treatment recommendations, medication
adherence, and home care support by integrating multimodal patient data and providing automated assistance to patients. In
robotic surgery, reinforcement learning automates sub-tasks, enhances surgical precision, alleviates clinician workload, and
facilitates semi-autonomous procedures while upholding safety parameters.
IV. Furthermore, the review demonstrates that deep learning algorithms substantially surpass conventional methods in processing
intricate medical data, including electronic medical records and medical imaging. Models such as LSTM, BioBERT, and
transformer-based architectures showed effectiveness in extracting clinical information from noisy and inconsistent records.
The integration of structured and unstructured data enhances prognostic accuracy for conditions such as glaucoma and cardiovascular risk. Explainable AI instruments like SHAP and LIME improve transparency, while cultivating clinician trust.
V. The review demonstrates that sophisticated machine learning algorithms, such as Random Forest and XGBoost, attain elevated
predictive accuracy for equipment malfunctions and patient health hazards, so ensuring safety and economic efficiency.
VI. Integration trends demonstrate an increasing utilization of cloud-edge computing for real-time analytics, with lightweight
machine learning models implemented on IoT devices enhancing latency and energy efficiency. Although numerous studies
indicate favorable therapeutic outcomes, such as improved diagnostics, augmented decision support, individualized treatment,
and reduced healthcare expenditures—challenges persist.
6. Discussion
The integration of ML-IoT in healthcare shows considerable potential; however, it encounters critical challenges such as interoperability issues, latency, scalability limitations, data security risks, and ethical issues. Resource-limited IoT devices managing
sensitive medical information increase privacy vulnerabilities, whereas cloud and edge systems face challenges due to diverse data
types. Black-box models present issues related to transparency and fairness, while variable wireless protocols may influence real-time
performance. Future research directions will be examined in detail, focusing on multilayered security, enhanced edge computing,
explainable AI, human-in-the-loop approaches, and emerging technologies such as quantum computing and nano-IoT.
6.1. Challenges and limitations
Healthcare systems have advanced tremendously due to the integration of ML and IoT. Internet of Things (IoT) generates a large
volume of real-time data from various sensors and devices, necessitating analysis due to their complex characteristics. ML algorithms
have demonstrated their crucial significance in the field of IoT. However, these technologies face some notable challenges which must
be addressed when applying ML algorithms in healthcare289
6.1.1. Data security and patient privacy
The healthcare industry has a number of challenges when integrating machine learning (ML) with the Internet of Things (IoT), such
as issues with data security, privacy, scalability, and data heterogeneity. Data security and patient privacy are major concerns for MLIoT based healthcare. Data security and privacy issues arise because of the continuous collection, transmission, and storage of sensitive
patient information. Also, IoT devices have limited resources and are vulnerable to security breaches. 72 % of hostile operations target
sensitive health information, such as genetic and EMR data, hence strong encryption and privacy-preserving measures are
crucial.290–293 Service reliability is also impacted by information security breaches, underscoring the necessity of all-encompassing
protection plans for IoT-enabled devices.294,295
6.1.2. Scalability and data heterogeneity
Scalability poses a considerable challenge in implementing ML-IoT solutions in the healthcare sector. The increasing prevalence of
IoT devices, sensors, and patients leads to a significant rise in data generation, resulting in challenges for infrastructure management.
Studies indicate that although decentralized learning approaches, such as federated learning and blockchain, effectively preserve

privacy, they face scalability challenges due to non-IID data, bandwidth fluctuations, and considerable communication overhead
among distributed nodes.296 The management of extensive and diverse healthcare data can lead to the overloading of cloud and edge
computing resources. This has a considerable impact on tasks that need low latency. Edge devices can have limited computational
resources and memory which makes it difficult to run complex machine learning algorithms locally. One major limitation is that the
model’s performance highly depends on the quality and the size of the dataset. This shows that the limited volume of dataset is a
significant challenge for healthcare.297
6.1.3. Challenges related to communication, network and low latency
Research and recent surveys have highlighted that communication, network reliability, and latency are one of the most crucial
challenges in the ML-IoT based healthcare system. Home-based or remote patient monitoring systems face additional challenges due to
heterogeneous sensor protocols (BLE, Zigbee, Sigfox, and LoRa), variable bandwidth, and device energy limitations, which can cause
unpredictable delays and network failures. Limited computational resources on wearable devices restrict local ML inference, making
lightweight edge AI models, compressed deep learning techniques, and job offloading essential to maintain responsiveness without
overloading hardware.298–300
6.1.4. Lack of interoperability and standards
Interoperability presents another critical challenge in ML-IoT healthcare ecosystems, which comprise devices and sensors from
various vendors employing diverse communication protocols and data formats. Also, the absence of universal standardized frameworks obstructs seamless data integration and coordinated care across platforms. Addressing these challenges is essential for realizing
the full potential of IoT in healthcare for ensuring reliable, secure, and patient-centered services.301,302 Manufacturers of devices
frequently use diverse communication protocols and data formats, which leads to fragmented ecosystems that impede scalability and
data aggregation. Efficiency, cross-device integration, and extensive healthcare deployments are still constrained in the absence of
internationally recognized standards.303
6.1.5. Algorithmic and ethical challenges
Recent studies highlight that ML-IoT systems in healthcare face some algorithmic and ethical challenges, mainly due to the opaque
characteristics of black-box models. Researchers emphasized the challenges faced by clinicians, patients, and stakeholders regarding
the absence of transparency and interpretability in AI-driven medical decision-making. Deep models do not clarify the process by
which inputs are transformed into outputs, leading to legal, ethical, and trust concerns in clinical settings.304 Furthermore, these
models may unintentionally exhibit bias, thereby jeopardizing equitable outcomes that compromise fairness. Research has highlighted
the importance of integrating Explainable AI (XAI) methods, including SHAP and LIME, to improve transparency, accountability, and
ethical integrity.305
6.2. Future research directions
The influence of IoT-ML in Healthcare 5.0, which has lasted since 2020,306is substantial and has influenced us to change our
perspective on conventional treatment approaches. According to predictions for 2020, the world smart health market has reached
1436 billion USD, and between 2020 and 2027, the average growth rate may further be expanded by 16.2 %.307Healthcare 5.0 focuses
on customization and patient-centric models, intending to establish lifelong partnerships and improved well-being. It included the
features of smart health care such as automated networks, cloud networking, artificial intelligence, big data, mobile internet,
biotechnology, and IoT308to advance healthcare sustainability, reduce costs, and enhance patient outcomes. Prioritizing
human-centric services aims to balance cost, service quality, and benefits, addressing the satisfaction of patients, healthcare workers,
and providers309. Fig. 7 illustrates the prioritization of Healthcare 5.0. There are several areas in this industry where making the
required changes can impact healthcare in the future.
To monitor the patient’s status a great number of solutions exist. However, there is still immense opportunity in the healthcare
system. Thus, it is crucial to find prospective technology. Fig. 8 illustrates the various future directions for researchers.
6.2.1. Security and privacy enhancement
For ML-IoT-based healthcare systems, security and privacy continue to be major obstacles.310 To stop eavesdropping and unwanted
changes, data transfer between nodes and processing units must be secured. While maintaining the confidentiality and integrity of
sensitive health records, cryptographic techniques can secure explicit data mapping and user identity.311,312 In addition to
privacy-preserving strategies like blockchain and differential privacy, energy-efficient and lightweight machine learning (ML)-based
data aggregation algorithms are required to mitigate these threats.313 System safety also requires the development of tamper-resistant
IoT devices and the strengthening of access control techniques.314It is essential to create ML-based aggregation techniques and
lightweight cryptography that strike a balance between resource efficiency and security.

6.2.2. Integration of emerging technologies
Nano ML-IoT is a significant future direction for healthcare, integrating nanoscale devices, Internet of Things connectivity, and
machine learning. The Internet of Nano Things (IoNT) has advanced considerably in the healthcare sector, providing expedited and
more convenient methods for diagnosis, monitoring, and treatment.315,316 Healthcare functions like electromagnetic detection,
transmission, and actuation are improved by combining opto-technology with ML-IoT-based systems.317 By linking medical equipment
and facilitating remote health data sharing, this integration makes smart healthcare possible.318 Contactless feature extraction and
enhanced data analysis are made possible by sophisticated signal processing techniques.319 Effective data aggregation requires
addressing performance degradation in dynamic and diverse situations.320–322 Through expert knowledge and ML-based techniques,
architectures such as IoT-HDHM-ML employ networks of wearable nodes to continuously monitor numerous patient parameters in real
time, hence boosting healthcare efficiency.323 Furthermore, Explainable AI (XAI) can provide interpretable and transparent predictions, helping clinicians trust and adopt ML-IoT systems in critical decision-making processes, while Quantum Computing offers the
potential to accelerate ML model training and support complex data analysis in genomics and medical imaging, further enhancing
healthcare applications. Future studies should concentrate on creating scalable, resilient opto-ML-IoT infrastructures that can function
in dynamic, diverse contexts.
6.2.3. Involvement of stakeholders
The involvement of Stakeholders including professionals in the fields of engineering and health sciences as well as patients is
crucial to make Healthcare 5.0 successful. Stakeholders in healthcare, also including patients, providers, and insurers, maintain a
single ledger that encodes pre-authorization requirements, ensuring transparency and accountability.324 Patients must be involved in
the design process and the ML-IoT technologies must be patient-centered.325 Additionally, while designing ML-IoT-based digital
healthcare systems, receiving feedback from users of such systems and considering individual requirements are also essential.326
Moreover, in the healthcare system, Blockchain provides additional benefits such as real-time calculations through the automation of
information distribution and it typically employs cryptographic-based techniques (such hash functions, asymmetric encryption, and
digital signatures) across different system stakeholders to help maintain trust throughout interactions.327
6.2.4. Standardization of protocols
To solve interoperability issues in healthcare IoT systems, standardization and synchronization are crucial.328 Data transmission
between new machine learning (ML)-based healthcare technologies and current electronic health records is made easier by ensuring
that data formats are uniform and analyzable. To facilitate the incorporation of cutting-edge healthcare solutions, policymakers should
give priority to data compatibility, sharing, and interoperability. The creation of protocols and universal data standards for ML-IoT
healthcare systems should be the main goal of future research. Integration can be improved by looking at automated mapping and
translation solutions between heterogeneous data sources. Policy-driven frameworks that direct the adoption of new technologies
while preserving compliance, compatibility, and safe data transmission across various healthcare systems could also be the subject of
future research.
6.2.5. Human-AI collaboration in healthcare
In the healthcare industry, human-AI collaboration refers to the use of AI systems in conjunction with people as partners to address
difficult issues, such as supporting clinical decision support systems (CDSS) in the diagnosis of different diseases including cancer.329,330 Human-AI collaboration facilitates augmented decision making. Augmented decision-making utilizes AI insights to assist
clinicians by providing evidence-based recommendations, thereby enhancing accuracy and minimizing diagnostic errors. Collaboration between doctors and AI, grounded in ethical and transparent practices, guarantees that human oversight, explainability, and
fairness are integral to patient care decisions. Medical professionals can choose the best machine learning methods utilizing
human-in-the-loop ensemble learning when human experience is incorporated into ML-IoT systems. This improves prediction accuracy
and model performance.331–333 Despite obstacles including bias in CDSS, skepticism about AI, and adoption issues, this partnership can
lessen the scarcity of qualified healthcare workers, enhance the quality of care, and lighten the workload of clinicians.334,335
Future studies should examine methods for teaching healthcare workers how to collaborate with AI and include these techniques
into healthcare education curricula. Wider adoption will be supported by research into ways to improve the usability, transparency,

6.2.6. Novel insights and future outlook
Future research in Healthcare 5.0 should focus on five critical domains: security, emerging technologies, stakeholder engagement,
standardization, and human–AI collaboration. An enhanced multi-layered security framework is required that combines machine
learning-driven data aggregation with lightweight cryptography and hybrid privacy-preserving techniques such as federated learning,
blockchain, and differential privacy. Such frameworks should incorporate tamper-resistant IoT hardware and context-aware access
control to improve the overall confidentiality as well as system resilience. Future research in Healthcare 5.0 should prioritize a
multilayered approach that integrates security, emerging technologies, stakeholder involvement, protocol standardization, and
collaboration between humans and AI. The integration of advanced technologies such as Nano ML-IoT, multimodal data fusion,
scalable opto-ML-IoT infrastructures, energy-efficient wearable networks, and predictive analytics can also facilitate a dependable
healthcare system. Also, active involvement of stakeholders such as patients, clinicians, engineers, and insurers is crucial. Effective
patient-centered designs, transparency through shared ledgers and blockchain technology, and system modifications depend on the
active participation of stakeholders. Standardizing universal data formats and protocols will also enhance safe data sharing, ensure
compliance, and promote interoperability across diverse healthcare platforms. Moreover, enhancing collaboration between humans
and AI requires the incorporation of AI literacy and collaborative methodologies into healthcare education. This must be accomplished
for smooth integration of AI into clinical processes.
Overall, these directions highlight the novel insights and clear perspectives for future research in ML-IoT healthcare applications
while addressing the unmet research needs by prioritizing safety, technological adaptability, stakeholder inclusivity, interoperability,
and a focus on human–AI collaboration.
7. Conclusion
The incorporation of Machine Learning (ML) and Internet of Things (IoT) in healthcare has improved the overall accuracy of
diagnosis, operational efficiency, customization of treatment and clinical decision making. Recent advancements in these technologies
have enhanced patient outcomes and optimized healthcare processes, resulting in increased accuracy, efficiency and costeffectiveness. Nevertheless, challenges such as interoperability issues, scalability limitations, data security concerns, and ethical

considerations continue to be substantial barriers. To fully realize the potential of machine learning (ML) and Internet of Things (IoT)
in healthcare, it is essential to address these challenges through continuous research and technology developments. For mitigating
these challenges, future healthcare research should focus on strengthening security and privacy, integrating emerging technologies,
involving key stakeholders, standardizing protocols, and promoting effective human–AI collaboration. This will pave the way for a
future when personalized healthcare becomes the standard. Although ML and IoT have made significant strides in healthcare, their
application is not without substantial hurdles that must be carefully considered. This study conducts a critical and comprehensive
analysis of the recent advancements, applications, challenges and future perspectives of machine learning and IoT in the healthcare
sector. By prioritizing the mentioned essential domains, the healthcare sector will effectively utilize the advantages of machine
learning (ML) and Internet of Things (IoT), ultimately resulting in enhanced, easily accessible, and tailored healthcare for people across
the globe.

 Agriculture, Forestry and Other Land Use (AFOLU)

Executive Summary

11

Agriculture, Forestry, and Other Land Use (AFOLU) is unique
among the sectors considered in this volume, since the mitigation potential is derived from both an enhancement of removals
of greenhouse gases (GHG), as well as reduction of emissions
through management of land and livestock (robust evidence;
high agreement). The land provides food that feeds the Earth’s human
population of ca. 7 billion, fibre for a variety of purposes, livelihoods
for billions of people worldwide, and is a critical resource for sustainable development in many regions. Agriculture is frequently central to
the livelihoods of many social groups, especially in developing countries where it often accounts for a significant share of production. In
addition to food and fibre, the land provides a multitude of ecosystem
services; climate change mitigation is just one of many that are vital
to human well-being (robust evidence; high agreement). Mitigation
options in the AFOLU sector, therefore, need to be assessed, as far as
possible, for their potential impact on all other services provided by
land. [Section 11.1]
The AFOLU sector is responsible for just under a quarter
(~10 – 12 GtCO2eq / yr) of anthropogenic GHG emissions mainly
from deforestation and agricultural emissions from livestock,
soil and nutrient management (robust evidence; high agreement)
[11.2]. Anthropogenic forest degradation and biomass burning (forest
fires and agricultural burning) also represent relevant contributions.
Annual GHG emissions from agricultural production in 2000 – 2010
were estimated at 5.0 – 5.8 GtCO2eq / yr while annual GHG flux from
land use and land-use change activities accounted for approximately
4.3 – 5.5 GtCO2eq / yr. Leveraging the mitigation potential in the sector is extremely important in meeting emission reduction targets
(robust evidence; high agreement) [11.9]. Since publication of the IPCC
Fourth Assessment Report (AR4), emissions from the AFOLU sector
have remained similar but the share of anthropogenic emissions has
decreased to 24 % (in 2010), largely due to increases in emissions in
the energy sector (robust evidence, high agreement). In spite of a large
range across global Forestry and Other Land Use (FOLU) flux estimates,
most approaches indicate a decline in FOLU carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions over the most recent years, largely due to decreasing deforestation rates and increased afforestation (limited evidence, medium
agreement). As in AR4, most projections suggest declining annual net
CO2 emissions in the long run. In part, this is driven by technological
change, as well as projected declining rates of agriculture area expansion, which, in turn, is related to the expected slowing in population
growth. However, unlike AR4, none of the more recent scenarios projects growth in the near-term [11.9].
Opportunities for mitigation include supply-side and demandside options. On the supply side, emissions from land-use change
(LUC), land management and livestock management can be reduced,
terrestrial carbon stocks can be increased by sequestration in soils and
biomass, and emissions from energy production can be saved through

the substitution of fossil fuels by biomass (robust evidence; high agreement) [11.3]. On the demand side, GHG emissions could be mitigated
by reducing losses and wastes of food, changes in diet and changes in
wood consumption (robust evidence; high agreement) [11.4] though
quantitative estimates of the potential are few and highly uncertain.
Increasing production without a commensurate increase in emissions
also reduces emission intensity, i. e., the GHG emissions per unit of
product that could be delivered through sustainable intensification;
another mechanism for mitigation explored in more detail here than in
AR4. Supply-side options depend on the efficacy of land and livestock
management (medium evidence; high agreement) [11.6]. Considering
demand-side options, changes in human diet can have a significant
impact on GHG emissions from the food production lifecycle (medium
evidence; medium agreement) [11.4]. There are considerably different
challenges involved in delivering demand-side and supply-side options,
which also have very different synergies and tradeoffs.
The nature of the sector means that there are potentially many
barriers to implementation of available mitigation options,
including accessibility to AFOLU financing, poverty, institutional,
ecological, technological development, diffusion and transfer
barriers (medium evidence; medium agreement) [11.7, 11.8]. Similarly, there are important feedbacks to adaptation, conservation of natural resources, such as water and terrestrial and aquatic biodiversity
(robust evidence; high agreement) [11.5, 11.8]. There can be competition between different land uses if alternative options to use available
land are mutually exclusive, but there are also potential synergies, e. g.,
integrated systems or multi-functionality at landscape scale (medium
evidence; high agreement) [11.4]. Recent frameworks, such as those
for assessing environmental or ecosystem services, provide one mechanism for valuing the multiple synergies and tradeoffs that may arise
from mitigation actions (medium evidence; medium agreement) [11.1].
Sustainable management of agriculture, forests, and other land is an
underpinning requirement of sustainable development (robust evidence; high agreement) [11.4].
AFOLU emissions could change substantially in transformation
pathways, with significant mitigation potential from agriculture,
forestry, and bioenergy mitigation measures (medium evidence;
high agreement). Recent multi-model comparisons of idealized implementation transformation scenarios find land emissions (nitrous oxide,
N2O; methane, CH4; CO2) changing by – 4 to 99 % through 2030, and 7
to 76 % through 2100, with the potential for increased emissions from
land carbon stocks. Land-related mitigation, including bioenergy, could
contribute 20 to 60 % of total cumulative abatement to 2030, and 15 to
40 % to 2100. However, policy coordination and implementation issues
are challenges to realizing this potential [11.9]. Large-scale biomass
supply for energy, or carbon sequestration in the AFOLU sector provide
flexibility for the development of mitigation technologies in the energy
supply and energy end-use sectors, as many technologies already exist
and some of them are commercial (limited evidence; medium agreement) [11.3], but there are potential implications for biodiversity, food
security, and other services provided by land (medium evidence, high

agreement) [11.7]. Implementation challenges, including institutional
barriers and inertia related to governance issues, make the costs and
net emission reduction potential of near-term mitigation uncertain. In
mitigation scenarios with idealized comprehensive climate policies,
agriculture, forestry, and bioenergy contribute substantially to the
reduction of global CO2, CH4, and N2O emissions, and to the energy
system, thereby reducing policy costs (medium evidence; high agreement) [11.9]. More realistic partial and delayed policies for global land
mitigation have potentially significant spatial and temporal leakage,
and economic implications, but could still be cost-effectively deployed
(limited evidence; limited agreement) [11.9].
Economic mitigation potential of supply-side measures in the
AFOLU sector is estimated to be 7.18 to 10.60 (full range:
0.49 – 10.60) GtCO2eq / yr in 2030 for mitigation efforts consistent with carbon prices up to 100 USD / tCO2eq, about a third of
which can be achieved at < 20 USD / tCO2eq (medium evidence;
medium agreement) [11.6]. These estimates are based on studies that
cover both forestry and agriculture and that include agricultural soil
carbon sequestration. Estimates from agricultural sector-only studies
range from 0.3 to 4.6 GtCO2eq / yr at prices up to 100 USD / tCO2eq, and
estimates from forestry sector-only studies from 0.2 to 13.8 GtCO2eq / yr
at prices up to 100 USD / tCO2eq (medium evidence; medium agreement) [11.6]. The large range in the estimates arises due to widely
different collections of options considered in each study, and because
not all GHGs are considered in all of the studies. The composition of
the agricultural mitigation portfolio varies with the carbon price, with
the restoration of organic soils having the greatest potential at higher
carbon prices (100 USD / tCO2eq) and cropland and grazing land management at lower (20 USD / tCO2eq). In forestry there is less difference
between measures at different carbon prices, but there are significant
differences between regions, with reduced deforestation dominating the forestry mitigation potential in Latin America and Caribbean
(LAM) and Middle East and Africa (MAF), but very little potential in
the member countries of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation
and Development (OECD-1990) and Economies in Transition (EIT). Forest management, followed by afforestation, dominate in OECD-1990,
EIT, and Asia (medium evidence, strong agreement) [11.6]. Among
demand-side measures, which are under-researched compared to supply-side measures, changes in diet and reductions of losses in the food
supply chain can have a significant, but uncertain, potential to reduce
GHG emissions from food production (0.76 – 8.55 GtCO2eq / yr by 2050),
with the range being determined by assumptions about how the
freed land is used (limited evidence; medium agreement) [11.4]. More
research into demand-side mitigation options is merited. There are
significant regional differences in terms of mitigation potential, costs,
and applicability, due to differing local biophysical, socioeconomic, and

Agriculture, Forestry and Other Land Use (AFOLU)

cultural circumstances, for instance between developed and developing regions, and among developing regions (medium evidence; high
agreement) [11.6].
The size and regional distribution of future mitigation potential
is difficult to estimate accurately because it depends on a number of inherently uncertain factors. Critical factors include population (growth), economic and technological developments, changes
in behaviour over time (depending on cultural and normative backgrounds, market structures and incentives), and how these translate
into demand for food, fibre, fodder and fuel, as well as development in
the agriculture, aquaculture and forestry sectors. Other factors important to mitigation potential are potential climate change impacts on
carbon stocks in soils and forests including their adaptive capacity
(medium evidence; high agreement) [11.5]; considerations set by biodiversity and nature conservation requirements; and interrelations with
land degradation and water scarcity (robust evidence; high agreement)
[11.8].
Bioenergy can play a critical role for mitigation, but there are
issues to consider, such as the sustainability of practices and
the efficiency of bioenergy systems (robust evidence, medium
agreement) [11.4.4, Box 11.5, 11.13.6, 11.13.7]. Barriers to large-scale
deployment of bioenergy include concerns about GHG emissions from
land, food security, water resources, biodiversity conservation and livelihoods. The scientific debate about the overall climate impact related
to land use competition effects of specific bioenergy pathways remains
unresolved (robust evidence, high agreement) [11.4.4, 11.13]. Bioenergy technologies are diverse and span a wide range of options and
technology pathways. Evidence suggests that options with low lifecycle emissions (e. g., sugar cane, Miscanthus, fast growing tree species,
and sustainable use of biomass residues), some already available, can
reduce GHG emissions; outcomes are site-specific and rely on efficient
integrated ‘biomass-to-bioenergy systems’, and sustainable land-use
management and governance. In some regions, specific bioenergy
options, such as improved cookstoves, and small-scale biogas and
biopower production, could reduce GHG emissions and improve livelihoods and health in the context of sustainable development (medium
evidence, medium agreement) [11.13].
Policies governing practices in agriculture and in forest conservation and management need to account for both mitigation
and adaptation. One of the most visible current policies in the AFOLU
sector is the implementation of REDD+ (see Annex I), that can represent a cost-effective option for mitigation (limited evidence; medium
agreement) [11.10], with economic, social, and other environmental
co-benefits (e. g., conservation of biodiversity and water resources).
