product to the fertiliser which is typically generated in biological
treatment of food waste. Implementation of fly larvae composting
allows implementation of a system where food waste is viewed as
a resource and generates high value products unlike in conventional systems where at best a partial recovery of energy and plant
nutrients is possible. The larval biomass resulting from fly larvae
composting can be used as feed for animals, further reducing the
overall system emissions since other sources of feed (e.g. soybean)
can be replaced (Allegretti et al., 2018).
Other potential emissions from the degradation process, such as
methane (CH4) and nitrous oxide (N2O), may be a concern, as they
are in conventional food waste treatment methods such as composting and anaerobic digestion (Møller et al., 2009; Pipatti et al.,
2006). Emissions of CH4 and N2O are relevant to investigate, as
they have GWP of 34 and 289, respectively, over 100 years (IPCC,
2013). Studies focusing on LCA of waste management systems
and investigating fly larva composting as one of the alternatives
highlighted knowledge gaps in inventory data on emissions from
fly larvae composting as a food waste treatment (Allegretti et al.,

2018; Mertenat et al., 2019; Salomone et al., 2017). These LCA
studies use emission data for other insect species to overcome
the lack of data. A recent LCA study by Mertenat et al. (2019) evaluated direct emissions from BSF treatment of food waste and found
that they were lower than in conventional composting. However,
further evaluation based on homogeneous feedstock and carbon
and nitrogen balance is necessary to evaluate the effect of substrate and process parameters on the emissions. To our knowledge,
direct CH4 or N2O emissions from fly larvae composting of food
waste have not been determined to date under controlled laboratory conditions. Emissions of CH4 typically occur due to methanogenic microbe activity under anaerobic conditions and can be
expected to be low in fly larvae composting, due to larval movement mechanically turning the substrate and making it more aerobic (Cickova et al., 2015). Emissions of N2O occur from processes
such as nitrification and denitrification in aerobically degraded
organic material and depend on both substrate properties and
microbial activity (Ermolaev et al., 2015). Overall low N2O emissions have been reported for Neomyia cornicina fly larvae treating
cattle dung, an effect attributed to inhibition of microbial degradation activity and nitrogen assimilation within larval biomass
(Iwasa et al., 2015),. Fly larvae of Hermetia illucens have been
reported to modify the microbiome of their surrounding substrate
(Jeon et al., 2011; Varotto Boccazzi et al., 2017). However, the
effects of this on emissions of N2O have not been investigated.
Another relevant gas associated with aerobic degradation of
organic material is ammonia (NH3), as it contributes to acidification and eutrophication (IPCC, 2014). This gas can represent a
major pathway of nitrogen losses in conventional composting
(Jarvis et al., 2009). Ammonia has been reported to cause odours
and even to create a hazardous environment for workers in fly larvae composting and can represent a major pathway for nitrogen
losses from the compost produced (Cickova et al., 2015; Cickova
et al., 2012; Lalander et al., 2015). The pathway for NH3 emissions
can be expected to be similar to that in conventional composting.
Several factors are decisive for NH3 emissions during composting;
when aerobic degradation occurs at a high rate, organic nitrogen
mineralisation produces ammonium (NH+4) as the primary product
(Paredes et al., 1996). Ammonium is converted to gaseous form
(NH3) when the substrate pH shifts towards alkaline and the rate
of NH3 emission increases with aeration and temperature (Rynk
and Richard, 2001).
High efficiency in fly larva composting on optimal substrates
makes this method attractive for use as a major food waste treatment method (Lalander et al., 2019). However, further process
improvement is needed, as organic degradation in the process is
not complete (Lalander et al., 2018). BSF larvae-associated bacteria
have been suggested as a means to improve the efficiency in the fly
larvae composting process (Yu et al., 2011). Pre-treatment of the
substrate with these bacteria could potentially improve nutrient
availability to the larvae, as parts of food waste are otherwise slow
to degrade (Yu et al., 2011; Zheng et al., 2013). Alternatively, seeding the substrate with BSF-associated bacteria at the start of larvae
treatment could accelerate the process of larval microbiome
adjustment, while also stimulating degradation to some degree
(Xiao et al., 2018; Yu et al., 2011).
The aim of this study was to evaluate GHG and NH3 emissions from fly larvae composting treatment and the effects of
pre-treatment and seeding of substrate with BSF larvaeassociated bacteria on the efficiency and rate of the fly larvae
composting process and the amount of emissions produced.
The results of this study are key in performing further life cycle
assessment (LCA) evaluation of fly larvae composting as a
waste management alternative and for comparing its performance to other waste treatment alternatives, currently there
is lack of such data.

2. Material and methods
2.1. Materials
In all treatments performed in this study, food waste was used
as the substrate for the larvae. This food waste was sourced from a
local canteen at SLU (Uppsala, Sweden) and represented a mixture
of food preparation waste, food scraps and unsold prepared food.
The food waste had a dry matter (DM) content of 24.9 ± 2.9% of
wet weight (WW), volatile solids content of 92.3 ± 0.5% of DM,
pH of 4.42 ± 0.63 and density of 1.09 ± 0.06 g mL1 on average
(n = 3). The collected substrate was homogenised, divided into
feeding portions and stored at 20 °C until use, prior to which it
was thawed and allowed to reach room temperature for up to
12 h. In all treatments, 5-d-old, >0.2 cm long BSF larvae obtained
from a colony continuously running since 2015 at SLU (Uppsala,
Sweden) were used.
2.2. Study layout
All treatments were performed in 11 cm deep small boxes with
dimensions of 21  17 cm giving a treatment surface of 357 cm2 to
which 700 larvae were added, giving a larval density of 2 larvae
cm2. The larvae density and feeding rate of 30.0 ± 0.3 mg dry matter larva1 d1 were selected to ensure sufficient nutrition and
avoid overcrowding in accordance to previously established recommendations (Diener et al., 2011). The boxes were incubated at
28 °C during the 14-day treatment period to obtain larvae in the
fifth instar. The larvae were added by weight based on individual
larvae weight determined on a smaller sample. Three treatments
were compared: Treatment L was standard fly larvae composting,
where only fly larvae were added to the food waste; in treatment
BL, fly larvae and a spore-forming bacteria consortium isolated
from the gut of BSF larvae were added at the start of the composting; in treatment PBL, the food waste was pre-treated in open
boxes at 28 °C for 7 days with the same bacteria consortium as in
BL, after which fly larvae were added (Fig. 1). Spore-forming bacteria were chosen due to simplicity of their implementation as inoculum in future applications but also to avoid possibility of recycling
pathogens. At the end of the experiments, the larvae were picked
out, weighed and enumerated. Based on the final number of larvae,
their survival was calculated in relation to the initial number. The
treatment residues were weighed and sampled for analysis of dry
matter content (DM), total volatile solids (VS) and total nitrogen
(N). All treatments were performed in triplicate.
2.3. Bacterial isolation
Twelve BSF larvae (BSFL) reaching instar 5 (reared in food
waste) were picked out and washed in deionised water and then
in disinfection solution (70% EtOH). The disinfected larvae were
manually chopped to pieces and immersed in 10 mL
(4 BSFL/10 mL) nutrient broth (1 g/L Lab-Lemco powder, 2 g/L
yeast extract, 5 g/L peptone and 5 g/L NaCl, National Veterinary
Institute, Uppsala, Sweden) at 70 °C for 10 min. After cooling to
room temperature (RT), 1 mL of broth from each tube was spread
on taurocholate gelatine agar (TGA) plates (£ 14 cm; Miclev, Sweden) and the plates were incubated at 37 °C for 24 h. Five visually
different colonies were clean-spread on TGA plates and incubated
at 37 °C for 24 h. Single individual colonies were taken and heattreated once more in the nutrient broth (as described above). For
each colony, upon reaching RT, 10 mL of broth were spread on a
TGA plate and the plates were incubated at 37 °C for 24 h. Once
again, single colonies were collected from each plate and cleanspread on TGA plates that were incubated at 37 °C for 24 h. The

2.4. Material sampling
Substrate samples were collected from the initial food waste
mixture and from residues left at the end of the treatments
(Fig. 1). These were analysed gravimetrically for DM content by
drying at 80 °C until stable weight and for VS content by incineration at 250 °C for 2 h, followed by 550 °C for 4 h. Homogenised food
waste density was estimated by filling graduated cylinders and
measuring the volume and weight of the substrate. For total nitrogen (total N) determination in food waste, 0.5 g of material was
boiled in concentrated sulphuric acid (H2SO4), following the procedure described in Lalander et al. (2015). The samples were neutralised using 10 M sodium hydroxide (NaOH), diluted 1:50 in
deionised water and digested using SpectroquantÒ Crack-Set 20
(1.14963.0001). The nitrate concentration in the digested solution
was then determined at 340 nm using the SpectroquantÒ nitrate
test (1.09713.0002). Larvae total N was analysed externally (AgriLab AB, Sweden) in dried ground samples using a modified SSISO 13878 method and LECO CN-200 analyser. Treatment residue
total N was analysed in the same way as larvae, but an additional
NH4-N measurement was performed on a wet sample using a FOSS
TECATOR FIAstar 5000 Analyzer and following a modified method
supplied in instrument application notes (AN 65/84, ASN 01/92
and ASN 02/92) and added to the total N value. The maturity of
treatment residues was measured after adjusting its DM content
to 28% (on average) by addition of dry sawdust (93% DM), using
the SolvitaÒ test following the procedure provided by the supplier.
2.5. Gas sampling
Emissions of GHG (CO2, CH4 and N2O) and of NH3 were sampled
using a closed chamber technique. Each treatment box and a

battery-driven fan (Rubicson, Kjell & Co Elektronik AB, Sweden)
were placed in a chamber closed with an airtight lid, equipped
with a sampling port and pressure normalisation loop tube (1 m
long, £ 4 mm) for approximately 60 min. Frequency of gas sampling (Fig. 1) was selected to balance the ability to perform multiple treatments in triplicates and provide a sufficient resolution for
gas emission dynamics. The gas samples were taken at intervals of
0, 15, 30 and 60 min using a 60 mL syringe and transferred to gastight N-evacuated 20 mL glass vials in pairs, which were later analysed by gas chromatography (GC) (Clarus 500, Perkin Elmer, USA)
for CO2, CH4 and N2O following the procedure described in
Ermolaev et al. (2015). At each interval, after taking the two gas
samples for GC analysis, NH3 gas concentration was measured
directly by connecting the opening of a NH3 gas detection tube
(105SD, 105SC, Kitagawa, Japan) to the sampling port and extracting the sample using a Kitagawa gas pump (AP-20, Kitagawa,
Japan). The volume of extracted gas was recorded, as it resulted
in chamber gas dilution through the pressure normalisation tube.
This was compensated for by calculating the gas concentration
using the known concentrations in the sample and room air and
the known volumes of the chamber and extracted samples,
described as:

2.6. Data analysis
The concentrations measured at the intervals were used to calculate the emission rates in g min1 for all gases, using the slope
estimation in the linear regression (LINEST function in Microsoft
Excel 2016). This produced CO2 emission rate values with a high
level of accuracy (R2 > 0.99, n = 18), confirming linearity of gas concentration increases during all sampling periods. Due to very low
concentrations of CH4, often close to background level, if a negative
slope was obtained in linear regression of the four interval measurements, the emission rate was assumed to be zero. Due to even
lower emissions of N2O, and since N2O concentration did not
increase in the interval measurements in the majority of cases, it
was assumed that N2O emission rate was zero if R2 was below

0.9. Based on the calculated gas flows, total emissions of all gases
were estimated using trapezoidal rule integration of emission rates
over time between sampling points (Holman, 2001), and assuming
that the emission rates were constant from the start of treatment
up to the first gas measurement and from the last gas measurement to the end of treatment. Such assumption, while imprecise,
was necessary to make an estimation of total emissions and it
was used to avoid underestimating the total emissions. Analysis
of variance (ANOVA followed by the Tukey’s HSD tests) with 95%
confidence interval was used to verify statistically significant differences between the inflow material and treated material and
between treatments. For comparisons of inflow material treated
material and larvae produced, variables such as bioconversion ratio
and material reduction were calculated on dry matter basis as previously described by Lalander et al. (2019). All statistical analyses
were conducted in R (R Core Team, 2016).
The total GHG emissions were evaluated using GWP values of
34 and 298 for CH4 and N2O, respectively, over 100 years according
to IPCC (2013).

3. Results
3.1. Material reduction and bioconversion ratios
The conversion efficiency was similar for all treatments, but
with a slightly greater average mass reduction (52.3 ± 4.2) and larvae bioconversion ratio (27.9 ± 3.7) in the bacteria and larvae (BL)
treatment (Table 1). However, there was high variation between
replicates and no significant difference between treatments was
found. Similarly, no significant difference between the treatments
was found for any of the parameters analysed. The residues
remaining after the treatments had a DM content of 22% on average, which was lower than that of the initial food waste (25%)
(Table 1). Larval size differed slightly between the treatments,
but the differences were not significant (Table 1). Larval survival
estimation was based on initial number of larvae extrapolated
from a smaller sample and the final number of larvae enumerated
in their totality. The final number of larvae exceeded the initial
estimation by 22% in one of the replicates and by 1% in another
in treatment BL. In those cases, the survival was assumed to be
100% and the initial larvae numbers were adjusted to 856 and
710, respectively, bringing the average survival in that treatment
to 98.3%. With such an adjustment, the larval survival in treatment
BL was significantly higher than in treatment PBL, although with a
relatively high P value of 0.05 (Table 1).
Residue maturity was low across the treatments, with a compost maturity index (CMI) of 2.3 on average (n = 9), indicating that

the residues could be classified as very active compost (Table 1).
While CMI is calculated based on SolvitaÒ measurements of CO2
and NH3 emissions, in our treatments these measurements generally showed no detectable NH3 (n = 7) and high CO2 concentrations
(data not shown).
Overall, the majority of available DM and VS remained in the
products after the treatment, and 67–78% of initial dry solids and
VS available in the substrate was recovered in the larvae and residues after treatment (Table 2). Most of the water initially available
in the material was recovered in the residues (Table 2), resulting in
relatively low residue DM (Table 1). Larvae contained 10–17% of
the initial water, while 18–31% of water was lost during the treatment (cf. Table 2). As water is also generated in the process of respiration, it was possible to estimate the amount of water produced
based on the VS loss. On average, 64.3 g VS was lost during the larvae composting in treatments L, BL and PBL, while an additional
30.3 g VS was lost, on average, in the pre-treatment of PBL (cf.
Table 2). Based on the oxidation reaction of the average food waste
formula (Haug, 1993) it was estimated that, on average, 34.2 g of
water were generated during the larvae composting step in all
treatments and an additional 16.1 g during pre-treatment of PBL
due to VS loss in respiration.
Larvae contained a higher amount of N (60.7 mg N g1 DM, on
average) than the food waste substrate (Table 2), while the residues contained a lower amount. However, from a mass balance
perspective, over a half the initial N ended up in larvae and the rest
was recovered in the residues (Table 2). Total N in all treatment
products was close to 100% of the initial N, suggesting high N
recovery, however most likely also caused by variation between
the replicates and possible underestimation of initial N amount
in the food waste. Variation associated with analytical methods
and process development in pre-treatments and treatments in
some cases resulted in overestimation in N balance due to counteractive combinations of such variations.

3.2. Gas emissions
The CO2 emission rates and patterns were similar during the
larvae composting step in the different treatments. The CO2 emission rate peaked during the second measurement on day 7 of fly
larvae composting, reaching 7.4 mg min1 on average across the
treatments, and then declined slightly by day 11 to 5.6 mg min1
(Fig. 2A). Total emissions of CO2 were similar across all treatments,
excluding any emissions from pre-treatment (Fig. 2B). Total emissions of CO2 in the larvae treatment step were on average 96.5 g
CO2 kg1 initial food waste on a wet weight (WW) basis (Fig. 2B,
Table 3).

The CO2 emissions during the pre-treatment step in the PBL
treatment were estimated from VS loss as suggested by Haug
(1993), assuming a carbon fraction of 55% of VS. This resulted in
an additional 51.5 ± 13.7 g CO2 kg1 initial food waste (WW) being
produced on average in the pre-treatment step, assuming that all
the carbon in the lost VS was converted to CO2.
In all three treatments, the CH4 emission rates were relatively
low and they generally declined from start to end of larvae composting (Fig. 2C). Initial CH4 emissions at the beginning of larvae
composting in treatment PBL were lower on average than in the
experiments without pre-treatment and were closer to CH4 emission rates measured on day 11 of those experiments (Fig. 2C). This
difference was not significant for any of the sampling days, but
when comparing the emission rates grouped by day and treatment,
the CH4 emission rates in treatment PBL were significantly lower
than those in treatment BL (P = 0.005). The lower CH4 emission
rates resulted in lower overall total CH4 emissions (Fig. 2D, Table 3).
Total emissions differed between treatments and were significantly lower in the larvae composting step of the PBL treatment
with pre-treated substrate (P = 0.02) than in treatment BL, where
bacteria and larvae treated the substrate (Fig. 2D). The emissions
did not differ significantly between treatments L and BL or
between treatments L and PBL (Fig. 2D). The CH4 emissions were
not measured during the pre-treatment step and were not included
in the comparisons, but they could potentially increase the total
CH4 emissions from the whole PBL treatment process.
The N2O emissions did not show any specific pattern and the
majority of the values measured were very close to background
levels (Fig. 2E). The flux values were often assumed to be zero, as
the interval measurements in the chamber produced low R2 values
(R2 < 0.9, n = 9 of 27) due to both initial N2O concentration close to
background levels and no concentration increase in the chamber
over the measuring period. The N2O results presented here are thus
an estimate of the actual emissions.
The estimated N2O emission rates varied between replicates
and thus the mean values had relatively high standard deviation
(Table 3). The emission rates during larvae composting in treatment PBL were so low that they were not significantly different
from zero (Fig. 2E). This resulted in cumulative N2O emissions in

this treatment being very small, and the standard deviation being
comparable to the mean of the replicates (Fig. 2F, Table 3). Overall,
cumulative N2O emissions from the larvae composting step were
not significantly different between the three treatments and
showed large variation. The N2O emissions from the pretreatment step in treatment PBL were not measured.
Ammonia emissions were below the detection limit of 0.2 ppm
in all cases (n = 27).
4. Discussion
4.1. Process efficiency
Bioconversion ratio and substrate reduction were not significantly different between the treatments, as evidenced by the similarity in total CO2 emissions between the treatments, indicating
that a similar amount of the VS content in the substrate was converted to larval biomass (Table 1, Fig. 2A-B). Mean estimated total
CO2 emissions in all treatments were 96.5 g CO2 kg1 initial food
waste (WW basis), corresponding to a loss of 53.8 g VS (based on
carbon conversion), which was less than the overall average of
64.3 g VS estimated to be lost from the mass balance (Table 2). This
difference could be explained by either underestimation of the
total CO2 emissions, emissions of other volatile substances not
measured in this study or inaccuracy in VS measurements.
Overall, after larvae composting in all treatments, approximately half of the initial VS was recovered in the residues (Table 2).
The relationship between ash, VS and DM only changed by 2–5
percentage units, from around 92 to 98%, as some minerals were
taken up by the larvae together with VS. The high proportion of initial VS remaining in the residues suggests that, even after larval
composting in all treatments, the residues could still be considered
only mildly degraded (Table 2). This was confirmed by the low SolvitaÒ CMI value obtained for the residues (Table 1). This is typical
for fly larvae composting of food waste, as BSF larvae grow quickly
and thus consume the most easily digestible parts of the substrate
(Li et al., 2011; Li et al., 2015). The part of VS converted by the larvae (representing bioconversion ratio on a VS basis) was 21 and
28% of initial VS in treatments L and BL, respectively (Table 1),

Lalander et al. (2019) where a lower bioconversion ratio of 13.9%

40 mg DM larvae1 d1, suggesting that a feeding rate of 30.0 mg

Overall, the nitrogen balance indicated that, of the initial N in
the food waste, over a half was recovered in the larvae and the rest
in the treatment residues (Table 2). In treatment L, 97% of the initial N in the substrate was recovered in these two fractions, while
in treatment BL 100% was recovered. This indicates small N losses
from the system. In treatment PBL, the high N recovery in the two
fractions produced suggests that there was no major N loss either
during the pre-treatment step or during larvae composting. Two
major factors were identified as reasons for the very high N content
in the fractions produced in relation to the initial N in all treatments (Table 2). The primary factor was probably underestimation
of total N value in the incoming food waste, as the initial sampling
may not have reflected the total composition of the material due to
unexpected inhomogeneity of incoming material. In fact, another
study performed on food waste from the same source reported a
higher initial N value (49.5 mg N g1 DM; unpublished data) than
found here (35.4 mg N g1 DM; Table 2). The second factor was
deviation in substrate analysis (the method has a 10% error). The
N content of the larvae has been shown to be consistent within a
certain range for BSF larvae and does not depend strongly on initial
N, as long as it is within an acceptable range for their growth
(Lalander et al., 2019).

4.2. Gas emissions
The CO2 emissions were similar between the treatments
throughout the study and showed a similar pattern, with higher
CO2 emission rate measured on day 7 of the experiments and a
slight decrease on day 11 (Fig. 2A). This emissions pattern differs
from that in the thermophilic composting process, where an initial
peak is typically observed early in the microbial degradation process, when easily available substances are consumed by the proliferating microorganisms (Ermolaev et al., 2015). A second peak
associated with process temperature increase if the compost
becomes thermophilic, and with more substances becoming easily
degradable at such temperatures, can be expected (Ermolaev et al.,
2015).
In fly larvae composting, the substrate development had a lower
effect on the CO2 emissions (Fig. 2A-B). Furthermore, in treatment
PBL with pre-treated substrate, there was no significant difference
in CO2 produced during larvae treatment compared with the other
two treatments, suggesting the larvae themselves are the major
source of emissions, since the bacteria introduced in pretreatment (PBL) and seeded at start of the treatment (BL) would
contribute to CO2 emissions due to their respiration in addition
to that of larvae themselves (Table 3). The near linearity in cumulative CO2 emissions could also be expected, as the larvae grow in a
nearly linear way (Lalander et al., 2019) and thus their respiration
could be expected to increase accordingly (Banks, 2014). No strong
correlation (R2 = 0.53) between CO2 emission rates and larvae size
was observed in our experiments, but it was significant
(P < 0.0001) and in the cases where larvae were small, the emission
rates were also smaller, while the CO2 flux was never below
0.003 g min1 after the larvae reached a size of 0.2 g (Fig. 3). This
means that while there was a significant correlation with larvae
size, it could not explain all the variance in CO2 production rate.
Larger variation in CO2 emission rates later in the process can be
related to multiple factors, including the establishment of a microbial community, resulting in a larger contribution of microbial res-

The CH4 emissions dynamics suggested that during the process
of larvae treatment, the material becomes less anaerobic, thus
reducing CH4 production rates during larvae composting
(Fig. 2C). There was only a weak correlation (R2 = 0.43, 0.42 and
0.38 for treatments L, BL and PBL, respectively) between CH4 emission rates and treatment time, mostly due to variation in CH4 flux
measured in different replicates (Fig. 2C–D). However, parts of the
substrate remained anaerobic as CH4 production continued,
although at much slower rate on days 7 and 11 (Fig. 2C–D). In aerobic composting, the CH4 emissions typically increase 4–10 days
later in the process, due to a combination of factors, including a
longer time required for methanogen population growth and thermophilic temperatures (Ermolaev et al., 2015; Ermolaev et al.,
2012; Jäckel et al., 2005). In our fly larvae composting treatments
the opposite was observed. The reduction in CH4 emissions with
treatment time could be associated with larvae growth, as they
turn material more efficiently when they are larger and thus aerate
it more (Cickova et al., 2015).
Overall, the total CH4 emissions from the treatment period were
similar between the two treatments without pre-treatment, with
no significant difference, while these emissions were significantly
smaller in treatment PBL compared with BL (Table 3). The total
CH4 emissions were very small, one-thousandth of the level
observed during conventional composting (Ermolaev et al., 2012).
This likely relates to the majority of the process being aerobic, performed in thin layers and constantly turned. When compared on a
carbon basis, the total CH4 emissions represented 3.3 g of VS loss
(5.3% of total VS), only a fraction of the carbon emissions compared
with CO2, which was calculated to be responsible for losses of
53.8 g VS (87%) on average during all treatments.
The CH4 emissions from pre-treatment in PBL were not measured. While it was possible to estimate the emissions of CO2 from
VS loss due to degradation during the pre-treatment period
(Table 3) with relatively high certainty, the CH4 emissions were
more difficult to predict. Two possibilities were considered: (1)
No CH4 was emitted during pre-treatment, which was supported
by the results obtained for conventional composting, when there
is typically a delay in peak CH4 production of 4–10 days
(Ermolaev et al., 2015; Ermolaev et al., 2012) and production is
associated with thermophilic temperatures (Jäckel et al., 2005),
which were not reached during pre-treatment in our experiments.
(2) The emission rate during pre-treatment was similar to that
measured during the first sampling in the PBL treatment, in which
case the total emissions during the 7 days of pre-treatment were
an estimated 0.61 ± 0.27 mg CH4 kg1 FW, bringing the total CH4

emissions in treatment PBL to 1.63 ± 0.70 mg CH4 kg1 FW, a value
still lower than in the other treatments (Table 3).
The results obtained indicate very low (or no) N2O and NH3
emissions, as also indicated by the total N recovery in the N balance (Table 2, Fig. 2E–F). A lack of detectable NH3 emissions was
confirmed by the SolvitaÒ measurements (Table 1). The lowest
reading, 4.5 out of 5 units, was detected only from residues in
one out of nine replicates in all treatments. In a study by
Lalander et al. (2015), NH3 emissions from fly larvae composting
were detected (olfactory identification) and confirmed through N
balance, indicating a loss of up to 50% of initial N through emissions to air. Moreover, that study reported higher pH in the residues, which would enhance the NH3 emissions. The low NH3
emissions in the present study could be dependent on several factors. First, the final residue pH was 5.1 on average (Table 1). Second, there may be a lack of NH+4 in the residues, as also observed
by Green and Popa (2012), which is likely due to larval assimilation
of N-containing molecules such as proteins. On the other hand,
Cickova et al. (2015) suggest that in fly larvae composting, substantial NH3 emissions can be expected from the increasingly aerobic
process due to larval movement in the substrate. Those authors
also suggest that the material can dry out or warm up and the
pH of the residues can become alkaline, which was not the case
in the present study (see Table 1). Third, other studies reporting
high ammonia emissions from fly larvae treatment have used manure as substrate (Cickova et al., 2012; Iñiguez-Covarrubias et al.,
1994), and manure can be expected to contain higher concentrations of degraded N forms and generally have a higher pH. These
may be associated with microbial degradation of remaining
organic N and other forms of N excreted by larvae due to their
metabolism, such as uric acid (Bursell, 1967). The importance of
moisture and pH changes should be investigated in future experiments, to extend knowledge on NH3 emission dynamics during fly
larvae composting. In conventional composting, it has been
reported that factors such as process temperature becoming thermophilic and pH increasing above 6 are responsible for the NH3
emissions (Ermolaev et al., 2015).
The residues in all treatments were not stabilised during larvae composting (Table 1) and the SolvitaÒ test indicated stability
similar to that of fresh compost. Thus the treatment residues
require an additional treatment step for stabilisation. Previous
studies have shown that Salmonella spp. and viruses (reoviruses
and adenoviruses) are inactivated in the larvae composting process, but not parasites (Ascaris suum) (Lalander et al., 2013;
Lalander et al., 2015). During additional treatment steps to stabilise and sanitise the residue, there is a risk of additional emissions, and thus the optimal conditions for emissions reduction
have to be maintained and emissions monitored. In a full-scale
environmental assessment, management of the residues needs
to be included.

4.3. Perspectives
Fly larvae composting not only performs a valuable function in
the form of organic waste management, but also generates a valuable product in the form of larval biomass (Lalander et al., 2018).
When the emissions from a waste treatment alternative are being
compared, a comprehensive systems analysis should be performed,
where results from multiple studies are incorporated. Such a study
should consider the value of larvae biomass as the product. In such
cases, emissions per unit mass of larvae and per ton of dry feed
replacement produced can be estimated (Table 4). This study
focused on the direct emissions from the treatment step. The CO2
equivalents of emissions of CH4 and N2O were 1/1000 of the actual
CO2 emissions when expressed per ton of dry larval biomass produced (Table 4). Treatment PBL produced less CH4 and N2O than
the other two treatments, but total emissions of CO2 nearly doubled, which resulted in significantly higher total emissions per
ton DM of larvae produced including CO2, CH4 and N2O in treatment PBL comparing to L and BL (P < 0.00005). However, this did
not result in a significant increase in bioconversion ratio, indicating
that such pre-treatment is unnecessary (Tables 2 and 5). A similar
conclusion can be drawn when looking at emissions per 1000 larvae also resulting in significantly higher (P < 0.0005) total emissions in treatment PBL comparing to L and BL (Table 4). A
complete system evaluation should thus complement the results
obtained in this study with other relevant impacts and when other
feeds are replaced with larvae produced.
Evaluation of direct emissions from fly larvae composting
enables comparison of this treatment with treatment steps in other
common organic waste treatment alternatives, such as composting
and anaerobic digestion (Table 5). Emissions of CO2 during fly larvae composting are of biogenic origin and may be considered non-

In such an interpretation of total GHG emissions from fly larvae
composting, the total emissions are very small, only around
0.38 kg CO2-eq. ton1 food waste treated (Table 3). A recent study
by Mertenat et al. (2019) on emissions of CH4 and N2O from larger
crate fly larvae composting reported lower total CH4 and higher
N2O emissions (Table 5). However, the N2O emissions pattern
was different from that in the present study, with emission peaks
appearing after feeding events (Mertenat et al., 2019). In the present study, the gas measurements were performed less frequently
and before the feeding events, to avoid overestimation of the emissions associated with system disturbance due to feed addition.
Similar N2O emission peaks to those appearing directly after feed
addition have been observed in composting, at the start of the process, if the food waste contains nitrate (Ermolaev et al., 2015). This
suggests that further investigation may be necessary, with more
frequent gas measurements and nitrate content evaluation of
incoming food waste.
Organic waste treatment alternatives often include several process steps that may contribute additional direct GHG emissions to
the overall system total. In anaerobic digestion, additional emissions can be expected due to biofilter emissions and digestate storage and during upgrading and combustion of biogas (Møller et al.,
2009). Since an additional treatment step is necessary for fly larvae
composting residues, additional NH3 or N2O emissions can be
expected if the residues are still relatively moist, similarly to possible emissions during the curing stage of the composting process
(Ermolaev et al., 2012).
The emissions from fly larvae composting residue posttreatment have not yet been evaluated. Direct and indirect emissions during all the process stages for fly larvae composting have
to be performed to allow fair comparisons.
5. Conclusions
Overall GHG emissions from fly larvae composting of food
waste using BSF larvae were comparatively low. CO2 from food
waste degradation was the major GHG emitted, with total emissions of 96 g CO2 per kg food waste treated. Emissions of CH4
and N2O were equivalent to 0.38 kg CO2-equivalents per ton food
waste treated (assuming GWP over 100 years). No NH3 emissions
were detected, which was reflected in total N mass balance over
the treatment cycle.
There was no significant improvement in material reduction or
bioconversion ratio when food waste was seeded with larvaeassociated bacteria, compared with food waste treatment with larvae alone. Moreover, there was no significant effect of different
treatments on total GHG emissions.

a b s t r a c t
Volatile emissions from decomposing animal waste are known environmental pollutants. The black soldier fly, Hermetia illucens (L.), is being evaluated for industrialization as a means to recycle wastes and
produce protein for use as food and feed. We examined the ability of black soldier fly larvae to reduce
odorous compounds associated with animal wastes. Black soldier fly larvae were reared under laboratory
conditions on poultry, swine, and dairy manure at feed rates of 18.0 and 27.0 g every other day until 40%
reached the prepupal stage. Volatile emissions were collected and analyzed from freshly thawed as well
as the digested waste when 90% of the black soldier fly larvae reached the prepupal stage. Volatiles were
also collected simultaneously from manure not inoculated with black soldier fly larvae (non-digested)
and held under similar conditions. Manure samples were analyzed for relative amounts of nine select
odorous volatile organic compounds: phenol, 4-methylphenol, indole, 3-methylindole, propanoic acid,
2-methylpropanoic acid, butanoic acid, 3-methylbutanoic acid and pentanoic acid. Black soldier fly larvae
reduced emissions of all volatile organic compounds by 87% or greater. Complete reductions were
observed for 2-methly propanoic acid in digested poultry manure, phenol, 4-methylphenol, indole and
all five fatty acids in digested swine manure, and 4-methylphenol, indole, 3-methylindole and all five
acids in digested dairy manure. This study is the first to identify volatile emissions from manure digested
by black soldier fly larvae and compare to those found in non-digested manure. These data demonstrate
additional benefits of using black soldier fly larvae as a cost-effective and environmentally friendly means
of livestock manure management in comparison to current methods.
Capsule: Black soldier fly larvae are capable of altering the overall profile of volatile organic compounds
and reducing levels of targeted odorous compounds in livestock manure.

1. Introduction
The decomposition of manure is responsible for environmental
emissions, such as greenhouse gases, ammonia and other volatile
organic compounds (VOCs), which are pollutants and pose potential health risks (FAO, 2009). Between 100 and 330 VOCs and volatile fatty acids are generated by concentrated animal feeding
operations (CAFOs,) depending on management practices and the
species of animal involved (Cai et al., 2015; Powers and Bastyr,
2004; Schiffman et al., 2001). The compounds most associated with
or responsible for the odor of manure are phenols, indoles, alcohols, organic sulphides, and volatile fatty acids (Hales et al.,

2012; Kuroda et al., 1996; El-Mashad et al., 2011). For example,
Hales et al. (2012) found that 4-methylphenol was responsible
for 67.3% of odor activity in dairy manure. The key odorous VOCs
in poultry manure were butanoic acid, 3-methylbutanoic acid,
dimethyl trisulphide, indole and skatole (Yasuhara, 1987). These
VOCs, which are noxious odors, can also negatively affect humans
by posing potential health risks to those living in communities surrounding animal farming facilities (PEW, 2008). VOCs responsible
for strong odors contribute to higher levels of tension, depression,
and anger experiences by those working or living in close proximity to areas with heavy animal farming (Barrett, 2006).
With the increasing amount of manure and the need for a
sustainable method of management, fly (Diptera) larvae have
become an alternative means to process this resource. Black solider
fly, Hermetia illucens (L.) (Diptera: Stratiomyidae) larvae (BSFL)
have been studied as a means of manure management because of

 214

K.V. Beskin et al. / Waste Management 74 (2018) 213–220

several beneficial abilities. First, BSFL reduce organic matter, such
as livestock manure. Sheppard (1994) observed significant reductions in poultry manure (50%) in one study, and in another study
reported 56 and 42% reductions in dry weight, depending on
whether manure had water added to it or not (Sheppard, 1983).
Newton et al. (2005) observed a 39% reduction in the dry weight
of swine manure processed by BSFL. Myers et al. (2008) documented a 58% and 33% reduction in dry matter of manure from
BSFL fed 27 g and 70 g of dairy manure daily, respectively. In a
study comparing poultry, swine, and dairy manure, the dry matter
of all three manure types was reduced by 37% (Oonincx et al.,
2015).
In addition to the reduction of dry matter of manure, nutrients,
which in excess can be detrimental to the environment, are
decreased. BSFL reduce the nitrogen content of poultry manure
by 62% (Sheppard, 1983). During the digestion of dairy manure,
BSFL reduced concentrations of nitrogen and phosphorus by 30–
50% and 61–70%, respectively (Myers et al., 2008). When BSFL were
allowed to feed on poultry, swine, and dairy manure, nitrogen content was reduced by 80, 37, and 30%, respectively (Oonincx et al.,
2015). Importantly, adult black soldier flies do not need to feed
and their non-synanthropic nature has earned them the label of
a non-pest species (Furman et al, 1959). However, to date, the
impact of black soldier fly digestion of manure on VOC production
has not been examined. The purpose of this study was to assess
how the digestion of poultry, swine, and dairy manure by BSFL
impacts select odorous VOCs.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Acquisition of flies
The H. illucens larvae were from a colony established in 2014
from eggs from a colony maintained at the Coastal Plains Experiment Station, University of Georgia, (Tifton, GA) and are now maintained at the Forensic Laboratory for Investigative Entomological
Sciences (F.L.I.E.S.) Facility at Texas A&M University (College Station, TX). Adult flies were maintained in a 2.6  1.3  1.3 m wooden cage fitted with metal screening, in a greenhouse maintained
at approximately 29 °C. Adults were allowed to oviposit in three
7.0  5.0  0.3 cm pieces of corrugated cardboard (Booth and
Sheppard, 1984) held together with masking tape and placed on
the lid of a 30.0  15.0  11.0 cm plastic shoe box containing one
kilogram of Gainesville diet (Hogsette, 1992) saturated with water.
A 13.0  5.0 cm portion of the lid was removed and replaced with
metal screening on which the cardboard pieces were placed; this
approach allowed volatiles to escape from the wet Gainesville diet
and attract gravid flies, but prevented the flies from contacting
and/or ovipositing directly into the media instead of the cardboard.
The cardboard was removed from the cage after eight hours, and
eggs were removed from cardboard using a sterile plastic spatula
and weighed. One gram of eggs was then placed in a 0.5 L plastic
container, covered with a paper towel secured with a rubber band,
stored in a walk-in environmental chamber (29 ± 0.3 °C with 60 ±
5.1% relative humidity and 14:10 L:D cycle) and checked every 12
h until hatch. Two hundred grams of Gainesville diet at 70% moisture was added to the container once larvae eclosed. Newlyemerged larvae were allowed to feed for four days in the environmental chamber prior to use in the experiment.
2.2. Acquisition of manure
Three different livestock manure types were used in this study.
Poultry manure was collected from layer hens housed at the Poultry Science Research, Teaching, and Extension Center at Texas A&M

University in College Station, TX, USA. The hens were fed a mixture
of corn and soybean meal that is considered typical layer diet, consisting of 18.5% crude protein, 2.5% crude fat and 2.4% crude fiber.
Swine manure was collected from sows raised by Schroeder Genetics in Anderson, TX, USA. The sows were maintained on cubes containing 14.0% crude protein, 2.8% crude fat, and 6.5% crude fiber
formulated for gilts, sows and adult boars. Dairy manure was collected from cows maintained at the Southwest Regional Dairy Center in Stephenville, TX, USA. The diet for these animals consisted of
16.1% crude protein, 5.0% crude fat and 28.1% crude fiber. The
majority of this diet is composed of a mixture of corn silage
(32.0%), ground corn (22.5%), and concentrate pre-mix (19.4%)
composed of canola and soybean meal.
Each manure type was collected on site within 12 h of excretion, using a shovel and two 19 L buckets with lids, sterilized prior
to use for manure collection. The manure was transported to the F.
L.I.E.S. Facility where it was homogenized in the buckets and transferred to individual 3.78 L self-sealing plastic freezer bags and frozen at 20 °C until used. Manure was removed from the freezer
and allowed to thaw for 24 h at room temperature before being
used. Thawed manure was stored in a refrigerator at 4 °C.

2.3. Experiment design
One hundred 4-d-old larvae were placed in 88.7 ml plastic bathroom cups (Georgia-Pacific LLC, Atlanta, GA, USA) and assigned to
one of the three manure types (poultry, swine, or dairy) and one
of two feed rates (18.0 or 27.0 g every other day). Feed rates used
were based off the methods of Myers et al. (2008) who used 300
larvae and feed rates of 27, 40, 54 and 70 g of manure per day.
The feed rates used in this study are therefore modified from this
due to only 100 larvae being used and feeding occurring every
other day. Preliminary experiments were conducted to confirm
the scalability of these feed rates (unpublished data).
Containers without larvae were used as controls and subsequently referred to as non-digested manure. These containers
received manure assigned at a given feed rate in similar fashion
to those with larvae. Three replicates for each feed rate and manure type with and without larvae were used. Containers were
placed in a randomized block design among three levels of a shelving unit in the environmental chamber maintained at 29 ± 0.3 °C
with 60 ± 5.1% relative humidity and 14:10 L:D cycle The experiment was replicated twice (Fig. 1).
Initially, larvae in each replicate were provided manure at the
assigned amount and allowed to feed for four days. Larvae and contents of the cup were then transferred to a 1.89 L ReditainerTM
EXTREME FREEZETM deli container (Clear Lake Enterprises, Port
Richey, FL, USA) and fed every other day. Manure was weighed
directly into the containers using a ScoutÒ Pro Balance (Ohaus, Parsippany, NJ, USA). Containers were then covered with a 25.4  25.
4 cm piece of tulle to prevent contamination.
Containers were checked daily for post-feeding larvae (i.e., prepupae, Sheppard et al. 1994), which were removed and identified
by the cuticular color shifting from opaque to black (May 1961).
Additionally, to monitor the progress of larval feeding, manure in
each container was shifted using forceps that had been sterilized
with 70% ethanol. Separate forceps were used for each manure
type to prevent cross contamination. Feeding of larvae terminated
when 40% of the larvae reached the prepupal stage (Sheppard et al.
2002). VOCs were sampled from the digested group and a matching randomly selected sample from the non-digested group of
the same manure type and feed rate, when approximately 90% of
the larvae reached the prepupal stage. This level of pupation was
selected as it would also represent industrialized production of
BSFL.

USA) containing a 9.0 mm 300 ll insert (Thermo Fisher Scientific,
Waltham, MA, USA) using N2. An additional 5.0 ll of 80 ng/ll nOctane (Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA) was added to each sample as an internal standard. Samples were capped and stored at
20 °C until analysis at the Geochemical and Environmental

using a using a Hewlett-Packard 6890 gas chromatograph with a
Hewlett-Packard 5973 mass selective detector (Hewlett-Packard

Injections of 1 ll were performed in splitless mode with an

4. Discussion
BSFL digestion of manure reduced the emission of select odorous VOCs across all manure types and feed rates tested when compared to amounts present in the initial manure. BSFL were adept at
reducing select VOCs at rates of 87% or greater. In the case of 4methylphenol, indole, skatole and the five fatty acids examined,
no levels of VOCs were detected in either digested swine or dairy
manure (i.e., 100% reduction). In addition to the benefits presented
in previous studies, such as reductions in dry matter (Sheppard,
1994), nitrogen and phosphorus (Myers et al., 2008) and pathogenic Gram-negative bacteria (Erickson et al., 2004; Liu et al.,
2008), the ability of BSFL to reduce VOC emissions, particularly
those associated with the offensive smell of manure, is an additional benefit to their use as a manure-management tool.
The reduction of select odorous VOCs is believed to be in part
due to a decrease of moisture (Brinton, 1998). In the current study,
moisture content data (Fig. 2) indicate that manures both with and
without BSFL were lower in moisture than freshly-thawed manure.
At both feed rates (18 and 27 g), BSFL reduced the moisture content
the most in dairy manure; particularly at the 18 g feed rate. Dairy
manure also experienced the greatest decreases in moisture at the
18 g feed rate for non-digested manure. The differing levels of
moisture reduction experienced by the manure types was expected
due to the longer larval development times seen in swine and dairy
manure compared to poultry. Furthermore, non-digested manure
experienced greater moisture loss at the 18 g feed rates likely
due to differing surface area to volume ratios compared to that
at the 27 g feed rate. For example, Miller et al. (1974) found that
poultry manure with a higher surface area was rendered into a
more granular like texture when digested by Musca domestica
(Miller et al., 1974). At both feed rates, larvae reached 90% prepupation significantly faster on poultry manure than on swine or
dairy (data not presented).
The extended development time of BSFL on the certain manure
types could be due to lower nutritional quality (i.e. calories, protein
and fat content) (Zhou et al., 2013). For example, Oonincx et al.
(2015) observed longer development times with larvae fed poultry,
swine and cow manure compared to a control diet of poultry feed
(144-215 vs 20 d). Similarly, Nguyen et al. (2013) found that larvae
reared on pig manure experienced a significantly longer median
time to adulthood (55.33 ± 2.14 d) compared to those reared on a
standard diet of poultry feed (42.17 ± 1.30 d) (Nguyen et al.,
2013). In fact, median time to adulthood was significantly longer
for larvae fed manure compared to those reared on other substrates (liver, kitchen waste, fruits and vegetables) used in the
study (Nguyen et al., 2013).
Possibly the increased BSFL development times observed with
swine and dairy manure in our study gave the larvae more time
to reduce the moisture content via digestion and aeration. Similarly, because VOCs were taken at 90% prepupation, BSFL digested
and corresponding non-digested controls for these manure types
incubated longer than poultry manure samples and continued to
lose moisture in the environmental chamber. Thus, the digested
and non-digested swine and dairy manure treatments had lower
levels of moisture than poultry manure. The increased moisture
reduction in dairy and swine manure might affect the presence
of VOCs, such as volatile fatty acids in the samples. However, in
some instances, the BSFL were more adept at reducing VOCs than
manure without larvae. For example at the 27 g feed rate, the

lower moisture content of BSFL digested manure could explain
the complete reduction of 2-methylpropanoic acid in poultry manure, and phenol, 4-methylphenol, and indole in swine manure.
The ability of the BSFL to reduce the moisture content of the
substrate on which it feeds likely impacts the microbial populations responsible for generating many odorous VOCs as many of
these microbes are negatively affected by moisture content
(Hansen, 1976). Tate (1978) determined survival of Escherichia coli
to be greatest in organic soils that were under flooded conditions;
Hagedorn et al. (1978) determined E. coli populations to be highest
in a water table following a major rainfall. Similarly, Streptococcus
faecalis degrades rapidly under low soil moisture conditions
(Kibbey et al., 1978). Moisture content of manure and the effect
on bacteria survival have been less thoroughly studied; however,
Wang et al. (1996) suggested that dehydration of manure could
contribute to the die off E. coli O157:H7 and observed this with
fecal Streptococci spp. in a later study (Wang et al., 2004).
Himathongkham et al. (1999) examined the survival of E. coli
O157:H7 and Salmonella typhimurium in cow manure and slurry
and reported similar results: these microbes persisted in wastes
with higher moisture contents.
A reduction in microbial populations in manure digested by the
BSFL could also contribute to reduction in targeted VOCs. Lalander
et al. (2013) saw a 6 log reduction in Salmonella spp. in human
feces with BSFL digestion compared to a less than 2 log reduction
in the control feces, which had no larvae. Poultry manure inoculated with Salmonella enterica serovar Enteritidis that was digested
by BSFL experienced pathogen populations 2.5 log lower than control samples without larvae after three days (Erickson et al., 2004).
Lalander et al. (2015) observed a decrease from 107 CFU g 1 to
below 1 CFU g 1 in Salmonella spp. in compost reactors that were
supplied a mix of human and pig manure, and organic wastes
and allowed to be digested by BSFL. Liu et al. (2008) inoculated
dairy manure with E. coli and observed that larvae were successful
at reducing the pathogen loads in the manure across all treatments; however, their ability to reduce the pathogen was affected
by the amount of manure they were provided and the temperature
at which the experiment was conducted. The greatest reduction of
E. coli occurred with a manure amount of 50 g at 27 °C which
decreased after 72 h from 7.0 log CFU g 1 to 0.23 ± 3.39 log CFU
g 1.
Reduction in microbial populations reduces many odors associated with manure, as VOCs are the coproducts of different metabolic pathways, which serve as waste products or potential
signals and cues for the microbes (Mayrhofer et al., 2006). Bacteria
from several genera are responsible for many of the odorous VOCs
found in manure (Mackie et al., 1998). Streptococcus spp. are capable of producing ammonia, five of which have been found in
swine manure (Russell, 1979). Peptostreptococcus spp. metabolize
peptone and amino acids into volatile fatty acids including acetic,
formic, propionic, caproic, isobutryic, isovaleric, and isocaproic
acids (Mackie et al., 1998). Other bacteria in genera such as Eubacteria, Lactobacillus, Escherichia, Clostridium Propionibacterium, Bacteroides and Megasphaera are responsible for the production of
odorous VOCs such as volatile fatty acids indole and sulfur containing compounds (Mackie et al., 1998; Zhu, 2000; Le et al., 2005).
A study by Mayrhofer et al. (2006) found positive correlations
between the production of VOCs and the enhancement of microbial
growth and conversely negative correlations between microbial
inhibition and VOC emissions during the breakdown of household
biowastes over a course of 16 d. This relationship between
microbes and specific VOC emissions has been demonstrated by
several studies (Senecal et al., 2002; Lechner et al., 2005; Jünger
et al., 2012) with the hopes of uniquely identifying human bacterial pathogens from specific volatile fingerprints to circumventing
biases caused by DNA extraction procedures (Mayrhofer et al.,

2006). Such studies support the concept that the microbial structure of manure affects VOC emissions.
Investigations into how different treatments of manure (e.g.,
freshly excreted versus thawed manure and rearing temperatures)
effect digestion and subsequent VOC emissions are needed.
Yasuhara (1983) saw differences in volatile profiles from samples
of fresh poultry manure, manure that was immediately frozen
and manure that was allowed to age before freezing. Husted
(1994) found that methane production from dairy manure
increased when stored at higher temperatures. Gibson et al.
(1987) noted that different temperature regimes affected the
growth of Clostridium botulinum spores in pork slurry. Therefore
it is reasonable to hypothesize that different temperature regimes
could affect the microbial communities in manure and alter VOC
emissions.
5. Conclusions
This study demonstrated the ability of BSFL to reduce levels of
odorous compounds emitted from different livestock manure types
(e.g., 100% reduction of indole and fatty acids in swine and dairy
manure, Table 1). This, along with aforementioned benefits, makes
BSFL an attractive alternative means of manure management that
is both environmentally and economically friendly. Not only would
those using BSFL to process manure experience lower levels of odor
emissions, but also an increased reduction in dry matter
(Sheppard, 1983), pathogens (Erickson et al., 2004) and overabundant nutrients (Myers et al., 2008). All the while larvae are acquiring valuable biomass, and they in turn could be used as feedstock
for poultry (Hale, 1973), swine (Newton et al., 1977) and several
species used in aquaculture (Bondari & Sheppard, 1987; StHilaire et al., 2007; Kroekel et al., 2012). Furthermore, larval stock
has also been successfully rendered into biodiesel (Li et al., 2011;
Zheng et al., 2012). Those implementing a BSFL system on site
could reduce the need for ancillary management equipment, lower
feed costs, and generate profit by selling larvae or larval-based
products.

 Abstract
Black soldier fly larvae (BSFL) have been proven to reduce greenhouse gas emissions in the treatment of
organic waste (e.g., domestic biodegradable waste, DBW). However, the microbial mechanisms involved
have not been fully understood. The current study mainly examined the dynamic changes of carbon and
nitrogen, greenhouse gas emissions, the succession of microbial community structure, and changes in
gene abundance in DBW under BSFL treatment (LT) and non-aeration composting (NC). We found that of
the organic waste supplied, 29.9% carbon and 55.0% nitrogen were stored in BSFL. For every 1kg of dry
matter of organic waste consumed, 655 g CO2, 0.80 mg CH4, and 2.26 mg N2O were emitted from LT,
significantly lower than those from NC. 16S rRNA gene sequencing results showed that the BSFL
increased the relative abundance of Methanophaga, Marinobacter, and Campylobacter during the
bioprocess, enhancing the consumption of CH4 and N2O. The metagenomic data showed that the BSFL
reduced the ratio of (nirK + nirS + nor)/nosZ in the residues, thereby reducing the emission of N2O. In
addition, it increased the functional gene abundance of nirA, nirB, nirD, and nrfA, making nitrite more
inclined to be reduced to ammonia. The BSFL mitigated greenhouse gas emissions by redistributing
carbon and nitrogen and remodeling the community and function of microbiomes during the DBW
bioconversion.

1. Introduction
Recently, black soldier fly larvae (Hermetia illucens L., BSFL) bioconversion technology has been widely
recognized as a promising biotechnology for the treatment of domestic biodegradable waste (DBW),
livestock manure, and sewage sludge (Qin et al. 2022; Wang et al. 2022; Wang et al. 2023). This
technology can not only convert organic waste into organic fertilizer (Xiang et al. 2022), but also harvest
larvae for animal feed and biofuel production (Parodi et al. 2020). However, organic waste emits a large
amount of greenhouse gases (CO2, CH4, and N2O) during the bioprocess, which is harmful to the
environment (Akdeniz 2019). Studies have shown that BSFL bioconversion technology can significantly
reduce greenhouse gas emissions compared to traditional composting (Pang et al. 2020). However, few
studies have been focused on how BSFL reduce greenhouse gas emissions during organic waste
treatment.
Through the processes of nitrification, denitrification, and nitrogen fixation, N2O was produced and
emitted during bioconversion (He et al. 2021), and CH4 emissions also depended on CH4 production and
oxidation (Sun et al. 2022). Thus, when assessing N2O and CH4 emissions, the nitrogen metabolism and
methanogenesis functional microbial community should be fully considered. Researchers found that the
emission intensity of N2O was positively correlated with the functional gene abundance of nirK, nirS, and

nosZ. (Chen et al. 2023). In addition, methanosarcina, methanoculleus, and methanobacterium were the
most abundant methanogenic genera in the aerobic composting of livestock manure (Sun et al. 2022).
Many studies suggested reducing greenhouse gas emissions by adding additives (biochar, lime, etc.) and
changing composting conditions (temperature, aeration, etc.), all of which without exception affected the
Page 2/22

 microbial community structure (Chu et al. 2022; He et al. 2021; Sun et al. 2022; Zhang et al. 2023). The
BSFL caused a significant impact on the microbial community in organic waste, and it also formed a
unique microbial community in its own intestines (Zhan et al. 2020). Therefore, it is necessary to study
whether the microbial community changes caused by BSFL alleviate greenhouse gas emissions during
the BSFL bioconversion. The latest developments in metagenomics have promoted research on the study
of non-culturable microorganisms (Xiang et al. 2024). Metagenomics can analyze microbial diversity and
identify proteins, enzymes, and biochemical pathways related to nitrogen metabolism and
methanogenesis process. The current study used metagenomic analysis to investigate the dynamic
profiles of the functional structure of microbial communities in larval intestines and residues, which is
important for understanding the emission mechanisms of CH4 and N2O during the process of BSFL
bioconversion.
In this study, we conducted two experiments in a full-scale project for DBW treatment, i.e., inclusion with
BSFL (LT) or non-aeration composting (NC). The principal goals of this study are to (i) understand the
redistributions of carbon and nitrogen in each component (i.e., larvae, residual material, and gaseous
emissions), and use mass balance to calculate the flow direction of carbon and nitrogen; (ii) investigate
the evolution of bacterial community structure through 16s rRNA analyses; (iii) reveal the dynamic
changes in the functional structure of microbial communities in larval intestines and residues using
metagenomics analyses. This study provides a new insight on understanding of greenhouse gas
emissions during BSFL bioconversion for the treatment of organic waste.

2. Materials and methods

2.1. Experimental design
The full-scale BSFL bioconversion project for DBW (food waste, kitchen waste, and fruit and vegetable
waste, etc.) treatment established by the HangZhou GuSheng Biotechnology Co., Ltd. was in YuHang
County (30°24′10.8″ N, 120°09′43.3″E), HangZhou City, ZheJiang Province, China (Deng et al. 2022). Raw
DBW was collected from nearby villages and towns, including rural households, farm product markets,
and food catering companies. After removing non-biodegradable substances (e.g., plastic, wood, and
glass), a pulper was used to process the collected DBW into a slurry that was then passed through a 3.5
mm sieve. Appropriate amounts of rice husk powder were added to adjust the moisture content of the
slurry to ~ 75%.
The BSFL bioconversion unit was housed within a plastic greenhouse featuring a sequence of
bioconversion pools, measuring 14 m × 2 m × 30 cm (L×W×H). A continuous feeding strategy based on
operational experience was applied to treat DBW. Briefly, 100 kg DBW was manually applied to each pool,
and then four-day-old BSFL (2nd instar) were introduced into the pools to initiate the process of DBW
bioconversion (i.e., LT). The inoculation intensity was equivalent to the emergence of larvae from 35
grams of eggs per ton of DBW. Afterwards, the DBW was fed according to Fig. S1. Another pool was filled
with the same amount of DBW without larvae added (non-aeration compost, i.e., NC). Commencing on
Page 3/22

 November 9, 2020, the experiment spanned 14 days and was replicated three times for each treatment.
DBW samples for both LT and NC were collected bi-daily starting from day 0 prior to feeding. Fresh BSFL
samples were concurrently gathered from the larvae treatment every two days. Samples were temporarily
stored in a portable refrigerator and transported to the laboratory within 4 hours. Fresh larvae samples
were chilled on ice for dissection after surface sterilization twice using 70% ethanol and cleaned twice
using sterile water. Based on methods described in (Gold et al. 2018), the midgut was dissected for
subsequent DNA extraction (LI). Simply, the midgut is the part between the proventriculus (a valve with a
potentially grinding function) and the Malpighian tubules (shaped as a slender tube). Fresh samples were
either processed immediately or stored at -80°C before downstream analysis.

2.2. Measurement of greenhouse gas fluxes.
In situ, reactor-atmosphere fluxes of CO2, CH4, and N2O were measured using a static flux chamber. The
chamber consisted of a polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA) box of 20 cm in height, 30 cm in length, and 25
cm in width with a threaded access cap and a gas valve. The cap was fitted with a gas-tight O-ring for
installing a thermometer, and the gas valve was used for gas sampling. The top of the box was equipped
with an axial fan to promote sufficient mixing of internal gases. The chamber was connected to a
stainless-steel base collar of the same size but only 5cm in height, which was used to reduce lateral gas
flux before sampling. The stainless-steel base collar of the chamber was inserted into the DBW and left to
equilibrate for roughly 30 min before sampling. The gas valve was closed and the axial fan was started.
Gas measurements were taken at approximately 20-min intervals, for a total of five measurements. For
each measurement, 100 ml of gas was collected using an air pump and Teflon FEP airbag (Teflon® FEP,
China). CO2, CH4, and N2O concentrations in samples were measured by gas chromatography as
described by (Zeng et al. 2018). Concentrations were then converted to nmol/m3 at ambient pressure and
temperature using the ideal gas law. Atmospheric flux (Jatm ) was calculated from the concentration (C0)

 2.3. Waste reduction calculation and analysis of
physicochemical parameters
A real-time weighing and monitoring system was set for collections of daily input of DBW, residue mass,
and fresh larvae yield. The reduction rate of DBW was calculated using the input and residue mass.
Temperature, pH, and moisture were measured as described in our previous report (Tao et al. 2023). Total
carbon (TC) was determined with a Elementar Vario El cube-type element analyzer (Elementar Vario EL
Cube, Elementar, Germany). The total Kjeldahl nitrogen (KN) was tested according to the procedure of
(Wang et al. 2023) after digesting the dry samples using the concentrated H2SO4–HClO4 acids. NO-3-N
and NH + 4-N were analyzed using a continuous flow analytical system (Shimadzu, JAPAN) (Xu et al.
2023). Levels of crude protein, crude fat and ash in samples were tested by standard methods coded as
GB/T6432-1994, GB/T6433-2006 and GB/T6438-2007, respectively (Deng et al. 2022).

2.4. Community DNA extraction
For all samples (NC, LT, and LI), total community DNA was extracted using 0.25 g of DBW or intestinal
tissue. Extractions were performed using the QIAamp® PowerFecal® DNA Kit (QIAGEN, Germany)
according to the manufacturer’s instructions. To verify successful DNA extraction, the DNA concentration
and purity were quantified with a TBS-380 fluorometer (Turner Biosystems, Sunnyvale, CA, USA) and a
NanoDrop 2000 spectrophotometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA), respectively.
Electrophoresis was performed with 1% (w/v) agarose gels before the use of DNA extracts from the
respective microbes.

2.5. Marker-gene sequencing and analysis
High-resolution marker-gene (16S rRNA) analysis was performed on an Illumina Novaseq PE250 platform
for all samples. qPCR was used to estimate total bacterial and archaeal biomass. The primer pair 341F
(CCTAYGGGRBGCASCAG) and 806R (GGACTACHVGGGTWTCTAA) was used to amplify the V3-V4
regions of the bacterial 16S ribosomal RNA gene. 2% agarose gel electrophoresis of PCR products was
carried out to test whether the products were amplified successfully. 2% agarose gel electrophoresis of
PCR products was carried out to test whether the products were amplified successfully. The Illumina
Novaseq PE250 platform was selected for double-end sequencing with an average of 30,000 raw reads.
Pandaseq software was used to merge paired reads. Clean reads were obtained after quality filtering.
Raw data for high-throughput sequencing are available at Mendeley Data
(https://doi.org/10.17632/rxdgmvx4x9.1).

2.6. Metagenomics sequence, assembly, and analysis
All samples from LI and LT, as well as NC samples from days 0, 6, and 14, were chosen for shotgun
metagenomic sequencing. The DNA was treated with Covaris M220 (Gene Company, Shanghai, China) to
produce fragments of ~ 300 bp for paired-end library construction. Paired-end sequencing was performed
on an Illumina HiSeq 4000 platform (Illumina, San Diego, CA, USA) at Majorbio Bio-Pharm Technology
Co. (Shanghai, China). Low-quality reads (length < 50 bp or with a quality value < 20 or having N bases)
Page 5/22

 were removed using Fastp v0.20.0 (https://github.com/OpenGene/fastp). The reads were then trimmed
by removing host DNA (Hermetia illucens (L.)) with BWA v0.7.17 (https://github.com/sghignone/bwa). A
total of 2,451,107,634 clean reads were generated with an average of 48,060,934 reads per sample. The
metagenome was then assembled as contigs having a minimum length of 300 bp and open reading
frames (ORFs) were predicted using MetaGene (http://metagene.cb.k.u-tokyo.ac.jp/). All predicted genes
(90% sequence identity and 90% coverage) were clustered using CD-HIT
(http://www.bioinformatics.org/cd-hit/). The longest genes in each cluster were chosen as representative
sequences to construct a non-redundant gene catalog. The raw metagenomic data were deposited in the
National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) Sequence Read Archive (accession number:
SUB13374969).

2.7. Statistical analysis
One-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) was performed using SPSS 22.0 and the results were tested for
significance. A P-value of < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. The line chart, bar chart, and
Sankey chart were created using Origin 2023b (OriginLab, Los Angeles, USA). For the exponential model,
parameters P and k were fitted via non-linear regression using the nls() function in R (Fig. S2, 3, and 4;
Table S1), and h was denoted the effective chamber height in m. For taxonomic annotation, usearch
(http://drive5.com/usearch/manual/dereplication.html) was used to determine data quality as well as
identify and remove chimeric sequences. Operational taxonomic units (OTUs), obtained according to a
97% similarity threshold, were compared with the Greengenes database
(http://greengenes.secondgenome.com/) to obtain the bacterial community structure and composition
information for the samples. For functional annotation, sequences were aligned to the KEGG database
using BLASTP (BLAST Version 2.2.28+, http://blast.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/Blast.cgi) searched with an e-value
cutoff of 10− 5.

3. Results and discussion

3.1. Changes in carbon and nitrogen
We measured the mass, moisture, temperature, and pH values of the residues to characterize the
bioconversion process (Fig. S1), and the physical and chemical properties of inputs, residues, and larvae
are shown in Table 1. The results showed that the degradation rate, temperature, and pH in the BSFL
treatment (LT) were higher while the water content was lower, compared to the non-aeration compost
(NC). The total carbon (TC) and total Kjeldahl nitrogen (KN) in the LT decreased by 13.9 g/kg and 2.76
g/kg, respectively, which were 13.9 times and 3.70 times higher than those in the NC (Fig. 1a, b). This is
attributed to the lack of aeration in the NC, resulting in low microbial activity (Rincon et al. 2019). On the
contrary, the peristalsis of the larvae and their own respiration ensure the oxygen supply in LT, allowing
for rapid degradation of TC and KN.
