cleaning, peeling, and nucleating procedures involved in their industrial
processing. Furthermore, the presence of enzymes makes them susceptible to enzymatic browning, thus making waste generation an unavoidable outcome during the processing stage (Zhu et al., 2023). In
developing countries, fruit and vegetable waste ranges from 15 % to 50
% of harvested produce and is typically generated before reaching the
market (Gardas et al., 2017). Worldwide, approximately 0.3 and 15.6
million tons of kiwi residue and citrus peel waste are generated annually, respectively (Zhu et al., 2023). Furthermore, global grape pomace
from grape processing accounts for 5-9 million tons annually (Zhu et al.,
2023).
By-products from fruits and vegetables are rich in various beneficial
compounds, including vitamins, carotenoids, alkaloids, proteins, dietary
fibers, and polyphenols. Fruit waste, in particular, comprises cellulose,
lignin, hemicellulose, and other polysaccharides (Nabi et al., 2024).
Therefore, there is considerable potential to recover these natural
components from such residues within the framework of the circular
economy. The citrus industry generates around 50–60 % of by-products,
totaling over 60 million tons globally (Wedamulla et al., 2022). These
residual materials comprise peels, pulp, seeds, and leaves and are rich in
bioactive compounds like polyphenols, carotenoids, pectin, essential
oils, and enzymes. Orange peels are among the most prevalent waste
products in the food industry and serve as a rich source of carotenoids.
The carotenoid content in orange peels is estimated to be around 97.4
μg/g when acetone is employed as a solvent (Murador et al., 2019). An
enhanced carotenoids extraction yield of 65,350 μg/g from orange peels
was achieved using hydrophobic deep eutectic solvents (DES) consisting
of Menthol and Camphor, along with an ultrasound extraction method
with an ultrasound intensity of 60 % and an extraction time of 20 min
(Viñas-Ospino et al., 2023).
Pomegranate juice processing plants produce a significant amount of
waste, comprising fruit residues such as seeds and outer peels. The peel,
consisting of the exocarp and mesocarp, accounts for approximately 50
% of the total weight of the fresh pomegranate fruit, and its chemical
composition varies depending on cultivar type (Lacivita et al., 2023).
This amounts to over 1.9 million metric tons per year globally (El Barnossi et al., 2021). The exceptional properties of pomegranate fruit peels
(Punica granatum L.) are well-documented, as they contain a plethora of
bioactive phytoconstituents, notably phenolic compounds like hydrolyzable ellagitannins, anthocyanins, and flavonoids (Singh et al., 2019).
These compounds are renowned for their antioxidant, antimicrobial,

antifungal, antiviral, and antidiabetic activities (George et al., 2019;
Lacivita et al., 2023).
Waste and by-products generated from tomatoes, the second most
important vegetable crop Worldwide, are rich sources of carotenoids
(lycopene, beta-carotene, lutein), flavonoids, phenolic acids, tannins,
dietary fibers, and vitamin C (Khatib et al., 2023). These compounds
contribute to the potential health benefits of tomato by-products,
including antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects, cardiovascular
protection, and potential anticancer properties (Natali et al., 2023).
Recently, Khatib et al. (2023) reported a polysaccharide yield of 6 % (w/
w based on dry matter) for dried tomato by-products using water at
100 ◦ C. They revealed that tomato polysaccharides are rich in rhamnose,
with galacturonic acid content ranging from 22.3 % to 33.8 %. Additionally, they found that their degree of methylation (DM) and degree of
acetylation (DA) varied from 8.86 % to 71.00 % and from 8.57 % to
19.42 %, respectively, depending on the solvent nature and temperature
(Khatib et al., 2023). The observed variation in DA and DM levels could
influence the functional and biological characteristics of polysaccharides recovered from plant by-products and waste, thereby
determining their suitability for use in food and cosmetic industries.
Polysaccharides extracted from the by-products of red bell peppers, a
versatile vegetable cultivated and utilized globally, demonstrate notable
anti-inflammatory, anti-complement, immunomodulatory, and chemopreventive properties (Adami et al., 2018). Additionally, these polysaccharides can be extracted at a yield nearing 10 % (Khatib et al.,
2023). Red bell peppers also contain significant quantities of vitamin C,
dietary fibers, flavonoids such as quercetin and luteolin, and carotenoids
(Anaya-Esparza et al., 2021).
Dietary fibers, which form the structural framework of plant cell
walls, comprise both soluble fibers, such as mucilage and pectin, and
insoluble fibers, like lignin and cellulose. In lemon, orange, and grapefruit seeds, the content of soluble dietary fibers varied between 4.6 %
and 7.9 %, while insoluble dietary fibers ranged from 75.9 % to 82.2 %
(Karaman et al., 2017). The total dietary fibers in banana and mango
peels were 64.3 % and 69.8 %, respectively (Tlais et al., 2020). Banana
peels are mainly rich in insoluble fibers (56.8 %) like cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin, but contains also substantial amounts of pectin
(Arun et al., 2015). Dietary fiber consumption has been linked to
numerous health advantages, such as a decreased risk of diabetes, cancer, hypertension, obesity, and cardiovascular and gastrointestinal disorders (Hasan et al., 2024; Tlais et al., 2020).

Carrots, commonly juiced for their refreshing taste, result in a substantial number of by-products – up to 40 % of the original weight (Tlais
et al., 2020). These by-products, mainly carrot pomace and peels,
contain a high concentration of valuable compounds like dietary fibers
(pectin), carotenoids (β-carotene), phenolic acids, minerals and vitamins. Thanks to their antioxidant, antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory and
antimutagenic activities (Gulsunoglu et al., 2019), carrot by-products
are gaining traction as a promising source of natural ingredients for
functional foods or additives.
Date palm by-products are made of fibrous materials mainly generated during harvest (leaflets, mesh, rachis, spadix stems, and petiole)
and date processing by-products (immature or spoiled dates, pollen,
seeds, and press cake). Date palm biomass contains many valuable
compounds, including dietary fibers, flavanols, carotenoids, phytosterols, and tocopherols (Manai et al., 2024). Many innovative extraction
methods have proven to be effective in extracting phenolics, dietary fibers, flavonoids, carotenoids, and carbohydrates from date palm
biomass, including ultrasonication, subcritical water extraction,
subcritical fluid CO2 extraction, subcritical fluid extraction, and
microwave-assisted extraction-deep eutectic solvent extraction
(Ghafoor et al., 2022; Kehili et al., 2024).
Large amounts of by-products are produced during the extraction of
olive oil, including leave, pomace stones, and wastewater. Olive byproducts are cheap and constitute a source of bioactive and functional
compounds with a wide range of health benefits (Otero et al., 2021).
These bioactive compounds include for leaves (phenolic compounds,
mainly secoiridoids, flavonoids and substituted phenols); pomace
(phenolic compounds, essential amino acids, sugars, organic acids, and
mineral nutrients); stones (cellulose, hemicelluloses, lignin, and
phenolic compounds), and wastewater (phenolic compounds, pectic

polysaccharides, and lignocellulosic residues) (Khwaldia et al., 2022).
2.2. Grain/cereal by-products
Global cereal production, surpassing 2.8 billion tons annually, generates substantial by-products (FAO, 2023). Around 400 million tons of
corn, wheat, and rice harvest residues are burned yearly (Salazar-López
et al., 2019). Industrial processing steps (milling, decortication, etc.)
discard by-products like the pericarp, aleurone layer, and germ. Cereal
by-products represent a valuable source of dietary fibers (e.g., β-glucans), proteins, bioactive peptides, lipids, phenolic compounds, phytosterols, and other health-promoting elements (Fărcaș et al., 2022).
Brewer's spent grain (BSG), the main by-product of beer production,
represents a significant waste stream. With global beer output reaching
around 180 million tons annually, BSG production is estimated at
roughly 20 % of that volume (López-Linares et al., 2020). This complex
mixture, primarily composed of barley husks and seed coat fragments,
boasts a valuable nutritional profile. BSG contains 30-50 % carbohydrates and 20-30 % protein, making it a potential source of valuable
bioproducts (Karlsen and Skov, 2022). However, its perishable nature
and complex composition have traditionally limited its use to low-value
animal feed. While research explores utilizing BSG to extract valuable
compounds like arabinoxylan and prebiotic oligosaccharides (Sun et al.,
2024), achieving economic viability for large-scale production remains a
challenge. A recent study by Sun et al. (2024) proposed a promising and
cost-effective approach for industrial BSG valorization. This three-step
method utilizes ammoniation pretreatment, enzymatic hydrolysis, and
fermentation to convert BSG into valuable products: single-cell protein
(SCP) and arabinoxylo-oligosaccharides (prebiotics). Notably, the process successfully yielded from every 1 kg of BSG approximately 310 g of

Several cereal processing by-products from large-scale industries,
such as BSG, rice bran, wheat bran, and corn bran, have been identified
for their high protein content, making them suitable candidates for
producing hydrolysates with promising biological effects (Tlais et al.,
2020). Extensive research findings emphasize the feasibility of deriving
bioactive peptides from proteins sourced from brewer's spent grain and
rice bran, underscoring the significant value of these extracted proteins
from industrial by-products. These bioactive peptides, composed of
2–50 amino acids, exert beneficial effects on human health and food
products, including lowering blood pressure, scavenging free radicals,
and exhibiting antimicrobial properties (Gobbetti et al., 2018).
Cereal waste and by-products serve as rich sources of essential vitamins and micronutrients, primarily concentrated in the bran and
cereal germs. These processing discards are rich in both macrominerals
(calcium, magnesium, etc.) and essential trace minerals (zinc, iron, etc.)
(Z. Jin et al., 2022). Additionally, cereal by-products contain significant
quantities of B vitamins, including niacin, pantothenic acid, and thiamine (Verni et al., 2019). Notably, BSG primarily contains choline at
1800 mg⋅kg− 1, followed by smaller amounts of niacin, pantothenic acid,
riboflavin, and thiamine. Recovering valuable bioactive compounds
from BSG requires careful selection of processing methods to maximize
their utilization (Lech and Labus, 2022). Common techniques focus on
converting BSG's cell wall components (cellulose and hemicellulose)
into fermentable sugars through chemical and enzymatic hydrolysis.
This process liberates functional compounds trapped within the BSG
structure. Similarly, strategic extraction methods and pre-treatments
can significantly enhance the yield of vitamins and minerals from
cereal by-products (Lech and Labus, 2022).
Rice bran boasts the highest reported lipid content among cereal
brans at nearly 19 % dry weight, followed by wheat germ and corn bran
(Górnaś et al., 2016). These lipids are rich in health-promoting unsaturated fatty acids, particularly oleic and linoleic acids (Xu et al., 2021).
Additionally, rice bran contains a variety of bioactive compounds like
tocopherols, squalene, and phytosterols, which contribute to its antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties (Xu et al., 2021). A byproducts of wheat milling, wheat germ is a significant source of valuable nutrients, generating an estimated 25 million tons globally each
year (Fărcaș et al., 2022). It boasts a wealth of health-promoting compounds, including biopeptides, polyunsaturated fatty acids, and functional components like sterols, tocopherols, and antioxidants (Tlais
et al., 2020). On the other hand, wheat bran, a by-products of wheat
milling (around 15 % of the grain's weight) is rich in fiber, protein, and
healthy fats. Wheat bran is known to aid digestion, reduce the risk of
chronic diseases, and potentially have anti-cancer effects (Deroover
et al., 2020). Wheat bran's valuable composition includes dietary fibers,
polyphenols, sterols, and β-glucans, contributing to its health properties
(Fărcaș et al., 2022). Corn bran is rich in phenolic acids, with ferulic acid
being the most abundant, followed by vanillic, caffeic, and other acids
(Fărcaș et al., 2022). Additionally, corn bran is rich in anthocyanins,
making them valuable food pigments (Tlais et al., 2020).

products can reach up to 40 %, with in vitro protein digestibility ranging
from 70 to 85 %. Analysis of anti-nutritional factors revealed low phytic
acid content across all studied seed meals, but high tannin content was
observed specifically in grapeseed meal (Sá et al., 2021).
Extracted via cold pressing, chia seed oil stands out as a nutritious
botanical source rich in omega-3 fatty acids. This oil boasts not only high
levels of these essential fats but also a significant protein and fiber
content (Ferreira et al., 2023). Moreover, the cold-pressing process
yields a cost-effective by-product, rich in polysaccharides, which further
enhances the overall resource potential of chia seeds. Notably, a natural
gelling agent, a gum, can be extracted from this by-product as a substitute for gelatin and whey protein in bigel production (Alkabaa et al.,
2024).
Defatted sunflower flour, a by-product of extracting oil from sunflower seeds, is traditionally utilized in animal feed. Nonetheless, it offers a plentiful and economical protein source suitable for human
consumption. Sunflower seeds are rich in storage proteins, with 11S
globulins being the most abundant (accounting for 60-80 % of total
protein), followed by 2S albumins (20-30 %). Tonolo et al. (2024)
investigated bioactive peptides derived from sunflower protein isolate
(SPI), obtained from defatted sunflower flour. Following simulated
gastrointestinal digestion, the resulting peptide-enriched fraction
exhibited antioxidant properties in zebrafish, a live animal model
(Tonolo et al., 2024).
Though the exact composition can vary depending on the variety,
hempseeds boast an impressive nutritional profile. They pack a powerful
punch with 30-35 % of their weight in healthy fats (lipids), 20-25 %
protein, 30-35 % dietary fiber, and a wealth of essential minerals (Lan
et al., 2019). Rich in essential fatty acids, primarily linoleic acid and
α-linolenic acid, as well as α- and γ-tocopherols, hempseeds are prized
for their high oil content and unique fatty acid profile. Interestingly, the
cake obtained from hempseed oil extraction serves as a valuable source
of proteins, demonstrating favorable technofunctional properties such
as a high solubility index, emulsifying ability, and stability (MendozaPérez et al., 2024).
Due to their protein content, olive seeds, separated from the olive
flesh during the pitting step, have been used for extracting protein hydrolysates rich in bioactive peptides through enzymatic processes. These
hydrolysates have demonstrated antioxidant, antidiabetic and
cholesterol-lowering properties. Moreover, they showed stability during
simulated intestinal absorption using human intestinal cell models
(Bartolomei et al., 2024). Another by-product of olive oil production,
olive pomace, is the solid residue derived from the process. It retains a
notable quantity of residual oil and offers a source of triterpenes. These
include maslinic and oleanolic acids (triterpenic acids) as well as
erythrodiol and uvaol (triterpene dialcohols) (Schmidt et al., 2023).
Prickly pear seeds, comprising 2-3.8 % of the fruit, yield oil rich in
unsaturated fatty acids, primarily linoleic acid (Al-Naqeb et al., 2021).
The oil also boasts significant levels of vitamins (tocopherols, vitamin
K1) and sterols (β-sitosterol being dominant). Notably, γ-tocopherol is
the major tocopherol, outnumbering α and δ forms (Al-Naqeb et al.,
2021). However, the oil's composition, especially fatty acids and tocopherols, varies depending on geographic origin (Ettalibi et al., 2021).
Prickly pear seed oil exhibits antioxidant and antimicrobial properties,
antidiabetic potential, lipid-lowering effects, in vitro anticancer activity,
anti-inflammatory properties, anti-ulcer effects, and protection against
UV radiation (Al-Naqeb et al., 2021; Ferreira et al., 2024). Prickly pear
seed pomace, a by-product of seed oil extraction, is abundant in phenolic
compounds and exhibits potent antioxidant properties, along with
modest anti-inflammatory and anti-tyrosinase activities. Phenolic extracts obtained through an autohydrolysis process hold the potential for
use in cosmetic formulations due to their effective UV-screening abilities
(Ferreira et al., 2024).
Cold-pressed Sacha Inchi seed oil, extracted from the seeds of the
oleaginous Sacha Inchi plant, is prized for its richness in essential fatty
acids like α-linolenic acid and tocopherols. This oil has gained

Despite its efficacy in extracting heat-sensitive compounds, SFE requires
precise control of operating parameters (e.g. solvent flow, pressure and
temperature) and faces challenges related to cost and continuous
operation.
PLE employs solvent extraction at high temperatures and pressures
to enhance analyte recovery while maintaining the solvent in a liquid
state throughout the process. This technique disrupts cellular structures,
liberating both polar and non-polar compounds, including essential oils
from coriander seeds and citrus peels, carotenoids from tomato pomace
and carrot roots, anthocyanins from grape skins and blackberry fruits,
phenolics from oregano by-products and olive leaves, proteins from
soybean meal, and carbohydrates from potato peels (Barp et al., 2023).
PLE is a rapid, efficient, and solvent-saving technique that enhances
analyte extraction through increased temperature and pressure. However, the high cost of specialized equipment limits its widespread
application.
By applying short, high-voltage pulses, PEF induces electroporation,
creating pores in cell walls and enhancing mass transfer. This nonthermal, green, and cost-effective process has been effectively used to
release polyphenols, flavonoids, and anthocyanins from plum stems and
pomace, white mulberry leaves, olive leaves, blueberry press cake,
apricot pomace and kernels, quince peels, chicory roots, cocoa bean
shells, custard apple leaves, and flaxseed hulls; steroidal alkaloids from
potato peels; polysaccharides from jackfruit waste and corn silk; and
proteins from rapeseed stems and leaves (Chatzimitakos et al., 2023).
Membrane filtration, including nanofiltration, microfiltration, and
ultrafiltration, offers a sustainable and solvent-free approach for
isolating phytochemicals from plant-based waste and by-products. MST
has gained significant attention in the industry for its ability to
concentrate, purify, and separate valuable compounds. Offering high
recovery rates and selectivity, MST is particularly effective for recovering phenolics (e.g., phenolic acids, catechol, tyrosol, and hydroxytyrosol) from wine lees, grape marc, fruit seeds, and corn, olive, and
artichoke wastewaters (Castro-Muñoz et al., 2020).
Industry 4.0 technologies offer significant opportunities to enhance
the sustainability of green and novel extraction processes. By integrating
digital tools for energy efficiency, waste reduction, process optimization, and traceability, these processes can contribute to a more circular
and environmentally friendly manufacturing landscape. Real-time
monitoring, predictive maintenance, renewable energy integration,
data-driven decision-making, automation, and blockchain technology
are key elements in achieving these goals.

3. Emerging techniques for recovering bioactive compounds
Emerging extraction methods aligned with the “Green Extraction
Process” concept have been developed, prioritizing renewable resources, alternative solvents, energy efficiency, waste minimization,
process safety, and high-quality extract production (Chemat et al.,
2012). The use of green extraction methods such as microwave assisted
extraction (MAE), ultrasound-assisted extraction (UAE), enzymeassisted extraction (EAE), supercritical fluid extraction (SFE), pressurized liquid extraction (PLE), pulsed electric field (PEF), and membrane
separation technology (MST), to convert plant-based waste and byproducts into valuable bioactive compounds can promote a more sustainable model by reducing waste and generating new revenue streams.
The MAE technique utilizes non-ionizing microwave radiation (frequency 0.3–300 GHz) to rapidly heat solvents through interaction with
polar molecules within plant matrices, facilitating analyte extraction
(Bitwell et al., 2023). Essential oils from citrus peels, phenolic compounds from apple pomace, grape skins, olive mill wastewater, cereal
brans, soybean meal, rapeseed meal, and sunflower seed meal, pigments
from tomato and carrot peels, and blueberry pomace, and polysaccharides from apple pomace, citrus peels, sugar beet pulp, wheat and
oat brans, corncobs, and rice husk are examples of successfully extracted
bioactive compounds by MAE (Alvi et al., 2022). MAE offers significant
advantages, including reduced processing time, solvent consumption,
and energy usage, while producing higher-quality extracts at lower
costs.
UAE employs high-frequency sound waves to disrupt plant matrices
and enhance the extraction of target compounds. Cavitation, induced by
the rapid formation and collapse of bubbles, generates localized high
temperatures and pressures, leading to cell disruption and increased
mass transfer (Kumar et al., 2021). UAE is an efficient technique with
reduced extraction time and energy consumption, particularly suited for
extracting thermolabile compounds, though it may induce degradation
due to the formation of free radicals (Hasan et al., 2024). UAE has been
used to extract polysaccharides from wheat bran, rice husk, apple
pomace, pomegranate and grape skins; anthocyanins from blueberry
and raspberry pomace, cherry pomace, and blackcurrant pomace; and
carotenoids from tomato peels, papaya peel and pulp, mango pomace,
pomegranate waste, and carrot pomace (Martins et al., 2023).
EAE utilizes enzymes to disrupt plant cell structures, enhancing the
release of phytochemicals. This green and efficient method reduces the
use of solvents and energy compared to traditional extraction techniques. EAE has been employed to improve the extraction of a wide
range of compounds, including phenolic compounds such as flavonoids
and anthocyanidins from saffron tepals, wheat bran, pistachio green
hulls, bean shells, and brewers' spent grain; carotenoids from tomato
waste; and biopolymers from grapefruit peel, buckwheat husk, palm
kernel, and soybean meal (Streimikyte et al., 2022). However, challenges include high costs, scalability issues, and enzyme limitations in
breaking down plant cell walls.
SFE is a sustainable and eco-friendly method for extracting valuable
compounds from plant-based waste and by-products. This process utilizes solvents, primarily carbon dioxide (CO2), under specific temperature and pressure conditions that transform the CO2 into a supercritical
fluid. This state allows for efficient solubilization of lipophilic compounds (e.g., carotenoids, essential oils, and flavonoids) due to the
fluid's unique properties, including low density, viscosity, and surface
tension, combined with high diffusivity (Gan and Baroutian, 2022).

4. Plant-based waste and by-products and food sustainability
Food sustainability and more broadly sustainable development requires an integrated approach that takes into consideration environmental and social concerns along with economic development. Every
year, a staggering 1.3 billion tonnes of food are wasted or lost worldwide
(Durán-Sandoval et al., 2023). According to Roy et al. (2023) developed
countries, with a total population of 1.4 billion, threw away around 670
million tonnes of edible food, while developing countries, with a population of 6.2 billion, contributed around 630 million tonnes. These
figures stand in stark contrast to the global reality, where between 690
and 828 million people suffer from hunger, and 3 billion cannot afford a
healthy diet (FAO et al., 2022; Roy et al., 2023).
4.1. Environmental and social dimension
Reducing food waste not only benefits the environment but also
contributes to various social agendas by reducing greenhouse gas
emissions, enhancing ecosystem services, and enforcing sustainable
resource management policies (Table 1). Food waste accounts for 8-10
% of global greenhouse gas emissions and ranks as the third-largest
emitter globally, following China and the United States (S. You et al.,
2022).

Selecting the right approach for valorizing food waste is crucial for
cost-effective management and resource conservation (Roy et al., 2023).
The economic impact of food waste is closely tied to the valorization
processes used, with economic benefits depending on the derived endproducts (Table 1) (Kotykova and Babych, 2019). The significant economic cost of lost and wasted food, estimated at U.S. $680 billion in
developed countries and U.S. $310 billion in developing countries, underscores the urgency of effective management strategies (Laso et al.,
2020).
While some studies question the economic viability of food waste
anaerobic digestion, emphasizing the need for additional revenue
streams such as using biogas for vehicles or on-grid electricity to
enhance economic benefits (Flotats, 2019) others assert its feasibility,
particularly when supported by government subsidies (Papirio et al.,
2020; Roy et al., 2023). In the United States, converting industrial food
waste into lactic acids or biogas is estimated to generate significant
annual revenue (Papirio et al., 2020).
Incineration is identified as having the least life cycle cost compared
to other waste management options, though decentralized composting
of food waste is economically beneficial, with examples like on-site
incineration at Hong Kong International Airport showing promising
sustainability and economic savings (Lam et al., 2018). The economic
viability of food waste biorefineries hinges on factors like plant capacity,
product diversity, and integration with existing infrastructure (Roy
et al., 2023).
Studies have examined various economic indicators to assess the
profitability of food waste recovery scenarios, highlighting the influence
of market prices and economies of scale (Cristóbal et al., 2018). Integrating food waste biorefineries into existing facilities can significantly
reduce production costs and enhance economic sustainability (Lohrasbi
et al., 2010).
Overall, a comprehensive economic evaluation of food waste valorization requires considering waste stream availability and proximity to
biorefinery locations, factors often overlooked in previous studies
(Caldeira et al., 2020). Such considerations are essential for ensuring the
economic sustainability of food waste management practices.

5.1. Artificial Intelligence (AI)
Neethirajan (2023) defines AI as systems that precisely understand
data, learn from it, and apply it to carry out particular and customized
activities that mimic human behavior. In the contemporary era of Food
Industry 4.0, AI can be used for a lot of tasks in the food industry, in
instance, to track and improve food production and supply chains,
promote circular economy programs, among others. Therefore, AI can
lead to a more healthy and ethical food system by its potential to optimize the use of resources and reduce greenhouse gas emissions (Sharma
et al., 2021) associated to plant-based industry. Recent advancements in
AI technologies such as deep learning, image recognition, ML, and

For instance, by utilizing meteorological data, crop yields, and consumer demands, AI enhances agricultural practices and food supply
chain management, resulting in higher yields and less waste along the
supply chain (P. Kumar et al., 2022).
Waste sorting is tremendously important because it is an effective
way to achieve waste reduction. ML and computer vision are suitable
techniques to enable the development of waste material recognition and
classification systems. These systems can be trained to distinguish
various types of waste, including plastic, glass, paper, and even organic
waste from fruit and vegetable. In the study conducted by Zhang et al.
(2021), the authors demonstrated the effectiveness of a deep learning
algorithm for automatic classification of food waste based on images
captured by surveillance cameras in restaurants. This approach facilitates the identification and quantification of generated waste types,
thereby easing their management and subsequent processing. Additionally, Ortega-Fernández et al. (2020) examined the use of deep
learning techniques for intelligent waste management, focusing on accurate waste classification and optimization of sorting processes.
Regarding biogas production, Yang et al. (2021) utilized ML models
employing the Adaptive Neuro-Fuzzy Inference System (ANFIS) and
Least Squares Support Vector Machine (LSSVM) to forecast biogas
generation from diverse organic waste origins, including vegetables,
fruits, and food waste. These models identified key factors influencing
biogas production and optimized anaerobic fermentation conditions,
thus contributing to better utilization of organic resources and reduction
of greenhouse gas emissions. Similarly, Xiao et al. (2021) explored the
use of state retention neural networks (NARX) and backpropagation
(BP) methods to predict biogas production during the conversion of
organic waste into compost. By utilizing data on environmental conditions, waste characteristics, and microbial activities, their model accurately estimated composting yield and identified optimal conditions to
maximize biogas production.
AI can be utilized to optimize waste valorization processes such as
composting or methanization. For instance, predictive models based on
AI can be developed to monitor and control composting conditions to
optimize the organic waste decomposition process and produce highquality compost. A study conducted by Chiu et al. (2022) employed

ML techniques (based on random forest and long short-term memory) to
predict biogas production from food waste based on factors such as
waste composition, temperature, and humidity. These predictions
enable the adjustment of methanization process parameters to maximize
energy yield.
Another significant application is presented by You et al. (2017),
who compared several ML models for online classification of the calorific value of municipal solid waste burned in circulating fluidized bed
incinerators. By utilizing techniques such as artificial neural networks
(ANN), support vector machines (SVM), and random forests (RF), they
developed an online classification system capable of rapidly identifying
the composition and energy value of burned waste, thereby optimizing
the combustion process and energy production. Furthermore, Neto et al.
(2021) used ANN for modelling production biogas from fruit and
vegetable waste and predicting biogas yield and composition. The
response surfaces of the ANN model were found to be useful for defining
the optimum region in biogas production. It was observed that biodigestion of fruit and vegetable waste could lead to a highest cumulative
biogas production.
In summary, AI provides innovative solutions for optimizing waste
valorization processes, particularly through material recognition, classification, and biogas production forecasting. These advancements
contribute to better management of organic resources and the reduction
of greenhouse gas emissions, aligning industrial practices with the goals
of a circular and sustainable economy.

addressing food waste challenges across various stages of the food production and distribution process.
In conclusion, the IoT plays a crucial role in real-time monitoring and
control of bioprocess parameters, which is essential for enhancing the
valorization of plant-based food waste. IoT solutions not only optimize
industrial processes but also reduce costs and risks, thereby strengthening the efficiency and sustainability of the food industry.

5.3. Additive manufacturing or 3D Printing
With its potential for a wide range of uses in the food business, additive manufacturing, often known as 3D printing, is an emerging
technology that presents a fresh approach to food processing and the
creation of novel formulas (Lv et al., 2023; Piyush et al., 2020). The
method is designed to swiftly and simply create aesthetically pleasing
and nutrient-dense food items with little to no human involvement and
without costly tooling, resulting in more effective resource usage and
little to no waste (Lee et al., 2020). A great deal of work is being done on
3D printing technologies and given the immense promise and potential
applications of this technology, it is even becoming a new industrial
revolution (Campbell et al., 2011).
Through the use of 3D printing technology, plant waste and byproducts can be transformed in new, value-added products (Godoi
et al., 2016). This approach provides the food industry with the opportunity to create innovative products tailored to consumer preferences
and market demand (Lipton et al., 2015). For example, Grape pomace
was collected from industries and utilized as a key ingredient of a 3D
printing material for functional cookies (Jagadiswaran et al., 2021).

5.4. Smart sensors
Kerry (2012) identified sensors as a device utilized to detect, locate
and/or quantify energy or matter, providing a signal either for the
identification or measurement of a physical or chemical property. Cloud
computing services provide possibilities for data processing, storage,
and collecting that let sensors reach their full potential. The integration
of smart sensors with IoT, AI, and other Industry 4.0 technologies has
made smart sensors a crucial component of contemporary agriculture
and food supply chains, offering valuable data for executive decisionmaking. Smart sensors as part of a wide range of production equipment are used more and more in the food industry to monitor, control
and optimize numerous manufacturing processes in real time, while at
the same time improving food traceability and quality (Watson et al.,
2021). As food products evolve and production and processing conditions change, smart sensors are designed to be tiny, flexible, and
versatile.

5.6. Robotics
In recent years, major food firms have increasingly integrated robotics into their food manufacturing plants, significantly contributing to
the reduction and valorization of food loss and waste, particularly of
plant origin (Duong et al., 2020). In the agricultural and food industries,
robots now perform a wide range of tasks, especially when combined
with intelligent sensors, such as advanced cameras and vision systems,
and AI. These technologies enable precise, real-time monitoring and
decision-making, enhancing efficiency and reducing waste. Robots may
be broadly categorized into five types: collaborative robots, articulated
robots, delta robots, cartesian robots, and selective compliance assembly
robot arm (SCARA) robots (Riboli et al., 2023). These autonomous
systems offer several key advantages in food processing. Robots can
handle delicate and complex tasks quickly and skillfully, minimizing
damage to plant-based products during processing and packaging. By
maintaining high levels of cleanliness and precision, robots help reduce
the risk of contamination, thereby preserving food safety and extending
shelf life, which directly cuts down on food loss. Robots can operate
efficiently in various environments and perform tasks under specific
conditions that might be challenging for human workers, further preventing potential waste. (Aly et al., 2023).
Robotics plays a crucial role in transforming plant-based waste and
by-products into valuable products. Through precise sorting, separation,
and processing, robots can identify and repurpose usable materials that
might otherwise be discarded. This not only reduces waste but also
creates new revenue streams by converting by-products into ingredients
for other food products, animal feed, or bio-based materials, thus
contributing to a more sustainable and circular food system (IñiguezMoreno et al., 2023; Kshirsagar et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2022; Olawade
et al., 2024; Sarc et al., 2019).
For example, Onoda (2020) indicated the potential of robotic sorting
systems powered by artificial intelligence algorithms to separate and
sort waste, streamline the sorting process, and increase recycling rates.
In this process, a stereo camera recognizes images and distances, and the
robotic arm automatically sorts them (Ahmed and Asadullah, 2020).
Moreover, Soheyb et al. (2021) have proposed a solution based on robotics and IoT technologies for the management of smart greenhouses
that offers the farmer the possibility of monitoring, supervising and
controlling a large number of greenhouses to minimize waste and
damaged production without needing to physically intervene each time
for regular actions such as irrigation, fogging and aeration according to
the needs of food and plants.

5.5. Digital twins
Digital twins involve creating digital representations of real-world
products, processes, or physical objects. These representations integrate various technological advancements like IoT and AI to synchronize
physical activities with the virtual world. Digital twins come in statistical, data-driven, and physics-based models (Defraeye et al., 2021; Tao
et al., 2019; Van Der Burg et al., 2021; Verboven et al., 2020). They hold
the potential to enhance knowledge and streamline decision-making
across different sectors such as agriculture and food processing
(Defraeye et al., 2021; Van Der Burg et al., 2021; Verboven et al., 2020).
Furthermore, they could aid in predicting postharvest changes in food
quality and optimizing supply chains to minimize food loss (Defraeye
et al., 2021; Onwude et al., 2024).

aromatic plants. Their research highlights how these precise virtual

also open new avenues in the extraction methods of active compounds.
Digital twins provide detailed simulations and analyses of plant growth
conditions, enabling farmers to optimize resource use (such as water and
nutrients) reduce waste, and increase yields. Additionally, these virtual
models offer innovative solutions for more efficient and environmentally friendly extraction processes of beneficial plant compounds, such
as essential oils and medicinal substances. Moreover, digital twins present a valuable alternative for recycling organic waste generated by
these plants by converting it into biofertilizers. This approach not only
minimizes waste but also enriches the soil, thereby closing the production cycle in a sustainable manner. Overall, digital twins hold significant
promise for making the cultivation and use of medicinal and aromatic
plants more sustainable and efficient while providing novel solutions for
organic waste management.
Finally, digital twins represent an emerging technology with

medicinal and aromatic plants. By simulating growth conditions and
improving extraction processes, these virtual models not only reduce

5.7. Blockchain
Blockchain technology serves as a real-time, decentralized digital
ledger that securely records and manages transactions across a distributed network. Each transaction, or “block,” is linked in a chain that is
immutable and transparent, ensuring data integrity and accessibility
(Antonucci et al., 2019; Prashar et al., 2020). This technology is
particularly valuable in the food supply chain, where it enables the
precise tracking and monitoring of food products from farm to table. By
utilizing blockchain, data related to the production, transportation, and
processing of food can be securely recorded and easily accessed,
reducing inefficiencies and mitigating food loss and waste, especially in
plant-based products (Carey and Subramanian, 2021; Kör et al., 2022;
Wünsche and Fernqvist, 2022).
The ability of blockchain to provide detailed, tamper-proof records
ensures that every step in the supply chain is monitored, which helps in
identifying and addressing points where food loss occurs. Moreover, the
technology facilitates the valorization of food waste by enabling the
tracking and management of plant-based by-products, transforming
them into valuable secondary products. By ensuring that these by12

6. Conclusions and futures dimensions
The global food system faces risks and threats due to climate change,
pandemic, population growth, conflicts, etc., causing massive economic
loss. Coincidence of these risks can compound the effects on global food
security and nutrition. The European Union's Green Deal is a comprehensive set of policy initiatives aimed at making the EU's economy
sustainable and reducing greenhouse gas emissions to net-zero by 2050.
It supports a circular economy model, which aims to minimize waste,
reuse materials, and recycle products to reduce environmental impact.
In the perspective, plant-based waste and by-products are very important because they are valuable resources that may be reused to reduce
environmental impact and improve resource efficiency. In addition, the
food business may lower greenhouse gas emissions, preserve energy and
water, and lessen pollution from landfill disposal by making plant-based
waste and by-products valuable. Furthermore, converting these waste
streams into high-value products supports the circular economy, which
reduces waste and optimizes resource usage. The production of plantbased foods produces nutrient-rich by-products and innovative and
emerging technologies are being used to extract beneficial chemicals
from these by-products. In addition, recent research has shown that
Industry 4.0 technologies such as artificial intelligence, smart sensors,
3D printing, internet of things, and digital twins are being used in the
food industry to reduce waste and improve resource management.
Operating procedures in the food sector are currently being transformed
by digital technology. The use of digital innovations has significant
potential to transform the food industry's waste management, resource
allocation, and product innovation strategies. In addition to promoting
resource recovery through the circular economy, digitalization has
created new possibilities to avoid, minimize and recycle waste from
specific waste streams in order to provide high-quality secondary raw
materials for the waste recycling market and reduce environmental
pollution. By embracing digital innovation and adopting circular economy principles, food companies can increase their competitiveness,
reduce their environmental footprint and contribute to a more sustainable food system.
However, there are a few issues with Industry 4 technologies. First,
there are frequently significant upfront expenditures associated with
implementing these technologies. These expenses may be unaffordable,
particularly for small and medium-sized businesses. Furthermore, if new
technologies cannot be integrated with other systems or are incompatible with the current infrastructure, their implementation may prove to
be challenging. Privacy and data security issues also need to be
considered. Sensitive corporate data processing and collecting might be
risky, thus suitable security precautions must be taken. Ultimately, a
trained workforce is necessary for the efficient use of Industry 4.0
technology. However, some firms may find it difficult to acquire and
train such competent workers. Notwithstanding these difficulties, based
on results of previous research, Industry 4.0 technologies have shown to
have a significant impact on achieving sustainability and waste reduction goals. Thus, it is important to implement novel technologies as well
as multi-collaboration (such as scientists, food manufacturers, and food
technologists) for sustainable waste management in order to achieve
circular economy goals and promote sustainable development
objectives.
To maximize the impact of reducing food waste, future research
should prioritize the integration of Industry 4.0 technologies, such as AI,
blockchain, and smart sensors, across all stages of the food supply chain.
It is essential to evaluate the cost-effectiveness and scalability of these
technologies, considering their application in both developed and
developing countries. Additionally, research should focus on adapting
these technologies to accommodate various scales of food production

Waste-to-feed bioconversion using Hermetia illucens
Larvae: Current insights and prospects
Caisin Larisa*
Animal Resources and Food Safety Department, Technical University of Moldova, Chisinau, Republic of Moldova
ABSTRACT
The rapid growth of the global population, urbanization, and intensive livestock production has led to a surge in organic
waste generation and an increasing demand for sustainable feed sources. Black soldier fly (Hermetia illucens, BSF)
larvae have emerged as a promising solution for converting organic waste into valuable biomass. These larvae efficiently
degrade a variety of substrates—such as food waste, agricultural by-products, and animal manure—transforming them
into protein- and fat-rich biomass suitable for animal feed, biofertilizers, and other applications. This review summarizes
recent developments in the use of BSF larvae for waste-to–feed bioconversion. It explores larval growth performance,
feed substrate characteristics, biomass nutritional composition, processing advancements, and safety considerations. BSF
larvae consistently demonstrate high conversion rates and generate biomass rich in nutrients and bioactive compounds,
making them ideal feed ingredients for poultry, pigs, aquaculture species, and pets. Research has advanced in optimizing
rearing conditions and postprocessing methods to improve efficiency and product quality. Nonetheless, substrate
standardization, microbial risk control, cost reduction, and the development of scalable systems for industrial adoption
remain challenges. The review also addresses regulatory frameworks and social acceptance issues that influence BSFbased product commercialization. Hermetia illucens larvae offer an environmentally sound and innovative approach
to organic waste management while contributing to sustainable protein production. Their successful integration into
Circular Economy Models depends on further technological improvements, supportive policies, and stakeholder
collaboration. With continued efforts from researchers, industry, and regulators, BSF bioconversion can revolutionize
waste treatment and animal nutrition, thereby supporting a more resilient and resource-efficient food system.
Keywords: Bioconversion, Hermetia illucens, Insect protein, Organic waste, Sustainable feed.

Introduction
The growing problem of organic waste accumulation
resulting from agricultural, food, and industrial
activities is facing the modern world (Thyberg and
Tonjes, 2016). Agriculture—including both crop and
livestock production—generates millions of tons of
waste every year, such as crop residues (tops, husks,
ungraded produce), processing by-products (oil cakes,
pomace), manure, and poultry litter (Westendorf, 2000).
According to the Food and Agriculture Organization of
the United Nations (FAO), approximately 1.3 billion
tons of food waste are produced annually worldwide,
accounting for one-third of all food produced (FAO,
2013). In the absence of an effective disposal system,
these wastes, including straw, leaves, and food
processing residues, create serious environmental,
economic, and social problems.
The accumulation of organic waste leads to soil, water,
and air pollution, as well as greenhouse gas emissions
such as methane and carbon dioxide, which intensify
the greenhouse effect and contribute to climate change

(Levis and Barlaz, 2011). Improper manure and plant
residue storage results in methane and ammonia
emissions, which, according to Stephen M. According
to Ogle et al. (2014), agriculture accounts for up to
20% of global greenhouse gas emissions. Nitrate and
phosphate leaching from manure into groundwater
causes eutrophication of water bodies (Carpenter,
1998). Moreover, long-term storage of untreated waste
promotes the release of toxic substances, such as
hydrogen sulfide, and the proliferation of pathogenic
microorganisms, posing a threat to the health of local
communities (Zhang et al., 2021). In many countries,
especially developing ones, a significant share of waste
is landfilled or incinerated due to a lack of infrastructure
and technology, worsening environmental damage
(Wilson et al., 2006).
Population growth, which has reached 8 billion
people (UN, 2022), urbanization, and the expansion
of livestock farming, which also increases the
demand for animal feed, drive the growth in organic
waste volumes (Mottet et al., 2017). Traditional feed

Finding effective methods for organic waste utilization
has become a top priority amid a growing environmental
crisis. One promising solution is bioconversion using
black soldier fly larvae (Hermetia illucens), which
not only significantly reduces waste volume but also
produces valuable outputs, such as feed protein and
organic fertilizers (Van Huis, 2013). This approach
helps reduce landfill waste, produce sustainable
alternatives to conventional feed, and lower the agroindustrial chain’s carbon footprint (Gold et al., 2021).
The technology has been successfully implemented in
various countries, and its scaling and automation have
contributed to the widespread adoption of this model.
The black soldier fly larvae (Hermetia illucens) represent
a promising tool for organic waste bioconversion. This
insect species is characterized by rapid growth, low
maintenance requirements, and the ability to process
a wide range of organic materials—from food and
agricultural waste to manure and residues from the
food processing industry—efficiently.
The bioconversion process involving H. illucens larvae
is based on their natural ability to rapidly ingest and
transform organic matter into valuable biomass rich in
proteins, fats, and micronutrients. Simultaneously, the
overall volume of waste is significantly reduced, the
microbiological load is decreased, and environmental
pollution is minimized.
Compared with traditional waste disposal methods
(such as composting, incineration, and landfilling), the
use of black soldier fly larvae offers several significant
advantages. Research indicates that H. illucens larvae
can reduce the mass of organic waste by 50%–80%
within 10–14 days, while the substrate-to-larval
biomass conversion rate (bioconversion rate) ranges
from 15% to 25%, depending on the rearing conditions
(Diener et al., 2009; Surendra et al., 2016).
Thus, H. illucens represents an environmentally
friendly and highly efficient biological agent capable
of playing a key role in the development of sustainable
organic waste management systems and the provision
of alternative sources of feed protein (Macwan et al.,
2024).
This article reviews the environmental and health
impacts of organic waste accumulation and explores
innovative processing methods using larvae of the
black soldier fly (Hermetia illucens). This study aims to
systematically analyze the research and applications of
larvae as bioconversion agents for transforming organic
waste into high-value feed. This review examines
the biological characteristics, rearing technologies,
nutritional composition, safety, and regulatory
frameworks of larvae-derived products. Environmental

the Stratiomyidae family, is a dipteran insect species
that plays a significant role in sustainable development
due to its capacity to process organic waste and produce
valuable products such as protein-rich biomass and
biofertilizer (Diclaro and Kaufman, 2025). This species
has attracted considerable attention in agriculture and
the circular economy because its larvae efficiently
convert food scraps, manure, and agricultural byproducts into animal feed and fertilizer resources
(Sheppard et al., 1994; Van Huis, 2013).
Hermetia illucens stands out among insects because of
its unique characteristics. Adult flies do not feed and
are not vectors of pathogens, making them safe for use
in agricultural systems (Wang and Shelomi, 2017). The
primary value of this insect lies in its larvae, which can
process up to 75% of organic waste, reduce its mass
by 60%–72%, and transform it into a biomass rich in
proteins (35%–40%) and fats (15%–25%) (Surendra
et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2018). This makes the larvae
a promising feed source for poultry, fish, and pigs,
particularly in the context of the global protein shortage
(Makkar et al., 2014).
The ecological role of H. illucens is multifaceted.
The larvae significantly reduce the volume of organic
waste and help lower methane and other greenhouse
gas emissions (Diener et al., 2009). Composting
organic waste with BSF larvae resulted in significant
nutrient enrichment, with total phosphorus increasing
up to 32.4% (compared to 10.3% in the control) and
total potassium reaching a maximum mean increase
of 77.1%, thereby emphasizing the strong fertilizing
potential of the final compost (Sarpong et. al., 2019).
Moreover, the larvae contribute to pathogen reduction
by inactivating harmful bacteria such as Salmonella
spp. and Escherichia coli (with a 99.9% reduction),
thanks to their stable gut microbiota (Lalander et al.,
2013). They can also degrade microplastics, reducing
the mass of polystyrene by 30%–40% within 30 days
(Yang et al., 2023).
From an economic perspective, the species is highly
attractive: its larvae are used to produce protein meal and
oil, which can substitute conventional feed ingredients
such as soybean meal or fishmeal (Spranghers et al.,
2017).

BSF larvae have a highly efficient digestive system
that enables them to break down organic waste into
valuable byproducts, such as protein-rich biomass and
fertilizer. Their gut is equipped with digestive enzymes
to efficiently process various organic materials,
including amylase for carbohydrates, proteases for
proteins, and lipases for lipids. They possess a highly
efficient digestive system enriched with enzymes—
amylases (85 U/g) and proteases (~100 U/g)—capable
of breaking down carbohydrates, proteins, and lipids
(Wang and Shelomi, 2017). Optimal rearing conditions
include a temperature of 27°C–30°C, substrate
moisture of 60%–80%, and larval density of 2.5–5.0
larvae/cm². Larvae process food waste, manure, and
agricultural byproducts into high-value biomass
containing 40%–45.2% protein and 20%–35% lipids,
including antimicrobial lauric acid (Spranghers et al.,
2017).
High fiber content (>7%) slows larval growth, whereas
substrate pretreatment (e.g., fermentation, grinding)
can enhance bioconversion efficiency by 10%–15%
(Liu et al., 2018).
Pupal stage: At this stage, the larvae stop feeding
and begin to pupate. The adult fly emerges from the
pupa within 7–14 days. Environmental factors, such
as temperature and humidity, influence the duration of
this stage (Chia et al., 2018).
Adult stage: Adult flies live for 5–8 days, do not feed,
and focus exclusively on reproduction. They do not
pose a threat as pests because they do not interact with
food or crops (Sheppard et al., 2002).
Hermetia illucens makes a significant contribution to
the circular economy and sustainable agriculture. Its
ability to process organic waste reduces the burden
on landfills and mitigates greenhouse gas emissions,

Functional characteristics of H. illucens Larvae in
bioconversion processes
Hermetia illucens larvae can convert up to 50%–80%
of the mass of organic waste—including food residues,
pig manure, and agricultural by-products—within
2–4 weeks. Sheppard et al. (2002) highlighted their
ability to effectively degrade pig manure, significantly
reducing both its volume and environmental impact.
According to Bruno et al. (2025), the powerful
digestive system of larvae, rich in enzymes such as
lipases and proteases, enables them to break down
complex organic substrates. The larvae contain 40%–
50% protein and 20%–35% fat on a dry matter basis,
making them a valuable raw material for animal feed
(Lu et al., 2024).
Tahamtani et al. (2021) demonstrated that the inclusion
of live larvae in the diets of laying hens had no negative
effects on bird health or behavior and even increased
feed palatability, confirming their nutritional value.
Thongpea et al. (2022) further emphasized that larval
biomass is rich in essential amino acids (e.g., lysine
and methionine) and fatty acids (notably lauric acid),
making it suitable for use in both feed and biofuel
production.
Larvae convert low-value substrates into nutrient-rich
biomass (Rehman et al., 2022). Bruno et al. (2025)
emphasized that the larval digestive system—supported
by symbiotic microorganisms—efficiently decomposes
organic matter while accumulating proteins and lipids.
Sheppard et al. (2002) noted that larvae reared on pig
manure produce biomass suitable for feed, and Mou

 

et al. (2024) added that such biomass is already being
used in aquaculture and livestock farming. According
to Ogello et al. (2025) and Alagappan et al. (2025), the
highest protein content was observed in larvae reared
on mixed feed (49.2%), while the lowest was found in
those fed on poultry manure (39.1%). This indicates
that the substrate type has a significant impact on the
larval nutritional profile (Fig. 2).
Hermetia illucens larvae develop from egg to
prepupa within 14–28 days under optimal conditions
(27°C–30°C temperature, 60%–70% humidity),
ensuring high productivity. Sheppard et al. (2002)
described cultivation methods that optimize this
cycle, including the use of containers with controlled
humidity. Bruno et al. (2025) and Tomberlin et al.
(2015) reported that the physiological adaptations of
larvae enhance growth on various substrates.
These larvae are highly tolerant to a broad range of
substrates and environmental conditions (15°C–40°C
and varying humidity levels). Bruno et al. (2025)
explained that the digestive system of larvae adapts to
diverse waste types due to a wide array of enzymes and
gut microbiota (Nguyen et al., 2015).
Alagappan et al. (2025) and Park et al. (2015)
emphasized that this property makes bioconversion
products safe for use in animal feed.
Bioconversion using BSF larvae significantly reduces
landfill waste volume and greenhouse gas emissions.
Čičková et al. (2015) added that larval frass (excrement)
is a valuable organic fertilizer rich in nitrogen and
phosphorus, contributing to sustainable agriculture.

Bioconversion of BSF larvae requires minimal
infrastructure. Sheppard et al. (2002) described simple
container-based cultivation methods, while Alagappan
et al. (2025) (2024) emphasized the cost-effectiveness
of this technology, making it suitable for both smalland large-scale operations. Larval biomass is used in

Comparative nutritional profile of feed insects
Insect larvae are a rich source of protein, with content
varying depending on the insect species, developmental
stage, and nutritional substrate (Table 2). According
to various studies, the nutritional composition of H.
illucens larvae fluctuates based on diet, developmental
stage, and rearing conditions.
According to research, the crude protein content is as
follows: black soldier fly (Hermetia illucens) larvae
contain 42%–50% protein on a dry matter basis,
increasing up to 65% after fat extraction (Nekrasov et
al., 2022); green bottle fly (Lucilia sericata) larvae can
contain up to 60% protein when reared on optimized
substrates, such as mixtures including camelina oil
and mealworm (Tenebrio molitor) larvae, which
contain approximately 47%–53% protein (Oonincx

and de Boer, 2012). Based on the studies by Nekrasov
et al. (2019), Finke (2002), and Ewald et al. (2020),

The protein composition of insect larvae includes
a wide range of essential amino acids—such as
lysine, tryptophan, and methionine—whose profile
is comparable to soybean meal and fishmeal, making
insect larvae a promising alternative to conventional
feed ingredients (Al-Qazzaz and Ismail, 2016). For
example, dipteran larvae have higher lysine and
tryptophan contents than crickets or locusts. Hermetia
illucens larvae provide a valuable source of essential
amino acids (Table 4; Makkar et al., 2014).
Insect larvae also contain significant amounts of lipids,
ranging from 15% to 40% of dry matter, with black
soldier fly (Hermetia illucens) larvae containing up
to 35% fat. Notably, their lipid profile includes high
concentrations of lauric acid (up to 60% of total fat),
which possesses strong antimicrobial properties
(Ewald et al., 2020) (Table 5). Lauric acid and specific
antimicrobial peptides (e.g., cecropins and sarcotoxins)
found in larvae have been shown to reduce pathogenic
microbial load, thus potentially lowering the need for
antibiotics in animal production (Borrelli et al., 2021).

Larval fats provide a high energy value of 18–22 MJ/kg
and can be tailored to the nutritional needs of specific
animal species by modifying the larval substrate. Insect
larvae also supply important macro- and microelements,
including calcium, phosphorus, magnesium, zinc, and
B vitamins. Black soldier fly larvae contain up to
5%–8% calcium and 1%–2% phosphorus in their dry
matter, which is higher than that in many conventional
feed ingredients (Chobanova et al., 2024).
The carbohydrate content in H. illucens larvae
is relatively low, around 5%–10% of dry matter,
and the chitin fraction accounts for approximately
4%–7% (ranging from 3.9% to 7.2%), which aligns
with the estimated 5%–8% chitin as part of the total
carbohydrate component in the larvae (Wang et al.,
2020; Lu et al., 2022).
The energy value of insect larvae—18–22 MJ/kg of
dry matter—is comparable to that of concentrated feed
sources such as fishmeal, and their digestibility is high,
reaching up to 95% in poultry and fish, making them an
efficient feed component (Nekrasov et al., 2019).

growth performance and health status. For example,

The bioconversion process using H. illucens larvae
involves several key stages: preparation and loading
of organic waste, larval inoculation, substrate
decomposition, biomass harvesting, and further
processing into finished products (Diener et al., 2009).
The first stage involves the collection of organic
waste, such as food residues, fruits and vegetables,
agro-industrial waste, and by-products from food
processing. The waste is shredded, homogenized,
and adjusted for moisture content—ideally between
60% and 70%—if necessary. This preparation ensures
uniform access to nutrients and accelerates the feeding
process. However, the substrate must not contain toxic
compounds, antibiotics, or heavy metals, as these can
inhibit larval development and compromise the safety
of the final product (Barragán-Fonseca et al., 2024).
Figure 4 illustrates the reduction in organic waste mass
over time due to the activity of H. illucens larvae. The
initial waste mass is 100 kg. By day 10 of bioconversion,

less than 60 kg remains, and approximately 50
kg remains by day 14 (Dewi et al., 2024). This
demonstrates the larvae’s ability to reduce more than
50% of the organic material, significantly decreasing
waste volume and contributing to environmentally
sustainable waste management (Fitriana et al., 2021).
Inoculation of H. illucens larvae and initial growth
Inoculation is typically performed using larvae that are
3–5 days old. On average, between 5,000 and 10,000
larvae are introduced per 1 kg of substrate (Okpoko et
al., 2024). The larvae quickly penetrate the substrate,
thereby initiating the consumption of organic matter
and subsequent growth (Diener, 2009). Optimal
development occurs under the following conditions:
temperature of 27°C–30°C, relative humidity of 60%–
80% (Table 6), and darkness (Wang and Shelomi,
2017).
The average feeding phase lasts between 7 and 14 days,
during which the larval mass can increase by a factor
of 1,000–1,500 (Barragán-Fonseca et al., 2017). This
stage is characterized by the intensive degradation
of organic matter and the production of a by-product
known as frass, which can be used as an organic
fertilizer.
Figure 5 illustrates the exponential increase in the
mass of H. illucens larvae during a 14-day growth
period. The larval weight increased from 0.01 to 7.0 g,
confirming their high productivity under optimal
conditions (temperature: 27°C–30°C; humidity:
60%–70%) (Huang et al., 2025). The most intensive
weight gain occurred between days 5 and 11, after
which the growth rate stabilized. This dynamic allows
for accurate scheduling of larval harvest to maximize
biomass yield (Diener et al., 2009).

Feed efficiency and applications of Hermetia illucensbased products
The resulting protein meal and fats can be used as
components in compound feeds for broilers, laying
hens, pigs, fish, shrimp, and even pets. The larvae supply
animals with high-quality animal protein, B-group
vitamins, minerals (Ca, P, Mg), and fatty acids—
including lauric acid (C12:0), which has pronounced
antimicrobial activity. The use of H. illucens-based
feed allows the following: to replace up to 100% of fish
meal in aquaculture diets (Henry et al., 2015); improve
feed conversion ratios; reduce CO2 emissions and
resource consumption. Bioconversion of organic waste
using H. illucens larvae is a sustainable, economically
viable, and environmentally friendly technology. It
allows for efficient biomass recycling, waste volume
reduction, and high-quality feed ingredient production
suitable for industrial-scale use (Table 7).
Organic resources for bioconversion: suitable substrates
for Hermetia illucens
Bioconversion of organic waste using larvae of
H. illucens (black soldier fly) is becoming an
increasingly popular technology for sustainable
biomass management and feed production. The
process efficiency largely depends on the quality and
composition of the initial raw materials.
Food waste is one of the most common and accessible
types of raw materials for bioconversion. It includes
food scraps from restaurants, cafeterias, and
supermarkets, as well as vegetable and fruit peels
(Diener et al., 2011; Van Huis et al., 2013). Food waste
is characterized by high moisture and nutrient content,
which promotes rapid growth of larvae.
Agricultural residues—such as straw, crop tops,
grain processing byproducts, and vegetable and fruit
peels—are also used in bioconversion (Makkar et
al., 2014; Surendra et al., 2016). To enhance nutrient
accessibility, these materials often require pretreatment
(e.g., grinding or moistening).

Animal-derived waste can be used provided that it
strictly complies with sanitary regulations. This includes
meat and fish byproducts, poultry manure, and other
farm waste (Nguyen et al., 2015; Jucker et al., 2017).
However, such waste requires careful monitoring due
to the risk of pathogenic microorganisms.
Household food waste and industrial food processing
byproducts, including dairy residues and brewery
waste, are also recognized as promising raw materials
for bioconversion (Li et al., 2011; Lalander et al.,
2019).
Conversely, certain types of waste, such as inorganic
materials, toxic, or chemically contaminated substrates,
are unsuitable for bioconversion by larvae due to the
risk of contaminating the final product and reducing
processing efficiency (Gold et al., 2020).
Thus, selecting the optimal type of organic waste is
a critical factor for the successful application of H.
illucens larvae bioconversion technology to produce
feed and reduce environmental impact.
Factors affecting the efficiency of bioconversion of
organic waste by Hermetia illucens Larvae
The efficiency of organic waste bioconversion using
larvae of H. illucens (black soldier fly) depends on a

combination of biotechnological and environmental
factors that determine larval growth rate, substrate
utilization efficiency, and the quality of the final
product (Surendra et al., 2016; Lalander et al., 2019).
Temperature is a critical parameter that affects larval
metabolism and development. The optimal temperature
range for rearing H. illucens is approximately
27°C–30°C. Lower temperatures slow growth rates,
whereas temperatures above 35°C cause stress and
increased larval mortality (Diener et al., 2011; Nguyen
et al., 2015). A stable temperature ensures maximum
bioconversion efficiency and biomass quality.
Substrate moisture should be maintained within 60%–
70% to provide larvae with optimal feeding conditions.
Substrates with low moisture content limit nutrient
accessibility and reduce larval activity, whereas
excessive moisture promotes pathogen growth and
anaerobic processes (Jucker et al., 2017).
The chemical composition and physical properties of
the substrate significantly influence the bioconversion
efficiency. Protein- and easily digestible carbohydraterich substrates promote rapid larval growth and higher
biomass yield (Makkar et al., 2014). To enhance
nutrient availability, fibrous or tough materials require

pretreatment (e.g., grinding or fermentation) (Surendra
et al., 2016).
Larval stocking density: The optimal stocking density
varies depending on the substrate type and quantity
but typically ranges from 5,000 to 10,000 larvae per
1 kg of substrate. Overly high densities lead to food
competition, slowing growth, and increasing mortality,
whereas too low a density reduces system productivity
(Diener et al., 2011; Lalander et al., 2019).
Aeration and environmental conditions: adequate
oxygen supply and proper ventilation prevent the
accumulation of harmful gases (e.g., ammonia) and the
growth of anaerobic microorganisms, improving larval
growth conditions and reducing disease risks (Gold et
al., 2020).
Rearing duration: The optimal growth phase typically
lasts 10–14 days. Harvesting too early results in low
biomass yield, whereas overly prolonged rearing leads
to substrate overuse and reduced larval quality (Nguyen
et al., 2015).
Effective management of these factors significantly
enhances the efficiency of bioconversion using H.
illucens larvae, reducing waste volume, and producing
high-quality feed material. Optimizing rearing
parameters for each specific waste type is recommended
to maximize productivity.
Global Approaches and Innovations in
Bioconversion of Waste into Feed
Global spread of bioconversion technology involving
H. illucens
Bioconversion technology using black soldier fly
larvae (Hermetia illucens) has gained widespread
adoption across many regions worldwide due to its
high efficiency in processing various organic wastes.
Infrastructure for specialized farms cultivating H.
illucens larvae is currently developing in Europe, Asia,
North America, and Africa. These enterprises create
new value-added chains within the agro-industrial
complex by combining waste management solutions
with the production of high-quality feed ingredients (Li
et al., 2011; Lalander et al., 2019).
The main directions of technology implementation
include the following:
-  Food waste utilization: The technology enables
significant reduction of biowaste volumes at food
processing plants, supermarkets, and restaurants
while simultaneously producing high-protein
feedstock. This approach reduces landfill burdens
and lowers GHG emissions (Makkar et al., 2014).
-  Feed production for livestock and aquaculture: H.
illucens larvae biomass is used as an ingredient in
compound feeds for poultry, pigs, fish, and other
animals, reducing dependence on traditional protein
sources such as fishmeal and soy, with economic and
environmental benefits (Jucker et al., 2017).
-  The development of a circular economy. Organic
waste bioconversion is integrated into closed

5436

 

production loops where waste is converted into
valuable resources. After larval processing, residues
are used as organic fertilizers, promoting sustainable
agriculture and reducing environmental pollution
(Gold et al., 2020).
-  Scientific and technical innovations. The current
research focuses on optimizing larval rearing
conditions, improving feed product quality,
increasing bioconversion efficiency, and scaling
production processes. Simultaneously, regulatory
authorities in several countries are developing
frameworks to ensure the safety and standardization
of bioconversion products used in feed production
(EFSA, 2015, 2021).
Overall, the adoption of H. illucens larvae in organic
waste management and feed production systems
reflects a global trend toward sustainable development.
This technology addresses critical challenges related
to food security and environmental responsibility
by combining innovative biotechnology with the
principles of circular economy.
Waste bioconversion using Hermetia illucens Larvae in
different regions of the world
The development of bioconversion technology
using black soldier fly (Hermetia illucens) larvae is
advancing rapidly across various continents due to its
high ecological and economic efficiency (Opoku et al.,
2023). The successful integration of this technology
into waste management systems and feed production is
illustrated in the following examples.
European Union (Netherlands, France, and Germany).
The Dutch company Protix is considered one of the
global leaders in insect-based protein production. It has
successfully implemented H. illucens larvae rearing
technologies for processing food waste and produces
feed lines for pets, fish, and poultry. Their facility
processes thousands of tons of organic waste annually,
simultaneously producing high-quality protein and
organic fertilizers (Van Huis et al., 2013; Gold et al.,
2018).
Ynsect, a French company, is also developing large
industrial complexes focused on producing insectbased feed protein and fertilizers, investing heavily in
research and sustainable technologies.
Asia (China, South Korea, and Vietnam). In China, a
farm in Guangdong Province processes over 50 tons
of food and kitchen waste daily using H. illucens,
producing both protein feed and fat for use in pig and
poultry diets (Yu et al., 2020).
According to Nguyen et al. (2015), the use of H.
illucens larvae has become an important solution for
agricultural waste management in Vietnam and provides
local farmers with sustainable feed alternatives.
As part of a national strategy to reduce biowaste in
urban and suburban areas, South Korea is promoting
government initiatives to implement insect-based
technologies (Surendra et al., 2016).

The Kenyan startup InsectiPro collaborates with

In South Africa, the company AgriProtein is a pioneer

In the United States, ongoing research is exploring the

These examples from various regions demonstrate
the high potential of waste bioconversion using H.
illucens larvae as a tool for sustainable development.
They confirm that integrating larvae into agri-food
and environmental systems can yield both economic
benefits and a significant reduction in ecological impact
regardless of geography.
Industrial bioconversion of organic waste using
Hermetia illucens
In recent years, significant technological advancements
have emerged in the field of organic waste
bioconversion, particularly aimed at the industrial
scaling of processes involving the black soldier fly
(Hermetia illucens). These innovations encompass the
automation of production cycles and the enhancement
of engineering solutions for managing microclimate,
substrate, and insect development stages.
The development of automated larval rearing systems,
which include controlled modules for substrate delivery,
ventilation, temperature, and humidity regulation,
is a key technological breakthrough. For instance,
“containerized Black Soldier Fly Larvae production
units” enable the bioconversion cycle to be conducted
in closed climate-controlled environments with a high
level of biosecurity, allowing such facilities to be located
even within urban areas (Pahmeyer et al., 2020).
In addition, smart monitoring and control platforms
based on the internet of things and machine learning

 

have been introduced. These systems track larval
behavior, substrate consumption, and growth rates in
real time, enabling prompt environmental adjustments
to improve productivity and reduce processing time
(Avila et al., 2022).
Another significant achievement is the optimization
of logistics and engineering solutions for sorting and
drying larval biomass, as well as for the disposal of
residues (frass fractions). Modern installations can
produce standardized protein and fat feed ingredients
that comply with international safety standards (Van
Huis, 2020; Barragan-Fonseca et al., 2021).
Large-scale farms, such as Ynsect (France), Protix
(Netherlands), and AgriProtein (South Africa),
have become pioneers in the commercialization of
bioconversion technologies and have demonstrated
successful industrial-scale operations, processing tens
of tons of waste daily (Byrne, 2024).
Thus, technological advancements in waste
bioconversion using H. illucens are focused on
creating highly efficient, sustainable, and safe solutions
capable of providing alternative feed sources while
simultaneously reducing environmental impact.
Regulatory framework and safety assurance for
Hermetia illucens Larvae-derived feed products
With the advancement of waste bioconversion
technologies using H. illucens larvae, compliance with
regulatory requirements and product safety assurance
have become critical factors for the sustainable
integration of these solutions into the feed industry.
Regulatory authorities worldwide are increasingly
developing legal frameworks aimed at controlling
substrates, processing conditions, and final product
quality (Regulation (EU) 2017/893) (Table 8).
Use of black soldier fly Larvae (Hermetia illucens)
as a feed component requires strict compliance with
biological and chemical safety standards
The cultivation, processing, and storage of H. illucens
larvae for use in animal feed must adhere to stringent
safety protocols to ensure both biological and chemical
safety. The following key factors should be considered:
- Microbiological safety: Hygienic conditions during
larval rearing and processing are crucial for preventing
feed contamination with pathogenic microorganisms.
Controlling pathogens such as Salmonella spp.,
Escherichia coli, Listeria monocytogenes, and other
potentially harmful bacteria According to EFSA
(2021a), maintaining thermal treatment conditions
of at least 90 °C for 15 minutes effectively reduces
microbiological risks.
-  Chemical safety (Heavy Metals and Toxins): One of
the critical concerns is the absorption of heavy metals
(lead, cadmium, mercury) and mycotoxins from
substrates. Studies have shown that the concentration
of toxic substances in larvae can directly depend on
the composition of the substrate used; therefore,
prior chemical analysis is required for the application
of organic waste (Van der Fels-Klerx et al., 2018).
