Specific rates of growth, CO2 production, and feed assimilation
were highest in the smallest larvae and decreased as the larvae
approached maximal weight (Fig. 2A, C, E, G). The specific growth
rate and thus the specific feed assimilation rate reached highest
values at 45% substrate moisture content. From Day 2, when the
larvae had grown larger than 1 mg DW, and until growth stopped,
the specific CO2 production rate became linearly correlated to the
specific growth rate at 45% and 55% substrate moisture content
(Fig. 2B and D), as predicted by Eq. (3). At 65% and 75% substrate
moisture content, the relationship between the specific rates of
CO2 production and growth became linear only after Day 4 and
Day 5, when the larvae were larger than 5 and 6 mg DW, respectively. Until then, measured specific CO2 production rates were
inexplicable high and we cannot rule out that respiration measurements on the smallest larvae may have been affected by so-called
‘flask effects’ (Wightman, 1981). These larvae are fragile and the
separation of larvae from substrates during respiration measurements may have been stressful. However, only minor parts of the
biomass (1–6%) were produced these first days of growth and the
estimated NGEavg values (Table 1) can potentially have been
affected only little.
The cost of growth, Y = 0.38 and maintenance, m = 0.05 day1
were found by simultaneously fitting Eq. (5) to the estimated
NGE values in all cultures, during the parts of the growth phases
where the specific CO2 production rate depended linearly on the
specific growth rate (Fig. 2B, D, F, H). More than 90% of the biomass
was produced during these phases. These values described well the
linear relationships between the specific rates of CO2 production
and growth (Eq. (3)) as well as the non-linear relationships
between NGE and specific growth rate at all substrate moisture
contents. Similar cost of growth and maintenance were also found
by Laganaro et al. (2021). Thereby cost of growth and maintenance
metabolism seemed not to be affected by substrate moisture content, maybe with the exception of larvae smaller than 1–6 mg DW.
Key processes, which affected larval performances in this study are
depicted in Supplementary information, Fig. S4 and did include larval as well as microbial substrate utilisation. Particularly the latter
were affected by substrate moisture content.

3.2. Microbial activities
The substrate moisture content strongly affected the microbial
CO2 production in the substrates (Fig. 1B, D, F, H). At 45% and
55% substrate moisture contents, the overall CO2 emission vastly
exceeded larval CO2 production (Table 2). Microbial processes converted 12–22% of the substrate carbon into CO2, thereby making
this fraction unavailable for the BSF larvae. At 65% and 75% substrate moisture content, the BSF larvae dominated the CO2 emissions. Microbial CO2 emissions peaked already after 3–4 days at
45–55% substrate moisture content. The lower microbial CO2 emission rates at the end of the cultivations (Fig. 1B and D) suggest that
the most readily available feed compounds had been consumed
within the first week. Similarly during composting processes the
soluble and most available fractions may be degraded within less
than a week, giving rise to decreasing oxygen uptake rates (Xi
et al., 2005). Thus, microbial activities therefore affected the feed
value of the remaining substrate in late growth phases. Parodi
et al. (2020) also observed a peak in CO2 emissions 4 days after
BSF cultures had been started, where after the emission rates
decreased. The shorter growth phase and lower maximal weight
of prepupae in the driest substrates (Table 1) were likely results
of microbial deterioration of substrate availability and quality. It
should be noted that CO2 emissions into culture headspaces represent only a fraction of the microbial activities. Some CO2 may
remain dissolved in pore water and microorganisms may convert
substrate components into volatile fermentation products. Indeed,
culture mass balances from Day 0 to Day 19 (Supplementary information, Table S1) confirmed that the CO2 measurements did not
fully explain the overall decrease in substrate weight after drying.
Cumulative CO2 emissions and larval growth summed up to 87% of
the removed substrate at 45% substrate moisture content and only
45% at 75% substrate moisture content. A similar result (just 47–
75% carbon removal via CO2 and larval biomass) can be deduced
from Pang et al. (2020), who found that 5–17% of the carbon initially present in substrates made from pig manure and corncob
was lost via routes different from CO2 (9–12%), CH4 (less than
0.2%), and larval biomass (4–7%).
3.3. Metabolic performance

4. Conclusion

The carbon content in the BSF larvae, the cumulative amount of
carbon emitted as CO2, and the accumulated amount of carbon
assimilated by the larvae is shown in Fig. 2A, C, E, G. At the time

91 mg C, resulting in NGEavg between 0.52 and 0.62 (Table 1). Highest NGEavg was in the larvae reared at lowest substrate moisture

0.65) compared with our results using 49% carbon content. In all

performance in terms of cost of growth and maintenance in BSF
larvae is insensitive to differences in substrate moisture content
within a broad interval from 45 to 75% (64–107% of the WHC). This

substrate moisture contents. In this study, low substrate moisture
contents favoured microbial substrate degradation to CO2, resulting in comparatively short growth phases and small prepupae

Handling Editor: Jian Zuo

Edible insects are considered a sustainable alternative protein source. Several studies have indicated that
greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions from insects are generally low. These data were usually recorded in closed static
chambers, which did not reflect the actual rearing conditions. On the other hand, open respiration chambers
need high amounts of substrate and insects, making the analyses time consuming and expensive. In the present
study, a novel small-scale open gas exchange recording system for evaluation of GHG emissions from insects is
presented. The device consists of four independent respiration chambers, each one equipped with a pump for
supplying air, a flow meter and a septum for sampling the flowing air. A validation experiment was carried out
using black soldier fly larvae as model organisms and moistened chicken feed (dry matter 40%) as rearing
substrate. Three independent runs were conducted, each with two replicates, using 200 neonates larvae and 300
g of substrate. Moistened chicken feed (300 g) without larvae was used as control. Throughout the 12 days
rearing period, gas sampling occurred every 12 h. Data interpolation considering a linear tendency between two
successive sampling points was applied and overall amounts of gases were quantified as area under the curve.
Irrespective of the run, CO2 emissions in the insect-substrate systems increased during the initial 7 d of experiment, consistently followed by a rapid decrease. Multiple cross correlation analysis showed high reproducibility
(r ≥ 0.9), while significant differences in the CO2 emissions between insects-substrate system (range 7.76–11.88
g g− 1 dry insects) and sole substrate (range 0.20–0.33 g g− 1 initial dry substrate) were observed. Very limited
N2O (≤1.13 mg g− 1 dry insects) and CH4 (≤1.33 mg g− 1 dry insects) emissions were detected in this experiment,
indicating that the performed black soldier fly larvae rearing did not result in significant production of these
GHGs. Overall, the experiment showed that the novel device may be particularly suited for quick and reliable
estimation of GHG emissions from edible insects.

1. Introduction
Approximately 30% (15.8 Gt CO2-eq) of the overall (52.5 Gt CO2-eq)
global greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions are generated by the agro-food
system (Li et al., 2022). Excluding the non-food agriculture, the food
supply chain alone is responsible for 13.7 Gt emissions (Poore and
Nemecek, 2018), with 7.4 Gt of CO2-eq originating within the farm gate
(crops and livestock production) (FAO, 2022). Emissions from meat
production are estimated to be approx. 2.8 Gt of CO2-eq per year, accounting for 39% of the overall agriculture GHG emissions (excluding
transport and land use) (Li et al., 2022). A large part of such emissions is
shared among ruminant animals with cattle and sheep responsible for 30

and 24 kg of CO2-eq per kg of meat, respectively (FAO, 2022). Hence, it
is evident that the modern food system is unsustainable and requires
transformation.
Novel and future food sources have been described as perfect means
for ensuring the ecological transition of the food system while safeguarding the nutritional quality of the diet (Parodi et al., 2018).
Whether integrated with other novel food sources, inclusion of edible
insects in the daily diet may represent the turning point toward a sustainable food system (Mazac et al., 2022).
Research conducted to date has demonstrated that insects can efficiently grow on waste, by-products and decaying materials while
emitting very low GHG (Moruzzo et al., 2021). Despite insect rearing is

Although such systems can be useful for shaping a first idea on the insects’ gas emissions, they cannot be considered entirely accurate since
they do not simulate the actual insect growing conditions. Accumulation
of CO2 and moisture, and depletion of O2 within such chambers may
indeed lead to metabolic modifications, which, concomitantly, affect gas
emissions (Akbar et al., 2016; Boakye-Yiadom et al., 2022; Mertenat
et al., 2019). On the other hand, open systems (Matyssek and Herppich,
2020) may be difficult and costly to operate, needing huge amounts of
substrate and insects to detect very low concentrations of relevant gasses
(Parodi et al., 2020). Therefore, in order to measure insects’ gas emissions efficiently and cost-effectively, to compare various substrates and
to offer important information to entrepreneurs and policy makers,
small scale and efficient gas emissions monitoring systems need to be
developed. The aim of this study was to design and test a new emission
chamber for efficiently recording the GHG emissions of insects, while
simulating real rearing conditions. This paper presents and describes the
new device in the first part. In the second section, results of a validation
experiment are discussed. Black soldier fly larvae (BSFL) and moistened
chicken feed were used as model objects.

W = 12 cm). Through smaller silicon tubes (iØ = 1.0 cm), four pumps
((b), Daypower Luftpumpe LP36-12, Pollin Electronic GmbH, Pförring,
Germany) pushed the inlet air into each gas exchange chamber (c). Flow
rate of each inlet line was independently controlled and regulated by
adjusting the voltage of the pump.
For the outlet system (Fig. 1a, red pipes (e)) 1.0 cm-silicon tubes
(overall length 210 cm) were placed on the front cap of each chamber
and fixed through a 4 cm long polyamide semi-flexible pipe (Landefeld
Druckluft und Hydraulik GmbH, Kassel, Germany). At 200 cm, a Rotilabo T connector (Carl Roth GmbH & Co. KG, Karlsruhe, Germany),

In order to ensure exact temperature control, the entire system was

2. Description of the gas emission chamber
The innovative climate-controlled gas exchange system (Fig. 1a) for
continuous recording of insects’ gas emissions was based on a smallscale respiration chamber for measuring the metabolic activity of fresh
vegetables (Linke et al., 2010; Rux et al., 2017). The new system consisted of four acrylic glass cylinders (gas exchange chamber, V = 9.42 L,
H = 30 cm, Ø = 20 cm, Fig. 1b) in which boxes with substrate and insects
could be housed. Each cylinder could be hermetically sealed by a
removable front acrylic glass push-fit cap (Ø = 22 cm, W = 1 cm) fitted
with polyurethane frame closure connection (2.5 cm height). The closing system consisted of a rectangular aluminium rod (H = 3 cm, L =
24.5 cm, W = 1 cm) and a polyurethane-screened aluminium cylinder
(Ø = 5.5 cm, W = 1 cm). In each chamber, three sensors recorded
temperature, relative humidity and air pressure ((d), ALMEMO FHAD
46-C2 multi-sensor module, Ahlborn Mess-und Regelungstechnik
GmbH, Holzkirchen, Germany). Sensors, placed along the vertical central line of each unit and fixed through screw IP68 polyamide Cable
Glands connectors (Conrad Electronic SE, Hirschau, Germany), were
connected to a PC. Data were recorded at 1 min interval and analysed

3.1. Substrate and insects
Commercial chicken feed (all-mash A Mehl M.Cocc., Deuka companion GmbH, Düsseldorf, Germany) with an initial dry matter content
of 91.62 ± 0.07% was ground (10000 rpm) into a fine powder with a
knife mill (Retsch GmbH, Hann, Germany), applying three cycles of 10 s
each, separated by breaks of 30 s to homogenise the bulk. Aliquots
(133.5 g) of this powder were transferred into a transparent 2 L polypropylene box (Ikea Deutschland GmbH & Co. KG, Munich, Germany)
and moistened at approx. 60% of humidity by adding 166.5 g of distilled
water (final substrate mass 300 g). To avoid excess of free water on the
surface, prepared substrates were kept two days (48 ± 2 h) at 10 ◦ C
before adding larvae. For each run, four boxes with substrate were

Black soldier fly larvae (BSFL, Hermetia illucens) were chosen as
model insects. Neonates BSFL (less than 12 h old), generated from eggs
(Hermetia Baruth GmbH, Baruth/Mark, Germany) laid on corrugated
cardboard were used. Eggs were left to hatch without substrates in a
polypropylene transparent box placed in a climate chamber (30 ± 1 ◦ C,
70 ± 5% RH, 0:24 L:D). Eggs eclosion started approximately 36 h after
receiving the eggs and only the larvae originated in the following 12 h
(36–48 h from the purchase) were used in the experiment. Exactly 200
neonate larvae were carefully transferred in two of the four boxes with
substrate through a camel brush. All the boxes were closed with a
polypropylene transparent lid (Ikea Deutschland GmbH & Co. KG,
Munich, Germany) equipped with a rectangular hole (15 cm × 10.5 cm)
screened with polyester black mosquito net (1 mm × 1 mm mesh, HaGaWelt GmbH & Co. KG, Nordstemmen, Germany). Number of BSFL and
amount of feed were carefully defined with the aim of ensuring
approximately 125 mg of fresh feed/larvae/day or 50 mg of dry feed/
larvae/day as suggested by Diener et al. (2009) and Dzepe et al. (2021).
After adding larvae, all boxes were immediately transferred into individual gas exchange chambers, placed inside a Bio Line climate chamber
(27 ± 1 ◦ C and 70 ± 5% RH). Each gas exchange chamber was hermetically closed, drain pumps switched on and data recording initialized. No further feed was provided during the experiment.

fuel gasses for FID.
Air samples (2 mL) from the vials were directly injected into the GC.
Gas flow was set at 25 mL min− 1, oven temperature at 80 ◦ C, and FID
and ECD temperatures at 250 ◦ C and 325 ◦ C, respectively. CH4 concentration (detection range: 1–100 ppm) was measured directly from
the sample, while CO2 was converted to CH4 within a methaniser
operating at 380 ◦ C, prior detection by FID (detection range: 1–100000
ppm). N2O concentration was finally measured by ECD (detection range:
0.05–100 ppm). Effective gas concentration (ppm) was calculated by the
LabSolutions LCGC software (Shimadzu Deutschland GmbH, Duisburg,
Germany) using four standard calibration gas mixtures (Air Liquide
Deutschland GmbH, Düsseldorf, Germany). For each studied gas, intrarun accuracy of the GC was computed as average of the absolute difference between the recorded value and the average of three independent determinations performed on the same standard mixture.
3.4. Chemical analyses of substrates, larvae and residuals
Dry matter (DM), volatile solids (VS), ash, total nitrogen (N), total
carbon (C), total organic carbon (TOC), total sulphur (S) contents, and
gross energy were analysed on substrates, 12 d old-insects and residuals.
Additionally, ammonium (NH4–N), nitrate (NO3–N) and nitrite
(NO2–N), neutral detergent fibre (NDF), acid detergent fibre (ADF) and
acid detergent lignin (ADL) contents were determined in substrates and
residuals. Insects were analysed after lyophilisation, while substrates
and residues after oven-drying at 60 ◦ C for 48 h. DM and ash contents
were determined gravimetrically after oven-drying at 105 ◦ C overnight
(NFTA 2.1.4 official moisture method) and incineration at 550 ◦ C for 4 h
(DIN 38414-EN 12879), respectively. VS content was calculated by
difference between DM and ash. Total N content was determined with
the Kjeldahl method (AOAC, 2000-method 992.15), while C and S were
analysed with the element analyser VARIO EL (Elementar Analysensysteme GmbH, Langenselbold, Germany), following the producer’s
instructions. TOC was gravimetrically determined by quantifying the
amount of carbon released after sample combustion in acidic environment (DIN-EN 13137:2001–12), while total protein content was
computed by multiplying the N content with 4.76 for insects (Janssen
et al., 2017) and 5.70 for substrates (Sriperm et al., 2011). Gross energy
was determined on the samples dried at 105 ◦ C for 24 h, following the
oxygen bomb method (ISO 9831:1998), while NDF, ADF, ADL contents
were analysed according to the ISO 13906:2008 and AOAC 973.18
methods, using the Ankom 2000 Fiber Analyser (Ankom Technology,
Macedon, USA). Finally, NH4–N, NO3–N and NO2–N contents were
quantified with the ion chromatography system Dionex ICS-1000
(Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, USA) after samples extraction
with distilled water (NO2–N) or 0.0125 M CaCl2 solution (NH4–N and
NO3–N). Chemical determinations of substrates were performed in
triplicate, while insects and residues were analysed in duplicate. In both
cases, results from the same sample were averaged.

3.2. Experimental set-up and gas emission measurements
Experiments were repeated three times (three runs). Two independent replicates were performed for each run (six replicates in total).
Actual concentration of N2O, CH4 and CO2 emitted by insects and
substrates were discontinuously measured through GC analysis of the air
sampled from the inlet and outlet systems. Gas sampling was carried out
every 12 h (every day at 8:00 a.m. and 8:00 p.m. (± 30 min)), along the
entire insect rearing period of 12 d. At each sampling point, three gas
samples were sampled with a 25 mL gastight glass syringe (1025 TLL,
PTFE Luer Lock, Hamilton Company, Nevada, USA) equipped with a
Sterican Gr2-G21 0.8 mm × 40 mm needle and immediately conveyed in
a pre-evacuate (2.7 mbar of negative pressure) 25 mL glass vial equipped
with a PTFE/butyl rubber septum stopper.
Sampling started approximately 10 h after setting up the box inside
each gas exchange unit (stabilization period = 10 ± 1 h). CO2 and O2
concentrations, relative humidity and pressure inside each unit were
monitored before and after each sampling and the airflow rates were
adjusted to keep the relative humidity inside the unit between 65 and
75% RH.
To minimise the interaction with external environment, gas exchange units and climate chamber were not opened during the experiments. After 12 d, all gas exchange chambers were opened and the
rearing boxes were collected. BSFL were harvested from T1 and T2
treatments by handpicking them with forceps, carefully cleaned with
towel paper, counted and weighted on an analytical balance (CPA224S0CE, Sartorius AG, Göttingen, Germany). Mass of residuals (frass from
T1 and T2, substrate residuals from C1 and C2) was also recorded.

4. Results and discussion
The aim of this investigation was to test and validate the new gas
exchange chamber. Three independent runs and two replicates per run
evaluating the GHGs emitted by BSFL reared on moistened chicken feed
were carried out. Therefore, emissions of the system substrate + insects
(treatment T) were compared with the emission of the sole substrate
(treatment C), and experimental reproducibility was evaluated through
a multiple cross correlation analysis.
Although GHG emissions from insects are known to be highly variable (Parodi et al., 2020), the recovered data showed high inter-run

4.1. GHG emissions trends and experimental reproducibility
CO2 emissions from the treatments T (Fig. 2A, red curves) were low
at the beginning, increased after approximately 3.5 d, peaked between
day 5 and day 7 and decreased again up to days 8–9. Such bell-shaped
trend was observed in all the runs, with very good overlapping of
curves. Cross correlation analysis (supplementary material S1) displayed a strong significant positive intra and inter run correlation (r ≥
0.9) between treatments T, which suggested high reproducibility of the
process. The aforementioned dynamics have already been noticed by
other authors (Bekker et al., 2021; Ermolaev et al., 2019; Pang et al.,
2020a; Perednia et al., 2017), further supporting the validity of the
measuring procedure. The main explanation for this particular dynamic
might be found in the activity of BSFL and in the nature of the rearing
substrate. CO2 is mainly originated from microbial and larval metabolism (Boakye-Yiadom et al., 2022) whereby it is plausible to expect
low emissions at the beginning, followed by a fast increase and a final
reduction and stabilization. Bekker et al. (2021) also observed that with
a substrate moisture of 65–75%, larvae started producing significant
CO2 only after reaching 5–6 mg of mass. After this point, linear correlation between CO2 production and larval mass was usually observed
(Laganaro et al., 2021). In the present experiment, larvae less than 12 h
old were used. Consequently, they could have had a very low activity
during the first hours of experiment, explaining the low CO2 emission
observed at the beginning. As the larvae grew, their metabolic activity (i.
e., respirational activity) increased (Gligorescu et al., 2019), resulting in
higher CO2 release. Similarly, the reduction of CO2 release observed at
the end of each run could suggest a decline in larvae metabolic activity,
mainly due to the achievement of the critical mass (i.e., the minimum
mass to allow metamorphosis) as well as to a substantial reduction of the
readily available feed (Bekker et al., 2021; Gligorescu et al., 2019).
Chemical analyses of substrate before and after (frass) the BSFL growth
are shown in supplementary material S2. Considering the different dry
matter recorded for substrate and frass, a reduction of approximately
50% of total volatile solids was detected. It was accompanied by a significant decline in TOC (47–53%) and NDF (15–24%) contents, while
absolute amounts of ADF and ADL increased. Different from NDF, which
comprises cellulose, hemicellulose and lignin (Hindrichsen et al., 2006),
ADF and ADL represents the amount of only hemicellulose and lignin
(Peguero et al., 2023). While cellulose is known to be easily degraded by
BSFL, hemicellulose and lignin are not directly digested (Gold et al.,
2018), pointing out that after 12 d of BSFL composting, no easily
digestible substrate was available. On the other hand, although the insects might have had already reached a satisfactory weight for going
through the metamorphosis, they still appeared far from the pupal stage,
suggesting that provision of new fresh feed (re-feeding) could have
reactivated the metabolism, resulting in higher final larval weight and a
new CO2 emission peak (Zhang et al., 2021).
CO2 emissions from the sole substrates (Fig. 2A, green curves,
treatments C) were roughly stable during the first week of the experiment and increased slightly only after this period. In these substrates,
CO2 emissions could mainly be associated to microbial activity (Oonincx
et al., 2010) as high fungal growth was observed in every run. Microbial
activity is well known for playing a crucial role in substrate modification
and CO2 emissions (Ermolaev et al., 2019). Future studies should focus
on understanding the effect of microorganisms on the GHG emissions of
substrate with and without BSFL.
Concerning CH4 (Fig. 2B) and N2O (Fig. 2C), no clear dynamics were
observed for either treatments T or C. The absence of consistency on
such data was also confirmed by the cross correlation, which highlighted
no correlation at the inter-run level, although some positive correlations
were observed within the same run (supplementary material S1). One

4.2. Cumulative gas emissions and mass balance
Cumulative gas emissions highlighted that BSFL were mainly
responsible for producing CO2, while no significant emissions of CH4
and N2O could be detected (Table 1). It is in accordance with previous
studies that suggested very limited CH4 and N2O emissions, compared
with direct CO2 emissions (Lindberg et al., 2022).
Two-sample t-test carried out on the overall dataset detected significant difference between the system substrate + insects and the sole
substrate only for CO2 (P = 0.001), suggesting that BSFL were the main
contributors for the CO2 emissions of the system. An increase in CO2
emissions due to BSFL activity was also observed in the BSFL-mediated
composting process of manure when compared to classical composting
(Parodi et al., 2021). On the other hand, no statistically significant differences between treatments T and C were computed for CH4 (P =
0.406) and N2O (P = 0.428) cumulative emissions, confirming that
production of such gasses was mainly due to microbial activity on the
substrate, as already stated by Oonincx et al. (2010) and Parodi et al.
(2021). However, although significant differences in CO2 emissions
were detected across the entire experiment, the intra-run ANOVA
showed significant differences between treatment T and treatment C
only in RUN-2 (P = 0.002). This highlighted that other parameters, such
as environmental conditions, feeding status and larval metabolic activity
might have influenced the overall GHG emissions from insects. Possible
explanation for the no statistical significance in runs 1 and 3 could
indeed be the low number of larvae compared with the high amount of
substrate used in the present study as well as the already mentioned high
microbial activity. The later might also be the main explanation for the
higher amount of N2O recorded from the treatment T in RUN-1,
compared to the other runs. Furthermore, it should be noted that,
although not important differences were observed on the substrate
composition between different runs (supplementary material S2), the
insects reared on RUN-1 showed lower growth and slightly higher survival (Table 2). These two aspects together might have affected the
substrate turning activity, resulting in different air circulation within the
bulk and promoting the selection of specific microbial species, particularly active on denitrification and N2O production, as already observed
by Nigussie et al. (2016) in heartworm-mediated composting processes.
Chemical analyses of frass (supplementary material S2) originated along
the three runs support such statement. Although an increase in nitrate
and nitrite from substrate to frass was observed in all the run, the
amounts of both nitrate and nitrite measured in frass from the two
treatments in RUN-1 were significantly lower than those measured in
the frass from the other two runs. Since N2O is primarily originates from
nitrate and nitrite reduction (Thamdrup, 2012), lower concentration of
these compounds in frass may suggest higher denitrification. On the
other hand, it is also interesting to observe that the amount of nitrite in
residuals of treatments C from RUN-1 was significantly higher than the
amount of nitrite in residuals generated in runs 2 and 3. This suggests
that the denitrification process and overall N2O production are more
influenced by general environmental conditions rather than by the
presence and activity of BSFL. However, it should be mentioned that
such phenomena may not be universally applicable as higher larval
density and/or lower feeding rate could also impact the microenvironment inside the substrate (Chen et al., 2019).

CH4 emissions varied between 760 and 1328 mg kg− 1 of dry BSFL
(Table 1). Such values were within the range of published data (between
5.5 and 10066 mg kg− 1 of dry BSFL) (Boakye-Yiadom et al., 2022), and
confirms that methane production relies more on the rearing substrate
than on the BSFL. Indeed, high CH4 emission is only observed when
manure or decaying material is used (Parodi et al., 2021), while it is
negligible when chicken feed is the rearing substrate (Perednia et al.,
2017). However, it should be noted that our values are higher than
already published values on commercial feed (Parodi et al., 2020). Such
difference might be explained by the different experimental set-up
applied in our study. Specifically, while Parodi et al. (2020) reared
30000 larvae on 12 kg of substrate, a very limited larvae/substrate ratio
(200 larvae on 300 g of feed) was applied in our study. In such conditions, we might hypothesise that anoxic areas were generated inside the
substrate, favouring the growth of methanogenic bacteria, which may
have produced CH4 (Chen et al., 2019). Similar considerations could
also be valid for N2O. Emissions of this GHG indeed usually range between 0.33 and 118 mg kg− 1 of dry larvae (Boakye-Yiadom et al., 2022).
Significantly higher N2O emissions were recorded in our experiment,
ranging between 275 and 1130 mg kg− 1 of dry larvae (Table 1). The
higher N2O emissions measured in the present study might be explained
by the high feeding rate (i.e. 0.6 g of dry substrate/larvae or 50 mg of dry
feed/larvae/day) as higher feeding rate has been associated to higher N
emissions (Nigussie et al., 2017; Rossi et al., 2023). The high variability
observed in the present experiment was mainly due to the RUN-1.
Indeed, as already mentioned, smaller larvae were collected in such
treatments. The reduced mobility of smaller larvae within the substrate
could lead to lower oxygen dissolution and higher denitrification
(Thamdrup et al., 2012), which is also supported by the lower concentration of nitrate and nitrite in the frass (supplementary information 2).
Despite the differences in cumulative gas emitted across the three
runs, the mass balance of C and N in substrate + insects treatments
displayed an overall recovery of approximately 93% and 85–95%,
respectively (Figs. 3a and 4a). Similar recovery was also observed for C
in the sole substrate treatments (92–93%; Fig. 3b), while higher variability was detected for N (80–99%; Fig. 4b). Although such values are
still far from 100%, based on the observations of Parodi et al. (2020) and
Pang et al. (2020a) they can still be considered satisfactory. Specifically,
Parodi et al. (2020) observed an overall recovery rate of 95% for C and
101% for N by using a continuous air detection system, while Pang et al.
(2020a) were able to recover 87.48–97.90% of the initial C and
74.40–98.39% of the initial N, when BSFL were reared on food waste.
In the present study, the mentioned recovery rates were similarly to
those of these studies (Pang et al., 2020a; Parodi et al., 2020) and the
variability on gas emission quantification was lower than in Mertenat
et al. (2019). This indicates that the novel gas emission chamber works
and presents high capability for large-scale implementation. However,
while noteworthy performances were reached for C, the result remained

cumulative CO2 detection, thereby decreasing the evaluation errors.
Additionally, Pang et al. (2020b) and Chen et al. (2019) showed that
CO2 emissions were positively correlated with substrate C/N ratio and
moisture, respectively, suggesting that the substrate plays an important
role in determining the actual GHG emissions. Additionally, it should be
mentioned that 12 h old larvae were used in the present study, while
other studies usually used 3 d, 5 d, 7 d or 10 d old larvae (Boakye-Yiadom et al., 2022). As young larvae are more active in terms of metabolic
performances (Gligorescu et al., 2019), it could be hypothesised that
neonate larvae produced more CO2 than older larvae. This justifies the
higher emission detected in the present study and suggests that emissions from BSFL in other studies are probably underestimated. In the
present study, CO2 cumulative emissions computed per mass unit of dry
insects did not seem to be strongly related to the larval growth performances, although good correlation was computed between larval gained

0.0333). Low correlation was instead detected between substrate

correlation: ρ = − 0.60, P = 0.2417). It confirms the findings of Chen
et al. (2019), Eriksen (2022) and Laganaro et al. (2021), while contradicts Oonincx et al. (2010) and Lindberg et al. (2022), who observed an

to sampling frequency and accuracy of the detection method (Pang
et al., 2020a), as well as the absence of a NH3 detection system.
Although NH3 is not a direct GHG, it is often considered as main
responsible for water and soil pollution (IPCC, 2014). Additionally, it
might be oxidised to N2O (FAO, 2006; Iwasa et al., 2015) contributing to
increase its level in air. As NH3 production is usually favoured by high
temperature, elevated pH and increased substrate aeration (Pang et al.,
2020a; Zhang et al., 2021), it can be hypothesised that significant production of such gas occurred, especially during the first days of conversion (Chen et al., 2019). It was further suggested by the strong acrid
smell perceived at the end of the outlet system as well as by the significant increase of NH4–N concentration observed in both, T and C
treatments (supplementary material S2). NH4–N may originate from
protein degradation and mineralisation, as well as from nitrite reduction
(Alvarez et al., 2014; Kroupina et al., 2022). While nitrite reduction is
hardly conceivable in the studied conditions, mineralisation of protein
can be hypothesised. Considering that NH4–N production is known to be
responsible for increased NH3 emissions (Yan et al., 2018; Liu et al.,
2019), it is reasonable to conclude that significant NH3 production
occurred in the present experiment.
Different NH3 production could be the reason for the high variation
in the total N recovery of all treatments. Production of this gas is

extremely variable and depending on several factors, such as aeration
rate, moisture, temperature and pH (Groot Koerkamp, 1994). Although
detection of these factors was continuously carried out during the three
experimental runs, no significant variations were observed (supplementary material S5) between the runs, excluding a potential effect of
the environment on the overall NH3 emissions. On the other hand, it has
been hypothesised that different BSFL populations have different ability
on producing NH3 with not all the individuals being able to do it (Parodi
et al., 2020). Another explanation could be that NH3 emissions from
BSFL rearing were strongly impacted by the larval metabolic performances (Parodi et al., 2021) as well as by the substrate microbial activity
(Gold et al., 2018). Specifically, as BSFL grow, significant amounts of
uric acid are produced, which are typically converted into NH3 by microorganisms (Green and Popa, 2012).
High variability on percentage of N recovery was also observed in the
treatment C (Fig. 4b) indicating different intensities of nitrification
processes in the substrates. The analysed different contents of NO2-,
NO3- and NH4–N in the substrates (supplementary material 2) indicate
the volatilisation of a significant amount of NH4–N as NH3 (Ren et al.,
2018).

The present study showed that the novel gas emission chamber with
continuous airflow is well suited for fast and reliable estimations of GHG
emissions from edible insects. Although it was a first trial using the new
device, gases emitted by BSFL grown on chicken feed were detected with
high reproducibility in terms of CO2 emission rate. However, the same
level of reproducibility was not observed for CH4 and N2O emissions,
which were generally limited and substrate dependent. Cumulative
emissions computed as g g− 1 (gas/dry insect) were significantly higher
than previously reported values, likely due to the use of younger larvae
in this experiment. However, the absence of a continuous measurement
method and the assumption that the airflow was linear between two
successive measuring points might have led to overestimation of the
emissions. Acceptable overall C recovery was detected for all runs, with
values not significantly different from the ones reported in literature.
Rather low N recovery percentage was instead detected as no NH3
measurement was implemented.
Future studies should aim to improve the device by increasing the
number of chambers in order to increase the number of parallel repetitions, implementing high-accuracy continuous emission detection
systems and developing a NH3 quantification method. Other substrates
such as waste and manure, where CH4 and N2O emissions have already
been detected, should also be tested with the aim of validate the device

An Optimization Model for Process Traceability
in Case-Based Reasoning Based on Ontology
and the Genetic Algorithm
Yineng Chen , Xinghui Zhu , Kui Fang , Yanbin Wu, Yuechao Deng , Xiao He ,
Zhuoyang Zou , and Ting Guo

Abstract —A traceability system can quickly and accurately
query product supply chain circulation information. It is difficult to obtain processing information and achieve sharing
due to the big data, long duration, large amount of equipment and scattered and easily lost processing information.
In tracing the application of the case-based reasoning (CBR)
to product processing, we can solve the problem of establishing an accurate and complete mathematical model between
the processing information and product quality defects by
finding a target record in a large amount of historical data.
The traceability model of ontology and CBR uses the web
ontology language (OWL) for case representation to simplify
the CBR framework for big data, classifies process data and
standardizes information storage. A joint optimization algorithm based on the genetic algorithm (GA) and CBR is proposed
to establish an optimization model of process traceability, which is applied to case retrieval and reuse. This algorithm
optimizes the genetic operator by combining the optimal preservation strategy and roulette selection method and uses
an exponential-scale transformation method to stretch the fitness function. The experiments show that the optimized
traceability model can infer information from garbled codes, wrong codes and missing messages to quickly determine
the problematic products, thus effectively improving the traceability accuracy of product processing.
Index Terms — Ontology, GA, traceability optimization, CBR, processing information.

The traceability information of the product processing link
includes information on the raw materials, order, equipment,
finished products and other relevant information. It is not only
difficult to record and collect data but also error-prone in
data acquisition, which may cause confusion in product supply
chain data and even affect the accuracy of the system traceability information [11]. In addition, the traceability information
will change with product processing [12]. Therefore, to trace
the processing history of a product, it is necessary to trace
all the equipment and its environment in the whole process to
trace the complete information of the supply chain.
According to the time, batch, name, number and sequence
of warehousing, a new batch (material batch, MaB) will be
generated for the raw materials purchased from the processing
plant. After receiving the raw materials, the processed products are formed through key processing steps. However, the
processing steps are complex and uncontrollable. To solve this
problem, the processing information is based on processing
equipment in this paper. RFID technology is used to associate
the MaB with a processing batch (PiB). The generated RFID
tag is printed on the packaging bag or other transfer device
for identification, including the equipment number, equipment
name, date, time, temperature, and pressure. After processing,
the finished product batch (PoB) is formed, which is composed of the packing date, product name, product quality and
sequence. The map of the product processing information is
shown in Figure 2.
The MaB, PeiI (processing equipment information) and PoB
are recorded in sequence and closely related to each other. The
processing information to be queried can be inferred from
the relevant historical data. CBR [13] is used to solve new
problems by looking for specific knowledge in the experience
or results of similar historical cases. It has the advantages of
being a simple, fast and efficient problem solving method.
This method can transform knowledge, experience and models that are difficult to regularize in historical records into
intuitive understandings [14]. Product processing traceability

III. O NTOLOGY-B ASED T RACEABILITY C ASE
R EPRESENTATION M ODEL C ONSTRUCTION
Ontology can not only be suitable for the definition and
representation of product processing traceability cases but can
also be integrated into the general knowledge of the processing field. Moreover, ontology has a more mature modeling
language, query language and development tools [16]. It is
convenient to retrieve and modify the product processing
traceability cases represented by ontology.
Case representation mainly adopts eigenvectors or structures, both of which have advantages and disadvantages [17].
The advantage of an eigenvector representation is that it is
simple and effective, and the disadvantage is that the utilization
rate of processing data is not high enough to improve the
retrieval efficiency of cases [18]. The advantage of a structured
representation is that it makes full use of the knowledge of
the target case domain [19], such as traceability classification
knowledge. Since a structured representation uses a semantic network or framework to define the case structure and
knowledge, the two knowledge representations are nonformal
representation methods, which bring many difficulties for the
storage, modification and retrieval of cases. It is not only
difficult to share case knowledge and domain knowledge but
also complicated to manage and maintain the case base.
As a formal conceptual model, ontology can define both
the eigenvector and the structured representation method of
the case. In the ontology of knowledge representation logic
based on description logic (DL), DL is a decidable logical representation language that formalizes the description
of deterministic, shared knowledge within a domain [20].
According to the characteristics of product processing traceability, ontology-based case representation can be defined by
the following triple:
Case =< D, C, S >
where D is the definition set, C is the case set, and S is the
solution set.

that is used to represent the inclusion relationship is added
based on the eigenvector approach. The case structure definition steps for processing information traceability are shown in

During product processing, many different products may be
produced by the MaB. However, when the processing flow and
the raw material ratio are consistent, the same equipment is
used to process these different products, and their processing
environments are also similar. Therefore, there are too many
data points for product processing, and they are very similar.
In this case, it is difficult to retrieve the historical case that
matches the target case with the traditional case retrieval
or ontology similarity calculation method. To improve the
accuracy of case retrieval, this paper uses the genetic algorithm
to optimize the case retrieval model. The genetic algorithm
is a kind of intelligent search algorithm that has all the
characteristics of intelligent search [21]. In addition, it is a
global random search algorithm [22]. In contrast, using the

The genetic algorithm replaces the parameter space of the

the selection and genetic mechanism of individual bit strings
in the population. New excellent individuals are searched

A. Coding Scheme Design
The optimization solution of the genetic algorithm can
only be obtained by encoding the parameters that need to be
optimized; that is, the weights of the case attributes and cases
need to be coded. Due to the high complexity and similarity
of product processing traceability cases, the binary coding
method is adopted in this paper, which can quickly distinguish
each case by simplifying genetic operations such as crossover
and mutation.
The population in the genetic algorithm is composed of
individuals, each of whom represents a solution to a problem,
that is, a historical case. The more historical cases there are in
the population, the stronger the search ability of the algorithm,
and the more likely it is to obtain the optimal solution, but
the calculation time will be longer. The more binary digits
there are, the wider the range of attribute weights that can be
expressed, but the computational complexity of the algorithm
will increase. Therefore, this article adopts the case weight
attribute strategy, in which the attribute of each individual
includes the attribute of the case. The number of bits in the
binary code is designed separately according to the range of
each property, for a total of 76 bits. The setting of the number
of bits is shown in Table I.

C. Genetic Algorithm Generates a New Population
The selection operation in the genetic algorithm selects
good individuals from the parent population and inherits them
in the next-generation population. The selection operation is
used to determine the recombination or crossover as well
as how many offspring will be produced by the selected
individuals [25]. The selection operation is not only used to
determine the individuals in the recombination or crossover
but also calculates how many offspring individuals to produce. Although genetic algorithms can produce an increasing
number of excellent individuals, they are likely to destroy the
most adaptive individuals in the current population due to the
randomness of the genetic operators. Of course, the efficiency
and convergence of the genetic algorithm are affected. This
paper adopts the best retention selection method to retain the
most adaptable individuals in the next-generation group [26].

In this method, the individual with the highest fitness does not
participate in the operations of crossover and mutation, but
instead it is used to replace the lowest-fitness individual after
crossover and mutation in the current generation population.
Combining the optimal preservation strategy with the conventional roulette selection method will make the optimization
process of the genetic algorithm efficient and accurate. The
realization process is shown in Figure 8.

quickly acquired, but processing link information traceability
is rarely involved. Aiming to address the problems of complex

collecting and recording information, and error-prone data
acquisition, a joint optimization algorithm based on GA and

Composting has been used extensively as a sustainable approach for the management organic waste streams and
conversion into stabilized soil amendments and horticultural growth media. In addition to these products, the
composting process also generates by-products of microbial metabolism that includes gas (CO2) and energy
(heat). High rates of food waste and commercial organic waste generation, along with greater diversion away
from landfills, creates new opportunities to valorize these by-products from aerobic composting. Specifically,
integrating carbon dioxide recapture and recycling into Controlled Environment Agriculture (CEA) production
systems presents a pathway to circularize resources. CEA systems produce plants year round in an environmentally controlled space where elevating CO2 environments can boost plant production, creating a synergistic
relationship with composting processes. The review evaluated CO2 emissions from an array of open and closed
composting systems, as well as different feedstocks to demonstrate its potential for use in CEA. Rates of CO2
emissions varied widely, with a peak CO2 emission range of 0.32–429.27 g CO2–C kg− 1 d− 1 depending on the
aeration conditions and feedstock composition. Analysis of two hypothetical CEA scenarios reveals that integrating in-vessel composting as an on-site waste management process is comparable in cost to using natural gas
as a regular CO2 source. The quantity of composting feedstocks required to generate CO2 emissions for a single
tier and five tier CEA lettuce production system ranged from 3.38 to 69.94 kg dry biomass d− 1 and 9.93–205.50
kg dry biomass d− 1, respectively, but varied based on feedstock composition and compost operating conditions.
The long-term research goal is toward valorizing non-edible biomass of CEA systems to create a circular economy
model of commercial plant production.

1. Introduction
Rapid urbanization aligned with global population growth results in
significant quantities of organic wastes being generated annually (Bong
et al., 2017; Karak et al., 2012; Narayana, 2009). These include food
wastes from residential, commercial, and manufacturing sectors (Melikoglu et al., 2013; Julian et al., 2010) as well as secondary food processing by-products from industry or municipal wastewater solids
(Hackett et al., 1999; Villaseñor et al., 2011). Traditional methods of
organic waste management and disposal, such as landfilling (Louis,
2004) and incineration (Assamoi and Lawryshyn, 2012; Cherubini et al.,
2009) are unsustainable and a transition toward prevention, recovery,
diversion, and valorization of organic matter, as outlined by the food
waste/recovery hierarchy (US EPA, 2015a) has occurred. For instance,

modern landfill designs not only incorporate leachate collection and
treatment, but also methane capture as a bioenergy source,(Adhikari
et al., 2006; Behera et al., 2010; Themelis and Ulloa, 2007). Many waste
management authorities around the world are moving to ban landfilling
of organic wastes (Behera et al., 2010; BioCycle, 2018; California
Legislature, 2014; Government of Nova Scotia, 1994; Government of
Ontario, 2017). In Canada, some jurisdictions have either banned the
landfilling of organic waste (Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island) or
are in transitionary phases (Ontario) to do so (Government of Ontario,
2017). Despite this progress, food wastes (edible and non-edible)
contribute 23%, or 6 million tonnes, of the total Canadian municipal
solid waste (MSW) stream sent to landfill (Environment and Climate
Change Canada, 2020). Organics recycling programs are now aimed at
diversion and conversion into new products or developing energy

Furthermore, municipal and commercial sectors are valorizing organic
wastes through the processing or conversion of organic material into
marketable products, e.g. compost, growing media (Kabongo, 2013).
Organic waste generation is increasing at unprecedented rates due to
rapid urbanization and economic development globally (Muller, 2009).
Globally, from 2007 to 2017, the top five main crops (sugar cane, maize,
wheat, rice and potatoes) have seen an increase in production both on
account of food demand and for biofuel production, especially with
maize (FAO, 2019). Maize production increased from 792 million tonnes
in 2007 to 1.13 billion tonnes in 2017, while the other main commodities also experienced sizable increases: 606 to 771 million tonnes
(wheat), 656 to 769 million tonnes (rice) and 314 to 388 million tonnes
(potatoes). Similar production trends can be seen in meat, dairy, and egg
products, with chicken numbers increasing by 4.5 billion head in 2007
to 22.8 billion in 2017. Similarly an increase in fish production has gone
from 98 million tonnes in 1990 to 173 million tonnes in 2017, predominantly driven by the expansion of aquaculture (FAO, 2019). Global
food loss and food waste (FLW) ranging from unavoidable food production losses to avoidable waste,(including discards and unpurchased
material) is estimated to be 1.3 billion tonnes according to 2019 FAO
statistics, and within North America, the USA generates an estimated
168 million tonnes of FLW (FAO, 2019), while Canadian FLW is estimated to be 34.9million tonnes (Gooch et al., 2019).
In agriculture, animal manures and slurries have an intrinsic value to
the agricultural community, providing a source of energy and nutrients
in the form of nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, and micro-nutrients for
crop production. Similarly, food wastes have value past their original
purpose of human (or animal) consumption, as a source of energy and
nutrients in a range of valorization technologies. Anaerobic digestion
(AD) is one favoured approach for treating food wastes, using biogas as a
waste-to-energy fuel, with the resultant digestate land-applied for crop
production. The European anaerobic digestion market is projected to be
worth CAD$94.2 billion by 2026 (Global Market Insights Inc, 2020),
demonstrating the tangible economic value of recycling organic waste
materials. Anaerobic digestion can be a valuable and important method
of utilizing waste material, already an important component of the European energy mix (International Renewable Energy Agency, 2018). A
significant disadvantage of AD technologies is the large capital-intensive
infrastructure and government-subsidized electrical supply rates, as well
as a local land-base for disposal of the digestate. In North America, the
cost of infrastructure and jurisdictional variability on subsidizing or
supporting electrical generation from alternative energy sources are still
barriers for wide-scale adoption of AD(Canadian Biogas Association,
2019). Other routes for organic food wastes include rendering of animal
by-products (for protein meal and oil products), autoclaving and hydrolysis, incineration (or waste-to-energy), pyrolysis, gasification, and
plasma gasification. Each of these methodologies have benefits and can
produce valuable products, but are also associated with constraints on
the raw material composition, are capital-intensive to build and operate,
and at best are more suited to large-scale industrial settings where volumes of waste material generated are high, land is expensive, and energy
recovery is viable(NI Business Info, 2012).
Composting is a viable process to optimally manage the biological
decomposition of organic matter under aerobic conditions. As an aerobic
decomposition process, the resulting predominant products include
stabilized organic matter (compost), water, heat, water vapour, and
carbon dioxide (Diaz and de Bertoldi, 2007; Epstein, 2017). The quantity
of CO2, and of other gases (N2O and CH4), produced will be influenced
by a number of factors including aeration rate, mixing rate, feedstock
composition, C:N ratio (Jiang et al., 2011), moisture content (El Kader
et al., 2007), and the temperature profile during the process. Aerobic
composting is achieved through a number of different processes, ranging
from outdoor windrows or static piles to indoor in-vessel systems (US

EPA, 2015b). Han et al. (2018) evaluated the influence of ambient
temperatures on greenhouse gas generation from sewage sludge processed in a large-scale municipal composting facility. Evaluated over
three seasons (winter, spring and summer), Han et al. found clear
variation in CO2 emissions between the three different seasons, finding
higher totalCO2 emissions in spring followed by summer, and winter,
941.72 mg CO2 kg− 1 h− 1, 698.97 mg CO2 kg− 1 h− 1 and 220.54 mg CO2
kg− 1 h− 1, respectively. Compost has an established commercial and
agricultural value as a soil amendment, nursery growth media, and as an
approach to deal with organic wastes across a range of management
scales (Hubbe et al., 2010; Meyer-Kohlstock et al., 2013; Walker et al.,
2006). In the USA, composting comprises approximately 8.5% of MSW
(292.4 million tonnes) management processes(US EPA, 2017) and is
considered a core process, along with other technologies such as
anaerobic digestion and incineration(Ayilara et al., 2020; US EPA, 2017;
Razza et al., 2018). Municipal composting is challenging due to the
heterogeneity of material, high requirement for labour, time, and cost to
separate contaminants such as plastics, glass, and other materials, but
also due to the difficulty in controlling the source material. The final
product varies in quality and consistency between jurisdictions leading
to a price per tonne of compost ranging from CAD$30 to $130.
Increasingly, the economics of municipal organics diversion programs
face significant challenges ranging from high labour, infrastructure, and
transportation costs, to low market value for composted products.
Pandyaswargo and Dickella (2014) evaluated the economics of municipal composting in Asian cities, determining that factors such as: location, scale, processing methods, technology used, end-product quality,
tipping fees, government incentives or rebates, and the ability to find a
suitable market for the end-product drive financial feasibility. Coker
(2010) found that controlling costs and maximising processing capacities is fundamental in ensuring profitability of municipal composting
facilities (Coker, 2010), while the NorthEast Recycling Council stated
that 87% of US composting operations fail within five years without
government subsidies (Castagnero, 2014). Development of circular
economies, with emphasis on improved valorization of bio-waste
streams, can generate new opportunities to reduce operational costs,
improve efficiency of utilization, and build synergies with different
sectors of the economy (Masullo, 2017).
Composting of organics is a vital step in reducing greenhouse gas
emissions, reducing the impact of organics going to landfill and pushing
forward the concept of a circular economy where little to no material is
deemed valueless (Favoino and Hogg, 2008; Lou and Nair, 2009). The
economics of commercial composting systems comprises: 1) the initial
capital investment for infrastructure and machinery costs, and, 2)
ongoing expenses including labour, maintenance, utilities and local and
provincial waste disposal rates. Revenues are generated through gate
(tipping) fees and the sale of compost. Composting has become not only
more profitable due to the use of gate fees, but due to higher gate fees
associated with landfilling. The 2018 median gate fee for landfilling
within the UK was found to be CAD$182 tonne− 1 compared to CAD$78
tonne− 1 for in-vessel composting and CAD$40 for windrow composting
(WRAP, 2019). Murphy and Power (2006) evaluated four municipal
composting systems in Ireland, finding that the greater the size of the
system, the more economically viable they became. Profits generated
were shown to be predominantly from gate fees, although the sale of
compost also provided moderate contributions to revenues from these
systems (Murphy and Power, 2006). Similarly, Pandyaswargo and Premakumara (2014) evaluated the financial sustainability of six composting facilities in developing Asian countries, finding that medium and
medium-large facilities were the most viable, concluding that gate fees
and the sale of compost were important in making the facilities
economically viable; however, the selection of composting technology,
management practices, market access, and availability of carbon credits
were also key. Organic matter, from pre- and post-consumer food
wastes, animal and agricultural wastes, and municipal wastewater solids
have intrinsic value as sources of energy (carbon) and nutrients (Pham

Rapid expansion of controlled environment agriculture (CEA) in
recent years provides a new pathway toward food security and resource
recovery (Hagbert and Bradley, 2017). Innovative practices for
year-round CEA, as exemplified in the proliferation of vertical farming
systems, has clear potential to valorize and use residual organic biomass
from these systems toward improving production efficiencies and
reducing operational costs. Vertical farming was valued at CAD$2.89
billion in 2018 and is estimated to reach CAD$16.05 billion by 2026
(Patil and Baul, 2019). Controlled environment agriculture systems,
such as vertical farms, are energy and capital intensive, integrating
multiple components such as, HVAC for environmental control of temperature, humidity, and ambient gas composition, and electric lighting
systems. Plant growth is modulated through the use of targeted spectral
compositions using energy efficient LED lights and in many facilities
through carbon dioxide gas enrichment of the growing environment to
increase baseline productivity. These systems provide the benefit of
year-round production, including some reduction of the carbon footprint
associated with long distance transportation, but comes at the expense
of higher energy usage and cost. In contrast, large traditional greenhouse operations, including some with hydroponic systems, are
increasingly using technologies found in vertical farming systems to
improve production, including LED lighting systems (supplemental),
solar capture, water capture and reuse, and general improvements in
controlled environment systems (Kalantari et al., 2017). Integrating
technological advances in recapture and utilization of CO2 from composting of organic wastes can minimize the carbon footprint of CEA
operations and improve plant productivity rates. The vertical farming
sector (both large and small operations) is estimated to reachCAD$5.91
billion globally in 2021, and projected to reach CAD$26.12 billion by
2028 (Grand View Research, 2021). Vertical Farm systems are touted as
being more water efficient (Avgoustaki and Xydis, 2020) and productive
than conventional agriculture, while also reducing the carbon footprint
associated with food transportation(Al-Kodmany, 2018; de Oliveira
et al., 2020). Inherent advantages of vertical growing systems, and more
broadly CEA in general, are the capacity to recycle nutrients more efficiently, improved water use efficiency through capture and reuse of
irrigation/fertigation solutions, and reduced the use of pesticides. The
advantage of locally grown foods includes a reduced transportation
carbon footprint, and fresher products that are closer to market, and
thereby typically have longer [consumer] shelf life. Further, there is also
more direct support of local economies when production is based within
a given community. Global production of lettuce ranges from 26 to 29
million tonnes over an area of 1,227,358 ha, with an estimated
field-based production between 2.2 and 3.2 kg lettuce m− 2 yr− 1 (Naus,
2018; Shatilov et al., 2019). In contrast, VF systems are estimated to
generate 41 kg lettuce m− 2 yr− 1, which is 13–18.5 times more production per square metre (Barbosa et al., 2015; Benke and Tomkins, 2017).
However, if lettuce root biomass is approximately 10–20% of total fresh
biomass under aeroponic or hydroponic production, which would
equate to 4.1–8.2 kg root biomass m− 2 yr− 1, waste biomass generated in
VF systems under current annual yields would be 2.9 to 5.8 million
tonnes per year(Li et al., 2018). Under conventional agriculture, the root
biomass would remain in the soil, recycling the carbon back into the
system. However, in CEA or VF, current industry practices for residual
biomass include disposal at local waste facilities or landfills and offsite
composting where available. The cost of landfilling or recycling will
vary based on local gate fees, accessibility to centralized organics
composting facilities, cropping cycle, local by-laws, and the size of the
vertical farm. Disposal costs for CEA or VF facilities will depend also on

crop type, the amount of non-commercial residual biomass generated, (i.
e., root mass, stalk/stems/leaves) and the ratio of harvestable to
non-edible biomass (harvest index).Another significant implicit challenge in these production systems is the use of fossil fuels or
carbon-negative sources to enrich the growing environments with CO2
(Esmeijer and Bloem, 1999; Ghiat et al., 2021). The overall cost of CO2 is
not necessarily a major factor (in the absence of a carbon tax) but is
generated through consumption of fossil fuels(Ghiat et al., 2021; Poudel
and Dunn, 2017). Atmospheric enrichment of the production facility
beyond ambient CO2 can dramatically increase production and improve
profitability.
On-site processing of waste biomass in CEA or VF systems using invessel composting may have value by reducing third-party collection,
transport, and gate fee costs. Moreover, the potential exists for integration of in-vessel composting to utilize metabolic carbon dioxide in
plant growth rooms and to generate final compost media for use as a
nutrient source or seed growth media. With 592 cultivation licences
granted in Canada, the recent rapid growth of cannabis production facilities across Canada opens new opportunities for the recycling of waste
biomass into gas and heat by-products that can be utilized within the
closed growing environments (Health Canada, 2018). Many CEA
cannabis operations incorporate CO2 enrichment of the production
chambers using non-renewable resources. The capacity to integrate
these two types of technologies currently exists but economies of scale
related to soil-based production agriculture have been an economic
bottleneck. Currently, shifting public perception of the environmental
impacts from soil-based agriculture, increased demand for high value
fresh produce throughout the year, and the vulnerabilities in global food
supply chains exposed by the Covid-19 pandemic are opening up the
opportunities to capitalize on this technology integration (Market Line,
2020)(Storey and Heliospectra, 2021).
The scientific literature on composting focuses primarily on chemical
dynamics of open-air/open access composting systems and/or on the
generation of compost products (Reyes-Torres et al., 2018). A significant
gap exists within this body of scientific literature on how the composting
process and available technologies can be adapted to recapture CO2 gas
for utilization in other systems, such as vertical farms or CEA. This review aims to highlight the potential to valorize by-product gas, specifically carbon dioxide (CO2) from the composting of organic wastes from
municipal, commercial, or agricultural sources for use in vertical
farming and other controlled environment agriculture production
systems.
2. Methodology
To achieve a comprehensive review and analysis of data on CO2
emissions from composting, a systematic evaluation of the scientific
literature and government publications was undertaken (Fig. 1). Scientific databases used to identify suitable literature for inclusion in this
study were accessed and included: Google Scholar (http://scholar.
google.ca), Science Direct (http://sciencedirect.com), SpringerLink
(http://springerlink.com) and Web of Science (http://webofknowledge.
com).
Utilizing database search functions, key search terms were input
based upon defined parameters: 1) the main metric relating to CO2, 2)

(Fig. 1).
Each database provided a numerical value of results based on the

exists in the application of composts to soils with the use of biochar;
however, since the focus is on process generated CO2 rather than carbon
sequestration, journal articles where biochar was part of the composting

2.1. Data reporting
A challenge in reviewing and synthesizing the literature on CO2
emissions from composting is the large variation in how data are
measured, and units presented across studies. A number of different
analytical techniques and instrumentation are available for the capture
and measurement of CO2 gas, including gas chromatography, portable
gas analysers (IRGA), NSDAIR sensors, and alkali traps and backtitration using acids. While the various approaches can provide comparable results, there may be variations in the sensitivities and in the
format that data are presented. The data evaluated in this review originate from studies conducted under open and isolated conditions, which
affect the extrapolation of gas production in real-world settings. This
review classifies open systems as any system that is open to the atmosphere such as, windrows, aerated piles, and static piles. Closed or isolated systems include material enclosed within a vessel either at a
commercial, pilot, or lab/bench-top scale.

3. Overview of the decomposition process and composting
methodologies
The aerobic decomposition of organic matter occurs as biochemical
transformations of carbon and other elemental components, mediated
through an array of bacteria, fungi, and actinomycetes (Trautmann and

of microbial organisms, with bacterial species typically dominating,
followed by fungi, and actinomycetes. Dominant phyla in compost systems typically consist of Actinomycetes, Bacteroidetes, Proteobacteria,
Firmicutes, and Sordariomycetes (Huhe et al., 2017). Microbial groups
will degrade compounds based on energetic paths of least resistance,
typically in the order of carbohydrates, fats, proteins, cellulose and
hemi-cellulose, and lignin. Oxidative breakdown of primary compounds
to secondary metabolites and constituent chemicals are catalyzed by
enzymes released onto surfaces or in the pore solution (Huhe et al.,
2017). A proportion of the organic carbon is released as carbon dioxide
during the process of oxidative decomposition, typically 50–60% of the
total carbon is lost over time(Chang et al., 2019). The rate and quantity
of carbon loss during organic matter degradation in compost systems
varies as a function of management practices (Tiquia et al., 2002)
employed to ensure adequate levels of available oxygen, unsaturated
moisture conditions, and balancing the C:N ratio of the mixture(USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service, 2007).The consumption of O2
and the production of CO2 is a clear indicator of the aerobic processes
working within the compost system, while CH4 is an indicator of
anaerobic processes and N2O and indication of nitrification(USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service, 2000).
Composting can be divided into three phases of microbial activity: 1)
active, during which labile carbon is rapidly mineralized intoCO2 or
immobilized back to organic forms, 2) stabilisation, during which the
remaining carbon compounds are either more recalcitrant to degradation or more complex forms of carbon are created that are also resistant
to decay, and 3) maturing/curing, during which the final product of the
process yields a material that consists of organic and inorganic forms of
carbon that are in pseudo-equilibrium leading to a low rate of carbon
mineralization. The time frames for these phases of composting can
range from several months to years depending on the type of system, the
intensity of management, aeration conditions, and environmental conditions (Bidlingmaier et al., 2004) (Table 1).

because of the level of external controls imposed on the process, such as

and manage temperature, and leachate collection.
3.1.1. Open composting systems
Open composting systems are open to the atmosphere and subject to
the effects of the local climate, seasons and weather, impacting the rate
of decomposition and time to achieve a stabilized homogenous compost
product but can be conducted at a large scale (Composting Council of
Canada, 2006).
3.1.2. Windrow composting systems
Windrow systems are systems open to the environment and are
mechanically mixed using tractor drawn windrow turners or front-end
loading buckets. The mechanical mixing is conducted to enhance aeration, increase exposure of labile components located on the outside of
the pile, and to manage temperatures. The length of compost windrows
is typically determined by site and management factors, providing significant flexibility to compost facilities, but width and height are
generally each restricted to 3–4 m for effective composting and easy
access by normal farm equipment (CH2M HILL, 2013; Composting
Council of Canada, 2006; Groat, 2017). Windrow composting is heavily
dependent on operator skill, with operators monitoring the pile and
turning as necessary, with more frequent turnings leading to a faster
composting process. These systems are suitable for facilities receiving
very high volumes of heterogeneous feedstocks on a regular basis, i.e.
large municipal facilities, and where a large land footprint is available.
3.1.3. Aerated static piles
Aerated static pile composting is comprised of single batch-based
trapezoidal piles of heterogeneous feedstocks. Depending on the feedstock type, the materials may be layered, such as in animal mortalities,
or mixed prior to establishing the structure. These compost systems may
be aerated passively or by forcing (positive) or pulling (negative) air
through the trapezoidal compost pile. Once established, agitation only
occurs when piles are combined or moved to a different area for curing.
Piles often are covered with a layer of finished compost or wood chips,
which are then incorporated when the piles are moved. Static aerated
piles are generally used for biosolids, animal mortalities, or feedstocks
that have similar consistency. Enclosed aerated static piles operate
under the same principles as aerated static piles but are enclosed predominantly by plastic permeable membranes or organic matter is bagged and forced air is applied(CH2M HILL, 2013; Composting Council of
Canada, 2006; Groat, 2017). Aerated systems are typically found in the
agricultural sector for management of crop residues or animal mortalities. They are established as a low maintenance and relatively low-cost
management system.

3.1. Composting system design overview
There are different methods used for composting, from large-scale
windrow systems that are open to the environment, commonly found
in municipal systems, to closed in-vessel systems that having some type
of housing or container offered in a variety of sizes and requiring a
reduced footprint. There are four main types of composting systems that
are conventionally used, these being windrows, aerated static piles,
enclosed channel, and in-vessel systems, with a fifth less common system, hyperthermophilic composting (Campbell and Glasser, 2009;
Grunklee, 1998). Management objectives for processing organic wastes
through composting include: conversion of biologically unstable organic
wastes into more stable forms, reduction of the volume of organic waste,
improving sanitation conditions through the elimination of pathogens or
hazardous chemicals (hyperthermophilic), and retention of nutrients in
organic forms for reuse in agricultural or other production systems
(Groat, 2017; Rihani et al., 2010). Composting systems, regardless of
their scale, aim to provide an environment where aerobic decomposition

3.1.4. Closed composting systems
Closed composting systems are those not open to the atmosphere and
are either covered or contained or enclosed within a structure or vessel.
These systems often incorporate mechanical components for mixing and
managing the decomposition process resulting in a shorter time-frame
for decomposition (Composting Council of Canada, 2006).

3.1.5. Enclosed composting systems
Older in-vessel composting systems, referred to as in-vessel bays,
enclosed halls, or silos, are typically an enclosed or semi-enclosed
building with mechanical components that move material from one
end of the structure to the other. Enclosed channel systems operate using
mechanical agitation, with organic matter placed in long channels with
concrete walls. Turning machines are utilized to agitate the material and
move it from one end of the system to another, where the decomposition
process takes place throughout. Forced aeration is typically through

3.1.6. Vertical in-vessel silo systems
Vertical in-vessel silo systems offer a passive aeration system for
cage-suspended organic matter within a silo vessel. These systems have
several challenges related to odour control, build up of leachate in airflow channels, and the slow rate of decomposition due to lack of
agitation. Modified systems include the incorporation of aeration tubes
within the piles to aid in passive aerations. Critical to these systems is the
homogeneity of the feedstock with regards to particle size to ensure an
even composting process, therefore rotary drum systems may be utilized
as a pre-treatment.

3.1.7. Modular in-vessel systems
Modular in-vessel composting systems are fully enclosed and automated systems requiring direct energy input and are designed to provide
optimal composting conditions and feedstock homogenization, resulting
in an accelerated degradation process. The resulting output depends on
the system type, material retention time, feedstock types, and operating
conditions. The product may potentially require additional curing for a
final, stable product. In-vessel composting systems are more expensive
based on initial equipment requirements but require a smaller land base
and range in processing capacity (CH2M HILL, 2013; Composting
Council of Canada, 2006; Groat, 2017; Tetra Tech EBA inc., 2014).
Modular in-vessel composting may include environmental monitoring,
gas and temperature sensors, and mechanical mixing of material, along
with active aeration to provide more control over the composting process (Fig. 3).
Small modular in-vessel systems are designed to process 10 tonnes
per annum, medium systems can typically process up to 100 tonnes per
annum and large systems can process approximately 5,000tonnes per
annum. Processing capacity for many of these modular systems can be
scaled up through addition of modules. Scaling up from small systems to
large systems results in increasing complexity with respect to system
design, operational input, running costs (e.g. electricity consumption),
and logistics (Tetra Tech EBA inc., 2014).
These systems can take up a significantly lower footprint than open
composting systems but require higher initial capital investments.
Different systems may have a fixed capacity with limited scalability,
while other provide some flexibility on control of processing capacity to
allow for increased handling and processing capacity through the
installation of additional modules. A number of in-vessel designs and
flow through approaches are currently on the market ranging from nonmechanically agitated (static) in-vessel containerized composting systems to fully automated turned and air injected systems at a range of
different scales and configurations allowing for stand-alone or multiunit integration (Engineered Compost Systems, 2019; Green Mountain
Technologies, n.d.; Brome Compost Inc., 2019; Renewable Carbon
Management LLC, 2019; Global Composting Solutions Ltd., n.d.).
