total cost of the treatment process must be considered for waste treatment. After appropriate treatment and processing
of waste material, OWs are utilized as organic fertilizers for enhancing crop productivity along with mitigation of soil
pollution. Another important step is the transfer of waste material throughout the process i.e., from source to collection site, to storage facility, to treatment plants and at last to the site of implication [85]. It also involves the supervision
and after-care of disposal sites so that the waste and/or pathogens from the waste do not migrate into the population.
Till now, most of the research to utilize OWs has focused on conversion of these wastes for fertilizers, bio-energy
and biogas production [25, 87–89]. For instance, Babu et al. [39] revealed that biomass from agricultural waste may be
used to create second-generation biofuels and may serve as a fodder for animals and raw material industrial products.
In organic production systems, composted agricultural waste can replace energy-intensive chemical fertilizers [31, 90].
Thus, development of environmentally robust agri-waste residue/OW management technologies has the potential to
mitigate soil pollution in situ and ex situ, and contribute towards establishing a green economy in the area of agricultural
production. Composting, vermi-composting and biochar production are some of the predominant methods used in
recycling of organic wastes, which are subsequently used in sustainable agriculture for improving crop production [91,
92]. Various biological processes used in OW management are briefly discussed in this section.

4.1 Production of compost from organic wastes
Composting process provides the most efficient way of handling agricultural OWs and it has emerged as a basic and
valuable technique for preparing a nutrient rich fertilizer from OW materials [26, 37, 93]. Thus, OWs may be effectively
recycled in the system itself as organic manure that acts as a soil conditioner in agricultural soils improving soil’s fertility, structure, water holding capacity and buffering capacity [94]. Therefore, the process of composting is advantageous
for disposing OW materials from an ecological and financial standpoint. Composting involves the aerobic/anaerobic
and mesophilic/thermophilic breakdown of putrescible in organic waste by microorganisms and certain invertebrates
[9, 95]. This process has also proven to enhance pesticide degradation in soil as well as in compost heaps [96, 97]. The
final product of composting is a stable organic material, which is particularly relevant to agricultural production and
management of forest lands. Application of compost in soil has also helped in reducing loss of N from soil as compared
to application of fresh manure. Recently, Hang et al. [93] showed that fertilizers produced through composting process
contain higher organic matter, averaging 45.42%, compared to commercial organic fertilizers and bio-organic fertilizers.
It was predicted that organic matter content could be increased to 49.3% by optimization of equipment and composting
processes in Chinese organic fertilizer companies, which will potentially reduce annual carbon emissions by an estimated
3.07 to 6.97 billion kg of ­CO2 equivalent.
Based on the raw material used for the process, compost can be classified as green compost and brown compost.
Green compost is prepared from plant byproducts such as crop residues, leaf and litter waste and yard wastes. Brown
compost is prepared mainly from wet wastes such as animal manure, kitchen wastes and municipal organic waste [98].
Compost can also be classified as aerobic composting and anaerobic composting depending on the process conditions.
For instance, Foughal et al. [89] inoculated a mixture of agri-food waste including fish, vegetable, and poultry wastes
with Aspergillus niger for accelerating waste biotransformation in a 20-day process. A combination of all three waste
types with a tiny excess of poultry waste was found as the best, effective and secure mixture for biofertilization. Anaerobic digestion product had a higher potential for biofertilization than aerobic biotransformation product, according to
fertilization tests on tomato crops.
4.1.1 Aerobic composting
Composting done under aerobic conditions is the most popular and efficient technique of converting OWs into
compost (Fig. 2), which produces mature compost within a short time period [99]. During the process, the raw waste
material is biologically converted to a stable, pathogen-free and odour less product ready to apply in agriculture
and forestry [100, 101]. The product can be obtained within around 4 weeks with regular turning of compost pile
[91]. However, if the compost is not turned regularly, it may affect the quality and duration of compost. Sufficient
amount of oxygen and aerated conditions are required during the aerobic composting process. A compost pile containing organic waste, sufficient amount of moisture with balanced carbon and nitrogen ratio (C:N) is set up in pits
or in an open area. Mesophilic microorganisms (ideal temperature ranges from 20 to 45 °C) start to multiply in the

4.1.2 Anaerobic composting
Anaerobic composting is carried out in the absence of oxygen in an enclosed system, commonly known as digesters,
by utilizing anaerobic microorganisms. During this process, a mixture of different gases (primarily methane and carbon
dioxide, with traces of hydrogen sulfide and hydrogen), collectively known as biogas, is produced [94]. The methane
content determines biogas’ calorific value, while ­CO2 acts as a contaminant. The spent slurry or compost can be used
as manure in agriculture and forestry [114]. During anaerobic composting, superior compost and liquid fertilizer per
unit volume of raw material is produced as there is minimal nutrient loss as compared to aerobic digestion. However,

Another major disadvantage of this process is that it leaves many pathogens and weed seeds undestroyed, since higher
temperatures are not achieved during the anaerobic process. However, due to very hostile conditions, the pathogens
and weeds die gradually. Also, this is a costly and labor-intensive process, especially when applied on a large scale [116].
Anaerobic digestion (AD) of organic waste and biomass involves a series of degradation processes carried out by
microorganisms in the absence of oxygen, resulting in production of biogas and nutrients rich slurry or digestate [114].
The critical physico-chemical parameters that need to be assessed for optimal AD performance include contents of total
solids (TS), volatile solids (VS), pH, carbon-to-nitrogen ratio (C/N), and biochemical composition. The biogas slurry contains water (93%) and dry matter comprising of 4.5% organic matter and 2.5% inorganic matter. In addition, significant
amounts of both macronutrients (N, P, K) and micronutrients (Zn, Mn, B) are found in biogas slurry. Due to availability of
nutrients in the slurry/digestate, it is applied as a biofertilizer in agriculture and enhances plant growth. Therefore, many
small-scale anaerobic digesters were installed in several Asian countries leading to significant increases in production
of biogas and biogas slurry [117]. Depending upon the optimal degradation of organic waste by microorganisms, the
digested slurry also contains readily available plant nutrients such as amino acids, minerals, and bioactive compounds
including vitamins, humic acids, and hormones [118]. Therefore, application of biogas slurry under field conditions is
an efficient strategy for recycling of nutrients in agriculture farms, which also reduces the use of chemical fertilizers and
environmental problems globally.
Deng et al. [119] used an amino acid-derived ionic liquid, glycine hydrochloride, to enhance methane production from
anaerobic digestion of rice straw. The addition of glycine hydrochloride increased bacterial diversity and increased the
abundance of methanogens and archaea. The peak activities of cellulase, xylanase, and lignin peroxidase enzymes were
significantly higher than those of the control (without additive). The cumulative methane production was 115.56 mL ­g−1

the expression of microbial community nirK gene.
4.1.3 Production of humic substances
Humic substances (HSs) occupy 80% of organic matter in soil and significantly influence soil physico-chemical properties,
and have been widely applied for soil remediation agents, and adsorbents [124]. The biochemical reactions involved
in aerobic composting degrades organic matter and the products aggregates to produce ‘humic like substances’ [91,
125]. HSs are a core product of pre-controlled degradation and chemical oxidation of OWs, and a crucial indicator of

organic matter, from composts or vermi-composts or from mineral deposits [126]. Humic substances as well as their
compounds in soil (humins, humic acid and fulvic acid) are a result of interaction between organic matter, microbes
and plant roots [127, 128]. They can also be formed ex situ by controlled breakdown and oxidation of OWs resulting in
humic like substances. Since the HS extraction rate is very low by microbial degradation in nature, artificial humification
processes such as aerobic composting and hydrothermal treatment have attracted a great deal of attention as the most
important strategies in HS production [124].
The formation of HSs is complex process and is affected by the characteristics of the raw materials involved, the presence of compost additives, microbial activity, temperature, pH, the C/N ratio, moisture content, oxygen content and
particle size, all of which can interact with each other. Humic substances can be divided into humic acids (HAs), fulvic
acids (FAs), and humins based on their characteristics in alkaline and acidic solutions. However, HSs represent the same
functional groups and structural arrangements, which help to predict their structures. Functional groups represented
by phenol and carboxylic acid groups of HAs and FAs can provide various agronomic functions, such as plant growth
enhancement, water and nutrient retention, and disease suppression capacity. Thus, HSs can act as a soil amendment,
fertilizer, and plant growth regulator.
The effect of HSs varies with soil environment, the nutrient accepting plant, the dosage and method of application.
Humic substances strongly affect solubility of several plant nutrients such as P, Fe, and Cu, thereby increasing their plant
availability [129]. In addition, SOC, mainly HSs, can detoxify monomeric Al in acid soils, can strongly bind toxic heavy
metals, making them unavailable to the plant roots, and may strongly bind a vast variety of harmful organic pollutants
[124, 130]. The inclusion of farmyard manure (FYM) and its rotted or composted forms were found superior compared to
the separate application of straw and slurry to soil. Soils amended with polyanionic HSs shows enhanced cation exchange
capacity leading to increased nutrient uptake. Humic substances also stimulate ­H+-ATPase activity for uptake of nitrate
and other nutrients. They also help in stress mitigation by phenyl-propanoid metabolism leading to the production of
phenolic compounds [91, 124]. These functions of HSs enhance the reuse potential of organic waste compost products;
however, this requires scientific control of various composting parameters and appropriate application of final products.

4.2 Decomposition of organic waste material into vermicompost
Vermicomposting is a type of aerobic composting based on the decaying of organic biomass with the help of earthworms and some associated microorganisms. This is a mesophilic process, where the end product i.e., vermicompost is
a stable, humus-like material [131, 132]. The species that are used for vermicomposting are usually epigeic [133], and
they live in areas containing high amount of organic matter feeding on leaf litter, decaying plant roots or dung. Species
of earthworms used in this process remain on the soil surface and do not form permanent burrows. In this process, different earthworm species most commonly used includes Eudrilus eugeniae, Perionyx excavatus, Eisenia andrei, E. fetida
[132, 134], and Pontoscolex corethrurus [135].
With time, many variations in vermicomposting methodology have been developed. It may vary from composting
in windrows to completely automated, continuous-flow reactor arrangements [136]. The process of vermicomposting
occurs in two phases: (i) the active decomposition phase where the earthworms ingest organic waste, digest it and excrete
simplified organic matter. They also assist the movement and involvement of poorly mobile microbial communities.
Earthworms also fractionate the organic matter, thus allowing an increased surface area exposure to other decomposer
microbes [137], and during the maturation stage, earthworms travel to freshly added undigested organic waste. This
step is necessary to collect earthworm-free vermicompost while not disturbing the process. During the organic matter
decomposition by earthworms, it has been demonstrated that pathogen removal occurs while transportation through
the gastrointestinal track of the worm [138] and also during the process of composting. However, for complete pathogen removal and increased decomposition rate, combining of vermicomposting and composting is preferred. Similar to
composting process, vermicomposting also produces greenhouse gases like ­CO2 and ­N2O depending on the raw material
used [139]. The rate of decomposition, final product quality, worm mortality and greenhouse gas emission all depends
on the vermicomposting parameters and therefore, the process parameters must be kept under control.
Zhou et al. [140] provided an overview for future waste management developments using various microbial cultures either individually or in the form of consortium, supplements, bulking agents, or their amalgamations for process
improvement. Recent advancements in combining mathematical modelling, innovative supplements, and intelligenceassisted device designs with (vermi-) composting practices were highlighted. 4.3 Production of biochar from organic waste
Biochar is a compact solid attained after the thermo-chemical alteration of organic waste material in anaerobic environment [40, 143]. The Amazonian "Terra Preta" soils were first discovered in the nineteenth century by European explorers
in the Amazonian region that contain large amounts of biochar derived carbon with greater microbial activity, better
nutrient availability and crop production during exploration [82, 144, 145]. Recently, biochar has appeared as a potential
supplement to soils as well as composts with many positive outcomes [42, 146, 147]. Generally, the carbon stored by
plants via photosynthesis is returned to the atmosphere during natural decomposition of dead plants, thus completing
the carbon cycle [25]. However, converting dead biomass into biochar disturbs the carbon cycle by storing carbon in
stable form [40, 148].
Biochar is produced from various waste biomass sources, such as wood, manure, wheat or paddy straw, sewage
sludge and municipal refuse [41, 149]. Biochar is produced by the method of pyrolysis under controlled conditions. The
pyrolysis reactor’s temperature typically varies from 300 to 1000 °C. Pyrolysis of plant biomass results in three streams of
products: (i) noncondensable gases, (ii) a combustible bio-oil (liquid hydrocarbon) and water, (iii) biochar (solid byproduct) [150, 151]. The pyrolysis reaction can be either exothermic or endothermic based on the temperature of the reactants, but with decrease in reaction temperature, it becomes increasingly exothermic [152]. Also, the method should be
energy-efficient and pyrolytic gases should be utilized within the procedure to reduce emissions [153]. Compared to
pyrolysis at higher temperatures, instead of; pyrolysis at lower temperatures often results in a higher biochar yield and
an improved volatile matter composition [154]. There are estimates of exothermicity or energy yield of 2.0 to 3.2 kJ ­g−1
of biochar on slow pyrolysis [152]. Among different methods used for pyrolysis, microwave assisted pyrolysis is carried
out at 300–500 °C ranging from minutes to hours, whereas slow pyrolysis is performed at 300–700 °C, and it takes hours
[151]. At temperature range of 450–550 °C, pyrolysis hardly takes 1 min (fast pyrolysis) and flash pyrolysis is carried out
300–800 °C temperature within 1 s. Other pyrolysis methods include torrefaction (200–320 °C for hours), hydrothermal
carbonisation (150–400 °C for minutes to hours) and gasification (> 800 °C for seconds to minutes). This allows regulation
of physico-chemical properties of biochar.
Production of biochar also requires careful selection of feedstock and optimization of processing conditions to achieve
maximum possible stability. Zhu et al. [155] stated that one of the most popular management techniques for achieving
carbon neutrality in a circular economy is the pyrolysis of agro-residues into biochar. Agro-residues may be pyrolyzed to
make biochar, which can then be used as an alternative energy source, a soil conditioner, and a replacement for activated
carbon to create biochar that is more environmentally friendly and long-lasting. Krishnamoorthy et al. [156] reported that
biochar properties were significantly affected by feedstock type and pyrolysis temperature. Sawdust biochar (lignocellulosic biomass) produced at ­5000C had the highest struvite yield from urine (7.91 g ­L−1), phosphate (97.9%) and ammonium recovery (87.1%), and relative crystal size (85.2%) compared to the non-seeded treatment due to its higher surface
area, pore volume, and hydrophobicity of the biochar. Manure pellet biochar (non-lignocellulosic biomass) produced at
­5000C also exhibited performance comparable to sawdust biochar produced at ­5000C. Increasing pyrolysis temperature
increased biochar’s hydrophobicity, zeta potential, electrophoretic mobility and bulk density, irrespective of the feedstock
type, thereby improving the seeding process. The ash content of biochar was negatively correlated with its surface area,
pore volume, and particle size, but positively correlated with biochar’s bulk density and suspension stability. In another
study, Sun et al. [92] systematically investigated the effect of pyrolysis temperature on the structure of biochar prepared
from crop straw of three crops (cotton, alfalfa, and wheat). A higher pyrolysis temperature led to a higher aromatization
and graphitization degree of biochar and a numerical relationship between pyrolysis temperature and biochar surface
properties (functional groups, carbonization degree) was established. Pyrolysis temperature controlled the content,

4.4 Organic waste utilization as phytostimulants
Organic phytostimulants or plant biostimulants are complex and heterogeneous organic substances that improve plant
productivity and quality by activating different physiological and molecular processes in crop plants [157, 158]. Organic
phytostimulants contain materials or microorganisms that may act as fertilizers and increase plant nutrition processes
independently of the product’s nutritional level and may also enhance one or more of the following traits of the plant and/
or the rhizosphere of the plant, such as (i) nutrient usage efficiency, (ii) biotic stress tolerance/resistance, (iii) quality traits,
or (iv) availability of restricted nutrients in the soil or rhizosphere [157, 159]. Phytostimulants can originate from diverse
raw materials with different compositions that can significantly reduce the input of chemical fertilizers and agrochemicals in soils and hence, promote the environmental sustainability of agriculture. Their use as organic phytostimulants
provides an interesting possibility for reducing the environmental stresses on agricultural systems [157]. These organic
phytostimulants have been grouped into different families: seaweed extract, protein hydrolysates, humic and fulvic
acid, chitosan, beneficial microorganisms and other complex phytostimulants [160–162]. However, the mechanisms of
phytostimulants action are still being investigated. The main organic phytostimulants are summarized in this section.
4.4.1 Seaweeds extract
Seaweeds extract (SWE) or other plant extracts are either applied directly on soils or as foliar treatment in the form of
purified products (such as the products of polysaccharides such laminarin, alginates, and carrageenans) [163, 164]. Microand macro-nutrients, N-containing chemicals (betaines), sterols, and phytohormones including auxins, cytokinins, and
gibberellins are other components in seaweed extracts that support plant development [165]. The polysaccharides like
laminarin, alginates, carrageenans, or their products may result in gel formation to enhance water retention. The polyanionic compounds in SWE helps in the fixation and exchange of certain cations and HMs for soil remediation. SWE may
also involve some antioxidants or endogenous stress responsive genes regulators. Raja and Vidya [162] reported that
seaweeds extracts contain bioactive compounds that activate several signaling pathways and defense-related genes/
enzymes. Seaweed extracts and their components induce tolerance, mitigate stresses, can enhance nutrient efficiency
and boost growth under stress conditions in agriculture.
4.4.2 Protein hydrolysates
Protein hydrolysates (PHs) consist of peptides or amino acids, which are derived from the enzymatic or chemical hydrolysis of proteins, and are derived either from plants or animals. PHs are recognized as biostimulants for sustainable crop
production systems. PHs have been demonstrated to modulate N uptake and assimilation, stimulate shoot and root
biomass resulting in enhanced plant growth and yield of various crops [166]. Protein hydrolysates obtained from animals
acted as biostimulant for transplanted strawberry plants subjected to cold stress [167]. Some of the PHs may protect
plants against HMs, improve soil microbial biomass and activities leading to increases in micronutrient mobility and
soil fertility, which might be indirectly enhancing nutrient uptake and plant biomass [168]. Compounds such as glycine,
betaine and proline derived from PHs confer antioxidant activity and contribute to the mitigation of various abiotic
stresses [169]. However, the effectiveness of different PHs is dependent on various factors, including source, production
process and plant species.
4.4.3 Chitosan
Chitosan is a biodegradable and biocompatible polysaccharide obtained from partial chemical or enzymatic deacetylation of chitin. It is the second most common natural polysaccharide after cellulose. Due to its natural origin and multidirectional bioactivity of this polycationic polymer, chitosan is being used as a biostimulant, a plant protection product, an
elicitor, or an agent to increase the storage stability of plant raw materials [170]. Chitosan has antifungal, antibacterial,
antiviral, and antioxidant activity, and is involved in induction of plant defense mechanisms and regulation of metabolic
processes. The purified preparations obtained from brown algae such as laminarin and chitosan-based nanomaterials

4.4.4 Complex biostimulants
Complex biostimulants include non-pathogenic bacteria, mycorrhizal fungi and other beneficial microorganisms, which
inhabit the soil, rhizosphere, as endophytes or in phyllosphere [174–176]. These microbes improve soil fertility, and help
the plants by improving their nutrient uptake, by mitigating abiotic stresses and may prevent invasion of pathogens
and pests [160, 177–179]. Many microbial biostimulants increase crop yield and quality under pot house and field conditions [180–182]. Some antagonistic rhizospheric bacteria such as Pseudomonas and Bacillus, and fungal endophytes
like Trichoderma spp., Sebacinales, Phanerocheate etc. are being used as biocontrol agents and as biopesticides [147,
183, 184]. The symbiotic association of arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi (AMF) with crop plants is widely recommended to
promote sustainable agriculture [185, 186]. AMF treatment helps in absorption of macro- and micro-nutrients by plants,
in maintaining water balance and mitigating biotic and abiotic stresses [187, 188]. The tripartite associations between
mycorrhizal fungi, plant and rhizobacteria along with application of compost have been reported to improve soil quality
and increase plant health [189, 190].
Inoculation with mutualistic endosymbionts like Rhizobium and plant growth promoting rhizobacteria (PGPR) is mostly
favoured as biostimulants [191, 192]. Single or dual microbial inoculation was found as an efficient biostimulant in legumes with multifunctional growth promoting traits [193]. For instance, coinoculation of chickpea with Mesorhizobium
sp. Cicer strain Ca181 and Pseudomonas strains MRS23 and CRP55b, increased the nodule formation by 68.2–115.4% on
chickpea at 80 and 100 days after planting under sterile conditions in comparison to single inoculation of Mesorhizobium
strain [194]. Shoot dry weight ratios of coinoculated treatments at different stages of plant growth varied from 1.18 to 1.35
times that of Mesorhizobium-inoculated and 3.25 to 4.06 times those of uninoculated plants. In similar studies, Sindhu
et al. [195] reported that coinoculation of Bradyrhizobium strain S24 with Bacillus strains in green gram (Vigna radiata)
caused 1.28 to 3.55-fold enhancement in shoot dry mass at 40 days of plant growth. Coinoculation of Bradyrhizobium
strain with majority of Bacillus strains promoted the nodule number on green gram roots and also increased expression
of nitrogenase activity under pot house conditions. Under salt stress conditions, separate inoculations of Rhizobium sp.
LSMR-32 and Enterococcus mundtii LSMRS-3 improved sprouting of seeds, seed harvest, crop’s physical characters like
height and biomass, chlorophyll concentration, and nutrient assimilation as compared to uninoculated crops [196].
Inoculation with both these strains also enhanced the quantity of leghemoglobin, nodule number, and nodule biomass
along with phosphatase and dehydrogenase enzyme levels of soil. The link between the microbiome and plant health
has recently been reviewed [197] and microbiome applications showed significant impacts on plant development and
sustainable crop production.

4.5 Production of biofuels and chemicals from lignocellulosic biomass
Rapid population expansion and advancement in industrialization and modernization has led to a hike in the demand
of energy in recent years [198]. This has resulted in the depletion of conventional energy resources such as oil, natural
gas and coal. On the other hand, the use of fossil fuels has caused drastic pollution of air and water resources, along
with increase in global temperature and ozone layer depletion [2, 199, 200]. Recently, utilization of agricultural waste
for the production of energy has emerged as innovative technology for replacement of fossil fuels in the production of
sustainable energy [198, 201, 202].
Crop residues primarily consist of lignocellulosic biomass, which is widely available as a low-cost renewable feedstock. Nearly half the quantity of rice-husk produced in India is used as animal-fodder and the other half portion is
discarded in the environment or burnt by the poor farmers. Therefore, appropriate technology may be developed for
conversion of rice-husk into useful products after value addition including electricity and biofuel. Recently, many studies

also used in the paper-pulp and cardboard industries. The pulp of wood is primarily used for production of cardboards
and very low amount (only 4%) of the total crop waste is utilized. Thus, wide range of value-added products such as biocoal, biofertilizers, bio-bricks, bio-plastics, paper, biofuels, bioelectricity, chemicals, organic acids and industrial enzymes
are currently being produced from lignocellulosic waste, which has large impact on the economy [8, 202, 204].

5 Influence of organic amendments on different biological processes in soil
For providing sufficient food to exponentially increasing human population, intensive agriculture practices are followed
by farmers worldwide, which generates significant amounts of organic agricultural waste [8]. For processing of organic
waste, various biological technologies such as composting, anaerobic digestion, vermicomposting and biochar production are preferentially employed [89, 110, 113]. These sustainable and eco-friendly technologies ensure food security
along with mitigation of pollution problems. For instance, the amendment of compost, vermicompost and biochar to
the soil has been found to increase soil fertility, stimulation of beneficial microbial community, mitigation of HM stress,
suppression of soilborne pathogens and detoxification of pesticides leading to increased plant growth and crop harvest along with less dependence on chemical fertilizers [28, 32, 147, 206] (Fig. 3). Massaccesi et al. [62] reported that the
biomass of lettuce (Lactuca sativa L.) plants was increased from 2- to 2.5-fold in all compost and biochar amended soils
in comparison to the control after 45 days of cultivation.

5.1 Increase in nutrient availability in soil
Optimal environment, sufficient moisture, and the right quantity of nutrients are essential for the development of crop
plants. But, the soil’s potential to deliver nutrients is diminishing with time due to soil erosion, land degradation and
intensive crop production systems [57, 207]. For enhancing crop productivity, farmers use excessive amount of inorganic
fertilizers, which have deleterious effects on soil health leading to unsustainable yields [208], and also cause environmental pollution leading to public health hazards [6]. Continuous use of chemical fertilizers in the field also affects the
proliferation of beneficial microbial community in the soil [209]. In order to increase crop yield, it is necessary to upgrade
the nutrient distribution system in a sustainable way to provide adequate food to exponentially rising human population
[33, 210, 211]. The effect of different types of organic amendments (OAs) (i.e., unamended control, conventional farmyard manure (FYM), kraal manure, improved FYM, compost, vermicompost, urban waste, taroka, poultry droppings, pig
manure) and earthworm Pontoscolex corethrurus (Rhinodrilidae) inoculation was assessed on the growth and nutrition
of rice [135]. The poultry droppings had the best fertilizer performance, followed by improved farmyard manure and
pig manure in treatments without earthworms after eight weeks of growth. Recently, application of processed products
obtained from organic waste materials during composting, vermicomposting, biochar and phytostimulants has emerged
as novel agri-technologies for preparing nutrient rich fertilizers [32, 35, 106, 212].

5.1.1 Enhancement of nutrient availability by composting
Addition of compost in the farm soil increases nutrient levels and improves soil structure [9]. It also improves soil
fertility, porosity and soil microbial biomass [213]. A good quality compost is an excellent source of three macronutrients for the plant i.e., nitrogen, phosphorous and potassium (NPK). Although, as compared to inorganic fertilizers,
their concentrations in compost is low, but their regular application may fulfill the plants nutrients need, and hence,
reduce the application of chemical fertilizers. Also, addition of compost in soils can benefit by altering the soil’s heavy
metal bioavailability and can mitigate their toxic effects on animals and plants due to different processes such as
adsorption, precipitation and redox reactions.
The leachates obtained from the composting process (used as raw or diluted form) were found to serve as substrate for utilization by microbes involved in composting process in shake-flask fermentation assays. For example,
in comparison to raw leachate, Bacillus sp. thrived better in diluted leachate [214]. Amendments of leachates with
yeast and whey permeate improved the growth of Bacillus sp. and also the sporulation rate. Co-substrates produced
the greatest sporulation rate, causing over 89% of vegetative cells to produce spores. Results indicated that leachate valorization approach will reduce the volume of leachate waste for treatment and will also help the circular
economy produce biological amendments at a reasonable price. In another study, improvement in biological phosphorus transformation and nutrient content in composting products was observed by inoculation of kitchen waste
with phosphorus-solubilizing bacteria (PSB) [215]. Treatment with PSB considerably improved enzyme activity and
enhanced the levels of bacterial diversity, total P, Olsen P, citric acid P, and organic matter (OM) decomposition. In a
recent study, Priya et al. [216] explored the application of soil amendments compost (CMP) and gypsum, and signaling
compounds such as strigolactones (SL), salicylic acid (SA), SL and SA or SLSA, and coumarins to modulate symbiotic
root-microbe interactions for improving legume productivity in saline soils. The SLSA treatment outperformed CMP
in enhancing nodulation and AMF colonization. Only CMP induced a significant shift in the rhizosphere and root
microbiome structure. Increased abundance of AMF Rhizophagus in the rhizosphere and AMF Diversispora in the

5.1.2 Contribution of vermicomposting towards enhancement of nutrient availability
Soil amendment with vermicompost increased the amount of stored carbon under rice-rice cropping pattern [217] and
promoted root growth as well as ginsenoside content of Panax ginseng [218]. Supplementation of vermicompost with
recommended dose of inorganic fertilizers was found to enhance N, P and K content in soil in comparison to using only
inorganic fertilizers. Sahariah et al. [217] studied soil physical parametres during vermicomposting process and it was

in comparison to the addition of NPK alone or NPK with farmyard manure. Addition of vermicompost also enhanced
microbial biomass as well as their enzyme activities (dehydrogenase, urease, phosphatase and aryl sulfatase) in soil [219].
Increased microbial biomass and dehydrogenase activity was positively correlated with increased ammonical N, nitrate
N and orthophosphates. These factors increased nutrient cycling rates in soil and promoted synthesis of plant growth
regulating substances.
5.1.3 Enhancement of nutrient availability by biochar application
Biochar amendment in soil results in increased nutrient cycling and improvement in soil fertility, water retention capacity
and enhanced microbial activities and also influenced soil characteristics [42, 146, 220, 221]. Different biotic and environmental stresses in soil were found to affect the mineralization rate of biochar [222]. Biochar addition to soil has also been
reported to reduce greenhouse gas emissions from soils [148, 223]. The biological, chemical, and physical characteristics
of soil can all be considerably enhanced by biochar [221], including soil pH, nutrient availability, cation-exchange capacity (chemical properties); bulk density, porosity and water retention capacity (physical properties); and improvement
in microbial population, variety and activity of soil microbes (biological properties). The results of biochar application
on soil depends on different variables such as type of feedstock used, conditions at the time of biochar production, the
type of soil to which biochar is applied, together with the quantity of biochar used [42, 222].
Amendment of biochar resulted in improved soil fertility and sequestration of carbon and also increased crop yield,
alleviated plant stresses, immobilized HMs and reduced their uptake by plants in soil contaminated with organic pollutants [40, 224]. Application of both compost and biochar to soil further enhances its agronomic values as well as
results in minimum nutrient loss, which can potentially replace nitrogen fertilizers [225]. Addition of biochar to composts
improved its properties and biochar amendment improved aeration in compost because of low density and high porosity of biochar, thereby increasing the humification process and overall microbial activities [226]. Also, because of high
sorption ability of biochar, it may reduce excess N loss from compost. Biochar can also immobilize organic pollutants
and HMs during composting and can lower emissions of greenhouse gases [224, 227]. Bouhia et al. [228] reported that
addition of biochar singly or in biochar-compost combination (BCC) in Zea mays grown in pots filled with alkaline soil
increased soil TOC, EC, and pH under greenhouse conditions. Furthermore, adding biochar and compost increased the
levels of macro- and micronutrients compared to those under single application of biochar. The soil fertility improved
significantly with regard to available P and K, N, and micronutrients. Although, single application of biochar had a negative impact on mycorrhizal symbiosis but single application of compost gave the best results in terms of plant growth
and soil fertility improvement.
Xie et al. [189] carried out four treatments in ginger field soil i.e., control (no compost or PGPR; CK), compost (TC),
compost + Bacillus subtilis (TC-BS), and compost + Bacillus amyloliquefaciens SQR9 (TC-BA). According to the findings,
TC considerably enhanced soil organic matter content by 17.34%, alkali hydrolysable nitrogen by 21.66%, available P
by 19.56%, and accessible K by 37.20% when compared to the control (CK). Neutral phosphatase, sucrase, and urease
activity in the soil all rose by 55.89, 35.59, and 57.21%, respectively. According to research by Ali et al. [229], initial reductive soil disinfestation (RSD) treatment, biochar amendment (RSD-BC), and collective applications of microbes (such as
Trichoderma and Bacillus spp.) and biochar (RSD-SQR-T37-BC) increased soil pH, soil organic carbon, and ammonium
in the treated soils while lowering nitrate concentration. Li et al. [109] provided an overview of biochar application for
organic waste co-composting and its biochemical transformation mechanism. As an amendment in composting, biochar worked in the adsorption of nutrients, the retention of oxygen and water, and the promotion of electron transfer.
Biochar addition caused changes in community structure, and mediated metabolic activities involved organic matter
degradation. The participation of biochar enriched the α-diversity of microbial communities at all stages of composting,

to chemical fertilizers and it offers a promising approach to a biogas-linked agroecosystem that restores sustainable
coordination between cropping and animal husbandry under an intensive agriculture production system. It helps in

5.2 Stimulation of beneficial microbes in soil
Specific microorganisms including bacteria, fungi, algae, actinobacteria, archaea, protozoa, and nematodes inhabit the
soil and rhizosphere, and influence the development and growth of crop plants [33, 182, 234, 235]. The interactions of
surrounding microbes with plants are controlled by exchange of signalling molecules in their environment [236, 237].
The narrow area in close contact with the surface of root, termed rhizosphere, is most affected area by microbial activities
[238]. In the rhizosphere, plant roots secrete a wide spectrum of metabolites in root exudates ranging from organic acids,
sugars, alcohols, amino acids, nucleotides, and secondary metabolites [239, 240]. These exuded plant metabolites play
important role in fostering beneficial interactions with the surrounding microbial community in the plants’ rhizosphere
and modulate the dynamics of plant–microbe interactions in fulfilling plant niche-based requirements [241, 242].
It has been estimated that in general bulk soil contains ­107 to ­109 bacterial cells ­gram−1 and there is almost 10 to 100fold more bacteria in the rhizosphere [243, 244]. Approximatly, 30,000 prokaryotic species inhabiting the soil have been
found to impact the development and productivity of plants [240, 245]. The configuration of rhizosphere microbiota
prominently affects the communications between plants and soil, thus helping plants in adapting towards adverse environmental conditions including biotic and abiotic stresses [178, 246, 247]. The soil amended with low concentrations (at
0.01% and 0.1%) of pyroligneous acid (PA; obtained from pyrolysis of lignocellulosic raw material) increased microbial
diversity and dehydrogenase activity in comparison to the control treatment and high concentrations (1% and 5%) of
PA amendment to soil [248]. Interestingly, population of the plant growth promoting bacteria (PGPB) i.e., Azospirillum,
Acetobacter, Beijerinckia, Bradyrhizobium, Herbaspiriluum, Mesorhizobium, Nitrosomonas, Pseudomonas and, Rhizobium
was stimulated at lower concentrations of PA.
The application of phosphorus fertilizer enriched with microorganisms including Paenibacillus polymyxa strain
CHT114AB, B. amyloliquefaciens strain AF75BB and Bacillus sp. strain CZP4/4 was found to improve enzymatic activity
and the genetic and functional diversity of the soil microbial communities [249]. The addition of compost and inoculation of beneficial microbes preferentially stimulated the specific microflora in the soil. For instance, ginger field soil was
treated with “compost (TC), compost + Bacillus subtilis (TC-BS), and compost + Bacillus amyloliquefaciens SQR9 (TC-BA)”
[189]. TC-BS treatment significantly upgraded soil bacterial variety than control treatment i.e., no compost or PGPR “(CK)
and TC, and relative abundance of beneficial Proteobacteria, Acidobacteria, Chloroflexi, and Bacillus” microorganisms
dominated. This study demonstrated that B. subtilis inoculation increased the variety of bacteria, changed the bacterial
population framework, boosted advantageous microorganisms, and encouraged a flourishing rhizosphere in soil from a
ginger field treated with tomato compost. In subsequent studies, five fertilization treatments i.e., “chemical fertilizer (CF)
and chemical fertilizer combined with biochar (CFBC), manure (M), MBC (manure combined with biochar and FMBC)”
decreased the ammonia-oxidizing bacteria (AOB) by 33.1–81.9% [105]. The redundancy analysis demonstrated that “pH,
available P, carbon to nitrogen (C/N) ratio, soil moisture content, nitrate nitrogen, and ammonium nitrogen” present in
the rhizosphere influence the population structure of ammonia-oxidizing archaea and ammonia-oxidizing bacteria.

Castellano-Hinojosa et al. [250] examined the effect of four citrus rootstocks and compost on the diversity, composition, and predicted functions of active rhizosphere bacterial communities. Variations in the active bacterial rhizobiome
were strongly linked to root nutrient cycling (C, N, and tryptophan metabolisms) and specific rootstocks, particularly in
soils treated with compost. Direct positive relationships between enriched taxa in treated soils and specific root nutrients
were detected. Liu et al. [251] investigated the impacts of adding ­FeSO4 and biochar to cattle manure and rice straw composts on functional genes controlling N loss, bacterial community, nitrification, and denitrification. Four treatments were
made including a control group (CP), and CP + 4% biochar (TG1), 4% ­FeSO4 (TG2), or 2% ­FeSO4 and 2% biochar (TG3). In

and narG gene (encoding membrane-bound nitrate reductase) in TG3 was higher than in the other groups, and TG3 was

a positive effect on the nitrification process by increasing the abundance of amoA and narG. Li et al. [252] performed
high-throughput sequencing of soil microbial community structure after treatment of cucumber with 5% (w/w) sweet
pepper straw biochar (SPSB) concentration and observed that this biochar concentration significantly altered soil microbial community structure and enhanced bacterial and fungal diversity. It increased beneficial bacterial groups (Firmicutes,
Actinobacteria and Bacillus) and modified fungal communities, with a decrease in Ascomycota and Aspergillus and shifts
in Penicillium abundance. Functional genomic analysis indicated enrichment in bacterial metabolic pathways and fungal
replication and expression genes.

5.3 Bioremediation of heavy metals
Heavy metals such as lead, arsenic, mercury, copper, nickel, cadmium and zinc are being accumulated in soils due to
various natural (volcanic eruptions and forest fires) as well as anthropogenic activities like application of chemical fertilizers, sewage sludge disposal, release of industrial waste, power stations emissions, fuel combustion by automobiles etc.
(Fig. 4). Although, some of these metals are essential for plant growth in trace amounts, but their excess concentrations
can poison the soil and negatively affect plant growth, physiology, metabolism and crop production. In soil, these HMs
are non-biodegradable [253]. The physical and chemical treatment of HM remediation in soils is a laborious, expensive
and non-sustainable process. Therefore, scientists are engaged in developing technology to sustainably remediate HMs
from agronomic soils by using different metal tolerant microorganisms as bioremediation agents [18, 21]. Furthermore,
mitigation of heavy metal pollution in soils through addition of compost, vermicompost and biochar has gained considerable attention because of its sustainability, low cost and health benefits [134, 254].

Under the abiotic stress caused due to accumulation of HMs, growth of soil microbiota and their functioning in
different ecological processes is negatively affected. Bioremediation involves the use of microorganisms to clean the
polluted environment by detoxifing different types of pollutants [21, 255, 256]. These soil microbes employ a variety
of mechanisms to survive under conditions of metal toxicity. They can store, alter, modify or detoxify HMs by binding,
immobilizing, oxidizing and volatilizing them [257, 258]. The basic methods of bioremediation of soil pollutants by microorganisms include biosorption, immobilization, bioaugmentation and biotransformation (Table 1). Generally, two types
of bioremediation i.e., in situ and ex situ methods have been adopted by metal tolerant microbes for successful remediation of HMs from soil. During in situ method, genetic engineering techniques are used, while in the ex situ method,
the contaminated soil is removed from its original site, moisturized and amended with nutrients [259] Some common
examples of metal-tolerant microorganisms include Bacillus, Pseudomonas aeruginosa (Zn and Cu), Citrobacter spp. and
Chlorella vulgaris (Cd, Pb, U, Cu, Au, Ni, Hg), Aspergillus niger (Cd, U, Zn), and Rhizopus arrhizus (Cd, Ca, Hg, Pb, Ag) [260].
Application of compost and biochar in soil also contributed in mitigation of HMs stress using physico-chemical
approach in the HM polluted soil [104]. The stoichiometric interactions between different microbial enzymes such as
N-acetylglucosaminidase, β-glucosidase, leucine aminopeptidase and acid phosphatase were examined after application
of heavy metals. Application of biochar to HM-polluted soils enhanced the activity of acid phosphatase and inhibited
activities of other enzymes. In addition, application of biochar-compost strengthened all these enzymes activities, which
were inhibited due to HMs. However, the stoichiometric ratio of C/P, C/N and N/P were changed due to application of
the biochar and compost. Along with alleviating the phosphorous-limitation in soils under copper stress, biochar also
alleviated the carbon-limitation in soils under Cd, As and Zn stress. Gao et al. [261] reviewed the recent advances in
bioaugmentation technology for efficiently removing poisonous contaminants from organic waste contaminated soils
by using microbes or their enzymes and bioremediation additives. A thorough overview of several bioaugmentation
techniques, including bacteria, fungi, their enzymes, and some other bioremediation additives, was provided. The longterm stability of wide-range bioremediation carriers, microbial/enzyme agents targeting coupled pollutants, desorption
of ecologically beneficial additives, and minute molecular biological stimulants were considered, while evaluating the
future of bioaugmentation.
Li et al. [262] used vinegar-residue biochar for remediation of heavy metal cadmium from contaminated water and
soil. Rwiza et al. [263] pyrolyzed lignocellulosic materials i.e., rice husks and maize hulls, which were burned at 500 °C to
create biochar, and were subsequently activated with KOH and ­ZnCl2 as activating agents. Compared to the raw hulls
and husk, the modified biosorbents absorbed ­Pb2+ more quickly and effectively. In comparison to the sorption capacity of 15 mg ­g−1 achieved by raw maize husk (CH), the KOH-treated maize husk biochar (KOH-CHB) acquired a removal
capacity of > 97 mg ­g−1 in the first 15 min. By pyrolyzing cannabis and cinnamon at various temperatures, Omidi et al.
[264] produced biochars that functioned as potential adsorbents. The Cd (II) adsorption onto biochars was successful at
pH 7.0 and at a temperature of 65 °C. A substantially shorter contact time and high ­Pb2+ removal by activated biochars
were likely caused by improved structures. The low-cost materials used in the current study showed the potential to
remove harmful ­Pb2+ from water at a reasonable price.
Foong et al. [265] presented a thorough examination of the use of biochar made from rice straw (RSB) to treat wastewater and remove various sorts of impurities. While magnetic biochar and electrochemical deposition have become
promising methods for biochar modification, acid-modified RSB has the ability to eliminate metal ions and organic
molecules. In another experiment, the highest relative reductions of HMs i.e., Pb, Cu, Cd, and Zn concentrations were
achieved in shoot of Chinese mustard (Brassica juncea Czern) at the level of 74.72, 69.19, 54.16, and 53.86, respectively,

5.4 Biocontrol of phytopathogens
Plant pathogens coupled with drastic climate changes are the major constraints for improving crop productivity and providing healthy food for ever-increasing human population. Various pathogenic microorganisms cause different diseases
on major crops affecting up to 20–40% annual losses in crop yields globally, which seriously jeopardize food security
and the quality of agricultural production [267, 268]. Farmers use excessive amounts of toxic pesticides for control of
phytopathogens and insects to minimize crop losses. However, injudicious application of these pesticides causes environmental pollution, development of resistance in pathogens, disturbs ecological biodiversity and even causes public
health hazards [5]. Hence, a sustainable and economical option is needed for controlling plant diseases and improving
crop yield. Recently, biological control of pathogens and pests by the use of antagonistic microorganisms (biocontrol
agents), their extracted bioactive metabolites or organic amendments has emerged as an environment friendly and cost
effective technology for controlling/killing the pathogens and suppression of plant diseases [269, 270]. These biological
methods of controlling phytopathogens will decrease the excessive use of agro-chemicals in crop fields and will reduce
the pollution as well as other health related problems [271–273].
In a stride to assess the significance of organic amendments on biological control of phytopathogens, different
amendments either singly or in combination with biocontrol agents were tested for suppression of the plant diseases.
For instance, pyroligneous acid (PA) or wood vinegar (an acidic reddish-brown aqueous liquid), possessing antifungal,
termiticidal and antimicrobial activities, has been produced through the pyrolysis of lignocellulosic raw materials [274,
275]. In another experiment, vermicompost application was found to reduce the number of parasitic nematodes and
encouraged the fungivorous and bacterivorous nematodes in soil [131]. In another study, three organic soil amendments
viz., cassava peel (Manihot esculenta, Cranz), sawdust (Gmelina arborea, Roxb) and leaves of Spanish cedar (Cedrela odorata
L.) were evaluated on the stalk rot disease of maize (Zea mays L.) caused by Fusarium verticillioides [276]. Interestingly,
maize plants subjected to cassava peels combined with C. odorata treatment showed significant reduction in disease
index and disease severity due to favourable competition with pathogenic fungi F. verticillioides. All these soil treatments
also showed significant growth promoting effects on plant height, leaves number, leaves surface area and stems girths
as compared to control plants.
Ali et al. [229] carried out initial reductive soil disinfestation (RSD) and applications of Bacillus (RSD-SQR), Trichoderma
(RSD-T37), and biochar (RSD-BC) reduced the incidence of wilt by 26.8, 37.5, and 32.5%, respectively in comparison to nonRSD treatments. Greater suppressiveness of Fusarium wilt and F. oxysporum was observed in treatments with RSD-SQRT37-BC and RSD-T37. In similar studies, use of integrated pest management (IPM) approaches statistically decreased the
Fusarium wilt severity of lettuce from 50 to 70% in comparison to untreated controls, in both fields under two consecutive
years [277]. The following treatments were used: (i) compost enriched with Trichoderma, (ii) combination of “Trichoderma
gamsii + T. asperellum, Bacillus amyloliquefaciens and potassium posphite”, and (iii) combination of “T. polysporum + T.
arviridus”. An increased crop yield was also observed in comparison to untreated controls. High-throughput sequencing
of bacterial and eukaryotic rRNA gene markers of rhizosphere microbiota was performed and it showed Proteobacteria,
Firmicutes and Actinobacteria as predominant phyla for bacteria and Ascomycota for fungi.

5.5 Remediation of pesticides and organic pollutants
For the management of pathogenic fungii, weeds, and insect pests in crop fields, a variety of pesticides, including
fungicides, herbicides, and insecticides, are often utilized. Nevertheless, fewer than 1% of the insecticides used in field
applications actually reach the pests [279]. The residual pesticides harm the environment and human health because of
their toxicity and environmental pollution [5]. In addition, various organic contaminants in agricultural soils including
detergents, dyes, lipids, phenols, oil and surfactants are continually being added in the soil through various processes.
Thus, the occurrence of pesticides and organic pollutants in soil is a major environmental concern. Use of single or
groups of bacteria, microbial-algae consortia, or organic amendments (compost or biochar) has been recommended as
a sustainable approach to decontaminate or detoxify the pesticides and organic pollutants from the environment [46,
75]. Ling et al. [280] reported that amendment of soil with Biochar500 or Biochar600 (pyrolyzed at 500 °C and 600 °C,
respectively) induces a shift in microbial community structure towards dominance of Gemmatimonadetes, Bacteroidia,
Alphaproteobacteria and Gammaproteobacteria classes and promotes faster mineralization of SOC, thus offsetting C
sequestration effects. The majority of soil derived ­CO2 efflux in biochar amended soils originated from recalcitrant components that were mineralized by the persistent organic matter decomposers.
The application of biochar and wood vinegar together prevented glyphosate pesticides’ hazardous leaking into the
aquatic environment [281]. In another study, humic acids exhibited a potent capacity to sorb cationic and hydrophobic
organic pollutants as it was shown that the functional groups of humic acid, such as quinones, may establish covalent
connections with aromatic amines or similar chemical molecules [282]. According to certain reports, lignin-modifying
enzymes (LMEs) such laccase and peroxidase can catalyse the oxidative coupling of 2,4-dichlorophenol to humic and
fulvic acids [283]. These hazardous residues that have been covalently bonded are efficiently detoxified since they are
not bioavailable. Thus, application of humic substances (HSs), LMEs or interactions between microorganisms’ and HSs
could offer a useful strategy for the biodegradation of organic pollutants and remediation of pesticides [127]. Recently,
Ni et al. [284] reported that combined application of corn straw biochar (CB, 2%) and low-molecular-weight organic acids
(LMWOAs, 10 mg ­kg−1) dissipated 86.58% of napropamide (amide herbicide) after 1 month of incubation. The napropamide in the soil was significantly absorbed by CB throughout this process, which drastically decreased its bioavailability.
The combined treatment boosted the relative abundances of microorganisms that take part in the biodegradation of
napropamide, accelerating the breakdown of xenobiotics in soil.
Zhou et al. [224] investigated the influence of biochar on toxicity mitigation and microbial community succession
in soil contaminated by polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon (PAH)-phenanthrene. The biochar-amended treatments (BC)
and biochar immobilized with the phenanthrene-degrading bacteria (MBC) showed significantly lower phenanthrene
removal rate (PRR) than the no-biochar treatments i.e., no biochar or inoculation (CK) and inoculation of phenanthrenedegrading bacteria (MB). The plant dry weight and height of the maize plants treated with BC, MB, and MBC were
significantly higher than those of the CK treatment, and the highest dry weight was observed in the MBC treatment
(biochar immobilized with the bacteria). Biochar amendment significantly changed the bacterial community structure
and strengthened the bacterial co-occurrence network. Furthermore, biochar amendment alleviated the toxicity or
stress of PAH on soil microbes. Bouhia et al. [32] isolated fungal species, FUN 06 (Galactomyces geotrichum), from olive

6 Plant growth stimulation and increases in crop yield
Amendments of soil with compost, vermicompost and biochar have been established as a effective method for increasing
crop yields, while lowering the need for chemical fertilizers, leading to sustainable agriculture [37, 57, 63]. In addition,
10–40% photosynthetically fixed carbon is deposited within the rhizosphere primarily as root biomass, exudates, and
microbial biomass as soil SOM [129, 239]. Moreover, combined application of organic amendments alongwith single or
consortium of beneficial microbes has been found to enhance biomass and yield of different crops under field and greenhouse conditions [37, 182, 286] (Table 2). The synergistic effects of organic amendments with beneficial microbes increase
the accessibility of nutrients including N, P, K, Zn and S, mitigate abiotic stresses and suppress plant diseases. Thus, supply
of carbon and energy resources from decomposed plant residues in the form of SOM alongwith root exudates help in
proliferation of beneficial microbial community. Subsequent expression of plant growth promoting activities of beneficial
microbes leads to stimulation of plant growth and increases in crop yield, contributing to circular sustainable agriculture
systems. But in some instances, some limitations have been reported, which restrict crop development in a variety of
agricultural settings. For example, the survival, viability and functionality of inoculated microbes under field conditions
are often different under laboratory and greenhouse environments due to competition with indigenous microbes and it
adversely impact the growth of crop plants [287]. Therefore, organic compounds, cell protectants, and nanoparticles are
frequently added to beneficial biofertilizer strains to boost their survival and effectiveness for improving crop yield [33].
The effectiveness of various organic amendments including compost, vermicompost and biochar on yield of different
crop varied depending on soil management, SOM content, rate of application and frequency of chemical fertilizers in
integrated nutrient management (INM) system as well as on the addition of other soil amendments. For instance, addition
of municipal waste compost at a dose of 80 tonnes ­ha−1 annually for 5 years, enhanced the wheat yield by 246% in comparison to untreated control in a field study [288]. In similar studies, Erhart et al. [289] reported 10% increase in the yields
of cereals and potato crop by application of of biowaste compost (23 tonnes ­ha−1 ­year−1) compared to unfertilized control
treeatment. Using INM approach, Diacono and Montemurro [290] showed that application of organic amendments along
with mineral fertilizers increased the plant growth and crop yield compared to application of soil amendment alone.
Recently, the development of ecological circular agriculture system has highly encouraged the use of biogas slurry
as an important kind of fertilizer owing to its high nutrient components, environmentally friendly and lower costs than
chemical fertilizers. Biogas slurry can be added directly to the crops or it may be used along with other organic amendments and synthetic stimulants. For example, Yu et al. [118] observed that amendment of biogas slurry in soil improved
the soil texture and enhanced the crop yield and fruit qualities of tomato. Similar studies carried out by Pathak et al. [291]
showed that seeds soaked in biogas slurry improved germination rates and increased seedling growth than untreated
seeds. Zhao et al. [292] sprayed biogas slurry on Capsicum plants in the field and it increased crop yields and prevented
the diseases. Addition of animal urine along with biogas slurry was found to increase its N content, resulting in increased
C:N ratio for easy nutrient accessibility to plants and soil microflora. On the other hand, long-term application of untreated
biogas slurry in crop lands has been found to adversely affect the crop yield, resulting in losses of crop yield and quality
[293, 294]. The continuous application of biogas slurry has also been reported to increase the accumulation of heavy
metals or genes for antibiotic resistance in soil [295, 296]. It may also cause leaching or movement of extra nutrients into

that addition of biochar to compost increased the levels of macro- and micro-nutrients compared to those under single

In a stride to establish the role of organic amendments on yield attributes and to reduce drought stress-induced damages in wheat (Triticum aestivum), Anee et al. [81] added different OAs consisting of compost, vermicompost and poultry

17%, whereas poultry manure amendment increased plant height by 16% under drought condition compared to control
plant. Vermicompost also showed the capability to reduce the level of lipid peroxidation and raised the proline content
by drought condition. Drought stress-induced increment of catalase, ascorbate peroxidase and glutathione reductase
activities were also efficiently modulated by the organic amendment application. Bornø et al. [301] used wood biochar or

7 Future perspectives and scope
Significant increases in the crop yields and quality of food production have been achieved by application of modern
agricultural technologies. Some of these technologies utilize chemical fertilizers, pesticides and plant growth regulators for securing sufficient crop yields to feed over seven billions of human beings on the earth. However, extensive
and injudicious uses of these agrochemicals have negative impacts on the environment, microbial diversity and
human health. Therefore, there is urgent need for sustainable agriculture, which relies on a better understanding of
organic waste management as well as beneficial interactions between plants and soil-inhabiting microorganisms.
Organic wastes can be processed and utilized in different forms and for various purposes in agriculture. They are
mainly utilized for improving soil’s physical and chemical properties, and for nutrient replenishment. In the last few
decades, soil contamination with organic and inorganic wastes, pesticides and HMs is also gaining much attention of
researchers. Multiple technologies have been devised to manage agricultural waste and to overcome soil pollution
[25, 31, 334]. But, all these technologies have some demerits when used individually. Therefore, there is a need to
develop integrated techniques or to modify existing methods to get maximum benefits for improving soil fertility
and crop production. The modifications or improvements must concentrate to develop sustainable methods, not
damaging the environment in the long run, easy to use, ethical, economical and affordable.
Most of the organic waste management practices and soil pollution mitigation methods employ different microorganisms at certain stage of agri-technology [28, 110, 113]. The selection of particular microbial strain is the crucial
step of any bioconversion technology. Although, microorganisms exhibit remarkable evolutionary capabilities but
their natural evolution is relatively slow. In such scenarios, bioengineering of beneficial microorganisms may be
helpful to enhance the bioconversion capacity of pollutants [335]. Recent developments in Microbiology, Molecular
biology and Biotechnology are providing the driving force towards engineering of better microbes for bioremediation
of polluted soil and to obtain improved microorganisms with desired characteristics. Mishra et al. [336] discussed
the profiling of microorganisms present in polluted sites using various techniques including culture-based and
omics-based approaches. The use of microbial electrochemical technologies was also reviewed for remediation of
pollutants. In addition, the effects of various treatment technologies for remediation of pollutants were evaluated
and future outlook and challenges were discussed.
The use of plant biostimulants and microbiome engineering has recently emerged as environment-friendly technology for improving nutrient use efficiency and mitigating biotic and abiotic stress resulting in plant growth promotion and increases in crop yield [159, 178]. Recently, genetically modified organisms (GMOs) or bioengineered
microbes have been developed for faster degradation and removal of soil contaminants such as pesticides, hydrocarbons, and HMs to restore soil health [335]. Applications of GMOs were found to improve the bioremediation
process by altering metabolic pathways that results in hyper-secretions of different biomolecules. In order to make
the soil productive and healthy, contaminated or polluted soils may be treated with GMOs, PGPR, AMF and other
soil additives for effective restoration of soil health [147, 333]. The resource efficiency may further be enhanced by
appropriate waste management and valorization processes of agricultural waste biomass into value-added products
for execution of sustainable circular bio-economy [337, 338]. Moreover, the synergistic effects of organic amendments
with beneficial microbes may become a preferred management option to provide valuable insights for fertilization
strategies in nutrient-poor ecosystems, benefiting both plant growth and crop yield components.

8 Conclusions
Production of organic agricultural wastes is unavoidable due to increasing food demand for exponentially growing
human population worldwide. But, the accumulation of unprocessed organic waste on soil is causing environmental
pollution. Different strategies and technologies used for organic waste management include composting, anaerobic
digestion, vermicomposting, biochar production, organic phytostimulants, and bioremediation of pollutants. Application of these processed organic wastes in the farm soil increased nutrient availability, stimulated the population of
beneficial microbes, caused remediation of heavy metals, inhibited the growth of phytopathogens, and detoxified
or degraded the pesticides and organic pollutants. Furthermore, fertilization of soil or crops with these processed
organic materials improved soil fertility and health; and stimulated plant growth resulting to increases in crop yields.

Thus, appropriate management of organic wastes by using recently developed technologies will not only reduce

Abstract— The AI-controlled Smart IoT-based Greenhouse
Monitoring System represents a cutting-edge solution for
precision agriculture. Leveraging the power of Artificial
Intelligence and the Internet of Things, this system
continuously monitors and optimizes environmental variables
within the greenhouse, including temperature, humidity, soil
moisture, and light levels. Greenhouse gases are the gases in
the atmosphere that raise the surface temperature of Earth.
Water vapor (H2O), carbon dioxide (CO2), methane (CH4),
nitrous oxide (N2O), and Ozone (O3) are some of the examples
for greenhouse gases. This article provides an overview of such
an automation workflow in greenhouse environments by
means of distributed wireless nodes. It makes use of both the
IoT and AI technique. Predictions are made through the AI
technique which makes use of CNN approach. After a
comparative study, sample results from commercial and
research greenhouse experiments with the IoT hardware and
software have been provided to show connection stability,
robustness, and reliability.

The black solider fly is indigenous to the southern United States and is now distributed

44

to warm temperate regions (Diener et al., 2009). The life cycle of the BSFL is divided into

45

four phases with an estimated lifespan of 44 days, depending on the environmental conditions

46

(i.e., temperature, moisture, and air supply) (Fig.1; Tomberlin et al., 2002). Mature flies have

47

no functioning mouth-parts and are not associated with transmission of diseases or considered

48

pests to humans or pets (Sheppard et al., 2002). Black soldier fly larvae (BSFL) have been

49

used in backyard and farm composting systems for decades, mainly to treat animal manures

50

(Tomberlin, 2001; Olivier, 2008). However, more recently, BSFL have been investigated in a

51

52

53

the best of our knowledge, there is limited prior research that has considered black solider fly

54

larvae as value-added feedstock for anaerobic digestion to generate biogas.

55
56

The capability to process putrescent wastes gives BSFL distinct advantages over
traditional composting and vemicomposting, which cannot generally accept meat and post2

 57

consumer wastes (Olivier, 2008). BSFL have the ability to rapidly consume large amounts of

58

a wide variety of organic wastes, including animal manure, fecal sludge, meat and kitchen

59

waste (Nguyen et al., 2015). In addition to being robust decomposers, BSFL contain

60

significant amounts of protein and lipids and have been investigated as a dietary supplement

61

to feed chickens, swine and fish (Alvarez, 2012; Newton et al., 2005). The high lipid content

62

of BSFL has also been investigated for its potential to create renewable biodiesel fuel (Zheng

63

et al., 2012a; 2012b). The cuticle (or larval skin) is composed of chitin, a long chain polymer

64

of N-acetyl glucosamine, which has been estimated to comprise approximately 10% of the

65

total BSFL dry biomass (Finke, 2007; Tomberlin et al., 2002). Chitin has proved versatile for

66

several medical, industrial and biotechnological purposes (Puvvada et al., 2012).

67

Unlike energy crops, BSFL would not compete with food production in agricultural land

68

usage, nor pose the associated environmental concerns such as soil erosion and pesticide

69

leakage to surface and ground water (EEA, 2006). Furthermore, BSFL have a high per-acre

70

productivity, fast growth rate, and can be grown on non-arable land areas. These qualities are

71

similar to algae production without the drawback that harvesting and valorization of algae

72

biomass require significant water use and high capital and operation costs, making it

73

economically challenging (Mussgnug et al., 2010). Moreover, production of energy crops and

74

algae depends on the photosynthetic fixation of CO2 and the limiting factor in such biological

75

energy processes is the conversion efficiency in the range of 1 to 3% of incident solar energy

76

(Miyamoto, 1997).

77

Like energy crops, BSFL have not been previously digested and thus may offer higher

78

bio-methane potential than manures or biowastes. Additionally, the characteristics of BSFL

79

biomass indicate that it could be a promising candidate for deployment in an integrated

81

conversion processes to produce multiple co-products including fuel, heat, electrical power

82

and value-added products such as fertilizer. A biorefinery concept developed around

83

anaerobic digestion could be suitable to treat various organic wastes and convert them to

84

multiple products, thus enhancing the economic viability of the integrated system. In a system

85

using BSFL as a feedstock, the BSFL could reduce the weight of other organic wastes and

86

convert them into more concentrated forms as an initial conversion step, or as a pretreatment

87

process prior to anaerobic digestion to enhance the digestion process. BSFL biomass can also

88

be used directly as animal feed or as feedstock to produce biofuel products (biodiesel and

89

biogas), with their residue serving as a valuable feedstock for anaerobic digestion process.

Application of big data in smart agriculture
Yingbo Zhang1)
Abstract
Using big data in smart agriculture represents a significant technological revolution in the agricultural
sector. This paper delves into the primary application areas of big data in smart agriculture, encompassing
precision agriculture, intelligent farming machinery, and sustainable agriculture. To begin with, big data
technology offers comprehensive data support for decision-makers in agriculture. Through real-time
monitoring and extensive data analysis, agricultural producers can gain more precise insights into soil
conditions, crop growth status, and other crucial information. Furthermore, implementing big data in
precision agriculture facilitates intelligent agricultural production by integrating precision fertilization,
irrigation, and pest and disease monitoring, thereby enhancing production efficiency. The advancement of
intelligent farming machinery also plays a pivotal role in enhancing the intelligence and efficiency of field
operations. Moreover, big data technology contributes to sustainable agriculture by providing scientific
support for agricultural decisions through data analysis on climate change, resource utilization, and other
pertinent aspects, thereby promoting the transition towards environmentally friendly agricultural practices.
Looking ahead, with continuous innovation and widespread adoption of big data technology, smart
agriculture is poised for significant development opportunities.
Keywords
big data in agriculture, smart agriculture technology, precision agriculture applications, intelligent
farming machinery, sustainable agriculture with big data

1. Introduction
The rapid evolution of big data technology is ushering in profound changes in the field of agriculture. In
recent years, due to the continuous advancement of information technology, the volume of data generated in
agricultural production has expanded rapidly. This phenomenon, commonly referred to as “big data,” has
emerged as a driving force behind the modernization of agriculture. The significance of big data in smart
agriculture is increasingly prominent, acting as a crucial support for enhancing agricultural production
efficiency and optimizing resource utilization. By adeptly collecting, managing, and analyzing this extensive
agricultural data, decision-makers in agriculture can gain more precise insights into various factors such as
soil conditions, weather patterns, crop growth, and market information. This, in turn, enables more intelligent
agricultural production [1-5].

The application of big data in smart agriculture first faces the challenge of data collection and
management. The data involved in agricultural production covers a wide range, including soil composition,
weather changes, and plant growth conditions. Various technologies such as sensors and satellite remote
sensing can be employed to monitor and collect this data in real time. Simultaneously, for such massive data,
scientific management and storage become the foundation for subsequent analysis. Therefore, constructing
an efficient big data collection and management system not only provides data support for smart agriculture
but also lays the groundwork for more in-depth decision analysis [6-10].
The application of big data in smart agriculture goes beyond data collection; it crucially involves
transforming this data into concrete decision support. Data cleaning, processing, and analysis become
indispensable steps. Through big data analytics, crop diseases can be identified, optimal planting times can
be determined, and market demand can be predicted, providing agricultural decision-makers with more
scientific and precise information support. The real-time and comprehensive nature of big data allows
agricultural decisions to be adjusted in real-time, minimizing production risks and enhancing agricultural
production efficiency. Therefore, the role of big data in decision support is considered one of the core drivers
of smart agriculture [11-15].
This paper aims to delve into the application of big data in smart agriculture, with a focus on analyzing
the impact of big data technology on various aspects of agricultural production and emphasizing its
importance for the development of smart agriculture. By comprehensively introducing specific applications
of big data in data collection, management, decision support, and more, the goal is to provide readers with a
profound understanding of big data technology in smart agriculture.
The structure of this paper is as follows. Starting from the introduction, the rise of big data in agriculture
and its importance to smart agriculture are presented. Subsequently, the paper is divided into two key sections.
The first part focuses on the collection and management of big data, providing an in-depth analysis of data
sources and collection technologies in agricultural production, emphasizing the necessity of constructing an
efficient big data collection and management system. The second part concentrates on the role of big data in
decision support, covering data cleaning, processing, analysis, and highlighting the crucial support provided
by big data to decision-making in smart agriculture. Through discussions on these two main aspects, readers
will gain a comprehensive understanding of the key applications of big data in smart agriculture, thus better
recognizing its role in improving agricultural production efficiency and sustainable development

2. Data collection and management in big data agriculture
2.1. Data sources in agricultural production
The sources of data in agricultural production are diverse and extensive, covering various aspects from
land to weather and plants. Firstly, soil composition is a crucial data source in agriculture. Through soil
sensors and detection devices, agricultural producers can obtain key information about soil nutrient content,
