and pH values, aiding in the formulation of scientific fertilization plans. Secondly, meteorological data plays
a vital role in agriculture. Weather stations and satellite technology can provide accurate meteorological
information, including temperature, humidity, and rainfall, offering real-time weather conditions to assist
farmers in planning planting and agricultural activities. Additionally, plant growth conditions are also an
essential data source in agriculture. Through image sensors and monitoring devices, practitioners can
monitor crop growth in real-time, facilitating timely measures against pests and diseases.
Among these data sources, agricultural producers can gain in-depth insights into critical elements such
as land, weather, and plants, enabling better production planning and decision-making. The high-quality
collection of this data forms the foundation of smart agriculture, laying the groundwork for subsequent big
data analysis and applications.
The diversity of data sources allows agricultural producers to comprehensively understand the conditions
of farmland, and scientifically formulate planting plans, and agricultural schedules. By fully utilizing modern
sensors and monitoring technologies, agricultural producers can not only increase production efficiency but
also achieve precise monitoring of the agricultural production environment. This not only helps improve
crop yield and quality but also contributes to reducing resource waste and environmental pollution. Therefore,
a deep understanding of data sources in agricultural production promotes the development of smart
agriculture, achieving a more sustainable and efficient agricultural production model.

2.2. Big data collection technologies
The successful application of big data in smart agriculture relies on efficient big data collection
technologies. Firstly, sensor technology plays a crucial role in agricultural data collection. Various sensors,
such as soil sensors, weather sensors, and image sensors, can monitor and collect multidimensional data in
real-time from the agricultural production environment. The widespread use of these sensors enables
agricultural producers to accurately obtain key information, such as soil nutrient content, weather conditions,
and plant growth status, providing real-time and comprehensive data support for smart agriculture. Secondly,
satellite remote sensing technology is also a significant means of big data collection. Through satellite remote
sensing, agricultural producers can obtain land information over a broader area, including land use conditions
and vegetation indices. This remote monitoring technology provides a more comprehensive and efficient
means of data collection for larger-scale farmland. Additionally, advanced agricultural machinery is
equipped with various sensors, enabling automatic monitoring of the agricultural production process, and
facilitating the real-time generation of data.
With the support of big data collection technologies, the acquisition of agricultural data no longer relies
on traditional manual collection or single-channel data sources but is achieved through automated and
intelligent means, enabling large-scale, real-time, and comprehensive data collection.
Building an efficient big data collection and management system is a prerequisite for the implementation

development of big data collection technologies, attention should be paid not only to the means of data

3. Big data analysis techniques
3.1. Data cleaning and processing
In the application of big data in smart agriculture, data cleaning and processing are crucial steps to ensure
data quality and usability. Firstly, data cleaning involves filtering, removing outliers, and filling in missing
values in the collected raw data to ensure accuracy and completeness. In agricultural data, environmental
factors and limitations of sensor equipment may introduce noise or outliers, and data cleaning effectively
enhances the credibility of the data. Secondly, data processing involves manipulating, organizing, and
calculating cleaned data to obtain higher-level information. In smart agriculture, data processing includes
using statistical methods, machine learning algorithms, etc., to extract valuable information from massive
data, such as crop growth trends, and pest predictions, providing scientific support for agricultural decisionmaking.
The effectiveness of data cleaning and processing is directly related to the reliability of subsequent data
analysis and applications. Through standardized data cleaning and processing procedures, practitioners can
obtain more accurate and reliable data, thereby enhancing the scientific and operational aspects of decisionmaking. Additionally, effective data cleaning and processing provide a high-quality data foundation for the
visualization and model building of agricultural big data. Therefore, data cleaning and processing play a
vital role in smart agriculture, laying a solid foundation for the in-depth application of big data.

3.2. Data mining and model building
In smart agriculture, data mining and model building are critical processes for transforming vast
agricultural data into actionable information. Firstly, data mining involves using various algorithms and
techniques to discover potential patterns and rules from extensive agricultural data. This includes operations
like classification, clustering, and association rule mining to extract useful information. For instance, through
data mining, agricultural practitioners can discover the optimal timing for crop growth under specific
meteorological conditions or identify potential factors affecting yields. Secondly, model building is the
construction of mathematical or statistical models based on data mining to better understand and predict the
behavior of agricultural systems. Machine learning algorithms play a crucial role in this process by learning
from historical data to establish predictive models, aiding agricultural decision-makers in making

scientifically sound decisions.
The goal of data mining and model building is to reveal patterns and associations hidden in agricultural
data through in-depth analysis, providing more accurate guidance for agricultural production. By
establishing predictive models, practitioners can better address risks such as climate change and pest
outbreaks, achieving precise management of agricultural production. Additionally, by continuously
optimizing and adjusting models, they can adapt to different environments and conditions, enhancing the
accuracy of predictions. Therefore, data mining and model building provide robust technical support for the
intelligence and sustainable development of smart agriculture.

3.3. Application of machine learning in agriculture
The application of machine learning technology in smart agriculture adds a new dimension to agricultural
decision-making. Firstly, through supervised learning algorithms, machine learning can utilize extensive
historical data to train models, predicting future agricultural trends and production conditions. For example,
machine learning models can be used to forecast crop yields and the probability of pest occurrences,
providing more accurate planting recommendations for agricultural producers. Secondly, unsupervised
learning algorithms play a crucial role in clustering and classification tasks in agriculture. Through clustering
analysis of different plots, plants, or soil types, machine learning helps agricultural practitioners better
understand the heterogeneity of land, providing a basis for precision management. Additionally, the
introduction of reinforcement learning algorithms makes autonomous and intelligent agricultural machinery
possible. Through the learning and adaptability of intelligent farm machinery, more efficient field operations
can be achieved.
The widespread application of machine learning in agriculture not only improves the efficiency of
agricultural production but also injects new vitality into the sustainable development of agriculture. By
continuously optimizing and adjusting models, machine learning technology can adapt to complex
environments such as different weather, land, and plant conditions, providing more personalized and accurate
solutions for agricultural decision-making. This allows agricultural production to better cope with challenges
such as climate change and resource limitations, optimizing resource utilization and driving agriculture
toward a more intelligent and sustainable direction. Therefore, the application of machine learning in
agriculture not only enhances the level of modernization in agriculture but also brings new possibilities for
the sustainable development of the agricultural industry.

4. Role of big data in decision support for agriculture
4.1. Demands for agricultural production decision-making
The demands for decision-making in agricultural production constitute one of the core driving forces
behind the development of smart agriculture. Firstly, with the continuous increase in the global population,

and intelligent. Agricultural producers need to make accurate planting decisions under constantly changing
weather conditions, scientifically allocate resources, and enhance crop yield and quality. Secondly, the
intensification of climate change imposes higher requirements on agricultural production. Irregular rainfall,
extreme weather events, and other factors disrupt traditional agricultural seasons and cycles, necessitating
more flexible adjustments to planting plans and irrigation schemes to adapt to the evolving weather
conditions. Additionally, intensified global market competition requires agricultural producers to finely
adjust the planting structure, engaging in intelligent agricultural production based on market demand.
These challenges and demands drive agricultural producers to seek more scientific and intelligent
decision support. The development of smart agriculture aims to meet the urgent need of agricultural
producers to make scientifically informed decisions by integrating advanced technologies in the face of
constantly changing environments. Smart agriculture not only focuses on improving production efficiency
but also emphasizes ensuring food supply within the framework of sustainable development, enhancing the
adaptability and resilience of agricultural production. Therefore, the demand for decision-making in
agricultural production propels the innovation and application of smart agricultural technologies, providing
robust momentum for the transformation of the agricultural industry.
In summary, the demands for decision-making in agricultural production are increasingly complex and
challenging, compelling agricultural producers to continuously seek more advanced technological means.
Through the introduction of smart agricultural technologies, agricultural producers can better cope with
uncertainties such as climate change and market fluctuations, achieving intelligent and sustainable
development of agricultural production. Thus, the demand for decision-making in agricultural production is
not only the driving force behind the development of smart agriculture but also an urgent requirement for
achieving modernization and sustainable development in agriculture.

4.2. Practical applications of big data in agricultural decision-making
The practical applications of big data in agricultural decision-making have yielded various achievements,
primarily evident in precision agriculture. Through large-scale data collection and analysis, agricultural
producers can obtain more detailed information, such as precise soil details, meteorological data, and plant
growth conditions, enabling precise fertilization and irrigation. This not only improves farmland utilization
efficiency, and reduces waste, but also helps enhance the quality and yield of agricultural products. Secondly,
significant progress has been made in the application of big data in agricultural production planning. By
analyzing historical yields, market demands, and other data, agricultural decision-makers can more
accurately predict future market trends, adjust crop planting structures, and implement more scientifically
informed agricultural production plans. Big data plays a crucial role in pest and disease monitoring and
control, allowing decision-makers to detect and respond to outbreaks earlier, ensuring the stability of

analyzing various data on agricultural production, financial institutions can more comprehensively assess
the operational status of farms, offering more personalized financial services to agricultural producers.
Additionally, big data has extensive applications in logistics and supply chain management. Through realtime monitoring and analysis of logistics data, the transportation, storage, and sale of agricultural products

product circulation.
Overall, the practical applications of big data in agricultural decision-making have profoundly changed
the way agricultural production operates. From precision agriculture to market forecasting, from pest and
disease monitoring to financial services, big data technology provides decision-makers in agriculture with
more comprehensive and accurate information support in different domains. This application not only
enhances the efficiency of agricultural production but also promotes the modernization and sustainable
development of the agricultural industry. Therefore, the practical application of big data in agricultural
decision-making provides agricultural producers with more innovative possibilities, driving the digital
transformation of the agriculture sector.

5. Application of big data in precision agriculture
5.1. Utilization of satellite remote sensing data
The widespread application of satellite remote sensing data provides crucial information support for
agricultural decision-making. Firstly, satellite remote sensing data can offer extensive, high-resolution
surface information in agriculture. Through data captured by satellite sensors, agricultural practitioners can
obtain detailed information about land use, vegetation growth, soil moisture, and more. These data not only
provide a comprehensive spatial perspective for agricultural production but also assist producers in better
understanding and monitoring changes in different land plots. Secondly, time-series analysis of satellite
remote sensing data can track agricultural seasonal changes. By comparing satellite data at different time
points, agricultural decision-makers can understand the dynamic process of plant growth, predict crop
growth cycles, identify potential issues promptly, and take corresponding measures. This is crucial for
planting plans, irrigation management, and pest monitoring.
The utilization of satellite remote sensing data plays a key role in precision agriculture. Through the
comprehensive analysis of multi-source satellite data, agricultural decision-makers can formulate more
intelligent and scientific agricultural strategies. For example, the health of vegetation can be assessed based
on vegetation indices, allowing timely adjustments to fertilization plans. Monitoring soil moisture enables
precise irrigation management. Moreover, satellite remote sensing data can be used to monitor the impact of
natural disasters such as floods and droughts, enabling proactive measures against agricultural disasters.

Therefore, the utilization of satellite remote sensing data not only provides timely and comprehensive
information for agricultural decision-making but also plays an irreplaceable role in improving agricultural
production efficiency and reducing disaster risks.

5.2. Role of drone technology in big data
Drone technology plays an increasingly crucial role in big data applications, especially in the field of
agriculture. Firstly, drones, equipped with various sensors and cameras, can efficiently and rapidly collect
various data in agricultural production. For instance, infrared cameras can be used to monitor crop growth
status, and multispectral sensors can provide useful information such as vegetation indices. This highfrequency, high-resolution data collection allows agricultural decision-makers to have a more comprehensive
understanding of farmland conditions, and promptly identify issues like plant diseases or nutrient
deficiencies. Secondly, drone technology achieves precise monitoring of large-scale farmland. Through
automatic flight and remote sensing technology, drones can cover vast agricultural areas in a short period,
providing detailed geographic information. This offers an efficient means for agricultural practitioners to
better formulate planting plans, and irrigation schemes, enhancing the sustainability and profitability of
agricultural production.
The role of drone technology in big data goes beyond data collection; it extends to supporting big data
analysis and decision-making. By incorporating advanced image processing and computing capabilities,
drones can process and analyze collected data in real-time, providing feedback to agricultural practitioners.
This provides powerful technical support for the development of precision and smart agriculture.
Additionally, drone technology plays a role in agricultural supervision, enabling precise monitoring of
farmland area, and crop planting conditions, contributing to accurate agricultural production supervision.
Therefore, in the era of big data, drone technology provides agriculture with more efficient, precise data
support, propelling agriculture towards digitization and intelligence.

5.3. Application of big data in precision fertilization and irrigation
The application of big data in precision fertilization and irrigation has brought revolutionary changes to
modern agriculture. Firstly, through big data analysis of soil nutrient levels, vegetation indices,
meteorological conditions, and other multidimensional data, agricultural decision-makers can formulate
more precise fertilization plans. Big data technology can monitor soil nutrient levels in real-time, analyze
crop growth status, providing scientifically sound fertilization recommendations. This not only improves the
efficiency of fertilization, reduces resource waste in agricultural production but also helps ensure the quality
of agricultural products. Secondly, the application of big data in irrigation management is equally significant.
Through monitoring soil moisture, meteorological conditions, and other data, big data technology can
intelligently adjust irrigation systems, achieving precise plant irrigation. This precision irrigation not only

promoting sustainable development in agriculture.
The application of big data in precision fertilization and irrigation not only enhances the efficiency of
agricultural production but also has a positive impact on the environment and sustainable agriculture. By
accurately understanding the needs of soil and plants, agricultural decision-makers can reduce unnecessary
use of fertilizers and water resources, lowering the environmental impact of agriculture. This lays the
foundation for the green development of agriculture. Additionally, the application of big data in precision
fertilization and irrigation provides a practical case for agricultural digitization, driving the development of
smart agriculture. Through the integration of big data technology, agricultural production gradually
transitions from experience-driven to data-driven and science-driven, providing more scientific and reliable
support for agricultural decision-making.

6. Conclusions
The application of big data in smart agriculture has already brought profound impacts, providing vast
prospects for the future development of the agricultural sector. Firstly, big data technology has offered a
fresh perspective and tools for agricultural production. Through real-time monitoring and extensive data
analysis, agricultural decision-makers can gain a more comprehensive and accurate understanding of critical
information such as farmland conditions and crop growth status, enabling them to formulate more
scientifically sound decisions. The application of big data not only enhances the efficiency of agricultural
production but also serves as an opportunity for the digital transformation of the agricultural industry.
Secondly, the influence of big data on smart agriculture manifests in various aspects, including precision
agriculture, smart agricultural machinery, and sustainable agriculture. With the support of big data,
agricultural producers can achieve precision fertilization, irrigation, and pest monitoring, thereby increasing
production efficiency. The development of smart agricultural machinery also contributes to more intelligent
and efficient field operations. Additionally, big data provides crucial information support for the sustainable
development of agriculture, assisting decision-makers in better addressing challenges such as climate change
and resource limitations.
In conclusion, looking ahead to the future, with the continuous development and widespread adoption of
big data technology, smart agriculture will usher in even broader development prospects. Future smart
agriculture will emphasize characteristics such as digitization, intelligence, and sustainability. Big data
technology will continue to drive scientific and intelligent decision-making in agriculture, enhancing the
adaptability and resilience of agricultural production. Concurrently, addressing challenges like data security,
quality, and technology accessibility will be essential to promote the healthy development of smart
agriculture. In the future, big data will continue to bring more innovation to agriculture, propelling the
agricultural industry toward greater modernization and sustainability.

In this study, the changes in the chemical and biological characteristics of a grape marc vermicompost during a
two-year production period were studied to determine the time required for completion of the maturation phase
and production of stable vermicompost. Grape marc was added to the surface of a vermireactor monthly for two
years. At the end of the experiment, the resulting vermicompost was 100 cm deep and consisted of layers of fresh
(top) to processed (bottom) grape marc approximately 15, 30, 180, 360, 540 and 720 days old. Several chemical
and biological characteristics were measured in each vermicompost layer at the end of the experiment: the
moisture content; pH; electrical conductivity; organic matter content; total and dissolved carbon content; C:N
ratio; nutrient content; earthworm density; basal respiration; and the activity of 12 enzymes associated with the
carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus and sulfur cycles. The earthworm density increased 30-fold during the two-year
period. In addition, the pH and electrical conductivity as well as the organic matter, total carbon, dissolved
organic nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium and copper contents all decreased, while the calcium, sulfur, zinc and
manganese contents increased. Basal respiration and carboxylesterase, peroxidase and catalase activities were
highest during the ﬁrst 30 days. By contrast, the urease, acid phosphatase, alkaline phosphatase and arylsulfatase activities were greater after 30 days. The major changes in vermicompost occurred during the initial
phase of vermicomposting. However, the chemical and biological characteristics continued to vary during the
maturation phase because of microbial activity. Thus, the quality of vermicompost greatly depended on the
duration of the maturation (conditioning) phase; therefore, it was diﬃcult to determine the time required to
yield a stable product.

1. Introduction
Vermicomposting is an inexpensive, eﬃcient and easily applicable
biotechnological process in which potentially hazardous organic waste
is converted into a high-quality organic fertilizer (Shak et al., 2014; Lim
et al., 2016; Busato et al., 2016; Lv et al., 2016). In the vermicomposting process, earthworms and microorganisms act together to
alter the chemical, physical and biological characteristics of organic
waste, thus generating vermicompost (Domínguez et al., 2010; Lleó
et al., 2013; Gómez-Brandón et al., 2019). The ﬁnal quality of the
vermicompost depends on factors such as the chemical and physical
characteristics of the substrate used to feed the earthworms, the
earthworm species involved, the management practices used and the
length of the conditioning period (Bisen et al., 2011; Domínguez and
Gómez-Brandón, 2013).

⁎

The vermicomposting process can be divided into two phases. The
initial phase, also called the active phase, is characterized by intense
earthworm activity (Lores et al., 2006; Aira et al., 2007; GómezBrandón et al., 2011). During this phase, earthworms process organic
waste by ingesting, fragmenting and reducing the volume of the material and by assimilating readily biodegradable compounds (sugars,
organic acids, proteins, peptides) (Fornes et al., 2012; Domínguez et al.,
2019). Earthworms thus alter the physical and chemical characteristics
and the microbial composition of the substrate (Hanc et al., 2019).
The second maturation (or conditioning) phase of vermicomposting
begins as the earthworms move towards undigested substrate and is
characterized by a predominance of microbial activity in the wormprocessed material (Aira et al., 2007). The intensity and duration of the
maturation phase varies and depends on the characteristics of the active
phase of vermicomposting (Aira and Domínguez, 2008; Domínguez

such as the pH, C:N ratio, total and available contents of nutrients and
toxic elements, microbial biomass and vermicompost enzymatic activity vary continuously throughout the vermicomposting process (Aira
et al., 2007; Romero et al., 2007; Aguiar et al., 2013; Garcia et al.,
2014). These alterations ultimately determine the diﬀerent characteristics of vermicompost processed for diﬀerent lengths of time (Cao
et al., 2016; Khatua et al., 2018).
Studies monitoring the long-term dynamics of the chemical and
biological changes that occur in organic waste during vermicomposting
are scarce. Previous studies have strongly emphasized the role of
earthworms as agents that modify the characteristics of organic waste,
and little attention has been paid to the contribution of microorganisms
during the maturation phase. The aim of the present study was to determine the length of time required to yield mature, chemically and
biologically stable vermicompost from grape marc. With this aim, the
changes in the chemical and biological characteristics of grape marc
substrate during a two-year vermicomposting process were determined.

The organic matter was determined by the weight-loss method in a
muﬄe furnace (Schulte and Hopkins, 1996). The total carbon and nitrogen contents were determined by an elemental analyzer (CHNS-O
EA-1108, Fisons Instruments, USA), and the NH4+ and NO3− contents
were quantiﬁed in a continuous-ﬂow autoanalyzer (Bran+luebbe AA3,
Seal Analytical, Norderstedt, Germany) (Sims et al., 1995). Dissolved
organic carbon (DOC) was determined colorimetrically after moist digestion (K2Cr2O7 and H2SO4) of aliquots of 0.5 M K2SO4 extracts of the
samples (Cabrera and Beare, 1993), and dissolved organic nitrogen
(DON) was calculated as the diﬀerence between the amount of mineral
nitrogen (NH4+ and NO3) and the total extractable nitrogen (TEN)
(Cabrera et al., 1993). The TEN was determined in the same way as the
NO3− was after the addition of potassium persulfate and autoclaving
for 30 min at 121 °C (to oxidize the nitrogen to NO3−). To determine
the DOC, the potassium persulfate extracts were added to 0.16 M potassium dichromate, concentrated H2SO4 and 6% barium chloride (m/
v), after which the mixture was incubated for 30 min at 160 °C. After
24 h, the supernatant was removed, and the sample was analyzed in a
spectrophotometer at a wavelength of 590 nm.
The pH and electrical conductivity (CM35, Crison Instruments,
Barcelona, Spain) were determined in a 1:10 vermicompost:water suspension. The moisture content was determined by the gravimetric
method (Gardener, 1986). The phosphorus, potassium, boron, calcium,
copper, iron, magnesium, manganese, zinc and sulfur contents were
determined from extracts of dried samples subjected to nitric-perchloric
digestion; the contents were measured by an atomic-absorption spectrometer (Varian SpectrAA-250 Plus, Varian Inc., Walnut Creek, CA,
USA) according to the USEPA 3050B method. The available Olsen P
content was determined according to the methods of Olsen et al.
(1954).
The earthworm population was sampled with the same cylinder
(7.5 cm diameter × 12 cm height) at the end of the experiment and in
the upper layers of the vermireactor (the deeper layers did not contain
any worms or cocoons). The earthworms were classiﬁed as adults or
juveniles, and the number of cocoons and the biomass of the individuals
were quantiﬁed.
The microbial activity was determined by measuring the rate of CO2
evolution from 5 g (fresh weight) subsamples during a 6-hour incubation period. The evolved CO2 was trapped in 0.02 M NaOH and subsequently measured by titration with HCl to a phenolphthalein endpoint after the addition of excess BaCl2 (Anderson, 1982).
The 12 enzymes considered were associated with the carbon cycle

phosphorus cycle (alkaline and acid phosphatase), the sulfur cycle
(arylsulfatase) and antioxidative capability and microbial activity
(peroxidase, laccase and catalase). The enzymatic activities were determined according to the methods of Sánchez-Hernandez et al. (2015).

2. Materials and methods
2.1. Substrate and earthworms
White grape marc (Vitis vinifera cv. Albariño) was obtained from the
Terras Gauda winery in Pontevedra (Galicia, northwestern Spain) and
stored in cold rooms at approximately −4 °C until needed. The chemical and physical characteristics of the fresh grape marc used are
listed in Table 1. The earthworm species Eisenia andrei was used for
vermicomposting. The initial population density in the vermireactor
was 297 ± 20 individuals m−2, which consisted of 82.25 ± 16 mature earthworms m−2 and 215 ± 37 juveniles m−2, and there were
63 ± 18 cocoons m−2; the mean earthworm biomass was
58.4 ± 15 g m−2.
2.2. Vermireactor and experimental design
The experiment was conducted in a vertical deposition vermireactor
housed in greenhouse facilities belonging to the University of Vigo
(Vigo, northwestern Spain). The vermireactor consisted of a metallic
container (length of 1.5 m, width of 4 m, depth of 1 m and volume of 6
m3) ﬁtted with a dark cover. At the beginning of the two-year experiment, a basal layer of vermicompost (depth of 10 cm) that served as a
bed for the earthworms was placed in the empty vermireactor. A plastic
mesh (5 mm Ø) was placed on top of the basal layer (to prevent fresh
plant material from becoming mixed with the processed vermicompost), and approximately 150 kg of grape marc (depth of 6 cm) was
placed on top of the mesh. The grape marc was added monthly during
the two-year period as successive layers on the surface of the vermireactor. Thus, at the ﬁnal sampling time, the vermireactor contained a
layer of vermicompost with a depth of 100 cm, comprising layers of
fresh (top) to processed (bottom) grape marc approximately 15, 30,
180, 360, 540 and 720 days old (Fig. 1). The vermicompost in the reactor was watered daily with an automatic watering system to prevent
drying.
2.3. Sample collection
After 720 days, samples were collected from each of the layers,
corresponding to the diﬀerent stages of vermicomposting. To collect the
samples, the vermireactor was divided into 12 sections, each with a
surface area of 0.5 m2. In each section, one sample was obtained from
each of the six layers of vermicompost with a cylindrical sampler
(7.5 cm diameter × 12 cm height), for a total of 72 samples. The
samples were stored in plastic containers at −20 °C until chemical and
biological analyses.

2.5. Statistical analysis
The normality of the data was examined using the Shapiro-Wilk test
(p < 0.05). The nutrient and toxic metal contents were square roottransformed to fall within the normal distribution. A one-way ANOVA
followed by a Tukey test for pairwise comparisons of the means
(p < 0.05) was used to test the eﬀect of the vermicomposting production period on chemical and biological characteristics. These characteristics were subjected to a Pearson correlation analysis (p < 0.05)
in order to verify the relationships between them. To check the quality
and to better visualize the correlation, a principal component analysis
(PCA) was performed using the STATISTICA 7 program.

3.3. Chemical characteristics of the vermicompost
At the end of the two-year study period, most of the chemical
characteristics of the vermicompost were altered (Table 1). The main
changes in chemical characteristics occurred in the period between 0
and 30 days during the initial vermicomposting phase, especially within
the ﬁrst 15 days (Table 1). Among the 22 characteristics evaluated, 18
varied by > 18.82% (considering the potassium content) during the
initial phase, and only four characteristics varied by < 5.87% (considering the moisture content).
The chemical characteristics varied less during the maturation
phase than during the initial phase. Nonetheless, the values of some of
these characteristics widely varied, including the electrical conductivity
(−30.74%), DOC content (−30.79%), NH4+ content (−40.24%),
NO3− content (+39.13%), phosphorus content (−40.82%), and others
(Table 1). These changes were mediated mainly by the microorganisms,
as little-to-no earthworm activity occurred during the maturation
phase.
Relative to the values measured in the initial vermicomposting
period, the following characteristics decreased signiﬁcantly over time:

microorganisms only and not earthworms), from day 30 to day 720.

4. Discussion
Although high rates of earthworm reproduction have also been
observed in other studies (Monroy et al., 2006; Martínez-Cordeiro et al.,
2013; Domínguez et al., 2014; Domínguez et al., 2016), the increase
observed in the present study was markedly high for this type of substrate. In a previous study by Domínguez et al. (2014) on grape marc
substrate, the initial density of earthworms was approximately
300 m−2 but increased by slightly more than twofold within 70 days
(~700 individuals m−2); however, the density decreased after 112 days
(~600 individuals m−2) as the availability of food decreased. The authors demonstrated that when food was readily available, the E. andrei
population doubled every six months and increased by approximately
50% within the ﬁrst 15 days. The ﬁndings of the present study are
consistent with previous ﬁndings, as the increase in the earthworm
population can be explained by the monthly additions of substrate.
E. andrei requires an environment rich in organic matter to survive
and reproduce (Martínez-Cordeiro et al., 2013; García-Sánchez et al.,
2017). The conditions in the vermireactor were optimal for survival and
reproduction of the earthworms, as the moisture content, temperature
and quality of the organic waste were adequate (Yadav and Garg,
2016). The moisture content remained constant throughout the layers
of vermicompost (~80% moisture), demonstrating the eﬃciency of the
system in controlling this characteristic both at and below the surface.
According to Domínguez et al. (2014), a substrate moisture content
close to 85% is optimal for earthworm survival.
During the ﬁrst 30 days of vermicomposting, the earthworms rapidly degraded the grape marc, with consequent increases in nitrogen,
phosphorus, calcium, magnesium, sulfur, boron, copper, zinc, iron and
manganese contents. In addition, the physical and chemical changes to
the grape marc due to the feeding activity of the earthworms stimulated
microbial activity, which also helped to degrade the organic waste.
Signiﬁcant reductions in microbial activity and nutrient contents were
observed during the maturation phase (i.e., after 30 days of vermicomposting). The microbial activity probably decreased because of the
lower activity of the earthworms, considering that the fresh waste had
already been consumed and that more recalcitrant organic material was
present in the vermireactor. The reduction in the total or available
contents of most nutrients during the maturation phase can be explained by immobilization of the nutrients in the earthworm and microorganism biomass or sorption by the vermicompost. However, the
increases in calcium, magnesium, sulfur, zinc and manganese contents
were probably due to a shrinkage eﬀect as the mass of the waste decreased (Lv et al., 2016).
Signiﬁcant changes in most of the evaluated chemical parameters
occurred during the maturation phase, although there was no earthworm activity in the older layers. The microbial activity continued,
albeit at a low level, and gradually altered the chemical characteristics.
In addition, owing to the humiﬁcation of organic matter, chemical
compounds such as functional groups (e.g., carboxylic and phenolic
groups) were generated and reacted with the various substances present
in the vermicompost, thus further altering the dynamics of availability
of many chemical elements (Dores-Silva et al., 2013).

3.4. 3.4 Biological characteristics of the vermicompost
Microbial activity decreased greatly during the two years of vermicomposting (Fig. 2). CO2 production was highest (p < 0.001,
CV = 31.74%) within the ﬁrst 30 days, followed by a sharp decrease
until 360 days, after which it remained low.
The enzymes displaying the highest activity within the ﬁrst 30 days
included the carboxylesterases (p = 0.005 for NA and p = 0.0184 for
NPB), protease (p = 0.0272), peroxidase (p = 0.006) and catalase (p =
0.0013) (Fig. 3). The ﬁrst three are involved in breaking down organic
compounds, and the last two are associated with antioxidative and
cellular activity. These results correspond to the microbial activity
evaluated by basal respiration, which was greater at the beginning of
vermicomposting than later during vermicomposting (Fig. 2).
The urease, acid phosphatase, alkaline phosphatase and arylsulfatase activities increased after 30 days (Fig. 3). These enzymes are
involved in breaking down organic compounds, indicating that biochemical changes in organic matter continued to occur during the
maturation phase. The β-glucosidase, arginine deaminase and laccase
activities did not vary signiﬁcantly during the vermicomposting process.

Lakshmi et al. (2014), as vermicomposting progresses, the availability
of carbon compounds to microorganisms decreases, reﬂecting the reduction in microbial biomass and, in turn, urease activity.
Alkaline phosphatase activity was greater in the intermediate period
of vermicomposting (30 to 360 days), during which there was relatively
high substrate availability and appropriate pH for activity. The high pH
and the high available phosphorus content (Olsen P) in the initial layers
in the vermireactor led to a decrease in acid phosphatase activity
(Fernández-Gómez et al., 2010). The activity of this enzyme was greater
after 180 days of vermicomposting, when the vermicompost was more
mature, which favors phosphatase activity (García-Sánchez et al.,
2017).
Arylsulfatase activity increased after 180 days of vermicomposting
when there was greater availability of organic esters containing sulfate
(high Stotal). Arylsulfatase is inhibited by a high concentration of boron
(Khafaji and Tabatabai, 1979), which was observed at the beginning of
vermicomposting. The boron content decreased after 180 days, which
may have allowed greater arylsulfatase activity.
The peroxidase and catalase enzymes behaved similarly, as the activity of both was high in the initial phase but decreased as the vermicompost matured. These enzymes are involved in oxidative stress
and are produced in greater amounts as microbial metabolism accelerates. In addition, the generation of reactive oxygen species increases
in the presence of excess copper (Cabiscol et al., 2000), as observed in
the initial layers of vermicompost. Liu et al. (2012) reported that
earthworms cause an increase in catalase activity in vermicompost as a
result of their own activity or by favoring microbial activity.
The ﬁndings demonstrate that vermicomposting in a vertical deposition vermireactor greatly increased the earthworm density and that
the vermicomposting process altered the chemical and biological
characteristics of the vermicompost, which was derived from plant
waste. The action of the high density of earthworms led to an increase
in microbial activity, with increases in the activity of some enzymes at
the beginning of the vermicomposting process (in the original wormprocessed material), further degrading the grape marc. Consequently,
the contents of organic matter, carbon, dissolved and total nitrogen and
some nutrients increased. The ﬁnal quality of the vermicompost depends on the intensity of the active phase. However, signiﬁcant changes
in the chemical and biological characteristics of the vermicompost also
occurred during the relatively long maturation phase. Owing to the
absence of earthworms and the humiﬁcation of organic matter during
this phase, the microbial activity was low but continuously and gradually altered the chemical characteristics. Thus, the quality of the
vermicompost depended on the length of the maturation phase because
of alterations in chemical and biological characteristics during the twoyear vermicomposting process.

The copper content was greater in the vermicompost than in fresh grape

copper content decreased during the maturation phase, probably because of strong adsorption of the metal to organic matter promoted by

Earthworms accelerate the decomposition of grape marc, which in
turn causes high microbial activity (measured as basal respiration) at
the beginning of the process of vermicomposting followed by a decrease
in the mature phase (Soobhany et al., 2015b). From 30 days onwards, a
decrease in microbial activity occurred because of the reduced availability of labile carbon compounds (Huang et al., 2013; Soobhany et al.,
2015a). This ﬁnding was reﬂected in the enzymatic activity within the
vermicompost. Regarding the enzymes involved in the carbon cycle, the
carboxylesterase activity decreased after 30 days of vermicomposting.
These enzymes are serine hydrolases and are very important with respect to the environment, as they are involved in the detoxiﬁcation of
anticholinesterase pesticides (organophosphorus and methylcarbamate). The activity of microbial carboxylesterases increases in the
presence of earthworms (Sanchez-Hernandez et al., 2014), as observed
in the present study, in which the highest activity of these enzymes was
observed in the layer with the highest density of earthworms
(< 30 days).
Regarding the enzymes involved in the nitrogen cycle, only protease
and urease activities changed with vermicomposting time. The protease
activity increased because of the greater amount of plant waste available during the ﬁrst 30 days of the vermicomposting process, which
resulted in an increase in NH4+ content (Aira et al., 2007). The urease
activity increased as the NH4+ content decreased (180 days) but then

5. Conclusions
The grape marc rapidly degraded during the initial phase of vermicomposting (< 30 days) due to the intense activity of the earthworms and microorganisms. The changes caused by microorganisms
during the maturation phase continued to signiﬁcantly alter the vermicompost, making it impossible to determine the length of time required to produce a chemically mature and biologically stable vermicompost.

 Abstract
Thousands of academic articles have been written about the various facets of the
Internet of Things (IoT). Added to those are books of multiple flavors, conference
proceedings, and a host of web-based content authored by a diverse cast of IoT
community constituents. While there are many examples of successful IoT application
solutions, participating technologies and how best to use them, are still relatively
immature. These solutions are complex, geographically diverse, incorporate a broad
spectrum of ever-evolving technologies that allow organizations to gather new data,
create new value and do new things they haven’t been able to do effectively before.
Despite the promise, excitement, and future thinking that leads organizations to
pursue IoT projects, many of those projects have fallen short of original expectations.
Too many projects fail, never making it past the pilot stage for many reasons. Authors
elsewhere have written and are continuing to write about those IoT experiences, so
they are not addressed in this paper. Instead, this paper looks at three critical data
issues arising from the deployment of IoT solutions: 1. The magnitude of data being
collected and stored from IoT solutions, and challenging if all such data is necessary;
2. How little of this data is actually being used and why; and 3. The concerns held
by many users about poor data quality, what causes it, and what can be done about
it. At the heart of every IoT solution are multitudes of sensors of all shapes, sizes,
and purposes. It becomes apparent that sensors may be the largest source of data
defects that when unresolved contribute significantly to poor solution data quality.
To better understand this premise, this paper looks at the challenges inherent in
sensor-generated data and possible approaches for mitigating its impact.

Introduction
The evolving quest for incremental organizational value is a primary driver for implementing sensor-driven solutions. Pursuit of value; new capabilities; better performance; reduced operating costs; optimized operations; better customer experience;
some may not even know...Value may be perceived or manifested in so many ways.
The technology propelling this growth is the Internet of Things, or IoT, and
encompasses the billions of devices worldwide connecting directly or indirectly to
the Internet. These devices communicate machine to machine, passing multitudes
of diverse data types and formats at widely varying speeds between them. Since
the introduction of the Internet and the World Wide Web in the 1980s and 1990s,
the drivers of growth have been applications, services, and data aimed at allowing
humans to seek out and find information and content in which they have an interest.
This activity continues to grow at compounded rates each year and remains central
to the overall growth of the Internet.
The IoT is one of the core evolving technologies built around the developing universe of sensor-based devices that can measure finite physical events and conditions,
convert those readings to data that is shared with other devices to make selected
adjustments in the physical environment, and then store that data as prescribed so
that it can be made available to authorized data consumers for their use and analysis. This data is stored in data warehouses, clouds, lakes, ponds, and "puddles,"and
is accumulating at astounding rates.
With the advent of increasingly smaller and more capable microchip sets in the late

1

 1990s, industrial innovators began to focus on the development of digitally-enabled
sensors and controllers to replace their long-established analog predecessors wherever
they might be. While the early transitions encountered many obstacles and challenges, these became the digital ancestors of the billions of such devices that today
comprise the IoT.
One of the primary defining characteristics of IoT devices is that they communicate with other like and supporting devices through machine-to-machine connections.
Another defining characteristic is that each type of device is designed for a particular
set of one or more functions or tasks and generates real-time data attendant to its
intended purpose. The number of devices comprising the IoT is increasing at an
extraordinary rate. The IoT is the market and technology supergroup of segments
that include Industrial IoT, Industry 4.0, Internet of Systems, and other less pervasive variants centered around machine-to-machine (M2M), sensor, radio, audio, and
video devices that generate data that traverses private and public networks. Component networks include a wide variety of power and bandwidth ranges, protocols, and
transport technologies.
Through evolution and continuing innovation, the scope of what these devices
can do, as well as how effectively they do it, has brought them to today’s smart
devices that are more intelligent, faster, cheaper, and more capable than ever. This
rapid-paced evolution is expected to continue at least through the new decade. IoT
devices include the sensors/actuators, the controllers they talk to, and the objects
of which they are a part. Their respective physical sizes, designs, and operating
configurations are tailored to their specific roles, locations, and environments in which
they are intended to operate. They may be small enough to operate in finite Nanospaces, or large enough to survive in hostile industrial operating conditions. An IoT
device intended to perform a specific set of functions or tasks in one particular set of
circumstances may look and operate very differently than a like device in a different

2

 set of circumstances. While some IoT devices may communicate directly to other
devices connected to the Internet, most don’t. In many implementations, IoT devices
belong to a closed network that includes a gateway that manages that connection to
the Internet. And the solution community is struggling on many fronts to manage
semi-structured data across a controlled infrastructure. The challenges are likely to

2.1

Defining Data Quality

While much has been written about data quality, there is no clear agreement about
what it is, how it should be measured, and how it should be managed. The perspective
of what data quality is varies by context and the interests of its primary stakeholders.
Most agree that data: 1. should be of sufficient value to justify the expense and effort
to collect it; 2. should deliver what it is expected to represent; and 3. should be of
sufficiently good quality that it is readily usable and trustworthy by all interested
consumers. While many efforts are underway to reach an agreement all can adopt,
as of this writing, there is still no universally accepted standard for defining data
quality, but there is a significant degree of commonality of concepts to which nearly
all authors about the subject seem to agree.
The concept of data quality actually describes two sides of the same coin. One
side is about supply, defining the manner in which a physical entity or event will
be represented in digital form. Here, the term data quality describes the conceptual
framework around how well data attributes have been defined and captured to reliably
portray a physical entity or event it is all intended to represent at a particular moment
in time. When every attribute and data characteristic accurately and completely
represents that physical entity or event as intended, the data is deemed to be of high
quality and can be used confidently as a digital proxy for that entity at the particular
moment of time. In contrast, data is deemed to be of lower quality as the data is
increasingly less able to serve as that reliable digital proxy for that entity or event
due to error, missing or incorrect values, corruption, and so on.[7]
The other side of the coin is about demand. Here, the term, data quality, asserts
the degree to which a data consumer can confidently use this particular data to satisfy
specific needs and requirements–that it is fit to meet their purpose. Data deemed to
8

 be higher quality should meet their purpose more effectively than lower quality data
that as it degrades, at some point will be unable to meet their purpose.
A serious point of tension that is often ignored or unrecognized in this assessment
of fitness for purpose, is the presumption by many that what is defined and provided
on the supply side is fully consistent with requirements and needs of all potential
data consumers and stakeholders representing the demand side. That is, that they
all are happy with what is being produced. This is very often NOT the case. In too
many cases, decisions are made around what the supply-side data product is going
to contain, how it will function, what data validation and formatting rules will be
used, and what might be stored in the metadata file, all without ever talking with
their community of potential or probable consumers and stakeholders. Meanwhile,
members of that community have requirements and needs that they can only assume
will be met in the data produced. And they are very often disappointed.
So, the story around data quality is very much like the story of the Ford Edsel
in the late 1950s. At that time, Ford Motor Company was looking for a new breakthrough model that would set the company apart from the rest of the industry and on
a new path of market success. Ford engineers went to great lengths to develop a car
with sleek lines, plenty of power, new features, and quality parts and craftsmanship.
Ford invested considerable sums in retooling their production lines and parts inventories in preparation for the Edsel’s market and production launch. Unfortunately, sales
of the new Edsel were dismal, far below even their worst expectations. They did not
understand what went wrong. Here clearly was a well-engineered automobile, that
was roomy, comfortable, powerful, and demonstrating the finest craftsmanship. Why
weren’t people buying it? Fundamentally, the car was ugly and hit the market just as
the industry was moving away from big heavy cars in favor of slightly smaller, lighter,
sportier, and less expensive models. No one wanted it. They wanted something very
different. So it is with data quality. It only is achieved when the supply-side data

9

 product delivers effectively what the demand-side community wants in the manner
that they need it and can use it.[3]

2.2

Big Data Characterizations

Big data brings an added set of dimensions to the challenge of good data quality. A
substantial portion of the data in the big data universe comes from sensors in the IoT.
Laney [44] originally proposed three "V" characteristics to describe the important
challenges driven by Big Data. Since then, many authors have proposed various
numbers of combinations of these and other such characteristics, including several
that have limited application in the discussion of IoT impacts.[58] [52] [57] [59] [67]
The most common and most applicable to the quality of data accumulating from IoT
solution sensors are these:
• Value - This is where it all starts and where it all ends. Value should serve as a
constant reminder that data is only truly useful if it is worth collecting and is
of sufficient good quality that it successfully fulfills its intended purpose. There
is no merit in investing in an IoT solution if the data it creates isn’t sufficiently
useful in providing the intended value.
• Volume - It is the volume of data that makes it Big Data. The IoT creates enormous amounts of data, quantum levels more than ever before. The challenge
this creates is that many of the more traditional methods of data quality improvement are now more difficult if not fully impracticable because they don’t
scale enough to accommodate the challenges of massive stores of data. Any
data set that is typically larger than what a single machine can effectively handle is generally considered Big Data. In this environment data is stored and
processed in blocks across multiple machines.

10

 • Velocity - Velocity is the measure of how quickly data is created, processed and
made available to consumers. Higher velocities compress real-time processing
cycle times and influence where such processing is done. Velocity also relates
to latency. Lower latency demands require processing to be done nearer to the
creation point.
• Validity - Validity asserts that all acceptable values and formats are consistent with the rules that have been prescribed for given data records and attributes. Because of data volume and volatility, machine learning processes and
algorithms, and statistical methods may be used more frequently confirm data
validity.
• Volatility - Volatility measures how long data remains useful. This can be
critical because the active life of certain data instances may be very short coming
from IoT sensors due to the frequency of data observations which can be made
as often as 5-10 per second (for example).
• Variety - Each IoT sensor type generates data in its own format and content.
Many are functionally related to others for context, synchronization, and data
preparation processing.
• Veracity - The magnitude of the data being processed and stored brings newer
challenges on multiple fronts. Veracity provides the assurance that data is
consistently and reliably what it is represented to be and that consumers and
stakeholders can trust the facilities, infrastructure, and processes that carried
the data from its point of origin to its point of consumption.

2.3

Dimensions of Data Quality

Just as there are many views around varying aspects of Big Data, there are likewise
many perspectives on how to characterize and measure it. Like a fine diamond, data
11

 quality has many facets or dimensions that help describe it. Many authors have
written many papers summarizing, explaining, defining, and extolling various lists
of such dimensions as they might apply in various contexts. A systematic scoping
review of the literature suggests that data quality dimensions and methods with real
world data are not consistent in the literature, and as a result, quality assessments
are challenging due to the complex and heterogeneous nature of these data.[9] [58]
[16] [17] [18] [32] [33] [35] [41] [59] [64] [65] [67]
However, in 2021, the work group Data Quality of DAMA Netherlands carried out
research into definitions of dimensions of data quality. It collected definitions from
various sources and compared them with each other. The working group also tested
the definitions against criteria derived from a standard for concepts and definitions:
ISO 704. The result is a list of 60 dimensions of data quality and its definitions.
Going forward, wide adoption of this definition standard should provide an authoritative reference upon which future assessments and discussions can be based, as well
as providing a framework against which the plethora of author-created lists can be
rationalizeddama21.
Selected from some of those lists, the dimensions that follow appear to be most
applicable to characterizing data generated by sensors and subsequently processed
by IoT application solutions. Each dimension here is described as it is expected to
be under the best of circumstances, or at least widely prevailing "normal" conditions.
But outages occur, devices fail, errors happen, data is lost or becomes defective,
communications channels get congested, and any number of like incidents can arise
that can impact data in various ways. As a result, questions about "something less"
need to be considered and are suggested here for further thought.[61] [28]
• Accuracy - Data is a faithful, reliable, and correct depiction of the actual entity
(e.g. person, place, event, or object), property, or condition it is expected to
represent. It should be readily verifiable through direct comparison to the real
12

 thing or other reliable data source. Questions:Does every attribute need to be
exactly what it is expected to be, to be useful? Which attributes cannot be
inaccurate in any way? Can some attributes be less accurate than others? How
inaccurate can each attribute be to be sufficiently representative and acceptably
useful? What is the impact on actions taken, analyses performed, and decisions
made using records containing inaccurate attributes?
• Completeness - All expected attributes about the entity are fully captured in
the data elements specified to represent them. Each data element is populated as intended based on specific or historical knowledge establishing what
should be captured, the format it should take, and the values or value ranges
that best represent the entity characteristic. When defined, data attributes
are usually deemed mandatory, variable, or optional and are expected to be
populated accordingly. All intended data attributes representing the specific
entity constitute a record. All intended records constitute a data set or file.
Any number of methods may be used to determine the level of completeness
and non-compliance, and to insert or replace selected values outside what is intended using historical profiles. Questions: Which mandatory attributes must
be complete to allow the record to be used? Which mandatory attributes can
be unpopulated with little to no consequence? What is the impact on actions
taken, analyses performed, and decisions made using records containing important but incomplete attributes?
• Consistency - Each instance of a particular data element is populated using
the same format, value or range of values, and validation rules as every other
instance of that same data element. All of the intended data attributes for
each record instance are expected to be the same. And all like records are
expected to be the same within data sets or files. And further, subsequent data

13

 sets or files containing records relating to the same entity and entity instances
are expected to be the same as earlier data sets or files for the same entity
and entity instances. Measures of consistency can be determined by comparing
randomly selected instances of like records, and against historical profiles of
that particular record type. Questions: Do consistency expectations apply
to all attributes or only to selected ones? To what extent can patterns vary
without degrading or negating the usefulness of the impacted records? To what
extent might such discrepancies impact actions taken, analyses performed, and
decisions made using records containing inconsistently populated attributes?
• Integrity - The concept that "it’s all there", with no corruption at any level: no
garbage or lost elements in one or more records, no garbage or lost records in
a data sets or files, hashes are accurate and intact, and relationships between
data elements, records and files are also fully intact and correct. Questions:
If such issues are discovered, how might they impact actions taken, analyses
performed, and decisions made? How large of a gap between the good data
can needed actions tolerate, analytical computations mitigate, and decisions
accommodate?
• Reasonability - While not as specific or clear as other data quality measures,
reasonability questions if the depicted data and records make sense. Are the
values and relationships what they should be? Do the patterns seen in the data
fit similar patterns derived from historical data? Such measures tend to be
subjective are contextual based upon the nature of what the data represents.
Questions: What are the boundaries of reason beyond which data can’t or
shouldn’t be used? How might those boundaries be defined?
• Timeliness - The measurement of data timeliness must be considered within
the context of its volatility, or rate of change. Data that changes infrequently is
14

 considered static and is usually not subject to this dimension of measurement.
Data not considered static is considered volatile. As the rate of change (rate of
refresh by newer data) increases, there is less time to use the current instance.
In higher volatility situations, the current data needs to be evaluated and acted
upon before the next instance arrives. There must be time between the two
instances to allow this. To do so, the time between when it is created and the
time it becomes available to be used (latency) must be as short as possible.
Questions: What is the impact on operational and analytical continuity if the
timely regular flow of particular data streams are disrupted? What is the impact
of too much data at one time? What is the impact of large gaps? What is the
impact of streams getting out of sequence? What is the impact of flows slower
or faster than expected?
• Validity - Essential to both consistency and reasonability, validity measures the
extent to which data attributes have the values they are expected to have, are
formatted correctly, and have the level of precision specified. Validity rules are
specific to particular data attributes. Certain attributes are assigned values
matching entries in lists of acceptable choices specified for that attribute wherever it may be used. Value choices may or may not be driven by values assigned
to other attributes using specified conditional rules. For example, attribute A
may be assigned a value within the integer range of 0-5. Attribute B is conditionally assigned a textual value selected from a table based on the value in
attribute A. Other examples include ensuring that: a textual value representing
a phone number is formatted a specified way; a numeric value representing a
unit price is formatted and computed to three decimal places; or a numeric value
representing atmospheric temperature is shown as degrees Fahrenheit formatted to one tenth of a degree and within the range +/-150 degrees. Questions:
Which attributes must follow their respective formatting and validation rules
15

 without exception to be acceptable and useful? Which attributes can be allowed to have values that violate formatting and validation rules? What is the
impact on actions taken, analyses performed, and decisions made using records
containing attributes with validation or formatting rule violations?

2.4

Metadata

In 2015, McKinsey Consultants estimated that data consumers spend 65% or more
of their time, trying to find the data they need, discovering where the data has come
from, learning about what issues have been identified since the data was created,
assessing what treatment has been applied to the data to this point, and determining
what else may need to be done to the data set or file to get it to a state where they
can actually use it.
Good metadata is a critical component of good data quality, particularly for Big
Data files and data sets originating from sensor-generated data streams in the Internet
of Things. Metadata should be a close companion to every data set, file and stream
as it is created or updated. It should be subject to a similar level of quality standards
as the data it describes. Good metadata should be able to tell an interested consumer
just about anything that needs to be known about the data set or file. In IoT world,
metadata is particularly essential to track the journey of each new data stream as
it is processed and ingested into the Big Data data stores where it will come to rest
while it awaits further processing or analysis by stakeholder data consumers. The
goals of the IoT technosphere is for all important aspects of any architecture and
application solution be automated to provide humanless assessments, controls and
event information through machine-machine interaction.
Like the data itself, comparable standards and practices should be in place for
establishing and maintaining metadata. Event journaling and core documentation
creation should be embedded in the data set, file, or stream metadata file at ap16

 propriate action and control points throughout application solution coding to ensure
that necessary information is included every step of the way and easily accessed by
every user authorized to learn about and access it.

IoT Sensor Quality Challenges
There are IoT devices of every shape, size, technology, purpose, and environment.
Functionally, they can be grouped into a few general categories that include sensors,
actuators, and controllers.
3.0.1

Sensors

The role of the sensor is to monitor and capture data related to its intended purpose,
and pass it along to other IoT devices, or place it directly on the Internet for downstream processing. They may be used singularly or in combination to provide more
robust perceptions of particular situations at specific moments in time. Typically,
sensors have passed their data to connected controllers for evaluation and indicated
action. Increasingly, sensors are being built with their own limited computational
and data evaluation capabilities. This allows them to operate more autonomously
and act more quickly when circumstances suggest. For example, a sensor may determine that ambient light levels have decreased below an established threshold, and
then acts to turn lights on. It may also interact with proximate motion sensors and
clocking sensors to determine when or if those lights should be turned off.
There are several categories of sensors that include the following:
• Mechanical sensors measure both static and dynamic forces of movement in the
physical world. Examples include accelerometers, gyroscopes, inclinometers,
scales, and touch.

18

 • Geospatial sensors ascertain where objects are in physical space including altitude and orientation, and are frequently associated with many types of mechanical and environmental sensors. These often are considered the core of a
wide variety of sensor packages used by many government agencies, scientific
research, and higher education for their observations of land, water, and, air
conditions around the world.
• Environmental sensors monitor physical conditions proximate to their respective location. Examples include temperature, humidity, pressure, light, sound,
motion, proximity, altitude, attitude, direction, location, and imaging. In many
respects, some of these may be used singularly or in combination to emulate
the human senses of sight, sound, and sensations.
• Chemical sensors detect the presence or absence of targeted chemical and biological substances and conditions. In many ways, they emulate the human
senses of taste and smell, but to a much greater degree. Examples include air
and water quality, smoke, gas detectors, and substance detection, to name a
few.
• Medical sensors are all designed to monitor and collect data regarding the many
aspects of the human body. Examples include heart rate, pulse, temperature,
blood glucose, and oxygenation level, neural activity and feedback, and respiration rate.
• Radio Frequency Identification Devices (RFID) are designed to enable asset
identification and movement. There are two classes of devices: chip-based tags
containing stored static data and a radio antenna, and readers that receive
the tag radio signal and captures and stores the resident data from the tag.
The reader is considered the sensor and tags are what they sense. There are
