Source: Mouser Electronics (mouser.com/Sensors/)

20

 for a sensor to have as many as twenty or more configuration options. Many just have
one. There are several hundred manufacturers of sensors and related components.
3.0.2

Actuators

The role of the actuator is to initiate a specific change in the environment based on
data coming from sensors, either directly or through associated controller(s). Examples of such changes might include: turning something on or off, increasing or
decreasing speeds, flows, pressures, or temperatures. In many cases, actuators may
create and insert data into the network indicating what actions they initiate and that
it was executed successfully or not. Virtually all of the characteristics of sensors apply
generally to actuators as well.
3.0.3

Controllers

The role of the controller is to take data from sensors, process it, and ultimately
determine if an adjusting action is needed, what actuator(s) need to make those
adjustments and to what extent. The intelligence to make these assessments and
determinations are usually held in the controller. However, increasingly more of the
intelligence is being built into the sensors and activators, as well as incorporating
inter-connectivity that enables them to talk directly with each other and handle routine, and less complex, exceptions without needing to defer farther into the network.
Functionally, any proximate processor can be tasked to perform the needed sensor/actuator processing. Sensors, actuators and controllers are being integrated into
integrated chip packages to reduce latency and overall power consumption. An increasing number of such chip packages are being deployed in newer solutions. Larger
volumes of data, more complex analysis, and time sensitivity is likely to drive demand
for these as they hit the market.

21

 3.1

Sensor Concerns

The world of sensors is vast and influence the design, definition, features and functions
of IoT application solutions with variants aimed at the differences in the environments
within which they will be deployed. Much can be discussed about each aspect of the
chosen architecture, device selection and use, deployment specifications and so on,
but they will not be discussed here.[34] [47] This paper is about how selected characteristics of sensor data and the environments within which they are implemented,
impact the quality of data into and out of IoT application solutions.[66] Some of
common characteristics are introduced and discussed.

3.2

Sensor Data Characteristics

Sensors live in the physical world. Each has a very specific purpose and is so designed.
One specific type of sensor may have many performance variants and be built using
any number of form factors to fit particular needs. An increasing number of sensors
are in micro-electromechanical (MEM) categories may be as small as one millimeter
and are often packaged with similar sized sensors of other types.[6] Environments may
be harsh and hostile towards sensors and related electronics, and can have detrimental
impacts on the quality of the data they create. They are often placed in hard-toreach locations making them difficult to support and maintain. They are built to
communicate be it other sensors, actuators, local controllers, or across a variety of
networks. As the key components of much larger, and often very complex application
solutions within the Internet of Things, the quality and reliability of the data they
generate is intrinsically critical to the overall value of the overall solution of which
they are a part. But, they are vulnerable to a variety of issues that can impact that
data quality and reliability.[26] [61]
Some of the more important characteristics that make this so include:

22

 • Low Cost - The fundamental driver for today’s sensors is having the needed
fundamental functionality at the lowest possible cost. This sets the parameters
within which everything else about sensor design, function, form factor, onboard processing, and storage must come together. Each of the characteristics
that follow in one way or another are controlled by the need to keep costs low.
This has been, and continues to be, a critical success factor for enabling the
design and deployment of IoT application solutions. Because of the quantities of
sensors required to meet solution objectives, manufacturers are concerned that
higher per-unit sensor costs may push solution costs too high to justify and
dampen deployment volumes. As will be discussed further here, manufacturers
are being pressed to improve what they can provide without materially raising
costs.
• Technical Limitations - The form factors of newer generations of sensors are
getting smaller, more digital, and more varied. Lines are more often blurring
between sensor, actuator, and processor functions, and more processing is being
attempted on board. Previous analog functionality is being shifted to digital
when it is expedient and cost effective to do so. And the migration to MEM
architectures and designs is increasing. As a result, there is very limited real
estate available for the actual sensor elements, memory, processor, and power
source. Sensor packages growing increasingly smaller; some are now as small
as a millimeter. Research is being done now on moving several selected sensor
elements and packages into the nano-micro-electromechanical (NEM) range.
Mass-scale deployment economics attempt to keep costs as low as possible,
against the rising pressure to expand on-board functionality and computing
power.
The consequence of all this is that there is limited to no available resource on
most sensors to help resolve the issues that are discussed in this section. But
23

 that may not be case going forward based on the work device manufacturers
are devoting to expand on-board computing, storage, and memory, particularly
in devices that are using hard-wired low-voltage power sources. This trend may
extend to devices not on local power as the needed technologies mature enough
to allow them to do so.
• Power - All sensors need power. Bad things can happen when sensor power
is lost or becomes unstable. Sensors are most likely to stop functioning, or
may function minimally without the level and stability of power needed to do
what it is expected to do. Machines may go down due to the loss of sensor
control. Data production may stop or be delayed. Many are hard-wired to
low-voltage premise power feeds. A wide variety use batteries, while others
use ambient light, solar cells, and various other forms of harvested energy. For
example, RFID tags scavenge power from readers when activated. While newer
generations of ultra-efficient, ultra-low-power batteries and power cells are in
development in the labs,[60] there is much to be done to advance them to the
their point of readiness for wide spread service. Power must be sufficient for
the sensor to make observations, convert them to digital, develop its reading,
store the results in registers in memory, format output observation data and
transmit it to designated receiving nodes.
Unfortunately, premise power isn’t always as stable and consistent as all would
expect. Interruptions or spikes in premise power, however minute can disrupt
the flow of sensor processing and can cause garbled, missing, incomplete, or
inaccurate data to be captured and transmitted. Many premise-based sensors
include batteries to help mitigate these negative impacts. A subset of these
are designed to run from the battery to provide stable, consistent power and
are kept charged by the premise power. The other subset uses batteries for
backup that take over when premise power becomes unstable or unavailable.
24

 The objective in all cases is to keep the sensor running with sufficient quality
power to do its job while minimizing data defects.
Battery-powered sensors are designed to run for long periods of time with
healthy batteries designed for service lives of several years with some lasting as
long as ten years. Battery specification and selection is critical to the longevity
of the sensor. Sensors that depend only on battery power are designed to be
ultra low power and very power efficient in their operation.[39] Battery life is
a function of rated power and capacity divided by the average cycle depletion
rate. The cycle depletion rate is the sum of the power needed for the sensor to
make, evaluate, record, and transmit the data from one observation. Each resident component in the sensor has its own power demands and affects directly
the cycle depletion rate. The sensor component has a specific cycle demand on
power as does the memory and processor components. Larger memories and
faster processors typically have higher demands on cycle power. The communications component may demand even more. A simple wired network connection
may demand minimal power while any one of the possible wireless connections
could take significantly more. If the sensor includes retransmission functionality
needed to assure data message delivery, power demand could rise substantially
to complete the impacted observation cycles when transmit errors occur.
The frequency of a sensor’s observations is a major factor in sensor longevity. A
sensor that makes an observation every 500 milliseconds will deplete its power
far sooner than the same sensor configured elsewhere to make observations every
15 minutes. Extreme temperatures may also impact performance and battery
life. Hotter temperatures tend to increase available power but shorten battery
life, while colder temperatures may impede performance but extend battery life.
Excessive moisture to an exposed battery can result in rust and corrosion and
cut short battery life.
25

 Sensor design, specification, and selection must consider all of these elements
and the dynamics they may bring to their deployed location, environment, and
function to find the best balance between power capacity, expected demand
and targeted service life. In the end, the first indication that there may be
a power problem is when sensor data errors begin to elevate or when data
from a particular sensor stop suddenly and don’t resume after a period of time.
Depending on the sensor, its function, and the nature of the data it is intended
to produce, this type of failure could be critical.
• Location - Where a sensor is placed, how it is mounted, how it is powered, and
how it is expected to communicate may all have some impact on a sensor’s
reliability and stability in the quality and consistency in the data it delivers.
Physical installation decisions together with often widely-variable ambient environmental conditions may also impact sensor performance, data quality and
device life. Dust, vibration, heat, cold, humidity, moisture, UV radiation, electromagnetic interference, and airborne chemicals are common conditions that
may attack sensor elements resulting in shorter device life, premature failure,
and consequently increasingly unreliable data.
• Noise - Generally, many types of sensors function by isolating and measuring specific attributes of signals fitting waveforms of certain frequencies and
amplitudes. As sensors make their observations, they expect to capture signal patterns that fit closely to the targeted pattern. Measurement algorithms
attempt to discern differences between what they capture and what they expected. Under ideal circumstances, sensors can reliably capture and measure
what they are designed to do and generate and transmit good data indicating
the observation’s results.
However, sensors can commonly encounter noise while taking their respective

26

 readings. Noise is defined as a random unwanted and unintended disturbance
in an expected electrical signal. Noise is environmental, some is atmospheric
and occurs naturally, while the rest is a product of proximate electrical, and
sometimes mechanical, activity. Electromagnetic Interference (EMI) and Radio
Frequency Interference (RFI) are very frequent causes. Virtually everything
electrical, electronic, or radio-related generates noise in some form. Most noise
is not a problem outside of specific, often narrow circumstances. It generally
only becomes an issue when that noise from certain external sources intrude
and interferes with the intended functional operation of a particular circuit,
chip, or component–such as a sensor, actuator, processor, and the like.
Resolving noise issues is often complicated and can take time. Some patterns
of distortion or signal alteration have become identifiable over time resulting
in filters or algorithms to mitigate their impact. Other patterns have to be
investigated using a variety of troubleshooting methods that may help isolate
and identify potential contributing factors.[46] For example, some of the possible noise mitigation actions might include: the sensor may need to be moved
from HVAC airflows to mitigate temperature fluctuations and convection cooling; machine vibrations may need to be dampened to reduce their effect on
the sensor; sensors may need to be moved to increase distance and minimize
impact; lights may need to be moved or shielded; nearby unshielded cables may
need to be moved; cellphones and other radio signals may need to taken away,
repositioned, or shielded; and other like actions dictated by the environment
and the nature of the effects that need to be identified and mitigated–if they
can be.
Unresolved noise will usually result in missing, garbled, inaccurate, or outlier
data defects that will need to be resolved downstream in the data channel.

27

 • Accuracy - Probably the most common and most concerning issues with sensorgenerated data are the continuing accuracy of the observations being reported
by each sensor. Noise, significant temperature fluctuations, and even extended
normal use can cause what is referred to as drift and happens to most sensors
to one degree or another. Drift is defined as the gradual increase in the gap
between what the device is measuring compared to the measurement it has been
calibrated to expect. As a result, data that appears complete and accurate is
actually not and becomes less reliable and useful.[5] The issue becomes: just
how inaccurate is this data, how long has it been inaccurate, and at what point
does it become unusable and need to be dropped? To reliably produce accurate
data, sensors need to be recalibrated as needed or at least checked regularly to
confirm they are providing measurements within the limits for which they have
been calibrated. All this said, it is important to note that sensor-generated
data is not perfect. There will always be some level of error that needs to be
recognized and accommodated.
The discussion about accuracy must also include some attention to precision.
Sensor precision refers to how finite a specific sensor measures what it is designed to measure. There might be hundreds of one sensor type, each with its
own design and function target. For example, temperature sensors have a wide
range of function targets. On one end, temperature sensors targeted to measure ambient air temperature might have a measurement range of -10 degrees
to +130 degrees Fahrenheit with a precision of one-tenth of one degree. On the
other end, cryogenic storage monitoring sensors could be targeted at the range
of -460 degrees to -238 degrees Fahrenheit with a precision of one-thousandth of
a degree. The point being that a temperature sensor isn’t usually one size fits
all. Within each sensor type there are often several models from various manufacturers, each with their differentiating characteristics. Sensor measurement
28

 data is often misinterpreted downstream because it isn’t clear which sensor produced it, only to find that the range and precision of the data isn’t what was
expected.
The explanation of the specific meaning of the data produced by a particular
sensor is usually provided by the manufacturer of that sensor. It may be different from other similar sensors so it is important for that sensor’s documentation
to be sure it is clearly understood.
• Duplication - Any number of operating interruptions or delays may result in
sensors duplicating data being sent downstream. Fluctuating power, communications issues, outbound sensor data transmission backlogs are all common
causes of resulting duplication.
• Connectivity - Sensors exist solely to make periodic prescribed measurements,
format the readings into data records (tuples), and send them somewhere else
across one or more methods of connection. For this discussion, the nature of selected possible connection options is unimportant here, but there are potential
impacting issues common to them all. Specific option characteristics, technologies, and protocols aside, their purpose is to reliably transport sensor-generated
data to its designated destinations. Each is expected to be configured to have
capacity sufficient to allow this data to move smoothly from its source to its
intended destinations. But that does not always happen. Some of the more
common issues that often arise include:
– Power fluctuations and outages can cause data streams to stop moving
data causing data to back up until the data stream path can be restored,
stabilized, and the data stream backlogs cleared. If more data collects in
the backlog than the stream can accommodate, data will likely be lost or
corrupted.
29

 – Each sensor is configured to make an observation at regular intervals. The
minimum interval cannot be any shorter than the time required to initiate
and complete one observation cycle. Within each observation cycle, the
sensor generates a certain amount of data. For some sensors, that amount
of data is limited while others may generate considerably more. The size of
any particular sensor data stream is a product of the size of its generated
observation record and the frequency of its observations. Observations
need to be scheduled often enough to fulfill the motivating value requirements, but no more frequent than necessary to avoid overwhelming the
data stream’s bandwidth and potentially loosing or significantly delaying
data.
– Every data path has an established capacity within which the data may
flow. Data moves freely along that path as long as its volume and speed
don’t exceed the path’s established capacity. When that capacity is reached,
upstream data slows and gradually pushes the blockage further upstream
creating a larger backlog. Here too, data loss or corruption becomes increasingly likely. In streams where low latency is required, such delays can
cause poor or missed response to a critical real-time action request.[8]
• Fusion - In many cases, the data from one sensor is not enough be useful or
actionable. Data from multiple proximate sensors are often needed to provide
better context and meaning.[2] [4] [43] [49] For example, temperature measured
at sea level may be quite different than temperature measured at the top of a
300 foot tower a short distance away. Without further information, explaining
the difference between the two proximate readings is difficult. Adding altitude
sensor data at each location helps show why a difference may exist. To take
this further, temperature is usually not that useful without also knowing the
relative humidity. So, to be useful in a broader context, sensor data represent30

 ing temperature, relative humidity, and altitude need to be brought together
to compute adjusted data values that may be more meaningful. This process
is referred to as sensor data fusion. In this process, the GPS (or other) location, and date and time must be incorporated to complete the record(s) to be
transmitted.[63] [56] [62]
For sensor networks that have been deployed for several years, it is the responsibility of the solution provider/developer to establish how all of these elements
are to be brought together to create the contextualized data instance(s) and
transmit them. Where standardized requirements can be established, manufacturers are developing integrated multi-sensor packages that accomplish this
fusion on single components. There are some challenges arising out of this
fusion that may also impact data quality.
– Observation synchronization is critical to fusion success. In established
deployments, participating sensors may not be close enough together to
allow the intended fusion processing to be done within the observation
interval established for them. This would require this fusion to be done
further down stream. Deployments incorporating integrated multi-sensor
packages mitigate this problem and are likely to be more suitable for realtime, low-latency requirements.
– Just one of a participating group of sensors that gets out of sync or is
delayed in providing its data, can compromise the ability of the fusion
process to keep up with the steady flow of observation data from all participating sensors. As has been discussed in other circumstances, delays in
process flows will cause data to back up and are likely to result in data loss
and corruption. Observation cycle interval timing needs to be adjusted to
minimize the frequency of such issues.

31

 – Date and time synchronization between related sensors is essential to the
ability to correlate and draw meaning from their observation readings.
Shorter observation intervals require this more than with longer intervals.
When intervals are shorter, the time between observations is less and tolerance for incongruity between them decreases and increases the possibility
of error between them. At some point, the incongruity of times will create
confusion over to which observation in a series the outlying sensor’s data
belongs. This could trigger a potential duplicate resolution issue with the
collective observation group immediately before or after the observation
group to which it should belong, and, will likely create a missing data
situation for the observation group to which it actually belongs.[30] [31]
[29]

4.1

The Core Value of IoT Solutions (IoTS)

It is easy to become overwhelmed with, not only the vast volumes of IoT devices,
but the seemingly endless and creative things they do, how they do it, and how
they work together to achieve their collective missions. None of these exist for their
own sake but for the data they create and curate and the value that data represents
for the organizations that deploy it in the first place. Each deploying organization
places a value on the role each device plays and the data produced. For some, the
value is episodic or event-related providing some level of understanding about them.
For others, it is gaining a more timely understanding of operational norms and as
much as they can about exceptions or anomalies. These understandings are derived
from appropriately timed and scaled analytical processes embedded in data value
life cycles. From these understandings, their respective aims are to save money,
improve efficiency, optimize operations, learn nuances of their business they didn’t
know before, and a host of other reasons and motivations. This is why they do all
this.
The core value of IoT devices, and the ecosystems within which they perform,
is how they are used to solve a myriad of problems, enable greater value, and fulfill
mission-critical functions in a wide variety of ways. As sensor electronics and processing capabilities improve, more sophisticated and smarter applications and their
constituent solutions are being developed and deployed for the new value they are

33

 intended to provide. They become then, the foundations for future innovations.[1]
Some examples includes the following.
• Factory floor automation: Nearly every aspect of shop floors, production lines,
refinery systems, materials provisioning, and a host of robotic devices are all
targeted for sensing or adjustments by IoT. Line optimization, waste reduction, product quality, energy conservation, cost efficiency, security, and product
tracking are all in the sweet spot for this space.

flow analytics, congestion management, smart traffic lights, accident detection
and response, emergency response management, security and law enforcement,
utility meter reading, smart building management, and clean energy management.

to the point where virtually every operating system in our vehicles are monitored and controlled. Today, innovation is pushing towards vehicle autonomy
and route auto-navigation. This will require sensor-bedded roads, among other
things. Included also are the developing interests in smart delivery drones.

actuators are used to manage grid health, flow levels, threshold tolerances,

 • Environment management: Just about everything in the physical world around

 of these are home personal hubs from the likes of Google and Amazon. There

4.2

An Example of Cost

At the heart of these solutions are sensors of all types, designs, and purposes, each
with its own role to play in the search for more and better information that can be
transformed and combined to yield new value. Sensors produce data–lots of it. And
adding more sensors to a particular solution can add dramatically to its complexity. Each type of sensor is configured to produce a new observation instance of data
many times a day. One sensor generating a 1Kb data record once each minute of
each day will generate 1,400 records and 1,400 Kb of data. Doesn’t sound like much.
Many sensors generate records at least once per second. This becomes 86,400 records
and 86,400 Kb each day. Depending on the environment and solution particulars, a
significant portion of sensors may multiple observations per second. A hypothetical
solution might have 100,000 sensors producing like data might yield 8.6 billion records
and 8.6 GB of data per day. And if the hypothetical fully-rationalized solution ob-

36

 servation processing cost is $1 perMB, then the daily cost would be $8,600 per day,
$258,000 per month, and $3,096,000 annually.
Few solutions would be this simplistic. Typical solutions may include many different kinds of sensors, each producing observation data instances with specific content
and size that is likely to differ from other solution sensor types. Each sensor will be
configured to generate event observation data records appropriate to its particular
need. In one solution, a specific sensor type might be configured to produce an event
observation data record once per hour while another instance of the same sensor in a
different application might be configured to produce one every second, yielding radically different record and data volumes each day. Some solutions may be deployed
using a fixed local infrastructure while others may use wireless or satellite services.
Choices like these will have much to do with transport and processing logistics, and
ultimately, cost. Many solutions deploy 5-10+ times the number of sensors discussed
in these examples.
sectionSensor-Based Solution Internal Controls While cost remains a consistent
consideration in the overall IoT value proposition, data quality, processing latency,
data volume, and overall solution performance are all critical factors that remain in
a precarious state of balance. To ensure that IoT solutions deliver high data quality,
they must include a strong system of internal controls aimed at preventing, detecting,
and correcting defects or conditions that may compromise data quality.
4.2.1

Preventive Controls

In the prior chapter, several sensor issues were identified and discussed. The discussion there established that the sensor world is young and still developing, and is yet
to reach a point of maturity where data quality assurance can be reliably and consistently delivered at highly confident levels. Consequently, there are many exposures
to the risk of poor data quality or loss. As a critical organizational asset, confidence

37

 in data quality and integrity is essential for deriving the value the organization needs
and expects. Preventive controls consist of various measures aimed at precluding the
occurrence of undesirable outcomes and defects that may compromise the high quality of data. Such measures are usually more extensive and complicated than other
types of controls, and invariably more expensive to implement and maintain.
Examples of preventive controls that could help reduce the impact of these might
include:
• Technical Limitations - A preventive measure for technical limitations and some
of the issues that arise as a result would be to make them more capable. This
is entirely doable. But, sensors are designed and produced to be functional at
the lowest cost–essential to justifying solutions financially. Increasing capacity,
functionality, and capability all drive up the cost per unit. Multiplying that
incremental cost by the number of units expected for a given solution can significantly change the financial equation. That said, manufacturers are finding
new ways over time for sensors to do more at less cost. So, over time, sensor
capabilities may become available that will help improve data quality.
• Power - Better power is a strong preventive measure for reducing data quality
problems. Investing in cleaner, more stable building power, and good quality,
long-life batteries would make an important difference when it comes to sensor
function and performance. But this also can be expensive. Power systems in
well-established facilities are what they are, and upgrading them can be costprohibitive, making it impractical to do. Batteries are getting better as the
technology evolves, but upgrading 10,000 sensors to take newer battery models
can be logistically difficult and will take time. And there is a cost to that as
well.
• Location - Protecting sensors from environmental contamination might also be
38

 an effective preventive measure for those devices where such action is possible.
Alternatively, investing in components that are sealed or encapsulated in material that is impervious to the elements may be an effective preventative measure
for prolonging the life of exposed sensor and sensor-related components.
• Noise - Noise is a complex and multi-faceted problem that can’t be easily mitigated. However, a notable contributing factor is electromagnetic radiation.
Some preventative measures can be taken to shield sensor and sensor components from such radiation. Machines can be shielded, network and electrical
wiring and cabling can be relocated or shielded, and other sources can be traced
to see if they can be mitigated. Such efforts can also be costly. Even so, stray
signals and remaining interference can still cause problems.
• Accuracy - Drift is inevitable with most sensors and is rarely preventable. However, some data problems can be prevented by ensuring that the most appropriate sensor and sensor components are deployed and accurately documented
so that they can be configured correctly to generate the intended data results
and precision.
• Duplication - Options for preventing duplications are limited. Perhaps more
capable onboard processing power may be able to at least minimize event observation record duplication, but probably not at this time.
• Connectivity - Investing in fault-resistant networks of sufficient capacity and
speed will help prevent data streaming flow-control-related problems and their
impact on data quality. However, upgrading existing networks can be quite
expensive.
• Fusion - Fusion opportunities are specific to the targeted solutions and the role
sensors or multi-sensor packages. Increasingly more of these are being built

39

 with sufficient processing capacity to perform on-board fusion tasks. As these
become more widely available may help prevent some of the fusion-related data
quality problems.
From these examples, there is support for the idea that implementing certain
preventive controls can mitigate some significant data quality exposures at significant
cost. As in all internal control systems, such efforts should be considered only if there
is sufficient cost-benefit, however that may be measured, for doing so. It is important
to recognize that a solution may consist of thousands of locations and sensors. It is
often impractical and too expensive to address all locations and devices. Areas where
higher concentrations of data quality loss or impact can be identified, should be the
better candidates for these kinds of remediations.
4.2.2

Detective Controls

Central to all notions of data quality management is the core principal that data
quality defects and issues should able to be identified, measured, and assessed. Systems of internal detective controls are designed and implemented to ensure that this
can be achieved as an intrinsic element of any ongoing IoT solution operation. This is
particularly important in the absence of strong, robust, solution design and preventative controls. The generally accepted elements of internal detective controls include:
environmental controls, risk assessment, monitoring operations activities, exchange
of information, and assessment. For the purposes of this discussion, these elements
will be adapted, for the purposes of this paper, to fit more appropriately the issues
and characteristics of IoT sensor-based solutions.[24] [25]
Environmental Controls

Environmental controls focus on ensuring that the end-end environment and infrastructure used by any particular IoT solution is secure, functional, and properly con40

 figured to create, process, move, and manage data flows that yield reliable, high
quality data. Because sensor-based IoT solutions involve such large volumes of data,
they need to operate effectively, efficiently, and reliably machine-to-machine with
no human intervention needed to capture, clean, and prepare data for down-stream
analytics and operational effectiveness measurement.
The foundational building blocks for solution environmental controls are assets:
the assets deployed to support the solution, and the data assets the solution brings
to life. To that end, such controls include the following:
• All devices are known and accounted for. Ensuring that when new sensors and
related devices are brought online, they become known to all asset management,
monitoring, and data management control processes.
• All changes to devices and the supporting infrastructure are fully coordinated.
Formal change management practices are followed when changing anything
about a solution element that could impact data quality.
– Sensor-affiliated devices: Sensors, actuators, controllers, processors, and
data processing computers are all considered assets and have specific roles
to play within the IoT solution they support. Each needs to be identified and known to the network and to solution management and control
functions. Once online, their status, health, and performance needs to be
monitored and measured. As solutions evolve, devices break or begin to
malfunction, devices need to be expanded or upgraded, or even retired.
In each of these cases, needed changes or updates need to be coordinated
and tracked, and confirmed back online and functioning properly when
the actions are completed. A fully functioning infrastructure supporting
an IoT solution is an essential foundation for dependable data quality.

41

 – Data formatting rules: Every solution device that creates or further processes data does so according to a specified set of data format rules. All
devices of a specific type are expected to adhere to the set of data formatting rules intended for them. As solutions evolve and mature, data format
rules expand or change and are assigned to pending of future updated rule
sets. In a coordinated fashion, the current set is retired and replaced by
the next designated set. At that point, all impacted devices should begin
complying with the new set. This should help ensure that any user or
process using that data does so according to the correct set of rules. This
is another essential part of the foundation for dependable data quality.
– Validation rule set versions: Like data formatting, most created data
records have a set of rules for validating that the data within them are
correct, complete, and have values within specified ranges, or that are
from lists of acceptable values. Like formatting rules, these are updated
from time to time and should also be managed through version control
and change management processes.
– Machine learning algorithms: Machine learning models and algorithms are
being used increasingly for data cleaning, enhancement, and transformation in IoT solutions. Many sensor-originated data streams may employ
ML processes for resolving data issues. Where they are used, all data
streams from the same device type should use the same version of models
and/or algorithms. As they are refined and updated, they should also be
managed through version control and change management processes.
Risk Assessment

In any IT solution, security and privacy protection are critical and essential elements
of application solutions. IoT solutions by nature have many parts, each of which
42

 should be expected to provide protections consistent with those provided by all other
solution components, and what the overall solution should be expected to provide
overall. As in any chain, the solution is only as strong as its weakest component. Due
to the general immaturity sensor-based IoT solutions, there remain many exposures
and risks that can negatively impact data quality, security, and privacy.
In 2018, the Open Web Application Security Project (OWASP) Internet of Things
working group published its list of Top 10 IoT security vulnerabilitiesowasp. They
describe them this way:
1. Weak, guessable, or hardcoded passwords: - “Use of easily brute-forced, publicly
available, or unchangeable credentials, including back-doors in firmware or client
software that grants unauthorized access to deployed systems.”
2. Insecure network services: - “Unneeded or insecure network services running
on the device itself, especially those exposed to the Internet, that compromise
the confidentiality, integrity/authenticity, or availability of information or allow
unauthorized remote control.”
3. Insecure ecosystem interfaces: - “Insecure web, back end API, cloud, or mobile
interfaces in the ecosystem outside of the device that allows compromise of the
device or its related components. Common issues include a lack of authentication/authorization, lacking or weak encryption, and a lack of input and output
filtering.”
4. Lack of ability to securely update the device. - “ This includes lack of firmware
validation on device [sic], lack of secure delivery (non-encrypted in transit), lack
of anti-rollback mechanisms, and lack of notifications of security changes due
to updates.”

43

 5. Use of insecure or outdated components: - “Use of deprecated or insecure software components/libraries that could allow the device to be compromised. This
includes insecure customization of operating system platforms, and the use
of third-party software or hardware components from a compromised supply
chain.”
6. User’s personal information misused: - “... stored on the device or in the ecosystem that is used insecurely, improperly, or without permission."
7. Lack of encryption or access control: - “... of sensitive data anywhere within
the ecosystem, including at rest, in transit, or during processing.”
8. Lack of device management: - “Lack of security support on devices deployed in
production, including asset management, update management, secure decommissioning, systems monitoring, and response capabilities.”
9. Insecure default settings: - “Devices or systems shipped with insecure default
settings or lack the ability to make the system more secure by restricting operators from modifying configurations.”
10. Lack of physical hardening: - “Lack of physical hardening measures, allowing
potential attackers to gain sensitive information that can help in a future remote
attack or take local control of the device.”
Vulnerabilities like these expose IoT solution elements and data to risks of hacking,
intrusion, and compromise that in the end, could result in losses significantly greater
than the solution cost; they need to be addressed. Every location and every device in
each location needs to be assessed and hardened. Nearly every sensor creates a data
channel that needs to be reviewed as well to find potential weaknesses. This is a big
topic with many nuances that underlie nearly every other facet of the IoT issues and
solutions discussed in this paper. The topic needs to be discussed in much greater
44

 detail in other papers and won’t be discussed further here. This does not lessen the
concerns and exposures discussed here.
Monitoring Operations Activities

The goal of all monitoring activities is to ensure that all data is flowing as expected
at all times throughout the universe of IoT solution elements. Monitoring capabilities
should be incorporated into solutions to inquire, test, confirm, and record in a log
the status of all monitored elements. Every element should be observed on a regular
schedule appropriate for the role that element plays in the overall solution. All
elements in the same role are likely to follow the same schedule. The frequency of
observation is likely to be a function of several factors like volume, role critically, time
sensitivity, degree of volatility,potential exposure to loss or error, and the probability
of risk that such a loss might occur. High volumes of critical time-sensitive data
may need to be observed every minute, while at the other extreme, low volumes of
non-critical, low volatility, low risk data might be observed hourly.[11] [14]
It is easy to imagine that if each of the monitoring observations generated data
records of their own that such volumes could be very large and could dramatically
compound the total volume of data produced by a particular IoT solution. For this
reason, monitoring would better take a "dashboard update" approach to logging.
With this approach, it is assumed that all is well throughout and it is sufficient to
simply track the most recent time of observation. So, other than the dashboard
attributes representing a particular solution element, no new data is generated for
positive observations.
However, it is rare that everything runs smoothly all the time; there are usually
some number of conditions or defects that need further attention and need to be
documented and tracked until they are resolved. Once discovered, these need to
be appropriately acted upon per processes prescribed in the category of corrective

45

 controls which are described in a later section in this chapter.
As stated, operations monitoring activities focus on discovering anything within
the IoT solution that may be considered anomalous or outside stipulated rules and
specifications. The methods for making such discoveries can sometimes be complicated and may be approached in a variety of ways. This is purposely left to the
solution designer to determine the best means of making these discoveries.[27] The
intention here is to suggest the general principles and objectives that might be used
to pursue such efforts. Examples of activity monitoring actions might include these.
• All expected data from all expected sources is present for all expected in-service
times. If there is a break or a gap in a particular data stream, which is it?
• All data is formatted as expected and complies with the current version of
validation rules and algorithms. Have current rules and templates been applied
to correct most data errors and defects coming from sensors? What else may
need to be looked at for further correction? Such might include:
– noisy data
– duplication
– missing or inaccurate attribute values
– outliers
– missing or broken records; records at random; in blocks; observed vs. unobserved
– evidence of sensor drift
– sensor & sensor data fusion errors
• Reliable file routing. Every solution sensor is the head-water of its own datastream that has a defined destination. At one or more process stops along the

46

 way, data records need to be validated, formats need to be checked, and identified defects fixed. Certain record attributes may be cross-validated with other
record attributes from other streams passing through the same process stop.
Many data streams are ultimately merged with others, some early on and others further down stream. Each stop is a designated computing venue in the IoT
datasphere described in an earlier chapter. Low latency, low-moderate volume,
and low processing demand data streams will most likely be processed in the
closest computing venue to meet solution requirements. All other data streams
will be mapped appropriately to computing venues further down stream.[10]
[12]
There are three primary control functions here that need to be incorporated.
1. Planned routing verification. Confirm that each data stream is flowing
from creation to destination as expected and on time. It is essential to
know that all is running smoothly. Breaks or gaps in data flows need to
be identified and investigated. Potential issues or losses may occur if data
isn’t arriving where it is expected to be when it is expected. For example,
a data stream from a sensor driving a process control function has a very
narrow window in which to fuse with data from other nearby sensors, clean
up the data, derive a collaborative reading, and send those results to an
actuator that may need to make an adjustment accordingly to the process
flow. If those results are late, or don’t arrive at all, adjustments may be
made at the wrong time or not at all. The process batch might be ruined or
become defective as a result. Events like these need to be localized quickly
and investigated for resolution, and tracked until normality is restored.
2. Routing exceptions. Most comprehensive solutions are designed to anticipate the possibility that planned primary data stream routes may fail.

47

 Edge or Fog hubs or gateways are inserted at key transfer points to manage traffic paths that host the various data streams. When the planned
routes become inactive, those hubs or gateways select alternate routes for
the data streams that are affected. These events create routing exceptions
that need to be tracked, monitored, investigated, and remediated to restore
the planned routes and move data streams back to them. For example, a
local wide area network route may fail and be rerouted to a 5G or satellite
route to bypass the downed primary route.
The fundamental issue this creates is the abrupt disruption in the data
streams impacted. They will no longer be present on the downstream legs
of the primary route, so they will need to be tracked as issues until resolved.
Notifications are needed to ensure that everyone that needs to, knows that
these routing exceptions are in effect. New temporary routes need to
be built and managed dynamically to look for those data streams at the
hub or gateway at the edge venue of the new route provider which could
be considerably greater distance away from the next normal computing
venue that will be looking for those data streams.[22] Once everything
is reconnected, a synchronization process is needed to reconcile continuity
issues such as gaps, overlaps, duplications, and corrupted records or blocks
of records. Events like these can be complicated and require full immediate
attention until all is back to normal using planned routes. Exposures and
risks are high in these circumstances that data quality and integrity can
become corrupted and compromised.
3. Routing performance metrics. Route planning is a critical operational
management function for an IoT solution of scale involving multiple sites,
multiple service providers, and multiple technologies. Most solutions do. A
solution with 10,000 sensors across 100 US locations will start with about
48

 10,000 data streams. Some of those data streams will be processed locally,
fulfill their purpose and be retired. Others may do the same but also
forward data to downstream computing venues in the fog, or the edge, or
on to one or more cloud service providers. Many data streams will be fused
or merged with others along the way, reducing considerably the number
of streams that will ultimately be inserted into the solution data stores.
Data stream routes could interconnect with a variety of technologies and
services for which the solution will need to keep track.[15]
How this is accomplished is very much a function of the solution itself
and the requirements it is designed to meet. What is essential to this
function is to be able to identify and track data streams that are losing
data, or processing slower than planned, may be making observations too
frequently or not often enough, and other conditions that may negatively
impacting data stream flows, processing performance, route throughput,
and ultimately data quality and integrity.
4.2.3

Corrective Controls

In this discussion of internal controls for IoT solutions, a variety of possible defects, errors, problems, and exceptions [collectively referred to as issues] have been identified.
Each has potential negative impacts on solution integrity, operations, performance,
and data quality. The system of detective controls is designed to identify any such
issues, and where within the solution the issue appears to be occurring. The purpose
of the system of corrective controls is to establish and follow processes to fix those
issues. Simply put, corrective controls take in identified issues, characterize and understand them, determine what is causing them and why(root cause), ascertain where
they are occurring, develop a plan for fixing them, execute the plan to fix them, and
confirm that those actions have corrected what was identified.

49

 What exactly is the issue? The answer to this question together with the information gathered to help support that answer needs to be clearly understood before doing
anything else. Questions that may need to be considered include: How can it best
be described? Is this a common issue? How frequently does it occur? When, where,
and under what conditions did it last occur? Under what conditions has it occurred
most often? Is there enough information to allow issues with similar characteristics
to be excluded from further investigation?
What is the root cause? Finding the root cause(s) behind an issue is fundamental
to developing a clear understanding of the factors that may be causing it. Particular
care is needed to distinguish symptoms from causal factors. Discovering the true
root cause(s) of an issue is a disciplined process seeking answers to questions that are
driven usually by the known or suspected issue circumstances.
Where is it occurring? Once the root cause(s) of an issue are understood, other
locations and/or impact points are investigated to determine where else the issue
is appearing so that they can also be fixed. Patterns often emerge during earlier
analysis that may point to like issues, even if they are not showing issues at the time.
For example, one particular sensor make and model in multiple locations might be
showing similar issues intermittently over time and the root cause findings suggest
that each is experiencing the same issue with a threshold limit parameter value in its
configuration table and needs to be remediated. In another example, the root cause
findings uncovered multiple related issues from several devices that happen to be
connected to the same hub. The hub was investigated and found to have an unstable
network interface card.
What is the plan for fixing it? Once it is clear what needs to be done to what to fix
the issue, a change management plan outlining the specific change steps and schedule
for each device and location. The plan should then be reviewed and approved by all
impacted stakeholders.

50

 Follow the plan to fix it. At the appointed times agreed between operations,
change managers, other interested stakeholders, the changes are made exactly as outlined in the plan in full coordination to minimize operating impacts. Plan steps should
be included to ensure that all related documentation and metadata are updated to
reflect the changes made.
Is the issue fixed? Part of that plan should include for each device and location
the steps to be taken to confirm that the changes were made correctly and they have
effectively remediated the identified issues and demonstrate the intended outcomes
have been achieved.

51

 Chapter 5
Conclusion and Future Work
The entire concept of the IoT is exciting and will provide fertile ground for innovative new development for at least the decade ahead. Time and creativity over time
will help spawn evolving ideas about using IoT-supporting sensors to solve important
problems, find better versions of today’s solutions, and do today’s things in better
ways, will all drive the creation of a host of new applications and their variant solutions and more data about virtually anything. However, the drive for these new
benefits cannot come at the risk of compromises and weaknesses in data security,
personal privacy, organizational intellectual property, and customer information.
As mentioned several times herein, all this is about data, lots of it. Even now,
there is so much of it that a substantial portion of what Gartner calls "dark data" never
goes anywhere or is ever used. Further, data needed for analysis must be discovered
and extracted from these mountains of potentially redundant and nonessential data.
A lot of data has a brief, useful life and may need to be extracted and destroyed
rather than kept. More attention needs to be directed toward where data is created
and where it needs to be processed or analyzed. Moving large amounts of data long
distances across the network is expensive, time-consuming, and may block others
from using the network when needed, particularly when low-latency response and or
immediate processing is required.
Navigating the layers of infrastructure supporting the IoT is a big topic with many
facets that this paper could not adequately discuss. However, it needs to be evaluated
closely regarding the data crisis that, in many ways, is already upon us.

52

 5.1

Thesis Questions and Conclusions

This thesis aims to discuss the issues surrounding sensor-generated data volumes and
data quality and find answers to the questions posed in the Introduction. Here then
are the findings and conclusions to those questions.
1. Given the increasing magnitude and velocity of sensor-generated data being produced, transported, and stored, the question must be asked: "is all this data necessary?" No! Not all collected data is necessary, nor does all data need to be
collected. And not all collected data needs to be kept. There should be a direct
correlation between the data that is collected, processed, and stored; and the
specific requirements that require it to enable the creation and ongoing production of new value targeted by senior organizational leadership. The literature
generally agrees that too few organizations have clearly defined what added
value they seek and the specific data needed to achieve it. Without such clarity
and focus, the default action then is to, generally, capture all data and try to
work out the value opportunities later. While this may be a practical approach
for certain kinds of value exploration, it is categorically not appropriate for all
situations.
The academic and trade literature identify this focus of action-to-value concept
as one of the central facets of sound data governance. But, unfortunately, the
typical organizational adoption rate is slow and modestly penetrated. Moreover,
implementation maturity and degree of compliance across most organizations
are considered low. Consequently, such organizations have not yet reached
a point where they clearly develop their value propositions and exercise the
discipline to identify the specific data needed to achieve it.
So, infrastructure providers continue to expand their capabilities to improve
their cost-efficiencies in the ways they transport, process, and store all the data
53

 their clients choose to generate and retain. And at current and projected rates,
there are mountains of data to come for the foreseeable future.
Meanwhile, middleware and application solutions providers are evolving their
wares to improve their clients’ ability to manage better the data they have and
the new data they create every day.
2. How much of this data is actually being used? No one seems to know for
sure. Estimates in the literature and industry sources vary widely, offering
little consensus on precise numbers–the data just isn’t tracked or recorded consistently to scale. In 2018, McKinsey analysts estimated that less than 4% of
sensor-generated data is used, primarily for anomaly detection and control. The
higher value uses of this data for optimization and prediction is limited and just
beginning to be explored. Industrial and business-to-business (B2B) applications appear to offer the greatest opportunities for value creation and growth,
followed by consumer-focused applications. The scientific data community is
increasingly adopting the IoT model as a part of its overall data management
transformation.[23] In so doing, it is expected to use a significantly larger portion of data collected, although small by comparison. Another higher use area is
the green-field deployment of IoT application solutions in developing economies
where value-connected data collection and retention is expected to be more
focused.
3. What strategies can be applied to materially reduce data volumes and their attendant resource demands and costs? In retrospect, the issue is not simply
reducing data volumes as much as it is collecting, processing, and retaining
only data that is of sufficiently high quality that it can be used readily to produce the value for which it is intended. As discussed previously, the following
support this premise:

54

 • Pragmatically, only data that is needed and is likely to be used to achieve
a specific purpose should be captured. Incurring all related costs for data
that isn’t likely to be used wastes time, money, and resources.
• Data may be deleted or archived appropriately when its purpose has
passed. However, if it needs to be retained, perhaps it can be done at
a lower cost.
• Data may be collected more frequently than needs require. Lowering frequencies produce less data overall and reduce associated costs and resource
demands accordingly. Of course, the opposite may need to be applied as
circumstances dictate. If the frequency of observations is insufficient to
satisfy requirements, they may need to be increased.
• Data may be useful at multiple levels and needs to be managed accordingly.
For example, data may be captured and used immediately to represent
the precise reading of a real-world circumstance and then evaluated by a
proceeding process as to whether or not a related actuator needs to make
an indicated adjustment as a result. If this is the only purpose for that
data, it may not need to be processed further downstream and deleted.
However, if that data instance also has analytical or predictive value, it
should be forwarded downstream and retained.
• In many cases, consecutive data instances may show the same values with
no appreciable or material differences. There may or may not be merit
in processing and retaining these instances. In these situations, it might
be appropriate to drop them or design solutions to summarize these consecutive series of inconsequential observation data instances and devise
methods for retaining and analyzing them.
4. What data quality challenges are a result of environmental and operational in55

 fluences on sensors supporting IoT? The past two chapters describe the nature
of sensor issues that can impact data quality in IoT application solutions. In
their current form of production and availability in the low-end cost range, they
have limited abilities to operate reliably in harsher environments and cope with
a wide variety of potential operational influences. However, the author’s research found no recent broad empirical numbers indicating the magnitude of
such errors on a regular basis. That said, the incidence of these errors tends
to be circumstantial. The most common sensor-related data issues are outliers,
followed by missing data, bias, drift, and noise. Less frequent issues include
constant values, data uncertainties, and stuck-at-zero.
In addition to their individual functional requirements, application solution
developers must also anticipate and resolve these errors. Further, the IoT environment has a host of security, privacy, and access control challenges that may
impact data quality and reliability; have not been researched as part of this
paper. Solution developers must incorporate needed controls and functionality
to mitigate as many of those challenges as circumstances allow.
5. What methods can be introduced or expanded upon to improve IoT data quality?
Data is most useful when it is of sufficiently high quality that it can be trusted
and is believed to reliably represent the real-world conditions accurately enough
to satisfy its intended purpose. When the level of data quality falls, so does the
trust and confidence in the data itself. At some point, it is considered no longer
useful and is either deleted or ignored. The issue here is that this is (hopefully)
data with a purpose. When it is deemed unusable, it creates a gap, be it a single
instance or block(s) of many data instances, and removes observations from the
data stream that are potentially consequential. While the literature identifies
various methods that may be applied to compensate for what has been lost, it
still may not be what was originally observed.
56

 As outlined in the previous chapter, the ability to detect potential errors is the
essential starting point for evaluating and performing appropriate corrective
actions needed to mitigate, as much as possible, the impacts such errors may
have on the integrity and reliability of individual sensor data streams. Each
type of error may lead to a specific course of correction and resolution and may
differ further depending on the sensor make and model creating the error. Realtime error detection and correction can be complicated because of the limited
time window within which such actions can occur. These typically leave little
time for time-consuming statistical or algorithmic solutions, while data streams
with no immediate processing demands can benefit significantly by applying
them.
In real-time conditions, few options may be available. In these conditions, time
may only permit the application of basic attribute pattern matches of various
types to determine if an error may exist. Options may include simply ignoring the erroneous instance(s) or substituting a statistically-derived Proforma
replacement to satisfy the real-time need. Faulty data instances are usually retained in the data stream so that they may be included in downstream detection
and correction processes.
A wide variety of approaches are suggested in the literature for detecting and
correcting defective/erroneous/anomalous data. Common methods include principal component analysis, artificial neural networks, Bayesian networks, Grey
prediction modeling, benchmark-based calibrations, Kalman filters, signal processing and filtering, association rule mining, clustering, k-nearest neighbor, and
value/mode decomposition. Depending on how they are used, some are more
suitable for detection, while others may be better for correcting or replacing
missing data. Even further, some are more suitable for certain types of errors
or defects, or even specific types or categories of sensors.
57

 As described previously, sensors have specific characteristics and purposes. The
data produced by each sensor make and model are usually distinct in the attributes captured and what values they should contain. Precise detection and
processing methods can be established and routinely applied to all data streams
originated by them. Benchmarks and profiles can be derived over time from the
community of similar sensors helping to improve detection, correction, and data
quality.

5.2

Future Work

Opinions vary broadly about how far things may be in developing and deploying
sensor-based application solutions. Many would probably agree that applications,
their assorted solutions, and underlying technologies are emerging from the "Early
Adoption" stage into the (very) "Early Majority" stage of the Technology Innovation
Life Cycle, and the low end of the steep "Improving" slope of the Technical Maturity Model with "Maturity" still a long way off. In many ways, IoT technology and
applications still fall far short of the inflated expectations and hype of the marketplace. The IoT is expanding on an extraordinary and accelerated scale regardless of
the current state of everything that must be there to achieve its ultimate potential.
Through this research effort, several key critical success factors were identified that
will need concerted industry focus to be achieved. These include the following:
1. Security, access, and privacy protections must be incorporated at all levels of
every solution and infrastructure element it uses to reach the levels of reliability,
confidence, and trust that are essential to realizing its full intended value and
innovative potential. There are far too many serious weaknesses and vulnerabilities today across all of the actors engaged in the development, deployment, and
operation of any given solution and are collectively negligibly "seamless." The
entire burden currently lies on the shoulders of solution providers and develop58

 ers to mitigate whatever they can or so choose. They will carry this burden,
expense, and liabilities until something much more broadly functional is available that they can use. Industry remedies need to be implemented as widely
as possible using universal standards that all can adopt and support. IoT infrastructure and solution security and privacy weaknesses are critical problems
and must be fixed. And it will take an enormous amount of effort over time to
get there. All other observations that follow are predicated on the presumption
that this must and will happen and will not mention it further.
2. One of the underlying visions of the IoT is dynamic machine-to-machine(M2M)
interoperability, the notion that each device is independent, self-managing, and
self-determining.[20] Each would seek out other devices and determine which
it should establish relationships with and which routes it should use to get its
data to where it needs to be. Such interoperability has been on the horizon for
many years, and many now see the IoT as a primary vehicle of innovation for
making it a reality. Others believe, however, that too much development and
deployment has been done "today’s way" to make this even marginally possible
over the next several years. Moreover, there have been virtually no industrywide efforts to standardize the essential transport, processing, and data hygiene
functionality and protocols that will be needed to enable even "baby steps" in
the direction of this lofty objective.
3. IoT connectivity is problematic today and represents solution-impacting limitations and challenges. Inconsistencies in coverage, bandwidth, and quality of
service (measuring throughput and error rates) across a given solution service
area make it difficult to ensure that data reliably gets to its designated destination. For example, selected solution elements targeted for certain wireless
services can’t be supported in some areas because the needed wireless service

59

 is not offered. As a result, some other form of connectivity may be required.
In some cases, it may be through an alternate provider. If data streams are intended for the primary provider’s Edge data centers, alterations may be needed
to accommodate differences between the two provider Edge service offerings. A
bridge between the participating Edge centers will need to be built to facilitate
data stream controls and flows.[10] If the alternate provider can only provide
lesser service levels, then error rates may be higher, latency may be higher, etc.,
adversely impacting data quality and solution performance. Several examples
of related problems will need further research and resolution if the IoT is to
become what it needs to and can be. Each variant adds complexity and added
effort to make it all work.[15]
4. Every device that has a role in the ongoing operation of an IoT solution needs
to be known and managed under a system of solution controls for various important reasons. Each device is an asset that must be tracked and managed
according to rules and processes applied to all other assets. Management features include applicable periodic maintenance and calibration, software version
control, physical location tracking, role assignment metadata updates, ongoing
performance metrics and service issues, support organization contact details,
other devices that it talks to, and the like. If it exists at all, the extent of this
functionality is a function of how the solution using it was designed. Establishing and maintaining this level of control is essential for operational reliability
and service management that begins to get very complicated when more of these
devices are shared by multiple solutions touched by multiple solution service
providers. The maturity and functionality of service management operations
capabilities will become a much bigger issue as industry providers, and solution
support organizations begin to drive towards ubiquitous M2M interoperability. A universal service-layer offering will be the essential foundation through
60

 which all solutions can manage what will become a very dynamic infrastructure
landscape.[19]
For example, a local hub supporting multiple wired sensors loses its connection
to a downstream Fog device. The hub searches for possible routes that will restore its path to nodes further downstream. An alternate path is found through
a 5G wireless connection through the provider’s Edge data center to the closest
node in the original data path. All this will need to occur dynamically and
automatically and will need to update all impacted device metadata and control processes. All stakeholders of all devices and impacted solution elements
will need to see what they are authorized to see and continue monitoring and
managing activities with the dynamic change forward.
5. As described in the previous chapter, each data stream needs to be managed
as it flows from its point of origination to its intended destination. A system
of controls needs to be incorporated into solutions to monitor and track each
data stream along its current path. Such controls ensure that all data from
all sources are present and accounted for and that variances that occur along
the way are adequately documented.[11] In most of today’s solutions, material
changes in devices, their status, and data paths are managed manually, some
better than others. Every break or change in a datastream’s path or flow must
be handled as smoothly as possible to minimize potential data loss or error.
Changes impacting low-latency data flows can break operational integrity if the
latency in the new path rises above critical latency thresholds. These processes
will also become much more complicated as device management becomes more
dynamic, as previously just described.[12]
As in the previous example, changes in device status and connectivity also
impact datastream monitoring and control processes. Changes in datastream

61

 paths will need to be instantly and dynamically logged to minimize the disruption of visibility to the flow and processing of the impacted data along its new
course. Similarly, there will be a need for a universal datastream flow control
layer that can provide all authorized stakeholders the access and control capabilities they will need to manage what they are allowed to do. Building such
a capability will take a major commitment of providers, developers, and other
stakeholders to develop the standards, protocols, and tools needed to make all
this possible.[13]
6. And last but not least, cost-sensitive sensor evolution and innovation need to
proceed forward as rapidly as possible. Critical to this effort is developing designs that bring increasing memory, computing, storage, and data flow control
on-board the sensor package or be readily adjacent. Incorporated into resident
capabilities should be self-diagnostic and error-detection functionality to preclude the need for downstream evaluation, particularly in real-time, low-latency
situations. In addition, self-healing and recalibration, and the reporting of suspected issues that be picked up downstream by monitoring processes. Finally,
device access security provisions need to be added and made manageable.
Sensor fusion management capabilities need to be added and expanded to facilitate the interconnection and fusion of data originating from adjacent contentand context-related sensors. As sensors evolve to manage more of these functions at internal low-latency speeds, responsibility for similar solution functionality can be taken off the shoulders of solution developers. Advancing functionality and capabilities aimed at improving data quality will challenge sensor
design engineers to innovate in ways that keep sensor costs as low as possible.

62

 5.3

Epilogue

IoT solutions are complicated with many moving parts. Some solutions span multiple geographic areas with large numbers of many different kinds of sensors tasked to
function in widely-varied operating environments using locally-available infrastructure service options and providers. As long as developers must cobble together solutions consisting of so many unique moving parts from multiple vendors and providers,
the task of developing world-class, high-reliability solutions yielding consistently high
data quality will demand an increasingly broad palette of skills, patience, money,
time, and most importantly, senior leadership support. Until the industry can successfully develop and deploy standards, protocols, and enabling tools for common
cross-platform services, today’s problems will continue to expand and become more
challenging to manage. The volume and velocity of device and data growth into the
foreseeable future may ultimately cripple or collapse, sooner than anticipated, solutions being deployed today. New approaches will be needed that is entirely woven
together with industrial-strength, bullet-proof, security, and privacy protections. All
manner of participating stakeholders will need to collaborate heavily to define and
implement the required standards and capabilities– much sooner than later!

Black soldier fly larvae (BSFL) efficiently convert biowaste into valuable animal feed. Sustainable and reliable
bioconversion is desirable to achieve optimal economic and environmental outcomes. Thus, science and industry
require an accessible research platform to study complex bioconversion processes under conditions mirroring
industrial-scale settings. In this study, industry-relevant respiration chambers were designed, tested, and replicated for BSFL feeding trials. Each open-circuit chamber housed three industrial rearing crates. The substrate/
frass and air temperature, mass change, NH3 and CO2 emissions, and relative humidity were measured. The
design was validated for CO2 recovery, airtightness, airflow homogeneity, and BSFL performance using firstly, a
uniform control substrate and secondly, uniform food waste across four parallel chambers. In a third trial, the
composition of food waste was varied across parallel chambers to detect differences in metabolic processes. For
trials using uniform substrates, low variability across chambers in performance parameters confirmed the
reproducibility and comparability of the design (e.g. bioconversion rate: <1%, final larval mass: ≤2 mg, standard
deviations, dry matter based). In contrast, the trial with varying food waste compositions showed a strong effect
on average substrate/frass temperature (e.g. 31.5 ◦ C vs 41.8 ◦ C) and final dry larval mass (e.g. 67 mg vs 40 mg).
This is the first study to systematically assess heat generation directly from heterogeneous food waste, a crucial
parameter for efficient BSFL bioconversion. These chambers provide an opportunity for science and industry to
thoroughly assess and understand the metabolic bioconversion characteristics. The findings are key for the
optimisation of sustainable bioconversion processes.

1. Introduction
Globally, almost one-quarter of the calories produced for human
nutrition are lost along the food chain and never consumed (Searchinger
et al., 2019). Next to saving resources, waste recycling within the food
system can enhance food security by preventing nutrient loss in landfills
(Gunders and Bloom, 2017; Irani et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2021). Food
supply chains are vulnerable, especially to evolving geopolitical and
climate change-related challenges (Ghadge et al., 2020). Larger urban
areas with increasing populations, space constraints, and limited selfsufficiency in food production are looking to decrease their sensitivity
to supply disturbances by incorporating food production pipelines

(Gulyas and Edmondson, 2021). Simultaneously, the wealth of urban
areas results in higher biowaste generation and consumption of animalbased food (Milford et al., 2019; Parfitt et al., 2010). From environmental and food security perspectives, cities can benefit from a circular
food system. This requires approaches that prioritise nutrient recovery
in a manner that can efficiently upcycle biowaste and provide agricultural input.
The black soldier fly larva (BSFL, Hermetia illucens) is an emerging
tool for biowaste recycling. It can feed on a broad range of biowastes (e.
g. manure, food industry by-products, municipal food waste, and
slaughterhouse waste) and convert the nutrients in the biowaste into
larval biomass (Banks et al., 2014; Gebremikael et al., 2020; Newton
