et al., 2005), which has myriad applications. For instance, the dry larval
biomass can contain 20 %–60 % protein and more than 25 % lipids,
which can be captured as valuable animal feed (Gold et al., 2018; Kim
et al., 2020; Siegrist et al., 2023) with potential animal health benefits
(Huis, 2020). When reared on underutilised biowaste streams, such as
food waste, BSFL can be more sustainable than current feed ingredients,
such as fishmeal (Smetana et al., 2019). Additionally, marketable substances, such as chitin or antimicrobial proteins, can be extracted from
the larvae (Ravi et al., 2020). Finally, the residues from the rearing
process (hereafter referred to as ‘frass’) are plant fertilisers (Schmitt and
de Vries, 2020). Due to their versatility BSFL become attractive for
urban biowaste recycling, which is intrinsically heterogeneous. Such
heterogeneous waste often exhibits significant variations in its properties, including its moisture content and its nutrient composition (AbdelShafy and Mansour, 2018). This variability can lead to common challenges in BSFL bioconversion, such as high heat production (Erbland
et al., 2021), insufficient frass drying (Lalander et al., 2020) and high
NH3 and CO2 emissions (Froonickx et al., 2023; Parodi et al., 2021).
Even though these processes are interrelated, they are not studied in
combination. Their elucidation is key since they can have dramatic
consequences for the efficiency and reliability of the bioconversion. For
instance, heat production can influence larval escape, growth and
mortality as well as the ability to separate frass and larvae, which are
operational problems that undermine the sustained economic and
environmental viability of this technology.
The bioconversion process has mostly been characterised by monitoring larval mass, biowaste reduction, bioconversion, and survival rates
in controlled feeding trials. Because BSFL live in their substrate/frass (i.
e. biowaste), the temperature can be significantly different from the
ambient temperature. Thus, the importance of substrate/frass temperature monitoring has been recognised recently but it has been monitored
by only a few studies (Erbland et al., 2021; Li et al., 2023). In fact,
Erbland et al. (2021) prototyped a ventilated incubator (six crates, 0.27
m2 per crate) that tracked mass loss and substrate/frass temperature
throughout BSFL bioconversion with chicken feed. The data suggest that
microbial activity plays an important role in the rearing of BSFL.
Nevertheless, there is a lack of research that attempts to reconstruct a
more comprehensive picture of BSFL bioconversion by measuring both
insect life history parameters and the abiotic environment by monitoring temperature fluctuations as well as the exchange of water and
emissions during the rearing process.
From answering fundamental biological questions to designing
climate systems for efficient BSFL bioconversion, the simultaneous
quantification of gaseous emissions and heat production during the
bioconversion is key. Respiration chambers are commonly used to
monitor gaseous emissions from living organisms to determine energy
and nutrient requirements and collect data for environmental impact
assessments of protein production. For instance respiration chambers
are used for the assessment of the metabolic activity of plants, soil, or
large livestock, such as cattle, however chamber size and the instruments used vary significantly (Albrizio and Steduto, 2003; Carbone
et al., 2019; Hammond et al., 2016; Heetkamp et al., 2015). Recent
evaluations of BSFL bioconversion have been conducted using dynamic
open-circuit respiration chambers, where gas concentrations were
continuously measured in ventilated chambers throughout the process
(Padmanabha and Streif, 2019; Parodi et al., 2020, 2021). Parodi et al.
(2020, 2021) monitored BSFL bioconversion with pig manure and an
industrial rearing substrate in an open-circuit respiration chamber
(three rearing crates per chamber, 0.15 m2 per crate or one rearing crate
per chamber, 0.5 m2 per crate). The goal was to track the development of
CO2, N2O, CH4, O2 and NH3 gas emissions and to calculate comprehensive nitrogen, carbon, and energy balances to assess the environmental sustainability of BSFL rearing. In contrast, Padmanabha and
Streif (2019) designed a low-cost chamber for automated BSFL rearing
and growth model development (Padmanabha et al., 2020, 2023). This
setup was capable of monitoring CO2 and O2 concentrations, air

temperature, and humidity, as well as the substrate/frass temperature
and humidity. However, it failed to capture NH3 emissions, which are
crucial indicators of larval protein metabolism and industrially relevant
air pollutants (Froonickx et al., 2023). Additionally, only a single crate
(0.12 m2 per crate), smaller than industrial size, was housed in their
setup. Consequently, there is a need for an accessible monitoring system
that can comprehensively assess the metabolic activity and trends in the
BSFL bioconversion processes of different substrates under conditions
that resemble practical implementation scenarios while adhering to
scientific standards.
Few studies have determined gaseous emissions (CO2, CH4, N2O and
NH3) from BSFL food waste bioconversion, mainly for environmental
impact assessments (Ermolaev et al., 2019; Lindberg et al., 2022; Mertenat et al., 2019; Pang et al., 2020). Large intervals between sampling
points complicate the determination of total emissions and neglect
common emission dynamics. Additionally, emission samples were
drawn from static systems (non-ventilated containers at the time of
sampling), in which increasing gas concentrations during measurement
could affect instantaneous larval and microbial activities, thereby
weakening the estimate. For instance, Guo et al. (2021) measured
gaseous emissions from commercial BSFL food waste bioconversion. The
sampling was performed at intervals of 4 h but only over a period of 3
days of the whole process, which did not enable the authors to draw
conclusions for the whole process. Unlike composting, a 6–7-day BSFL
bioconversion process is highly dynamic, and frequent sampling must
cover the entire process duration. For instance, CO2 emissions related to
larval and microbial activity can peak within hours, while NH3 emissions may surge only 2 days before the harvest of larvae (Coudron et al.,
2024; Parodi et al., 2020, 2021). Heterogeneous food waste is a challenging but key substrate in urban biowaste management and sustainable BSFL rearing and, therefore, needs urgent further exploration.
The aim of this study was to propose, describe, and validate an
industry-relevant bench-scale respiration system and use it for the first
time for the high-resolution characterisation of BSFL food waste
bioconversion. The system was validated for CO2 recovery, air flow
homogeneity, and its ability to capture the bioconversion within and
across parallel chambers using food waste in comparison to a reference
substrate. The results illustrated that a comprehensive BSFL bioconversion characterisation helps to understand BSFL food waste recycling
and to identify areas for further research. Therefore, this study established a tool to improve the bioconversion performance of BSFL with
urban biowaste for the production of feed and fertiliser for a circular
food system.
2. Material and methods
2.1. Respiration chamber for fly larvae bioconversion
The respiration system included four equally designed respiration
chambers that could be individually operated (Supplementary Fig. 1).
Fig. 1 depicts the general setup and components of the respiration
chamber, including the positions of sensors, whereas Table 1 depicts the
key system specifications. The respiration chamber was ventilated
through air inlet and outlet ducts for optimal sensor deployment and
determination of emission production and water removal from the
respiration system. The walls of the chamber were made of polyisocyanurate panels with an aluminium coating (30 mm; Kingspan,
Kingscourt, Ireland) to resist humidity and corrosion. For optimal
sampling and crate handling, the lid of the chamber was liftable from the
top, additionally tightened by rubber bands at the rim to ensure the
airtightness of the respiration system. The air inlet and outlet ducts were
covered with a plastic mesh (~1 mm) to prevent pests (e.g. insects) from
entering the respiration system and disrupting measurements. Unplasticised polyvinyl chloride (UPVC) ducts were connected to the inlet and
outlet of the chamber (Supplementary Fig. 2). Cable glands were applied
to seal the ports through which the sensor cables passed the duct or

2.3. Experimental design for technical validation

2.2. Bioconversion and respiration parameters

In the absence of larvae and substrate, the respiration system was
validated by completing tests on air tightness, air flow homogeneity and
CO2 recovery. Airtightness is crucial for avoiding drawing in ambient
air, which produces underestimated emission results. In addition, homogenous airflow is the key to ensure balanced heat and water transfer
throughout the three crates. CO2 recovery tests are the standard for
commercial high-tech respiration chambers for conventional livestock
to confirm airtightness, flow rate measurements, and validity of CO2
measurements. Airtightness was additionally confirmed for all chambers
according to Heetkamp et al. (2015) by placing soapy water under
maximum airflow at each crucial junction (lid, cable glands, and air
ducts) and confirming the absence of bubble formation.
Airflow homogeneity was determined in one of the chambers by
measuring air velocity across the chamber cross-section perpendicular
to the airflow at five predefined positions over each crate
(Supplementary Table 2) with a handheld hotwire anemometer (425,
Testo, Titisee-Neustadt, Germany). The anemometer was positioned in
the chamber via sealable ports at a constant airflow and 10 s mean air
flow velocities were measured for each position.
The CO2 recovery test was completed in all chambers based on
Heetkamp et al. (2015) and compared the difference in CO2 mass loss
from a commercial gas cylinder (99.8 % CO2) to the CO2 mass loss

In a third feeding trial on heterogeneous food waste, the composition

2.4. Experimental design for biological validation and heterogenous food
waste assessment
For the biological validation of the respiration system, i.e. the quality
of the setup to collect reproducible metabolic and rearing performance
metrics in BSFL feeding trials, the variability of measured parameters
within and across respirations chambers was assessed using different
rearing substrates. Metabolic metrics included substrate/frass temperature, CO2 production, and net mass loss of substrate and larvae,
whereas the two latter metrics were only measured on chamber level.
Rearing performance metrics were based on manually collected data
measured on crate level and included bioconversion rate, substrate
reduction, survival rate, individual larval mass, total frass yield, total
larval yield and frass moisture content. To this end, special focus was
placed on the variability of the measured parameters within and across
the respiration chambers (Fig. 2) in these trials. First, the variability
within the respiration chambers (or across crates in the same chamber)
was assessed to validate the performance of crates as biological replicates. As three substrate/frass temperature sensors were placed in each
crate, the substrate/frass temperature differences within the crates were
assessed. Second, the variability across the respiration chambers was
assessed to validate the performance of the respiration chambers as
biological replicates. Parameters reported as contents including the final
larval mass were aggregated as averages per chamber, whereas the
remaining parameters were aggregated as sums per chamber (e.g.
average frass moisture content per chamber and sum of larval yield per
chamber). Standard deviations thereof were used as measures of variability. However, to render results more comparable across metrics with
different units, the coefficient of variation (standard deviation divided
by mean) was used for the variables frass yield, total larval yield, water
removal, CO2 production, and mass loss of substrate and larvae.
Biological validation was completed in two separate controlled
feeding trials, one with food waste and the other with chicken feed used
as control. Each trial involved BSFL bioconversion in all four respiration
chambers in parallel. For the two trials, one uniform substrate was used
across all four chambers to assess the expected baseline variability of the
setup.

2.5. Substrate composition
Food waste consisting mainly of rice, noodles, and, to a smaller
extent, meat and vegetables was collected from a university canteen
(Ridge View Residential College, National University of Singapore,
Singapore), where it was disposed of within approximately 12 h before
collection. Following collection, the food waste was stored at 4 ◦ C until
use. Before the feeding trial, food waste was ground (Bio Universal
Shredder BG2-5,5, voran Maschinen GmbH, Pichl, Austria; see Supplementary Figure 4 for photos). Chicken feed provided by a local distributor was mixed with water to reach a final moisture content of 65 %.
Subsequently and before larvae addition, for efficient product separation at harvest, cocopeat was added to the food waste followed by
thorough mixing to absorb free water, according to Dortmans et al.
(2017), whereas in the trial with heterogeneous substrate across
chambers cocopeat was added to induce heterogeneity (Table 2 for
cocopeat contents).
2.6. Black soldier fly origin
The BSFL used in the trials originated from a laboratory colony
(National University of Singapore) that was maintained for at least 30
generations (Zhang et al., 2024) and initially set up based on wild caught
or laboratory cultures. Neonates and larvae of this colony were reared
on chicken feed and canteen food waste, respectively. For this study, fly
eggs from the colony were placed in an empty container covered with a
paper towel for 48 h (Deruytter et al., 2023). Neonates were nursed on
chicken feed (62 % water, 9 g of neonates, container: 37 cm × 50 cm × 9
cm). However, for the biological validation with food waste, an external
supplier (Ento Industries Pte Ltd., Singapore) provided larvae that had
been nursed on a vegetable-based substrate.
2.7. Feeding trials
The three trials were conducted using the described respiration
chambers (Table 2 for feeding trial parameters) located in a ventilated
laboratory on the National University of Singapore (NUS) campus with a
mean relative humidity of 82.8 ± 3.4 % and temperature of 28.5 ± 0.9
◦
C in 2023, based on one year long measurement from the inlet duct of
one chamber. At the beginning of the trial, the substrate was brought to
room temperature, thoroughly mixed, and sampled for compositional
analysis. Each rearing crate was then gradually filled with the substrate
(food waste or chicken feed) on a rotational basis to avoid batch effects.
Subsequently, an equal number of 5–7 − day-old larvae were transferred
into each crate. Using two spoons, three grab samples, covering the
entire surface and vertical substrate/frass profile, were drawn per crate
every second day during the trial and at harvest. Samples taken from the
same crate (for day 0 and harvest, substrate/frass was mixed instead)
were pooled before moisture content, pH, and individual larval mass
analyses, whereas material was returned to the respective crate. At
harvest, larvae were separated from frass by sieving, whereas if the
substrate was too clumpy for sieving larvae were manually picked, and
their mass assessed as rearing performance metrics. The total number of
larvae per crate at the beginning and at the end of the trial as well as the
larval mass were estimated based on random samples of approximately
100 larvae.

2.9. Data post-processing and analyses

3. Results and discussion

Comprehensive BSFL bioconversion process characterisation
included sensor-based estimation of CO2 concentration, NH3 concentration, airflow, air temperature, air relative humidity, substrate/frass
temperature, net mass loss of substrate and larvae, and manually
collected data to estimate rearing performance metrics: bioconversion
rate, substrate reduction, and survival rate. Sensor-based metabolic
process parameters (except for net mass loss of substrate and larvae)
were rounded and normalised via the software FarmOnline (SKOV). The
data were automatically transferred to cloud storage for post-processing,
visualisation, and statistical analysis in R version 4.1.3 (R Core Team,
2022) using RStudio (Posit team, 2023). Post-processing included the
removal of erroneous data when the chambers were opened for sample
collection based on air flow and CO2 dynamics. Airflow-based data
removal was conducted where differences between two consecutive
timepoints exceeded ± 5 m3 h− 1 because during closed operation air
flow differences were much lower than this cut-off. Because these
airflow changes had lag effects on the CO2 concentrations at the point of
measurement (outlet duct), removal of erroneous data had to be
extended. This outlier removal was based on the difference between
actual and smoothed data points based on local regressions (LOESS),
where < 1 % of total data was removed.
CO2 emissions were estimated every two minutes based on the difference in CO2 between the ingoing and outgoing air multiplied by the
current airflow, considering their specific volume at the current temperature (Supplementary Equation 1). Total water removal during the
feeding trial was estimated via an input–output based approach ie. the
mass and moisture content of water in the substrate versus in larvae and
frass. For a continuous, sensor-based approach of estimating total water
removal and substrate/frass dryness, the balance of water entering
versus water leaving the chamber via the air was calculated. Briefly,
sensor data for temperature and relative humidity were used to calculate
the absolute humidity in the ingoing and outgoing air via the respective
dew points (Sensirion AG, 2021), specific humidity, and water vapour
pressure (Cai, 2019). The absolute water removal per time step and the

BSFL bioconversion, an emerging technology for biowaste valorisation, still has significant process inefficiencies, particularly when
treating heterogeneous biowaste streams with varying compositions,
such as urban food waste. Therefore, this study proposes and validates a
novel respiration chamber system to investigate the impact of varying
substrate compositions on BSFL performance parameters that resemble
those of industrial insect farming to develop a more reliable and efficient
BSFL-based food waste treatment. For the first time, this study presents
highly resolved insights into the metabolic processes related to the
bioconversion of food waste with BSFL.
3.1. Technical validation
The respiration system was technically validated by measuring air
tightness, airflow homogeneity, and CO2. The results indicate that the
chamber performed well in terms of CO2 recovery. In addition, the
chamber exhibited some heterogeneities in the airflow velocity. In the
CO2 recovery test, 95–105 % of injected CO2 was recorded by the
respiration system (Supplementary Table 5). Concerning the airflow
homogeneity within the chamber, a trend of higher air velocities in the
middle of each crate and in the bottom crate was observed
(Supplementary Table 2). However, variabilities of air flow velocities
within and across crates were not high (standard deviations: within,
0.03–0.06 m s− 1; across, 0.05–0.06 m s− 1).
One advantage of the presented setup is the possibility of using three
stacked industrial-size rearing crates to serve as biological replicates and
mimic industrial conditions, in contrast to the open-circuit respiration
chamber by Padmanabha and Streif (2019). Yang and Tomberlin (2020)
investigated the impact of scale on feeding trials and demonstrated that
crate size is crucial for producing data representative of industrial BSFL
bioconversion. In contrast, Parodi et al. (2020) had a similar configuration to that of this study; however, the rearing parameters of their
three crates were not analysed separately, and airflow velocities over the

average temperature per crate. Hourly average temperatures across

Having robust measurements of substrate/frass temperature is
crucial because it is the environment in which larvae live and is,
therefore, a main factor for the larval development rate (Wang et al.,
2023). In fact, as shown below (Fig. 3A), substrate/frass temperatures

need for future studies to measure substrate temperature. Spatial differences in substrate/frass temperatures are expected in BSFL rearing
because of larvae roaming in swarms through the substrate/frass

camera to capture the entire spatial variability of the substrate/frass
temperature (Li et al., 2023), however only the surface temperatures
were considered here. With three continuously measuring substrate/
frass temperature sensors per crate, the setup of this study provides a
robust estimate. However, further research is necessary to identify the
optimal way to capture three-dimensional spatial variability.

3.2. Biological validation
Biological validation included determining metabolic and rearing
performance metrics during controlled feeding trials in the chambers.
Comparisons of variability within and between chambers were performed using uniform substrates across the chambers to further validate
the applicability of the chamber system for addressing research questions on feeding trials. Within-chamber validation included comparison
of rearing performance metrics across three rearing crates in one
chamber and the substrate/frass temperature within one crate. The
between-chamber validation included a comparison of all measured
parameters across the four parallel chambers (Fig. 2).
In general, the results indicated that the presented respiration
chambers provide rearing conditions that are well-suited for BSFL
rearing, while generating representative results. Metabolic and rearing
performance metrics in this study were even higher than those reported
previously (Erbland et al., 2021; Gold et al., 2018; Manurung et al.,
2016; Naser El Deen et al., 2023; Parodi et al., 2020). Survival rates were
around 90 %, final larval mass around 60 mg, bioconversion rates
22–28 %, substrate/frass temperatures > 36 ◦ C for several days, and
peak CO2 production rates between 20–50 g h− 1. Peak substrate/frass
temperatures of up to 50 ◦ C at individual spots likely did not provide
conditions that are optimal for larvae (Chia et al., 2018) but have been
reported previously in BSFL and blow fly larvae systems (Erbland et al.,
2021; Slone and Gruner, 2007), and proved that the proposed system
could be used to investigate the common issue of substrate/frass overheating. These generally high values for larval mass, survival rate and
substrate/frass temperature were expected, given that food waste and
chicken feed are among the most nutrient- and energy-dense waste
streams fed to the BSFL. In fact, the present study emphasizes the significant potential of food waste to be efficiently recycled via BSFL due to
its nutritional quality as reported previously (Naser El Deen et al., 2023).
For instance, Manurung et al. (2016) reported a final larval mass of only
less than 16 mg for BSFL fed with nutrient-poor rice straw. Notably
chicken feed and food waste used for the biological validation had
similar starch (food waste: 27 %, chicken feed: 30 %) and protein (food
waste: 24 %, chicken feed: 24 %) contents (Supplementary Table 3 for
more detailed information on substrate characteristics).

3.2.2. Baseline variability across chambers
The variability across the chambers was lower than the previously
mentioned variability within the chambers (Fig. 2, Supplementary Table
8). With both substrates, the variability was < 1 % for bioconversion
rate, < 0.6 ◦ C for substrate/frass temperature, < 3 mg for final larval
mass and 2 % for survival rate. Similarly, for both substrates, the variability (coefficient of variation) was < 2.5 % for larval yield, < 2.7 % for
frass yield, < 1 % for water removal, and ≤ 1.9 % for net mass loss of
substrate and larvae. Likewise, the variability in product composition
was low for fat and protein contents of larvae, varying by 0.55 g 100-1
g− 1 and 0.36 g 100-1 g− 1, respectively. Total CO2 production differed
moderately between chambers in the feeding trial with food waste with
a coefficient of variation of 8 %. However, in the trial with chicken feed,
variability of CO2 production was exceptionally high at 17 %. This
outcome might be due to nonuniform waterlogging in chicken feed
across crates, resulting in different microbial activities or other unknown reasons (Bekker et al., 2021). The sensor-based approach for
water removal estimation yielded higher average values and higher
variability than the input–output-based approach, which requires
further investigation. However, discrepancies in the average values

have been released based on the nutrient composition of food waste and

Generally, marginal variability across chambers has implications for
two possible applications of the respiration system. First, four chambers,
each with the same substrate, can be used as replicates to robustly estimate the average total CO2 emissions, time points of the highest CO2
production, substrate/frass temperatures, or bioconversion rates when a
specific substrate is converted. Second, the chambers can be used to
conduct parallel comparisons of the impacts of different substrates.
When the chambers are run in parallel, each with a different substrate,
the generally determined low across-chamber variability serves as a
reference and sets the bar for the effect size. For example, in trials with
uniform food waste or chicken feed across the chambers, the variability
in the final larval mass was 1 or 2 mg, respectively. Therefore, when
comparing the effects of treatments on larval mass across parallel
chambers, differences exceeding the 2 mg baseline may be attributed to
a treatment effect beyond the variability introduced by the use of
different chambers. A baseline of 2 mg is low considering that treatment
effects on the final larval mass are generally more pronounced. For
instance, NH3 pretreatments on substrates by Peguero et al. (2023)
changed final larval mass by at least 9 mg.
In addition to the provision of aggregated and endpoint values, the
respiration chamber system enables investigating and comparing temporal metabolic patterns of the bioconversion process (e.g. substrate/
frass and air temperature, relative humidity, gaseous emissions, and net
mass loss of substrate and larvae). For instance, CO2 production curves
showed consistent temporal patterns (maxima, minima, and slopes)
across chambers for each substrate but altered patterns between
different substrates (Supplementary Figures 7 and 8). With food waste,

the CO2 production rate rose steeply within the first 24 h of the trial,
slowed down until day 2, and peaked at a production rate of approximately 50 g CO2 h− 1 between days 3 and 4, after which it declined
continuously until harvest, intercepted by a short plateau phase towards
the end of day 5. In contrast, with chicken feed, the CO2 production
curve was skewed towards the end of the trial, with a slow start, peaking
at the end of day 5. Notably the initial larval mass was lower in the
chicken feed trial (Table 1) which might have caused a relative delay of
the CO2 peak. Across substrate comparisons show that the system is
suitable for highlighting and differentiating the effects of a changing
substrate composition on the bioconversion. Continuous time-series
data with small sampling intervals, as shown in this study, can be
valuable for improving process understanding, but comparative analyses of curves are often qualitative. Future research should explore the
feasibility of shape-based quantitative analyses of time series, which
could help identify and classify recurring metabolic patterns in
bioconversion processes, such as further investigating the contribution
of substrate/frass microbes versus BSFL to CO2 production (Bekker et al.,
2021). Potentially suitable methods for quantitative shape based analyses of biological timeseries have recently been described (Dove et al.,
2023).
3.3. Substrate/frass temperature, CO2 production and larval growth with
heterogenous food waste
After the biological validation of the setup, a feeding trial with heterogeneous food waste across chambers was conducted to assess the
potential of the setup to capture the resulting changes in the metabolic
processes in BSFL rearing. The introduction of compositional differences
in food waste across chambers led to a strong increase in the variability
of bioconversion parameters across chambers compared with trials with
uniform substrates across chambers. In fact, the variability across
chambers was higher for almost all parameters than the previously

assessed baseline, except for the larval survival rate, which was generally high (Supplementary Table 8). The final larval mass varied by 12 mg
larva-1 (coefficient of variation: 23 %). In fact, higher total CO2 production was accompanied by higher average temperatures in the substrate/frass, higher net mass loss of the substrate and larvae, and fastergrowing larvae, especially during the first half of the trial (Fig. 3). In
contrast, the bioconversion rate and final larval yield decreased with
increasing CO2 production. Likewise, the four food waste mixtures
exhibited distinctive patterns of CO2 production over time, whereas for
the same food waste mixture, the substrate/frass temperature and CO2
production showed highly similar patterns. Both CO2 production and
heat are indicators of metabolic activity; however, periods of strongest
CO2 production and larval mass growth aligned only for food waste with
2 % and 4 % cocopeat addition. Increased larval or microbial activity
might have been a driver of CO2 and substrate temperature (Bekker
et al., 2021; Erbland et al., 2021; Slone and Gruner, 2007). In this study
moisture contents differing across food waste mixtures by 3 % might
have had an influence on microbial activity and therefore on CO2 and
heat generation in the substrate, however Bekker et al. (2021) indicated
that rather differences in substrate moisture contents of 10 % lead to
decisive changes in microbial activity. Similarly, strong differences in
CO2 emissions from BSFL bioconversion were observed by Parodi et al.
(2020, 2021) notably by using very distinct inputs: an industrial rearing
substrate based on yeast concentrate and starch versus pig manure. The
peak CO2 emissions per larva were less than half of those observed in this
study. The CO2 production curves exhibited, depending on the substrate,
either one pronounced peak (similar to food waste with 4 % fibre
addition in this study) on rearing day 5 of the trial or a gentle, plateaushaped maximum (similar to food waste with 0 % fibre addition in this
study) from rearing days 5 to day 7, respectively. Total CO2 emissions
from pig manure were 40 % lower compared to the industrial rearing
substrate, whereas the authors suggested the lower nutritional quality of
the latter as an explanation. In this study a nutritional reason for an
increased biological activity is unlikely since the common bulking agent,
cocopeat, which was used to introduce variation in food waste composition across chambers, had a negligible nutritive value (80 % ADF and
17 % ash content). Additionally, the total amount of food waste per crate
did not differ. Notably, past feeding trials frequently used “food waste”
as one category when bioconversion parameters or the environmental
effects of BSFL rearing on different substrate types were compared
(Boakye-Yiadom et al., 2022; Naser El Deen et al., 2023). However, the
results of this study suggested that even the bioconversion of nutritionally similar food wastes can lead to process variabilities comparable
to those between pig manure and a highly nutritive industrial rearing
substrate. In fact, the implications for industrially relevant heat generation and resulting requirements for climate control systems are substantial. Based on the close association between heat and CO2 in
livestock systems (Pedersen and Sällvik, 2002), it can be estimated that
during the peak periods in this study, approximately 50 or 20 Watts of
heat was generated per crate, depending on the food waste mixture.
Extensive heat production requires cooling and therefore energy, which
is an environmental but also an economic concern for this waste management technology given that 25 % − 56 % of electrical energy consumption in livestock systems is used for cooling. The findings from this
study put into question the way substrates are currently categorised for
performance assessments and waste recycling. Further research is
necessary to identify the substrate characteristics that lead to the
observed temperature patterns, as the management of heat and larval
growth are key optimisable variables in the recycling of BSFL biowaste
(Li et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023). The presented time-series data
confirmed the potential of the chamber system to characterise and
improve the efficiency of food waste bioconversion processes.

chamber system that can be used to holistically investigate metabolic
processes in BSFL rearing under conditions that resemble those at the
industrial scale. Additionally, this study provides unique, highly
resolved insights into the metabolic processes that occur during BSFL
bioconversion of food waste. Validation trials confirmed the suitability
of the setup to address the research questions from a biological and
technical perspective. The low baseline variability within and across
chambers indicates that crates and chambers could serve as biological
replicates to discriminate the impact of different inputs on the bioconversion process. The present study, using the chamber system, showed
for the first time that the addition of a nutritionally negligible bulking
agent to food waste could lead to processes with strongly differing
temporal metabolic characteristics and products. Shown substrate
formulation dependent increases in CO2 emissions are highly relevant
for the environmental performance of the BSFL bioconversion. Future
work should focus on the technical refinement of the chamber, including
the achievement of an accurate estimate of the water balance and the
sampling of additional complementary metabolic indicators such as O2
and CH4 to compose full energy and material balances. The presented
chamber system should be used to further investigate the physical,
chemical, and biological characteristics of rearing substrates that drive
CO2 emissions, heat production, and larval growth in BSFL rearing. This
will pave the way for better prediction and control of bioconversion
processes, which is highly necessary when using heterogeneous biowastes. Additionally, these findings will help to reduce CO2 and NH3
emissions from BSFL bioconversion, thereby improving its environmental performance.

Abstract
The black soldier fly (BSF) has garnered the attention of the scientific community due to its outstanding efficiency in transforming organic
waste into raw materials that can be incorporated into the value chain. A bibliometric and bibliographic review was conducted to elucidate
the pivotal role played by the bioconversion of organic matter in shaping sustainable circular economy systems. The analysis revealed that
black soldier fly larvae (BSFL) have proven effective in the bioconversion of common waste, such as household and livestock waste, yielding
valuable biomass. Despite these advancements, the exploration of new sources of organic matter persists to mitigate its environmental
impact. Emerging technologies enable the efficient processing of BSFL biomass, yielding substitutes for environmentally unfriendly
materials. Although the literature emphasizes the advantages of BSF in constructing circular economy models, obstacles such as limited
legislation and insufficient incentives for producers, concerns about pathogens and contaminants, and low public acceptance of this species
are identified. However, the growing trend in scientific interest suggests that BSF could play a central role in building sustainable societies
in the future.
Keywords: black soldier fly; Hermetia illucens; circular economy; sustainability; bioconversion; use of waste.

Resumen
La mosca soldado negra (MSN) ha captado la atención de la comunidad científica debido a su destacada eficiencia en la transformación
de desechos orgánicos en materias primas integrables en la cadena de valor. Se llevó a cabo una revisión bibliométrica y bibliográfica con
el objetivo de elucidar el papel crucial que desempeña la bioconversión de materia orgánica en la configuración de sistemas sustentables
de economía circular. El análisis reveló que las larvas de MSN (LMSN) han demostrado ser efectivas en la bioconversión de residuos
comunes como desechos domésticos y ganaderos, generando biomasa útil. A pesar de estos avances, persiste la exploración de nu evas
fuentes de materia orgánica para mitigar su impacto ambiental. Tecnologías emergentes permiten procesar eficientemente la biomasa de
LMSN, generando productos sustitutos de materiales poco amigables con el entorno. Aunque la literatura destaca las ventajas de la MSN
en la construcción de modelos de economía circular, se identifican obstáculos como la limitada legislación, falta de incentivos para
productores, preocupaciones por patógenos y contaminantes y la baja aceptación pública de esta especie. Sin embargo, la creciente
tendencia en el interés científico sugiere que la MSN podría desempeñar un papel central en la edificación de sociedades sostenibles en
el futuro.
Palabras clave: mosca soldado negra; Hermetia illucens; economía circular; sostenibilidad; bioconversión; aprovechamiento de residuos.

1. Introducción
El cambio climático y el constante aumento de la población, acompañado de una mejora general en el
nivel de vida y el poder adquisitivo, han provocado un
constante incremento de la presión sobre los bienes y

servicios ambientales, especialmente en países en vías
de desarrollo (Bárcena-Ibarra et al., 2020; Leal Filho et
al., 2023). Ante estas circunstancias, los modelos
predominantes de producción y suministro resultan
limitados y poco efectivos para adaptarse a un futuro
más sostenible (Leng et al., 2022).

Dentro de este contexto, la economía circular se
presenta como una alternativa viable que busca minimizar los residuos y maximizar el aprovechamiento de recursos, fomentando la reutilización,
reciclaje y diseño de productos para cerrar los ciclos
de vida (Gomez-San Juan et al., 2022). En la
búsqueda de modelos multiespecíficos que
permitan abordar los problemas socioeconómicos
ante las crisis socioambientales actuales sobresale
una especie de insecto versátil sobre otras: la mosca
soldado negra (MSN) (Hermetia illucens) (Wade &
Hoelle, 2020). La MSN destaca por su capacidad de
transformar desechos orgánicos de diferente
origen en materias primas de alto valor nutricional,
agroalimentario e industrial (Woodley, 2009;
Mahmood et al., 2021; Amrul et al., 2022).
La capacidad que tienen las larvas de MSN (LMSN)
de reciclar la materia orgánica en descomposición
(MOD) abre la posibilidad de reincorporar al mercado un cúmulo de subproductos de todo tipo de
procedencia, incluyendo el sector agropecuario y
silvícola, la manufactura de alimentos, desechos
domésticos y restauranteros, entre muchos otros,
los cuales pueden convertirse en un problema de
salud pública si no son tratados adecuadamente
(Luperdi et al., 2023; Alagappan et al., 2022; Amrul
et al., 2022; Ioannou et al., 2022).
Diversos expertos concuerdan en que existe una
gran oportunidad de mercado en torno al aprovechamiento de la biomasa de MSN y sus derivados
(da Silva & Hesselberg, 2020; Alagappan et al.,
2022; Van Huis et al., 2021). Las implicaciones económicas, legales, ambientales y bioéticas en la cadena de producción de proteínas de origen animal,
coloca a la MSN como una de las alternativas más
viables sobre otros sistemas convencionales como
la ganadería y la acuicultura para un futuro más
sustentable (Skrivervik, 2020; Alagappan et al.,
2022; Milburn, 2023; Rehman et al., 2023). Sin embargo, aún se deben superar algunos obstáculos
para alcanzar este hito, ya que se debe garantizar
que los productos derivados de MSN estén libres
de contaminantes biológicos y químicos, cumplan
con las normas de bioseguridad alimentaria, cuenten con un mercado dispuesto a utilizarlos y que se
llegue a un consenso general que permita el
desarrollo de legislaciones nacionales y regionales
sobre toda la cadena de producción de MSN.
En los últimos 10 años ha incrementado exponencialmente el número de publicaciones científicas
donde se aborda a la MSN desde múltiples perspectivas, destacando su participación en la construcción de un futuro más sostenible. Sin embargo,
la normatividad y legislación que en torno al uso de
la MSN como parte del sistema económico no se

ha desarrollado a la misma velocidad que la generación de conocimiento en torno a la MSN
(Alagappan et al., 2022). Por todo lo anterior, es necesario conocer el estado actual del conocimiento
sobre la MSN como una especie potencial para su
incorporación en la transición hacia la economía
circular y los desafíos futuros. El objetivo de la presente revisión es elucidar el papel que desempeña la
bioconversión de materia orgánica utilizando la MSN
en la configuración de sistemas sustentables de
economía circular.

La participación de la MSN en el entorno de la sostenibilidad es amplia y puede abordarse desde
diferentes aristas, sin embargo, para fines prácticos
de esta revisión bibliográfica se exploró su papel en
la bioconversión de materia orgánica y en la
economía circular. Para dimensionar el estado del
conocimiento actual de la mosca soldado negra
desde las perspectivas de su papel en la sustentabilidad, bioconversión de residuos orgánicos y la

2.1 Generalidades de la Mosca Soldado Negra
La mosca soldado negra (MSN), Hermetia illucens
(Linnaeus, 1758) es un díptero perteneciente a la
familia Stratiomydae. Esta especie es nativa de
regiones tropicales, subtropicales y templadas del
continente americano, con temperaturas óptimas
de 25 a 30 °C, no pudiendo sobrevivir a menos de
5 °C (Lu et al, 2022). Debido a que la mosca puede
soportar diferentes condiciones de humedad, luz y
temperatura, se ha establecido en Australia, India,
Europa y África, después de ser transportada por
los humanos (Barragan et al., 2017).
En su forma adulta, el insecto es negro y alargado,
con tres segmentos (cabeza, tórax y vientre) y
ronda los 10–25 mm de longitud (Tomberlin &
Cammack, 2018). Tiene alas de color marrón y tentáculos que se proyectan desde la cabeza. En el abdomen cuenta con cinco segmentos con manchas
blancas. Los machos son más largos que las hembras, pero tienen alas y genitales finales más pequeños. Las hembras tienen longitudes corporales
entre 12 y 20 mm y alas entre 8 y 14,8 mm (Lu et al.,
2022). Este insecto experimenta una metamorfosis
completa, pasando por cinco etapas durante su ciclo de vida: huevo, larva, prepupa, pupa y adulto
(Figura 1). El ciclo de vida completo dura de 20 a 22
días bajo condiciones ambientales idóneas, con una
pupa durante los primeros 6 a 8 días y una metamorfosis adulta durante los últimos 14 días (Lu et al.,
2022). Sin embargo, la duración del ciclo de vida
puede variar de dos semanas a varios meses en relación con la temperatura, la humedad de la dieta,
la humedad relativa, entre otros (Tomberlin &
Cammack &, 2018).
La MSN no representa una amenaza para otros
organismos y no tienen afinidad por el cuerpo
humano ni por los alimentos frescos, por lo que no

son consideradas especies vectores o plagas en los
países donde habitan naturalmente (Lu et al., 2022;
Barragan et al., 2017).
Las LMSN han cobrado gran interés como alternativa para la alimentación animal, principalmente, y
en menor medida, para la humana debido a su importante valor nutricional (Tabla 2). Las etapas de
larva y pupa son las más ricas en nutrientes y dependen en gran medida de la calidad de los
sustratos de los que se alimentan, con alrededor de
14,7–39 g/100 g en base seca (bs) de grasa y 37–
56,2 g/100 g bs de proteína en base seca (Cammak
& Tomberlin, 2017; Caligiani et al., 2018; BarraganFonseca et al., 2017; Gligorescu et al., 2018; Liu et
al., 2017; Müller et al., 2017). Al respecto, Cammak
& Tomberlin (2017) han reportado que el perfil
nutricional de las larvas de H. illucens depende de
la composición de nutrientes de las dietas, por lo
que se puede lograr mayores porcentajes de
proteína, lípidos o carbohidratos en la biomasa de
larvas enriqueciendo el sustrato del que se
alimentan. La MSN también presenta un perfil de
aminoácidos esenciales y ácidos grasos, así como
un contenido de vitaminas y minerales muy
interesante y beneficioso para animales y humanos
(Oonincx & Finke, 2021; Bessa et al., 2020; Caligiani
et al., 2019).

2.2. Aprovechamiento de residuos orgánicos
La actual demanda de proteínas de origen animal
ha llevado a que cerca del 80% de las tierras cultivables se destinen a la ganadería, ya sea para el
establecimiento de granjas o zonas de cultivo para
la producción del alimento que se destinará a este
sector (FAO, 2015; Eldridge, 2016).

Esto supone una gran presión por la demanda de
recursos naturales y servicios ambientales de todo
el planeta, puesto que los casi 30 mil millones de
animales de cría (reses, cerdos, cabras y ovejas,
aves de corral, etc.) requieren no solo espacio y alimento, sino también altos volúmenes de agua
dulce, aire de calidad, cuidado, condiciones de
higiene, etc. (FAO, 2015).
En este contexto, numerosos estudios reconocen la
alta capacidad de la MSN para convertir desechos
orgánicos de diferentes orígenes en proteína animal, es decir, ésta es capaz de alimentarse de
sustratos bajos en proteína formados por
desperdicios, desechos y restos de alimentos,
granjas, agroindustria, entre otros, y transformarlos
en proteínas asequibles y de alta calidad relativa
para alimentar y nutrir animales y humanos
(Lalander et al., 2020; Surendra et al., 2020). Por lo
tanto, no es de extrañar, que en la revisión
bibliográfica palabras dentro de la semántica de la
bioconversión aparecieran frecuentemente como
“biotransformation”, “waste management”, “food
waste”, “waste”, “manure”, “waste treatment”,
“organic waste”, “circular economy” o “biomass”. Es
por ello que se considera a la MSN como una
especie “ecoeficiente” para la bioconversión de
residuos orgánicos en materias primas de alto valor
en el sector agroalimentario (Mahmood et al., 2021;
Amrul et al., 2022). Inclusive, la MSN es capaz de
reciclar gases de efecto invernadero, ya que
Lalander et al. (2020) encontraron que sus larvas
pueden tomar el 1,95–13,41% y el 5,40 – 18,93% del
carbono y el nitrógeno del sustrato, respectivamente, evitando así su liberación a la atmósfera.
La reducción del peso total, la biotransformación y
la tasa de conversión de diferentes sustratos por
medio de las LMSN se ejemplifica en la Tabla 3. Se
ha constatado que LMSN son capaces de reducir
entre 46,7–68% el peso total de MOD como
residuos de frutas y vegetales, industriales de trigo
y orgánicos municipales (Surendra et al., 2020).
Sobre estos mismos sustratos se observó un
porcentaje de bioconversión del 4,1–14% y una tasa
de conversión de alimento de 5,8–12,5. La biomasa

obtenida de las larvas de H. illucens alimentadas
con estos desechos presentan perfiles nutricionales idóneos para ser consideradas como alimentos potenciales para animales de cría monogástricos
y rumiantes (Khanal et al., 2023; Toral et al., 2022).

Los desechos animales de rastros vacunos, porcinos
y de aves también son un potencial recurso alimenticio para las LMSN (Luperdi et al., 2023). Unos pocos estudios, como el de Luperdi et al. (2023),
reportan que sustratos basados en diferentes subproductos de rastros de pollo y ganado incrementan significativamente la composición proteínica
(50,81% del peso seco) de las LMSN en comparación con el grupo control alimentado sólo con granos. Sin embargo, aún son necesarias más pruebas
sobre bioseguridad para el consumo de larvas
desarrolladas en estos y otros sustratos antes de ser
consideradas para la alimentación humana o
animal (Alagappan et al., 2022).
Por sus características de bioconversión, la MSN representa una alternativa amigable con el medioambiente para contribuir a la revalorización de los residuos sólidos orgánicos (Purkayastha & Sarkar,
2021; Amrul et al., 2022; Mahmood et al., 2021), es
decir, la MSN presenta alto potencial para ser la
base de un sistema de economía circular agroindustrial. En última instancia, el uso de la MSN para

2.3. Procesamiento y productos derivados de la
Mosca Soldado Negra
La bioconversión de residuos orgánicos por medio
de la MSN ofrece una amplia gama de posibilidades
para el sector industrial (Figura 2). Actualmente, las
LMSN son principalmente utilizadas para la alimentación de animales monogástricos (Joly & Nikiema,
2019), pudiéndose comercializar larvas vivas, larvas
deshidratadas o larvas en forma de polvo, ya sea
entero o desengrasado. Adicionalmente, Surendra
et al. (2020) mencionan que los principales productos que se pueden obtener de la cría y procesamiento de las LMSN son: proteína (para obtener
bioplásticos, hidrolizados proteicos y agentes emulsificantes), la grasa (útil para producir concentrados
para animales, biodiesel y agentes lubricantes), la
quitina (de la cual se puede obtener films comestibles, quitosano, aglutinantes e hilo quirúrgico), pigmentos extraídos de las moscas adultas, así como
los residuos llamados “frass”, de los que se obtiene
fertilizantes orgánicos y biogás.
2.3.1. Procesamiento
Luego de que las larvas alcanzan el peso adecuado
en la etapa de cría, se realiza una separación del
excremento generado durante la digestión de las
larvas y los restos de sustrato. Joly & Nikiema (2019)
indican que la técnica utilizada para separar las
LMSN del residuo de sustrato depende de la etapa
en la que se encuentre el animal al ser cosechado,
es decir, etapa larval o prepupal. Cuando la cosecha
se lleva a cabo en la etapa prepupal, el método más
común reportado en la literatura es la autocosecha, es decir, que las prepupas migran naturalmente del resto de sustrato para encontrar un sitio
de pupación. Las prepupas son guiadas a un lugar
determinado, generalmente a través de una rampa,
para ser cosechadas. La ventaja de la autocosecha
es que es un método simple y no intensivo en mano
de obra (Joly & Nikiema, 2019). Por otro lado, para
cosechar las larvas antes de que se conviertan en
prepupas, se utiliza un tamiz, ya sea manual o
automático (Dortmans et al., 2017).
Una vez cosechadas, las larvas requieren una etapa
que asegure su inocuidad microbiológica, así como
estabilidad para el transporte y almacenamiento. El
escaldado es una opción para sacrificar las LMSN,

ya que no sólo reduce la carga microbiana en la
biomasa y vacía el intestino de las larvas (Dortmans
et al., 2017), sino que también es rápido y menos
costoso, mitiga la oxidación de lípidos, aumenta la
estabilidad del color y mejora el sabor (Larouche et
al., 2019). Para realizar el escaldado, las larvas son
sumergidas en agua hirviendo por 2 min (Dortmans
et al., 2017).
No existe un consenso en cuanto a la mejor técnica
de secado de LMSN antes de su procesamiento y/o
almacenamiento, ya que existe una discrepancia en
cuanto a las ventajas y desventajas de algunos de
los protocolos de secado empleados (HernándezÁlvarez et al., 2021). En este contexto, el secado en
horno y al sol son más populares que otros métodos como el secado por microondas, liofilización y
al vacío. El secado en horno puede aplicarse en
temperaturas >60 ºC/2–12 h o hasta alcanzar una
humedad ≤ 10% (Charlton et al., 2015; Dortmans et
al., 2017; Joly & Nikiema, 2019). Sin embargo, una
desventaja del secado por horneado y solar es que
si se emplean temperaturas relativamente bajas (60
– 80 ºC) se extiende el tiempo de deshidratación y
no se garantiza una disminución significativa de algunos microorganismos como Ascaris suum, pero
sí sobre Salmonella spp. (Lalander et al., 2013). Otra
desventaja es que el secado a estas temperaturas
puede ocasionar rancidez de los lípidos de las larvas, por lo que las propiedades tecnofuncionales y
organolépticas de estas pueden verse afectadas
negativamente.
En muchas ocasiones, después de la cosecha, el sacrificio y el secado, las LMSN se procesan mediante
tratamientos térmicos (Hernández-Álvarez et al.,
2021). Estos pueden ser el escaldado, cocción, ultrasonicación, tostado, ahumado y horneado a altas
temperaturas (>105 ºC). Con estos tratamientos se
puede reducir la presencia de agentes microbianos,
modificar el perfil nutricional, reducir los tiempos de
deshidratación (cuando no se aplica un pretratamiento de secado) y conservar/generar características tecnofuncionales deseables (HernándezÁlvarez et al., 2021).
Las larvas deshidratadas (y en ocasiones tratadas
térmicamente) pueden ser sometidas a una operación de extracción de lípidos, con el fin de optimizar
su aplicación en alimentos animales. Esta extracción
se puede realizar mecánicamente, por medio de
una prensa o realizando una extracción química
con éter de petróleo. El polvo desengrasado puede
empacarse y comercializarse directamente.

El aceite extraído se puede utilizar como ingrediente en concentrados animales o como biodiesel
(Joly & Nikiema, 2019), sin embargo, debe de considerarse el fin para el que se requiere la fracción
lipídica, ya que el uso de solventes orgánicos puede
ser no adecuado para elaborar alimentos animales,
pero sí para biocombustibles y resinas industriales,
entre otros productos. Cuando existe un interés sobre la proteína es posible realizar etapas subsecuentes, como la molienda y la extracción acuosa
por medio de precipitación por variación de pH, lo
cual permite obtener desde concentrados hasta
aislados con proporciones proteicas entre 50% a
90% (Bußler et al., 2016). Asimismo, Edah & Owolabi
(2023) demostraron que la extrusión de LMSN
desengrasadas (con reducción de 60% de grasa) es
idónea para la producción de pellets que cuenten
con mejores características de flotación adecuadas
para la alimentación de peces.
2.3.2. Aplicaciones de la MSN para consumo animal
El aumento en el precio y la demanda de insumos
para la alimentación animal, exacerbada sobre todo
después de la pandemia de COVID-19, los conflictos bélicos de Europa Oriental y la llamada guerra
comercial China-Estados Unidos, han ocasionado
un aumento vertiginoso de los precios de la harina
de pescado, la soya y los granos para forraje (Attia
et al., 2023; Jia et al., 2022). Ante esta situación
varios expertos han propuesto a los insectos como
una fuente innovadora para suplir las necesidades
nutricionales de los alimentos, debido principalmente a su alto contenido calórico, lipídico y
proteico (Gasco et al., 2020; Ozhohanych et al.,

2023). Específicamente, la MSN se presenta como
una excelente alternativa para la alimentación de
animales debido a su alta capacidad como
bioreciclador de MOD y la rapidez y facilidad de
producción (Barragan-Fonseca et al., 2017).
Una de las principales aplicaciones que se propone
para la MSN es su uso en la alimentación de peces,
principalmente en la acuicultura. Al respecto, Muin
& Taufek (2024) compararon el rendimiento del
crecimiento de la tilapia híbrida roja al alimentarla
con LMSN y harina de pescado. Los resultados demostraron que los peces alimentados con la dieta
de LMSN exhibieron una ganancia de peso, una
tasa de crecimiento específico, un índice de eficiencia proteica y un índice de conversión alimenticia
significativamente mayores (p < 0,05) que los alimentados con harina de pescado.
Asimismo, Eide et. al (2024) concluyeron que la harina de LMSN es un ingrediente proteico alternativo
adecuado en inclusiones de hasta al menos el 8%
para el salmón del Atlántico en condiciones de
acuicultura industrial. Los investigadores realizaron
una prueba de alimentación para evaluar el impacto de LMSN en el crecimiento y la salud del salmón del Atlántico durante la fase de crecimiento en
agua de mar, en un sitio comercial en el condado
de Vestland, Noruega. Un total de 181.046 salmones
del Atlántico post-smolt se distribuyeron en seis
jaulas marinas duplicadas y se alimentaron con una
de tres dietas (una dieta de control similar a la comercial y dos dietas de prueba que reemplazaban
parcialmente el contenido de proteína de la dieta
de control con 4% y 8% de harina LMSN desgrasada). Los resultados mostraron que la inclusión de

Bermúdez-Serrano & Sánchez-Velázquez

harina LMSN favoreció el crecimiento y no tuvo ningún efecto adverso en la salud intestinal de los
peces. Además, no se atribuyó ningún cambio
histopatológico a la ingesta de comida de LMSN.
Asimismo, se demostró que la inclusión de LMSN
modula los procesos metabólicos asociados con los
lípidos, la respuesta a los estrógenos, la actividad
de los receptores inmunes (a las quimiocinas), la
fagocitosis y las vesículas extracelulares.
Los formuladores de dietas animales de cría y compañía también han comenzado a explorar la posibilidad de incluir a las LMSN como ingrediente alimenticio para satisfacer la demanda de los principales macro y micronutrientes (Barragan-Fonseca
et al., 2017). En la mayoría de los casos se propone
una sustitución parcial del concentrado animal con
LMSN, ya que una sustitución completa no ha resultado en un crecimiento satisfactorio del animal
(Barragan-Fonseca et al., 2017). Estos resultados
pueden asociarse al alto contenido de grasas y ceniza de las LMSN, a la forma de procesamiento de
las LMSN y los aminoácidos limitantes en las dietas
específicas de cada animal (Barragan-Fonseca et
al., 2017).
Los requerimientos nutricionales de los animales
domésticos, incluyendo los de compañía y los de
cría para alimentación, son muy variables y específicos entre sí (Tabla 4), por lo que es necesario
considerar aspectos como la edad, el tamaño, el
genotipo y el nivel de actividad físico de los individuos antes de la formulación (Castrica et al., 2018;
Dzanis, 1994; NRC, 1994, 2006, 2007, 2011, 2016;
Van Huis et al., 2013). Los criadores de animales
entienden estas necesidades, por lo que las dietas
son complementadas con diversas fuentes y
también son modificadas conforme avanza el
desarrollo de los animales.
Los formuladores de dietas animales de cría y compañía han comenzado a explorar la posibilidad de
incluir a las LMSN como ingrediente alimenticio

para satisfacer la demanda de los principales macro
y micronutrientes (Barragan-Fonseca et al., 2017).
En la mayoría de los casos se propone una sustitución parcial del concentrado animal con LMSN, ya
que una sustitución completa no ha resultado en un
crecimiento satisfactorio del animal (BarraganFonseca et al., 2017). Como ejemplo de ello, en un
estudio conducido por Facey et al. (2022) se sustituyó parcial o totalmente la dieta de pollos que
consiste en maíz-soya por LMSN (0% - 100%) durante 49 días, resultando las dietas de 12,5% y 25%
LMSN las que mostraron las mejores ganancias de
peso en los pollos y las de 50 y 100% LMSN las menores. Estos resultados pueden asociarse al alto
contenido de grasas y ceniza de las LMSN, a la
forma de procesamiento de las LMSN y los requerimientos aminoacídicos de estos animales
(Barragan-Fonseca et al., 2017; Facey et al., 2022).
Sin embargo, debe de entenderse también que la
composición nutricional de las LMSN está directamente relacionada con el tipo de sustrato alimenticio con el que se desarrollaron. La Tabla 5 muestra
la composición nutricional de LMSN crecidas en
cinco de los sustratos alimenticios más comunes.
Como se puede apreciar, la harina de pescado permite que las LMSN contengan una mayor cantidad
de proteína (42,50% bs), grasa (28,90% bs) y calcio
(0,32% bs), pero el contenido de fibra es relativamente bajo (3,02% bs), por lo que una dieta basada
mayormente en LMSN no es apta para reptiles y
aves de compañía, cuyas demandas de fibra son de
30–80 g/kg, además de que sobrepasarían fácilmente los requerimientos dietarios de grasa (30–55
g/kg). A diferencia de reptiles y aves de compañía,
para animales de cría, como cerdos, pollos de engorda y peces, las LMSN podría aportar la mayor
parte de los requerimientos de proteína y grasa, independientemente del tipo de sustrato en el que se
hayan desarrollado.

En cuanto a los beneficios de incorporar a las LMSN
en dietas de herbívoros estrictos como el ganado
vacuno, ovino-caprino y equino, algunas primeras
exploraciones han mostrado que la digestibilidad y
absorción de compuestos nitrogenados (como
proteínas y péptidos) de dietas enriquecidas con
LMSN para ganado vacuno son menores a las observadas en pollos y cerdos, mientras que la eficiencia en la conversión de fósforo fue considerablemente mayor que en pollos y cerdos (Oonincx et
al., 2015). Por otra parte, la formación y liberación
de amoniaco y metano se reducen drásticamente
en comparación con ganado alimentado exclusivamente con alimentos de origen vegetal (Jayanegara
et al., 2017).
Otros insectos como Zophobas morio, Alphitobius
diaperinus y Acheta domesticus han mostrado
también alto potencial para ser considerados como
alimento para animales de granja (Toral et al.,
2022), sin embargo, las ventajas ambientales y
económicas que conlleva la utilización de la MSN
para estos propósitos la colocan por encima de
estas y otras especies entomológicas.
Aún existe un gran campo de estudio abierto para
investigar el potencial de las LMSN como suplemento nutricional para animales de cría y de compañía. Por ejemplo, los sistemas experimentales de
inoculaciones bacterianas en sustratos y en los
propios tractos digestivos de LMSN han
demostrado efectos directos sobre la respuesta
inmunológica de estas, por lo que el campo de la
inmunología nutricional es una de las áreas que
puede tener un mayor impacto en el desarrollo de
productos alimenticios con características idealizadas (Vogel et al., 2018; Li et al., 2021; Keetanon et

al., 2023). Como esta existen muchas otras investigaciones que requieren de más tiempo para que
tengan resultados concluyentes.
2.3.3. Aplicaciones de los residuos de la LMSN
como fertilizante orgánico
Una de las áreas de estudio más recurrentes en la
bibliografía de los últimos 5 años sobre MSN es el
entendimiento y aprovechamiento de la capacidad
de las LMSN para digerir y transformar residuos orgánicos en compost de alta calidad con fines agrícolas (Lopes et al., 2022). Estos residuos pueden
incluir desperdicios alimentarios, estiércol animal,
desechos de jardín y otros materiales orgánicos.
Los desechos de la cría de LMSN, específicamente,
el excremento junto con restos del sustrato e insectos muertos es un subproducto que está ganando
popularidad debido a su alto contenido de compuestos orgánicos, nutrientes y potencial para su
uso como fertilizante orgánico para cultivos
(Oonincx et al., 2015), lo que cierra el ciclo de nutrientes y reduce la dependencia de los fertilizantes
agroquímicos.
El “frass” (como es conocido en inglés) es definido
por la Comisión de la Unión Europea como “una
mezcla de excrementos derivados de insectos de
cría, el sustrato de alimentación, partes de insectos,
huevos muertos y con un contenido de insectos de
cría muertos no superior al 5% en volumen ni superior al 3% en peso” (Reglamento de la Comisión
(UE) 2021/1925). Este subproducto se puede empacar y vender como abono orgánico, siempre y
cuando sea tratado térmicamente para reducir su
carga microbiana. El alto contenido de nitrógeno y
fósforo biodisponibles para la nutrición vegetal permite que el frass sea utilizado como suplemento o
sustituto de los fertilizantes inorgánicos que se utilizan para la producción de diversos cultivos. Esta
sustitución puede representar beneficios para los
suelos, evitando problemas como la eutrofización
(Chavez & Uchanski, 2021).
Diversos estudios comprueban la efectividad del
frass como fertilizante orgánico para mejorar la salud de las plantas, aumentar el rendimiento de
cultivos y la fertilidad del suelo. Tanga et al. (2021)
evaluaron el uso del frass de LMSN (FLMSN) en la
producción de maíz y obtuvieron un aumento del
rendimiento de hasta un 212% en comparación con
el fertilizante comercial Evergrow, mientras que un
tratamiento combinando de FLMSN con fertilizante
mineral resultó en un contenido de proteína y fibra
mayor en el maíz comparado a los otros tratamientos evaluados. Por su parte, Agustiyani et al. (2021)
evaluaron el efecto de la aplicación de FLMSN sobre el crecimiento de Pakchoi (Brassica rapa L.) y
