Experimental protocols
The present study had two principal research aims: i) Establish whether the small-scale experimental set-up are indicative of outcomes in large-scale production settings, and ii) to investigate the role of rearing temperature on growth, metabolism, and body composition.
Experiment 1: Large-scale production setting
Large-scale growth and metabolism experiments were performed twice under similar conditions in November 2021 and December 2021 at ENORM Biofactory A/S, Denmark. Respectively, 1.080 and 1.320 crates were placed within a 5 x 10.5 x 2.3 m rearing unit (Figure 1).
Each plastic crate (60 cm x 40 cm) contained ~7.5 kg of feed and ~11.200 seed larvae with a
weight of ~4-13 mg per larvae. Crates were stacked in racks that allowed ventilation of all
crates and the automated ventilation system recorded substrate and air temperature (°C) as
well as relative humidity (RH, %), airflow (L/min), and CO2 concentration (%) every 2
minutes from the outgoing air. The ventilation system of the rearing unit was programmed to
control airflow, temperature and humidity such that substrate rearing temperature averaged
~34°C with fluctuations confined between 32-38°C, and room air was generally maintained at
70-90% RH over the 7-day growth period.
Figure 1. Schematic overview of the large-scale facility

The concentration of CO2 (%) in outgoing air was measured with a DOL 19 CO2 sensor (dolsensors A/S, Denmark), and for calculations of CO2 production rate, incoming air was assumed to have a CO2 concentration of 410 ppm. The average annual CO2 concentration in
2021 was 413 ppm and atmospheric CO2 concentrations are generally slightly below average
in November and December (URL: https://www.co2.earth/daily-co2). Total airflow from the
ventilation system was recorded using an in-house calibrated system (SKOV A/S, Denmark).
Briefly, a pressure drop was recorded when air flowed across a damper and the recorded pressure drop was then converted to a flow recording using calibrations that considered the position of the damper. Airflow was recalculated to standard dry air by correcting for the temperature and humidity of the outgoing air and assuming a barometric pressure of 760 mmHg.
At the termination of the 7-day growth period, samples were collected from 12 crates (four
crates from the front, four from the middle, and four from the back of the room) for later
measurements of larvae growth and body composition (Figure 1). Larvae and frass from the

Experiment 1: Small-scale laboratory setting
In November 2021, a production crate with ~7.5 kg feed and ~11.200 seed larvae was randomly taken from the production facility at ENORM Biofactory A/S, Denmark, and transported for 1 hour to the research facilities of the Department of Biology, Aarhus University, Denmark. Upon arrival, feed and larvae were mixed and dosed in 7 round 1 L plastic chambers as
part of a small-scale respirometry setup (Figure 2). The 7 replicates contained 408 ± 13 g mix
of feed and larvae with similar larval density as in the large-scale experiments (~600 larvae
per chamber). The 7 respirometry chambers plus an empty control chamber were placed in a
35°C temperature-controlled cabinet and connected to an open-flow respirometry system allowing for hourly measurements of CO2 production rate and O2 consumption rate during the
subsequent 7-day growth period (see below for details about small-scale respirometry system). The substrate rearing temperature averaged ~35°C with fluctuations confined between
33-38°C. At the termination of the experiment larvae from each replicate were weighed and
sub-samples of larvae and frass were stored at -20°C for measurements of fractional water,
crude lipid, and crude protein content.
Figure 2. Schematic overview of the small-scale respirometry setup.

Experiment 2: Effects of temperature on growth and metabolism
In the spring of 2022, a series of experiments were performed to investigate the effect of rearing temperature on the growth and metabolism of BSFL using the small-scale respirometry
system. For all experimental temperatures, 580-605 larvae (3.4-6.2 mg per larvae) were
placed in ~400 g feed in 6 round 1 L respiration chambers. Each replicate chamber contained
a data logger (DS1921G Thermochron iButton, Maxim Integrated, USA) that recorded every
30 min to measure the variability and mean temperature. The four treatment temperatures:
27.0, 35.3, 39.4, and 41.9°C represent the average of the substrate temperatures recorded
across the 7-day growth period. CO2 production and O2 consumption were recorded hourly for
7 days with 2 empty chambers for control measurements. At the termination of the experiment, larvae from each replicate were weighed and samples were stored at -20°C for subsequent measurements of fractional water, crude lipid, and crude protein content.
The small-scale respirometry system
O2 consumption rate and CO2 production rate in the small-scale facility were measured using
open respirometry in 8 parallel respirometry chambers (diameter 15 cm, height 6 cm, volume
1 L) (Figure 2). During experiments, the respirometry chambers were placed in a temperaturecontrolled cabinet (Termaks, Norway) programmed to the desired treatment temperature. One
or two of the chambers were kept empty to record and control for background concentrations
of CO2 and O2 and the remaining chambers contained BSFL and feed. Small mesh nets on the
chamber in- and output tubes ensured that larvae could not escape. All respirometry chambers
were continuously flushed with air through gastight plastic tubes. Airflow through each chamber was controlled using a Flowbar-8 Mass Flow Meter System (Sable Systems, USA) and
airflow was adjusted (range 320-900 mL/min) to ensure a stable and equivalent loss of mass
as encountered under commercial conditions. Thus, loss of mass (primarily water) in each
respirometry chamber was controlled to ~30 g/day by adjusting airflow (drying) or in some
cases by adding MilliQ water.

Water, lipid, and protein content
Following the 7-day growth period, larvae and frass of individual crates or respirometry
chambers were weighed to assess total mass gain of larvae and to assess total loss of mass and
water in the feed. Subsequently we processed subsamples of larvae to assess water, crude
lipid, and crude protein content of the larvae.
The water content of either larvae, feed, or frass was determined by measuring the fractional
loss of mass following ~24 h of dehydration in an oven set to 70℃. To obtain crude lipid content, sub-samples of dried larvae were weighed and placed in perforated Eppendorf tubes that
were then placed inside a Soxleth apparatus. Here the samples were washed repeatedly with
petroleum ether over a 24-hour period to remove the lipid component. The lean samples were
then oven dried, and an estimate of the total lipid proportion was calculated from the difference in initial dry mass and lean dry mass. Another sub-set of dried larvae was taken from
each of the replicates to assess crude protein content. The dried larvae were ground with a
mortar and samples (~5-10 mg) were analysed for nitrogen content using a combustion analyser (Na 2000, Italy). Crude protein content was estimated by multiplying the nitrogen content by a factor of 4.76, which is a standardized conversion factor for protein to nitrogen ratio
in BSFL (Janssen et al., 2017). Crude lipid and crude protein content was, for the large-scale
experiments, only determined for the second round of experiments.
Data analysis
Data analysis and visualizations were performed in RStudio version 2023.09.1 with R version
4.3.2 (RStudio Team, 2023; R Core Team, 2023). Due to the small sample size with the largescale setup (n = 2), we were unable to statistically test for differences between the large- and
small-scale (n = 7) experiments.
One-way ANOVA tests were conducted to test for differences between temperature treatments (27.0, 35.3, 39.4, and 41.9°C). The sample size for each small-scale temperature treatment was n = 6, and assumptions, including normality and homogeneity of variances were
checked and met. Tukey’s Honest Significant Difference (HSD) test was used as a post hoc
test, and results were considered statistically significant if they met the criterion of p < 0.05.
Results
Comparison of growth and metabolism at large- and small-scale
In our initial experiments, we compared growth, metabolism, and CO2 production rates measured at large-scale production conditions (>8,000 kg, >12 million BSFL, n = 2) with values
measured under controlled small-scale laboratory conditions (~0.4 kg, ~600 BSFL, n = 7).
Formal statistical comparison between these systems was not appropriate given that data from
the large-scale experiments were only sampled in two independent replicates. Even so, the
data qualitatively supports that small-scale laboratory conditions can be considered representative of large-scale production conditions (Figure 3 and Table 2). Measurements of gas exchange from both small- and large-scale systems found the CO2 production rate to increase
slowly in the first 36 hours, after which there was a more potent acceleration in metabolism
during the subsequent 48 hours. In both systems, the CO2 production rate peaked after approximately 72-84 hours (Figure 3). Subsequently, the CO2 production rate declined steadily in the
small-scale chambers during the following 4 days while this decline was less pronounced and
more variable under the large-scale conditions. Integrating the total CO2 production over the
7-day growth period yielded a net CO2 production of 65.7 ± 1.0 L CO2 per kg wet mass in the
small-scale respiration chambers, while CO2 production was estimated 20-25% higher for the
two independent measuring rounds of CO2 production at large scale (82.6 and 78.0 L CO2 per
kg wet mass, respectively; Figure 3 and Table 2). Note, however, that measurements of CO2

the small-scale system, survival was estimated to 96 ± 5% with individual larval weighing 163
± 7 mg. When estimated as the proportion of initial dry mass, the harvest of larval dry mass
corresponded to 23.2 ± 0.9% and 24.7 ± 2% for the two rounds of large-scale production and
24 ± 0.7% for the small-scale respirometry chambers (Table 2). Finally, harvested larvae from
small- and large-scale systems were of similar body composition with a dry mass of 33.5 ±
1.7% and 30.7 ± 1.1% in the two large-scale production rounds and 34.5 ± 0.7% in the smallscale chambers. The dried larvae from large-scale production contained 33.0 ± 1.3% crude
lipid and 29.8 ± 0.5% crude protein (only assessed for one round of large-scale production)
which was similar to the larvae from small-scale chambers consisting of 33.3 ± 1.1% crude
lipid and 28.4 ± 0.5% crude protein (Table 2).

Effects of temperature on growth and metabolism of BSFL
Our initial experiment suggests that larval growth and metabolism in small-scale respirometry
chambers are representative of large-scale production systems, and we therefore continued to
investigate the role of rearing temperature on growth and metabolism in BSFL at 27.0, 35.3,
39.4, and 41.9°C in the small-scale system. As seen from the respiratory data, the dynamic
changes in metabolism during the 7-day growth period vary conspicuously with temperature
(Figure 4A). All treatments were characterized by sequential increases and decreases in gas
exchange that likely reflect how the “average larvae” in the respiration chambers develop
through larval instars. However, these transitions occur slower at low temperature (27.0°C)
where the final and largest peak in metabolism is reached after 6 days. In contrast, development and metabolism peaked earlier at 35.3 and 39.4°C while the developmental and metabolic transitions were more difficult to pinpoint at 41.9°C. Thus, the highest temperature was
most stressful limiting metabolism (Figure 4A). When the total metabolic expenditure during
the 7-day growth period was assessed from the total O2 consumption we found similar metabolic costs at the three lowest rearing temperatures with O2 consumption of 45.6 ± 2.9, 45.7 ±
2.4 or 46.2 ± 2.2 L O2 per kg initial wet mass at 27.0, 35.3 and 39.4°C, respectively. However,
metabolism was reduced to less than half at 41.9°C, where the 7-day O2 consumption was
only 22.1 ± 2.5 L O2 per kg initial mass (Figure 4B). A similar pattern was found for CO2 production, with the exception that total CO2 production was marginally, but significantly, lower

Discussion
Comparison of growth and metabolism at large- and small-scale
The data from the present study indicated that small-scale laboratory respirometry chambers
support gas exchange, growth, and metabolism in BSFL that is comparable, and therefore representative of, conditions in large-scale commercial conditions. This finding is based on our
efforts to evaluate the utility and relevance of controlled laboratory studies in relation to largescale facilities. Specifically, BSFL were reared at similar substrate temperature (~34-35°C)
and in similar diets in either small-scale controlled laboratory respiration chambers (~0.4 kg)
(Figure 2) or in the larger and more heterogeneous conditions that exist in a rearing unit at
ENORM Biofactory A/S (Figure 1) containing >20.000 times more feed and larvae in the system. Despite the massive difference in scale, we found remarkable similarities in growth and
energy conversion. Thus, survival, individual larval size, % dry mass, % crude lipid, % crude
protein, and final larval mass as a proportion of initial mass all differed by less than 10%

with the findings from previous studies, which found a higher larval weight in big scale
(crates of 2,060 cm2) compared to small scale (194 cm2) (Yakti et al., 2022). According to
Yakti et al. (2022), the difference is related to a higher substrate temperature in larger crates,
which may be avoided in the current experiment because of efficient temperature control in
both our small and large-scale systems (measured average was ~34-35°C, and fluctuations in
substrate temperature ranged only between 32-38°C). Yakti et al. (2022) also found that crude
protein content is higher and crude fat content is lower for larvae reared at small-scale compared to large-scale while we observed very similar body composition in our small and large
systems.
Unlike the similarities in growth data, we estimated CO2 production per kg initial wet mass to
be almost 20% higher in the large-scale system compared to the small-scale system (Figure 3
and Table 2). We speculate that a considerable part of this difference can be explained by the
different experimental methodologies used to assess gas exchange in large- and small-scale
facilities, respectively. Specifically, CO2 production measured at large-scale is experimentally
inferior to the controlled laboratory conditions because 1) CO2 concentration in the incoming
air is not measured directly (but assumed to be 410 ppm), 2) airflow in the rearing unit is assessed indirectly from a pressure drop across a damper, and lastly, 3) rearing rooms are not
completely airtight and the recorded airflow may also be confounded by occasional opening
of the entrance door during the 7-day growth period. Considering these methodological differences, a 20% difference is maybe not surprising between the well-controlled small-scale
respirometry chambers and the large-scale commercial facilities. Moreover, when CO2 production is recalculated relative to larvae production (g CO2/kg produced dry larvae mass) our
systems produce 1,632 ± 46 g CO2/kg dry larval mass for the small-scale systems and 2,164 ±
69 or 2,350 ± 282 g CO2/kg dry larvae mass for the measurements at large-scale. Both these
estimates are well within the range of previous studies (Ermolaev et al., 2019; Pang et al.,
2020; Parodi et al., 2020) where CO2 production from small-scale (>15 kg initial feed) produced between 1,394 to 2,750 g CO2/kg dry larvae mass (see table 2 in Parodi et al., 2020).
Comparing the large- and small-scale systems qualitatively, it is evident that the temporal development of CO2 production was initially similar between large- and small-scale systems,
particularly during the first two to three days of accelerated growth and metabolism (Figure
3). Conversely, the gradual reduction in CO2 production rate is more modest and variable in
the large-scale system which is likely due to a more heterogeneous growth and development
in the >1,000 different crates placed in the rearing unit. This differentiation in development is
confirmed by facility staff observations, revealing that crates taken from different positions in
the rearing room, may differ in developmental progression on days 4 to 6.
Based on this initial experiment we conclude that the detailed and precise quantitative estimate of CO2 production rate in our large-scale system was likely confounded by experimental
constraints. However, the qualitative information was similar between different months in the
large-scale system and thus comparatively informative (i.e. the level of CO2 production is informative of the intensity of larval growth). Furthermore, tracking the temporal development
of CO2 metabolism remains a powerful method for monitoring metabolism, growth, and development in both small and large systems (see discussion below). Finally, the close similarities in survival, growth, and assimilation between the large- and small-scale systems indicate
that small-scale respirometry chambers can be appropriate to investigate production-relevant
manipulations of BSFL production. This could include effects of temperature, humidity, diet,
texture, and microorganism interactions, that could affect growth efficiency in BSFL (Danieli
et al., 2019; Harnden and Tomberlin, 2016; Meng et al., 2023; Raimondi et al., 2020).

Effects of temperature on survival, growth, and metabolism of BSFL
Our study using small-scale laboratory respiration chambers at different temperatures showed
that rearing at 27, 35, and 39°C all support efficient growth in BSFL whereas 42°C causes a
severe, but sublethal, depression of growth and metabolism. Previous reports of BSFL have
found high survival (>80%) in the temperature range of 15-37°C (Chia et al., 2018; Raimondi
et al., 2020) while survival at 40°C is ambiguous with both low (Chia et al., 2018) and high
(Purkayastha and Sarkar, 2022) estimates reported in the literature. Here we confirm that
BSFL survives rearing under production-like conditions at temperatures ranging from 27.0 to
41.9°C while we found 100% mortality at 44.4°C (data from this treatment are not included
due to the fatal outcome). In our study design, we initiate the growth experiments using ~5-6
days old seed larvae, and the high survival at 41.9°C could therefore be linked to the shorter
exposure duration at this stressful temperature compared to previous studies (Chia et al.,
2018). Thus, the consequences of stressful heat exposure are determined both by the intensity
(the absolute temperature) and the duration of exposure (Jørgensen et al., 2021). Furthermore,
it is possible that later larvae stages are simply more resilient to high temperatures, and it has
previously been shown that the susceptibility to heat stress changes considerably between life
stages in BSF (Chia et al., 2018; Tomberlin et al., 2009). Despite the high survival at 41.9°C,
it is evident that this temperature is stressful, as it causes clear reductions in both growth and
metabolism (see below). Production systems with BSFL should thus avoid rearing temperatures above 40°C while the present study suggests that temperatures ranging from 27.0 to
39.4°C all support efficient development and growth of 4th to 7th instar BSFL (Gligorescu et
al., 2019). Thus, the metabolic rate at all these temperatures seems to end with a decline that is
indicative of a transition to a non-feeding 7th instar larvae (Figure 4). Furthermore, larvae size,
and total larvae growth after 7 days are fairly similar between 27.0 to 39.4°C (Figure 5B and
5C) confirming earlier reports describing temperature optima in BSFL (Chia et al., 2018; Raimondi et al., 2020; Harnden and Tomberlin, 2016).
Even if BSFL growth is well supported by a broad temperature range it is important to consider that small differences can be critical to optimize profitability in a large production facility. Optimization relates both to the efficiency of energy upcycling from cheap “low quality”
diets towards assimilation in the “high quality” larvae, but also to reducing the duration of the
rearing process. Regarding the efficiency of growth, the energy assimilation in larvae is determined by the relative energy allocation towards assimilation (growth) versus metabolism
(costs related directly to growth or maintenance) (Laganaro et al., 2021). This proportional
energy allocation varies with larvae age and dietary substrate and is also likely to be influenced by temperature and developmental stage (Laganaro et al., 2021; Bekker et al., 2021). In
our experimental design we estimated total growth over a fixed period (one week) and our
measurements do therefore not allow for a direct quantitative partitioning of the cost of
growth or maintenance metabolism during specific growth periods. Even so, the temporal
changes in CO2 production suggest that growth and metabolism are temperature sensitive
which may affect the efficiency of the BSFL production in a system where the growth period
is fixed. For example, Figure 4A clearly illustrates that the CO2 production rate fluctuates predictably with three CO2 peaks for each of the 3 lowest temperature treatments (27.0, 35.3, and
39.4°C). These peaks are likely representative of growth phases in the 4th, 5th, and 6th larval
instars and growth phases clearly proceed faster when larvae are reared at higher temperatures. These temporal patterns suggest that most larvae have entered the 7th non-feeding prepupal larval stage by the end of day 5 in the 35.3 and 39.4°C treatments. In contrast, the average larvae grown at 27.0°C likely only transitioned to the 7th instar by the end of day 7 shortly
before the termination of the experiment. Although larval instars were not assessed directly in
this study, these data suggest that continuous monitoring of metabolic intensity is a potential
tool to record larval growth patterns and thereby control (and limit) production time.

Effect of temperature on body composition
BSFL are known to accumulate anhydrous triglyceride (lipid) in the body during the last instars (Arrese and Soulages, 2010; Gligorescu et al., 2019; Talal et al., 2021) and this process
may continue even after they have transitioned to the non-feeding stage. Furthermore, it is
possible that rearing at different temperatures stimulates some internal biochemical pathways
that ultimately affect the larvae body composition in terms of proportional lipid and protein
content as has been suggested by findings from mealworms (Bjørge et al., 2018). Considering
the experimental design in the present study it is difficult to separate the direct effects of temperature from those of ontogeny (development) since the respiratory trace suggests that larval
development has progressed further at 35.3 and 39.4°C than at 27.0°C. Larvae harvested at
27°C are characterized by a lower crude lipid content (32.7%) compared to 35.3 and 39.4°C
(36.0 and 34.2%, respectively) suggesting that temperature and/or developmental stage might
be a contributing factor besides diet (Nguyen et al., 2015) affecting the macronutrient composition of BSFL. It is possible that larvae at 27.0°C had less time to process the lipogenesis
associated with the latest developmental stages compared to the two warmer treatments (35.3
and 39.4°C). This is consistent with the lower RER of 27.0°C larvae (1.10) compared to 35.3
and 39.4°C (1.17 and 1.15, respectively) which are indicative of different levels of total lipogenesis activity. Thus, lipogenesis from carbohydrates results in a net CO2 production that
contributes to the high apparent RER values, and RER values above 1 are common among
fast-growing animals (Talal et al., 2021) including BSFL (Parodi et al., 2020).
CO2 emission
Costs of growth (anabolism) and the basic costs of maintenance of larvae are associated with
considerable metabolic turnover, and furthermore, there is likely also a metabolic turnover
from the microbial community that lives in the feed and frass (Laganaro et al., 2021). As such
it is relevant to consider the CO2 budget of BSFL production as this represents an important
characteristic of this emerging “green” technology (Parodi et al., 2020). In the current study,
we show that the total emission of CO2 per unit of dry larval biomass increased as the temperature increased, showing a significant leap between temperatures of 39.4 and 41.9°C (Figure
5D). We speculate that the higher CO2 emission per g larvae produced at higher temperatures
is linked to a lower net growth efficiency, indicating that more energy is used for maintenance
relative to growth. Additionally, as discussed previously, warmer treatments also facilitated
faster development so some larvae at 35.3 and 39.4 °C presumably had >2 days where their
growth was halted, and the larvae were primarily utilizing stored energy after transitioning to
the non-feeding 7th larval stage. In the case of larvae reared at 41.9°C, CO2 emission per g larvae (Figure 5D) was considerably higher which, in addition to low growth efficiency, could
be linked to metabolic costs associated with heat stress such as production of heat shock proteins at the expense of growth (Gonzalez-Tokman et al., 2020). As mentioned previously, the
CO2 emissions measured are not produced from larval metabolism alone but include CO2 production from microbial metabolism in the feed (Bekker et al., 2021; Parodi et al., 2020).
Therefore, it would be relevant to study directly the effects of temperature on microbial metabolism and the contribution of microbial respiration in the overall system.
Conclusion
The data collected in this study qualitatively support that small-scale laboratory facilities are
representative of large-scale commercial facilities in terms of survival, growth, and metabolism. The present study also demonstrated that the production of BSFL is efficient across a
broad range of temperatures from 27.0 to 39.4°C with respect to survival, larvae size, total
larval dry mass, and body composition. Repeated CO2 measurements during the 7-day period
indicated that larval growth was fastest at 35.3 and 39.4°C suggesting that rearing at high temPage 11 of 22

Optimizing black soldier fly larvae (BSFL) production requires a better understanding of how diet composition
shapes growth, nutrient allocation, and metabolic efficiency. This study investigated whether respiratory measurements could serve as predictive, non-invasive tools for BSFL performance on diets differing in protein-tocarbohydrate (P:C) ratio. Larvae were reared for seven days on four experimental diets, with growth, survival,
gas exchange (O2 consumption, CO2 production, and respiratory exchange ratio (RER)), and body composition
(crude protein and lipid contents) measured across seven replicates per treatment. O2 consumption correlated
strongly with final larval biomass, while RER was closely associated with protein and lipid deposition. Larvae on
low-protein, high-carbohydrate diets accumulated proportionally more lipid, whereas protein-rich diets
increased crude protein content but required higher energetic investment. This demonstrates that lipid-rich
larvae grew more efficiently in energetic terms per unit accumulated biomass than protein-rich larvae. Across
diets, gas exchange variables reliably reflected growth dynamics, metabolic activity, and nutrient assimilation.
Integrating respirometry into rearing systems could enable real-time monitoring of insect biomass yield and
nutrient composition.

1. Introduction
The world faces pressing environmental challenges that impact
global food production, including climate change, soil degradation,
habitat loss, and the depletion of natural resources (Foley et al., 2011).
More sustainable food systems are essential to meet the increasing food
and feed demand driven by population growth while simultaneously
mitigating the impacts associated with greenhouse gas emissions, landuse, water scarcity, and food wastage (FAO, 2009; Foley et al., 2011).
One component of this more sustainable food and feed production is the
use of black soldier fly larvae (BSFL; Hermetia illucens (L.)) for converting
low quality organic material into nutrient-rich biomass (Broeckx et al.,
2021; Gold et al., 2020). This biomass can supplement traditional unsustainable protein sources (e.g. soybean and fishmeal) in livestock
feeds (van der Heide et al., 2021) and pet foods (Bosch & Swanson,

2021), and as an added benefit, the remaining frass after harvest of
larvae represents a high-quality plant fertilizer (Fuhrmann et al., 2022;
Lomonaco et al., 2024).
The ability of BSFL to feed on a wide range of organic materials is a
major reason why this species has become increasingly important
commercially (Purkayastha & Sarkar, 2022). Nevertheless, BSFL growth
rates, energy conversion efficiencies, and body compositions can vary
considerably with diet quality and macronutrient balance (BarraganFonseca et al., 2019, 2021; Eggink et al., 2023), and with other conditions such as moisture content (Bekker et al., 2021) or temperature
(Schøn et al., 2025). Diet composition, in particular the protein-tocarbohydrate (P:C) ratio and not just the total diet mass, has been
shown to strongly affect larval growth and body composition (Cheon
et al., 2022; Jensen et al., 2013; Lee & Jang, 2014; Rho & Lee, 2022).
Studies have demonstrated that nutrient-deficient diets that deprive

larvae of adequate protein or carbohydrate supply, as well as diets with
unbalanced P:C ratios, reduce larval growth and alter nutrient deposition patterns (Barragan-Fonseca et al., 2019; Berggreen et al., 2025;
Eggink et al., 2023). As a result, differences in diet can lead to substantial variation in BSFL body composition, ranging from 32-58% crude
protein and 15–38% crude lipids on a dry matter (DM) basis (see review
by Gold et al., 2018). Because variations in macronutrient composition
(encompassing both the levels and specific forms of protein, fat, and
carbohydrate) affect larval development, size, and composition, it is
important to understand in more detail how these dietary factors influence metabolism and energy conversion during growth. Similarly,
there is a growing interest in developing methods to monitor the progression of growth in actively rearing larvae, as repeated manual sampling and weighing is impractical, time consuming, and can disturb
larval behaviour and substrate structure, potentially affecting growth
dynamics.
Measurements of gas exchange (O2 consumption and CO2 production) as well as the respiratory exchange ratio (RER, VCO2/VO2) are
powerful indicators of metabolism, energy expenditure, and nutrient
assimilation under different dietary conditions (Parodi et al., 2020;
Schøn et al., 2025; Talal et al., 2021). BSFL utilizes aerobic energy both
for general maintenance of basal physiological processes, but also in
association with the direct cost of growth and nutrient assimilation
(Ferrannini, 1988; Talal et al., 2021) and studies have previously found
a close association between O2 consumption or CO2 production and total
larval mass gain (Eriksen, 2024; Schøn et al., 2025). However, this association may be affected by the rearing conditions, including the dietary conditions, as the energetics of growth is expected to differ
depending on the ratio of lipid and protein assimilation and because
different nutritional quality may affect the relative magnitude of
maintenance metabolism versus growth metabolism in ectotherms
(Goodrich et al., 2024; Laganaro et al., 2021). This may be further
complicated by the fact that in the BSFL rearing system the diet and
digestive tract microbiome also contribute to overall gas exchange rates
(Bekker et al., 2021; Fuhrmann et al., 2025; Parodi et al., 2020).
Nevertheless, continuous monitoring of gas exchange rates holds the
potential to provide important information on growth and body
composition in production systems. In this context, RER may be
particularly relevant to examine, as this metric reflects the combined
input from a range of metabolic processes related to both anabolism and
catabolism. RER reflects the catabolism of macronutrients where
oxidation of lipid, protein, and carbohydrate result in RER of 0.7, 0.83,
or 1.0, respectively (Schmidt-Nielsen, 1997). In addition, RER will increase as a consequence of lipogenesis from carbohydrates or amino
acids (Ferrannini, 1988; Talal et al., 2021), and RER measurements
therefore hold potential to indirectly monitor which macronutrients are
metabolized and assimilated.
The main objectives of this study were: (i) to assess how altering diet
macronutrient composition affects the growth, metabolism, and body
composition of BSFL, and (ii) to determine whether gas exchange measurements during rearing are predictive of BSFL production output in
terms of growth rate, quantity, and quality. To address these objectives,
larval growth, gas exchange (O2 and CO2) and body composition (crude
protein and lipid contents) were measured on BSFL reared on diets with
varying P:C ratios.

2.2. Experimental protocol
The study investigated how BSFL metabolism is affected by dietary
macronutrient composition by measuring gas exchange, growth, and
body composition of BSFL during seven days of rearing on four experimental diets. Experiments were performed over four consecutive weeks
using a blocked design where one or two replicates of each dietary
treatment was included each week, resulting in seven replicates of each
treatment. The experimental system allowed for hourly recordings of O2
consumption and CO2 production. Larval growth was estimated daily by
sub-sampling and weighing larvae from each replicate. At termination of
the experiment, larvae were separated from the frass using wet sieving,
and subsequently quickly dried with paper towels. Larvae were then
weighed and photographed to count the number of survivors using
CountThings (Dynamic Ventures Inc., California, US). All experiments
were performed in a climate cabinet at 27 ◦ C (Termaks KB8182, Bergen,
Norway) and constant darkness. Larvae sampled at the termination and
start of the experiment were stored at − 20 ◦ C before analyses of DM,
crude lipid, and crude protein contents.

2.5. Growth analysis
Respiration chambers with growing larvae were daily removed
briefly from the temperature cabinet to track changes in total mass (frass
and larvae) between days. On average the replicates lost 27.3 ± 3.4 g
day− 1, mainly due to removal of water vapor and CO2. During this
procedure, 15 randomly selected larvae were quickly collected and
weighed to assess average larval mass within each replicate. Three of the
15 larvae were sampled and frozen, and the other 12 larvae were
returned. Thus, during the experiment 18 larvae were removed from
each replicate. At the termination of the experiment all remaining larvae
were counted and weighed to enable calculation of survival and total
mass gain.
The total daily larval mass was estimated by multiplying the average
daily larval mass with the estimated number of live larvae on each day.
The estimate of live larvae accounted for the daily removal of 3 larvae
and used an assumption that mortality was evenly distributed across the
7-day rearing period. Specific growth rates (SGR) were calculated as the

2.4. Gas exchange measurements
The open-flow respirometry setup and protocol for gas exchange
measurements are described with greater detail in Schøn et al. (2025).
Briefly, eight custom-built, airtight respiration chambers (one empty
control chamber and seven experimental chambers) were placed in the
climate cabinet. Each chamber was provided with a controlled and
constant flow of room air (~ 600 mL min− 1) that continuously provided
O2 and removed water vapor and CO2. The inlet air flow for each of the
sequential chambers were regulated and recorded using a Flowbar-8
Mass Flow Meter System (Sable Systems). The recorded inlet flow of
moist air was later corrected for water vapour dilution using a factor of
0.9877, thereby expressing the inlet flow (V˙I) as dry air at ambient
conditions, assuming a room air temperature of 21 ◦ C, 50% RH, and an
atmospheric pressure of 760 mmHg.
To measure V˙O2 and V˙CO2, air was sequentially sub-sampled at a
rate of ~ 200 mL min− 1 using a SS-4 Sub-Sampler Pump (Sable Systems).
Sequential shifting between chambers was performed using an eightchannel RM-8 Respirometry Flow Multiplexer (Sable Systems). The
sampled air passed through a calcium chloride column for removal of
water vapor, and through syringe filters (Acrodisc syringe filter, 25 mm,
0.2 µm Supor membrane, Pall Corporation) to remove particles, before
passing through an O2 analyser (FC-2 Differential Oxygen Analyser
(Oxzilla), Sable Systems) and a CO2 analyser (LI-850 Gas Analyzer, LICOR Biosciences), respectively. The multiplexer shifted between each
chamber every 7.5 min, allowing the readings to stabilize. Only the
mean of the last 30 s of stable recordings was used, providing an hourly
measurement for each chamber over the entire 7-day period. Unstable
recordings of inlet flowrate, O2, or CO2, as well as outliers, were
removed and replaced by interpolation or extrapolation from preceding
and/or subsequent high-quality measurements, following the data
quality assessment protocol described in the Supplementary Materials.
The rates of oxygen consumption (V˙O2) and carbon dioxide production (V˙CO2) (mL min− 1) were calculated using Haldane-corrected
equations from the inlet flow rate (V˙I) and differences between inlet
and outlet fractional gas concentrations, accounting for unequal inlet
and outlet air volumes when RER ∕
= 1 (Withers, 2001). Inlet gas fractions
were estimated from the empty control chamber (FIO2 and FICO2) and
outlet fractions were measured from the experimental chambers (FEO2
and FECO2) within the same hourly cycle.

2.6. Water, lipid, and protein content
At the termination of the experiment, all harvested larvae from each
replicate were oven-dried at 60 ◦ C for three to four days until they had
reached a stable mass. Water content was calculated from the difference
between wet mass and DM, and sub-samples of dried larvae were taken
to estimate lipid and protein contents. To obtain crude lipid content,
samples of 1.76 ± 0.01 g dried larvae were weighed before they were
washed 5 times in 25 mL petroleum ether to remove the lipid fraction
(Jensen et al., 2010). Each round of washing lasted 48 h and after the
final round the defatted samples were again oven-dried at 60 ◦ C until
stable mass to allow for estimation of the crude lipid fraction (calculated
as the difference between initial DM and lean DM). Nitrogen analysis of
defatted, finely ground sub-samples (4.2–7.2 mg per sample) was performed using a combustion analyser (Na 2000, Carlo Erba, Italy). The
proportional crude protein content was then estimated by multiplying
the measured nitrogen content by a factor of 4.76, a standardized conversion factor for the nitrogen-to-protein ratio in BSFL (Janssen et al.,
2017). Total protein was estimated from lean DM and expressed as a
fraction of the total DM (before lipid removal).
2.7. Analysis of gross cost of growth and assimilation
To examine the relationship between energy consumption and energy assimilation, mass gain was converted into energy equivalents
based on mass gain of lipid and protein. For these calculations an
assumption of 37 kJ per g lipid and 17 kJ per g protein as energy conversion factors was used (FAO, 2002), respectively. Further, to assess the
energy used for aerobic metabolism VO2 was converted to energy
expenditure using a standard caloric conversion factor of 20.5 kJ per L
O2 (Schmidt-Nielsen, 1997).
2.8. Data analysis
Linear mixed-effects models (LMMs) were used to evaluate the effects of diet on parameters related to larval growth, gas exchange, and
larval body composition. The four diet treatments were included as fixed
effects, and experimental week was included as a random factor (model
structure: Diet + (1 | Week)) to account for the observed small week-toweek baseline variations. Model assumptions were assessed by visual
inspection of residual Q–Q plots and by residual diagnostics, with
normality and homogeneity of variances evaluated using Shapiro–Wilk

3. Results
Larval growth, gas exchange, and body composition varied by diet
over the experimental period. The experimental week was included as a
blocking factor in the experimental design, as larvae were supplied
weekly, resulting in distinct biological batches that could influence
performance outcomes. For some parameters, modest variation among
weeks was visible in the data (see example in Fig. S4). To account for this
structure, experimental week was included as a random factor in the
statistical models (LMMs), allowing diet effects to be estimated while
accounting for week-to-week baseline variation. Diet consistently
explained a large share of the variation across all response variables
(Table S1). Accordingly, for all response variables except survival rate,
diets differing in P:C ratio exerted a significant effect after accounting
for week-to-week variation, and this biologically relevant effect is
therefore the primary focus of the results and discussion presented
below.

3.1. Effects of diet on growth and body composition of BSFL

3.2. Effects of diet on gas exchange and metabolism

Larvae survived well and developed successfully on all diets, with
average survival rates ranging from 89-97% and with no significant
difference among diets (Table 2). While all diets supported substantial
larval growth, the final mass of larvae was significantly different across
diets after the 7-day growth period (Fig. 1A). Total larval yield was
highest when reared on the REF diet, followed by the mixed diets with
higher protein fraction (Fig. 1A, Table 2). The difference in larval
growth between diets was also evident from our analysis of specific
growth rates (SGR) (Fig. 1B, Table 2). From the SGR (Fig. 1B), it is
possible to see the change in estimated total biomass between two
consecutive days, where the biggest increase for P:C 1:3, P:C 1:5, and P:C
1:9 diets was found to be from day 3 to 4, followed by a more moderate
increase (and even slight decrease for the REF diet) in SGR per day.
The larvae reared on different diets had significantly different body
compositions at harvest (Table 2). Larvae reared on the P:C 1:9 diet had
significantly lower water content compared to those from the other
three diets. While the proportions of crude protein and crude lipid in the
DM did not differ significantly between REF and P:C 1:3, they were
significantly higher than found in larvae reared on diets with lower
protein content (P:C 1:5 and P:C 1:9) (Table 2). As the protein content
increased in the experimental diets, larval crude protein levels rose and
lipid levels dropped, resulting in larvae from the low-protein, highcarbohydrate diets exhibiting significantly elevated proportional lipid
fractions and reduced protein fractions (Table 2).

The dynamic changes in V˙O2 and V˙CO2 followed a broadly similar
pattern (Fig. 2A and Fig. S1), both showing that gas exchange rates
generally increased over the 7-day growth period but with different
temporal progressions and distinct patterns depending on dietary
treatment. For the commercial high-protein diet, REF, the V˙O2 increased
slowly during the first two days, after which the rate accelerated. V˙O2
spiked at three distinct time points: between day 1–2 (0.6 mL O2 min− 1),
day 3–4 (2.2 mL O2 min− 1), and day 5–6 (4.6 mL O2 min− 1), before V˙O2
declined considerably during the last 1.5 days of the experiment. A
somewhat similar pattern was found for the P:C 1:3 and P:C 1:5 diets,
but here the spikes occurred later and were more moderate. The P:C 1:9
diet displayed an even more delayed and reduced response with a small
spike around day 1.5–2.5, another by day 5.5, with indications of a third
increase in V˙O2 at the end of the experiment. Total VO2 differed
significantly among all diet treatments, with the REF diet showing the
highest O2 consumption, followed by progressively lower values in the
mixed diets with decreasing dietary protein content (Fig. 2A, Table 2).
RER values were > 1 across diets when estimated from the total gas
exchange over the 7-day growth period (Fig. 2B, Table 2). RERs differ
significantly among all four diets with lowest RER observed for the REF
diet and increasing RER values with increasing dietary carbohydrate
content.

4. Discussion
The purpose of this study was to evaluate BSFL growth performance,
metabolic activity, and energy conversion efficiency (energetic cost of
growth) using respirometry as a monitoring tool. Four experimental
diets with varying protein-to-carbohydrate (P:C) ratios were used; three
semi-artificial diets with identical formulations except for varying P and
C ratios, and a reference diet consisting of 100% chicken feed. Over a 7day period we recorded larval growth, V˙O2, V˙CO2, and fractional content of crude protein and lipid of the final larvae. As expected, diets with

protein-rich diet (P:C 1:3) resulted in 69.0% higher dry mass and 59.1%

At the time of harvest on day 7 the larvae from the different dietary

Notably, Eggink et al. (2023) found that even when carbohydrate-rich

stage, they still produced larvae with significantly higher lipid content
compared to larvae reared on protein-rich diets.

4.1. Effects of dietary P:C ratio on growth and body composition of BSFL
The four experimental diets varied in P:C ratios, but also in other
aspects, when comparing the REF diet (chicken feed) to the three semiartificial diets. For example, we added a higher proportion of indigestible cellulose as a structural component to the semi-artificial diets, and
the micronutrient concentrations also differed from that of the REF diet
(see methods and Table 1). These differences may contribute to a slightly
lower growth performance in the semi-artificial diets despite similar P:C
ratio in the REF diet and the high-protein semi-artificial diet (P:C 1:3).
Accordingly, the REF diet is primarily a valuable reference to earlier
studies (Schøn et al., 2025; Schow-Madsen et al., 2026), whereas the
three semi-artificial diets provide the best basis for direct comparison
and assessment of the effects of P:C ratio.

diets such that higher protein content accelerated development and
shortened instar duration as indicated by closer peaks in metabolism
(Fig. 2A and S1). Although larval instar was not measured directly in the
present study, these temporal profiles demonstrate the potential use of
gas exchange to monitor developmental dynamics non-invasively in
BSFL production systems (Schøn et al., 2025). For example, continuous
measurements of gas exchange can identify when the cohort of larvae

starts transitioning to the non-feeding 7th instar (large reduction in gas
exchange rates) which will then indicate when larval biomass is
approaching maximum. As an example, we observed for the REF diet
that oxygen consumption rate peaked between day 5 and 6 (Fig. 2A)
followed by our recording of maximal mass on day 6 (Fig. 1A). Larvae
reared on P:C 1:3 and P:C 1:5 had their final metabolic peak (likely
transition to 7th instar) between day 6 and 7, and for larvae reared on
the P:C 1:9 diet the gas exchange rates were still increasing at day 7.
These observations align well with Eggink et al. (2023), who found that
carbohydrate-rich diet (P:C 1:9) prolonged larval development by
approximately two days compared to diets with P:C ratios of 1:3.

Aerobic energy consumption increases with growth in BSFL and
other insects reflecting the cost associated with nutrient assimilation,
tissue synthesis, and increased maintenance cost of the growing larval
biomass (Eriksen, 2022, 2024; Ferral et al., 2020). While our experimental approach cannot directly partition the cost associated with either
growth or maintenance (but see Eriksen, 2022, 2024) we confirmed that

showed that O2 consumption per g biomass assimilated was slightly, but

aerobic “cost” is likely explained by the observation that larvae on the
REF diet reached maximal mass on day 6 while the cost for maintenance
metabolism continued also on day 7 and because the REF diet supported
growth of protein-rich larvae (see below). Because VO2-based estimates
of energy expenditure may include a contribution from microbial
metabolism, the energetic efficiency of growth reported here is likely
underestimated, which overestimates costs.
In a more detailed analysis, we associated the total energetic
expenditure (VO2 recalculated to kJ with a caloric coefficient of 20.5 J/
mL) to either the total energetic gain in lipids and protein (Fig. 3B) or to
protein alone (Fig. 3C). Larvae reared on the high-protein diet (P:C 1:3)
expended ~ 48% more metabolic energy per unit of lipid and protein
than larvae reared on the high-carbohydrate diet (P:C 1:9) (Fig. 3B).
Thus, larvae with proportionally high lipid allocation grew “cheaper” in
energetic terms which is consistent with protein synthesis being inherently more energetically demanding than lipid accumulation (Goodrich
et al., 2024; Laganaro et al., 2021; Talal et al., 2021). Conversely, we
found the energetic cost per unit of protein gain was ~ 44% lower in
larvae reared on the P:C 1:3 diet compared to P:C 1:9 (Fig. 3C). This
pattern suggests reduced efficiency of protein deposition under proteinlimited conditions while protein-rich diets seemingly facilitate a more
energy-efficient protein assimilation. We caution, however, that
isolating components of larval biomass assimilation and relating this to
the overall energy use of the whole bioconversion system should be
interpreted cautiously. This rough analysis does not directly partition
growth- and maintenance-related costs (e.g. Eriksen, 2022, 2024) and
protein-rich larvae likely have higher maintenance costs per unit mass
than lipid-rich larvae. Indeed, deviations between the unconstrained
(black) and origin-forced (red) linear models in Fig. 3C suggest that

ABSTRACT
Poor biowaste management contributes to greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions such as methane (CH4), carbon dioxide (CO2), and nitrous oxide
(N2O). Black soldier fly larvae (BSFL, Hermetia illucens) bioconversion offers a sustainable approach for treating organic wastes while reducing emissions and recovering valuable resources. However, the global warming potential (GWP) associated with BSFL treatment of different
waste substrates remains insufficiently characterized. This study quantified GHG emissions (CH4, CO2, N2O, and NH3) during BSFL bioconversion of human faecal matter (FM), pig manure (PM), and chicken manure (CM) using calibrated gas sensors. Emissions from BSFL-treated
substrates were compared with those of untreated controls, and a cradle-to-gate life cycle assessment (LCA) was conducted to determine
GWP in CO2-equivalent (CO2-eq). In the control treatments, GWP was highest in CM (0.194 kg CO2-eq), followed by FM (0.072 kg CO2-eq) and
PM (0.005 kg CO2-eq). BSFL treatment significantly reduced emissions across all substrates, resulting in GWP values of 0.011 kg CO2-eq for
CM, 0.006 kg CO2-eq for FM, and 0.001 kg CO2-eq for PM. The greatest reduction was observed in CM, indicating that BSFL treatment was
effective for this substrate. These findings demonstrate that BSFL bioconversion can substantially reduce GHG emissions from organic
wastes while supporting a circular bioeconomy approach to waste valorization.
Key words: biowaste valorization, black soldier fly, global warming potential, greenhouse gases, life cycle assessment
HIGHLIGHTS

• Black soldier fly larvae (BSFL) mitigate greenhouse gas emissions and ammonia.
• The BSFL treatment was most effective in chicken manure.
• BSFL technology leads to organic waste reduction.

GRAPHICAL ABSTRACT

INTRODUCTION
Poor biowaste management releases potent greenhouse gases (GHG) such as methane (CH4), carbon dioxide (CO2), and
nitrous oxide (N2O), which accelerate global warming and drive climate change (Hajam et al. 2023). Agriculture accounts
for approximately 12% of global greenhouse emissions, equivalent to 5.87 Gt CO2-eq. Over 65% of these emissions originate

from livestock production, with enteric fermentation as the dominant source contributing approximately 2.8 Gt CO2-eq, followed by manure management and manure left on pastures (1.2 Gt CO2-eq) (Symeon et al. 2025). The rising global
population will intensify meat demand and organic waste generation, amplifying GHG emissions (IISD 2020; Wang
et al. 2021). Sub-Saharan Africa generates over 62 million tons of organic waste annually, much of which is mismanaged
through open dumping and uncontrolled decomposition (Orhorhoro & Oghoghorie 2019). This challenge is more pronounced as rapid urbanization and expanding livestock production in Kenya are expected to markedly increase organic
waste by 2030, emphasizing the need for sustainable waste valorization solutions (National Environment Management
Authority 2021).
Poor organic waste disposal, often through open dumping or uncontrolled storage, results in the release of
greenhouse gases (GHG) such as methane (CH4 ), CO2, and nitrous oxide (N2O), which have high global
warming potential (GWP) and contribute significantly to climate change. These emissions are particularly pronounced in livestock and human wastes due to their high organic matter and nitrogen content, which promote
microbial decomposition and gas formation under anaerobic or poorly managed conditions (Amedh 2024). Globally,
livestock production generates large quantities of manure, estimated at over 4 billion tonnes per year. In many
regions, including developing countries, these wastes are commonly managed through open dumping, logoon storage, or rudimentary composting systems, which can lead to substantial GHG emissions and environmental
pollution (Lema 2025).
Livestock wastes such as pig manure (PM) and chicken manure (CM), together with human faecal matter (FM), are particularly important emission sources during storage, handling, and treatment. PM typically contains high moisture content
and readily degradable organic compounds, creating anaerobic conditions that favour methane production. CM, on the
other hand, contains high nitrogen concentrations that promote nitrous oxide emissions during decomposition. Similarly,
untreated FM can produce both CH4 and N2O due to microbial breakdown of organic matter and nitrogen compounds.
Composting of livestock manure, although widely used as a management strategy, can still contribute significantly to
GHG emissions, accounting for approximately 45–91% of total emissions from manure treatment systems, largely due to
release (Nordahl et al. 2023), while untreated human FM remains a significant source of CH4 and N2O emissions (Lambiasi
et al. 2024). These characteristics highlight the need for alternative waste management approaches that reduce emissions
while enabling resource recovery.
Black soldier fly larvae (BSFL, Hermetia illucens) bioconversion has emerged as a promising strategy for transforming
organic waste into valuable products while simultaneously reducing GHG and environmental pollution. Unlike anaerobic
digestion and composting, which can generate substantial CH4 and N2O emissions and require controlled infrastructure
(Aguirre-Villegas & Larson 2017), BSFL treatment operates with lower energy requirements and offers rapid waste conversion with nutrient recovery.
However, most existing studies have primarily focused on waste reduction efficiency, larval biomass production, and nutrient recycling, with limited comparative evaluation of greenhouse gas (GHG) dynamics and overall GWP across different
waste substrates. In particular, comprehensive assessments of GWP during BSFL bioconversion of FM, PM, and CM
remain insufficiently explored (Xiang et al. 2024b).
Furthermore, previous studies investigating GHG emissions during waste treatment have largely relied on advanced
analytical techniques such as gas chromatography-flame ionization detection (GC-FID), infrared gas analyzers, and differential optical absorption spectroscopy (Lambert-Girard et al. 2015; Shellie & Heng 2023). Although these techniques provide
high analytical accuracy, their application is often constrained by high operational costs, complex maintenance requirements, and reliance on laboratory-based infrastructure. This limits their suitability for continuous monitoring in smallscale or decentralized BSFL treatment systems (Boakye-Yiadom et al. 2022).
Therefore, this study integrates real-time gas sensing using (MQ-4 and MQ-135 sensors with life cycle assessment (LCA) to
quantify and compare CO2, CH4, N2O, and NH3 emissions from human FM, PM, and CM during BSFL bioconversion. By
evaluating the relative GWP of these substrates, the study provides insights into the environmental performance of BSFLbased waste treatment systems. GWP expresses the warming effect of different greenhouse gases relative to the emission
of 1 tonne of CO2, thereby providing a standardized metric for comparing the climate impact of different waste management
pathways (Shanbhag et al. 2024).

MATERIALS AND METHODS
Sampling and preparation
Fresh human FM was collected from a urine diversion dehydration toilet (UDDT) at Gachororo Primary School, Juja,
Kenya, while pig and CM were collected from a private farmer in Juja, Kenya. Non-degradable materials were removed,
and the substrates were mixed to obtain homogeneous samples. Samples were collected, dried at 104 ± 1 °C, and then
stored in air-tight containers for elemental analysis. The dried samples were later shipped to Aarhus University in Denmark,
Department of Biological and Chemical Engineering, for elemental analysis using vario MACRO cube CHNS elemental analyzer (Elementar Analysensysteme GmbH, Langenselbold, Germany) according to the procedure described by Muhammad
Firdaus et al. (2018). The elements (carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, and sulphur) were expressed as a percentage of the total
mass of the original sample. Ash content was determined based on an oven dry weight (ODW) basis, which presents the
mass of a sample after complete removal of moisture through oven drying as described in Equation (1) (Feng et al. 2005).

These sensors were selected due to their affordability, accessibility, and suitability for detecting emission trends in
resource-limited research contexts. However, the MQ sensor series is not a laboratory-grade instrument and therefore has
limitations in precision, cross-sensitivity, and susceptibility to environmental conditions. These limitations were mitigated
through calibration and repeated calibration and trials. The results were interpreted as indicative of concentration trends
rather than absolute values. While sensor uncertainty may have influenced the magnitude of calculated emissions, its
impact on the estimation of GWP was proportionally consistent across substrates, as all treatments were monitored
under the same conditions.
Bioconversion experimental setup
The experiment followed a randomized design in a greenhouse at Jomo Kenyatta University of Agriculture and Technology
(JKUAT), Nairobi, Kenya, with three homogenous mixed substrates (FM, PM, and CM). Each substrate was tested with and
without BSFL (control), each in triplicate. The larvae were collected from a colony on day 6 and then starved for 24 h before
being introduced to the substrates. The starvation period ensured that their guts were emptied, minimizing the risk of carryover effects from previous feeds that could otherwise bias experimental results (Shishkov et al. 2019). Six-day-old BSFL were
sampled by passing them through a 1.2 mm mesh screen (Nyakeri et al. 2019). Each treatment unit consisted of 250 pieces of
7-day-old larvae, which were fed on 0.25 kg of each substrate according to a procedure outlined by Vodounnou et al. (2024).
Calibrated sensors were then installed directly inside the ventilated substrate container (115 × 115 × 140 mm) in each treatment unit. DHT22 sensors were used to measure the temperature range (25.94–29.76 °C) and relative humidity level (42.93–
66.72%) within the greenhouse.
LCA for BSFL during the bioconversion process
This study used the cradle-to-gate approach, which provides a holistic view of BSFL environmental impacts throughout
its entire life cycle. The life cycle inventory (LCI) considered inputs (FM, PM, CM water, chick mash, BSFL eggs, and
BSFL), processes (larval rearing and bioconversion), outputs (gaseous emissions (CH4, CO2, N2O, and NH3) and frass),
as shown in Figure 1. Infrastructure construction, chick mash production, and downstream frass utilization were excluded
due to negligible contribution to system emissions. Foreground data were directly obtained from experimental measurements
of gas emissions (CH4, CO2, N2O, NH3), while background data were sourced from the ecoinvent database in OpenLCA
LCIA methods 2.4.0. The functional unit was the treatment of 0.25 kg of each substrate. The GWP associated with each
treatment was subsequently quantified using OpenLCA, an open-source LCA software.

(5) as described by Oyatokun (2023) under standard temperature and pressure conditions (25 °C, 1 atm) to standardize gas
concentration across treatments. This conversion assumes ideal gas behaviour, serving as a comparative indicator of emission levels rather than absolute flux.

RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
Temperature and humidity recorded
The recorded temperature exhibited relatively small fluctuations, with a mean of 27.75 ± 2 °C throughout a 15-day period. In
contrast, relative humidity displayed more pronounced variability, ranging between 60.72 ± 4%, as shown in Figure 2.
The recorded temperature (27.75 ± 2 °C) and relative humidity (60.72 ± 4%) fall within the optimal range reported for
BSFL development (25–30 °C and 60–70% RH), supporting active larval metabolism and microbial degradation. These conditions are considered favourable for efficient substrate conversion and consistent emission monitoring. Therefore, the
environmental conditions during the experiment were suitable for effective bioconversion. These findings highlight the critical role of environmental conditions in regulating BSFL bioconversion and GHG emissions, suggesting that future studies
should investigate these effects under controlled environments.

FM released moderate concentrations of CH4 (2,205.32 ± 160.00) and N2O (3,619.55 ± 100.00), indicating active anaerobic
degradation and substantial nitrogen mineralization. In contrast, PM had the lowest emissions across all gases, with CO2

and lower availability of degradable organic substrates. Overall, these differences highlight that the type and magnitude
of gaseous emissions during decomposition are determined by substrate characteristics, including organic matter quality,
carbon content, and C/N ratio, which in turn regulate microbial processes such as methanogenesis, nitrification, and denitrification. Similarly, a study reported high cumulative GHG emissions during composting from food waste and CM, where
CO2 was 186,127 ppm and 173,900 ppm, respectively, highlighting significant emissions of CO2, CH4, and N2O from different substrates tested (Zeng et al. 2023).
The BSFL-treated substrates recorded the lowest emissions across all the substrates tested. For instance, BSF_CM emitted
393.57 ± 1.50 ppm CH4 and 0.83 ± 0.01 ppm N2O, substantially lower than untreated CM. Similarly, BSF_FM and BSF_PM
showed drastic CO2, CH4, NH3, and N2O emissions compared to FM and PM, respectively, as shown in Table 3. The substantially lower emissions from BSFL-treated substrates indicate that the larvae rapidly consume and stabilize the organic
matter, reducing the availability of carbon and nitrogen for microbial processes such as methanogenesis, nitrification,
and denitrification. Lindberg et al. (2022) confirmed that during composting of fruit and vegetable waste, with or without
pre-treatment, CH4 and N2O emissions were very low (40–1,570 ppm) compared to CO2 (47,000–147,000 ppm). A study carried out by Xiang et al. (2024a) showed the same trend as the GHG emissions CH4, CO2, N2O, and NH3 were reduced by
the larval bioreactor by 62, 87, and 95%, respectively, compared to composting. BSFL treatment significantly mitigated the
emissions of CH4, CO2, N2O, and NH3. The reduction is mainly linked to improved aeration within the substrate and the
larval conversion of organic carbon and nitrogen biomass, which limits the microbial pathway responsible for GHG generation. Additionally, BSFL secretes antimicrobial compounds and enzymes that alter the microbial community, suppressing
methanogens and denitrifying bacteria responsible for CH4 and N2O generation. This combination of aeration, nutrient
assimilation, and microbial stabilization of organic matter lowers overall emissions (Li et al. 2025). The results demonstrated
that BSFL bioconversion significantly reduced GHG emissions from FM, PM, and CM, highlighting its potential as a climate
mitigation strategy. CH4 and N2O were particularly reduced, while CO2 and NH3 emissions also decreased substantially,
further supporting the role of BSFL in enhancing environmental sustainability.

Gas emissions from the bioconversion of the three substrates
Methane emissions from the three substrates
Among the control group, PM showed the lowest cumulative CH4 emissions, while CM showed the highest emissions.
Among the BSFL-treated substrates, BSF_CM recorded the highest cumulative CH4 emissions, while BSF_PM had the
lowest emissions, as shown in Figure 3.
Methane emission peaked during the first few days and declined towards the end, reflecting substrate depletion and
reduced methanogenic activity. The emissions were highest in untreated CM (3,544.37 ppm), FM (2,205.32 ppm), and
PM (148.58 ppm), and were substantially reduced by BSFL treatment to 393.57, 195.75, and 20.30 ppm, respectively, corresponding to reduction rates of 88.90% in CM, 91.13% in FM, and 86.34% in PM, with CM showing the highest mitigation
efficiency relative to its initial emission levels. The low C/N ratio of 8:51 in CM promoted rapid microbial degradation of
organic matter, enhancing anaerobic conditions that support methane production. As a result, the combined effect of
high ammonia levels and a low C/N ratio significantly boosted methane generation in CM, even under BSFL treatment.
BSFL treatment enhanced oxygen diffusion and substrate mixing, promoting an aerobic microbial pathway that converts
organic carbon to CO2 instead of CH4. This shift suppresses methanogenic processes, resulting in lower methane emissions.
Ermolaev et al. (2019) observed that BSFL feeding reduces the presence of readily degradable carbon compounds, thereby
limiting methanogenic precursors within the substrate. Matos et al. (2021) further noted that BSFL digestion converts a portion of organic carbon into larval biomass, thereby reducing the carbon pool available for microbial methane production.
Moreover, Symeon et al. (2025) emphasized that BSFL activity shifts microbial community composition, suppressing methanogens while enhancing aerobic and facultative microbial populations. These studies predominantly used closed chamber
systems with gas chromatography to quantify CH4 concentrations, ensuring precise and comparative assessment of gas emission during bioconversion. Collectively, all these studies confirm that BSFL bioconversion effectively mitigates methane
generation through biochemical stabilization and microbial regulation.

Nitrous oxide emissions on the three substrates
The N2O emissions from the tested substrates are presented in Figure 6.
The N2O emissions varied significantly across the substrates. All BSFL treatments resulted in a decline in cumulative N2O
emissions compared to the control groups. The most significant reduction occurred in CM, where emissions dropped from
44,294.91 ± 200.00 ppm to 0.83 ± 0.01 ppm, representing over a 99% decrease. FM recorded a sharp decline from
3,619.55 ± 100.00 ppm to 0.10 ± 0.11 ppm, while PM exhibited relatively low emissions, decreased from 0.55 ± 0.01 ppm
to 0.16 ± 0.60 ppm. The statistically significant p-values (2.56 × 10−6, 3.84 × 10−9, and 4.11 × 10−7) further confirmed
reduced N2O emissions across all BSFL-treated substrates. The observed trend results from the larvae’s capacity to assimilate
nitrogen into their biomass, thereby reducing the pool of inorganic nitrogen available for nitrification and denitrifying the
principal microbial pathway leading to N2O.
The relatively low N2O emissions can be linked to the elemental composition of the substrates. FM, with the highest nitrogen content (5.12%), recorded slightly higher N2O concentration, while overall emissions remained low due to limited
available nitrogen. However, BSFL treatment minimized N2O release by altering substrate conditions that typically promoted denitrification. The larval activity enhanced oxygen diffusion and anaerobic microsites, limiting the conversion of
nitrate to N2O. Additionally, nitrogen was immobilized in stable ammonium forms, thereby restricting substrate available
for microbial denitrification (Pang et al. 2020). As a result, nitrogen gases are minimized while the remaining frass retains
a higher nutrient value. These mechanisms collectively explain the lower N2O emissions and highlight BSFL bioconversion
as an efficient nitrogen stabilizing process (Mertenat et al. 2019; Zhang et al. 2024). These outcomes position BSFL treatment as a sustainable waste strategy that simultaneously mitigates emissions and enhances nutrient recovery, contributing to
circular bioeconomy goals.
Among the substrates, BSFL treatment achieved the highest CH4 mitigation in FM (91.13%), while CO2 and N2O
reductions were greatest in CM (99.85 and 99%, respectively); similarly, ammonia showed its highest reduction in FM
(98.89%). Overall, these results demonstrate the mitigation capacity of BSFL bioconversion, with its effectiveness varying
across gases and substrates depending on the waste characteristics and microbial dynamics. To further quantify the climate
implications of these emissions reductions, an LCA was conducted to translate gaseous concentrations into equivalent GWP
values.

CONCLUSION
This study quantified GHG emissions from CM, PM, and human FM, and evaluated the mitigation potential of BSFL bioconversion. The results clearly demonstrated that untreated substrates emitted substantially higher concentrations of
methane (CH4), CO2, nitrous oxide (N2O), and ammonia (NH3) compared to substrates treated with BSFL. Among the
untreated substrates, CM produced the highest cumulative emissions and GWP, followed by human FM and PM. BSFL treatment significantly reduced GHG emissions across all substrates. The corresponding reduction in GWP was 94.3% for CM,
91.7% for human FM, and 80% for PM. The highest mitigation efficiency was observed in CM, indicating that nitrogen-rich
substrates with low carbon-to-nitrogen ratios benefit most from larval bioconversion. These findings confirm that substrate
composition strongly influences emission dynamics and the overall climate mitigation performance of BSFL treatment.
The study addressed the key research question of whether BSFL bioconversion can effectively reduce GHG emissions
from different organic waste substrates. The results provide clear evidence that larval activity reduces emissions by enhancing substrate aeration, assimilating carbon and nitrogen into biomass, and suppressing microbial pathways responsible for
methane and nitrous oxide production.
Although conducted under controlled laboratory conditions, the findings provide a strong experimental basis for considering BSFL bioconversion as a low-emission alternative to conventional manure management practices. Future research
should focus on validating these results under field-scale conditions and assessing long-term operational performance. Overall, BSFL bioconversion demonstrates significant potential as a sustainable strategy for reducing GHG emissions from
organic waste streams.

Abstract: The study comprehensively evaluates low-cost CO2 sensors from different price tiers,
assessing their performance against a reference-grade instrument and exploring the possibility of
calibration using different machine learning techniques. Three sensors (Sunrise AB by Senseair, K30
CO2 by Senseair, and GMP 343 by Vaisala) were tested alongside a reference instrument (Los Gatos
precision greenhouse gas analyzer). The results revealed differences in sensor performance, with
the higher cost Vaisala sensors exhibiting superior accuracy. Despite its lower price, the Sunrise
sensors still demonstrated reasonable accuracy. Meanwhile, the K30 sensor measurements displayed
higher variability and noise. Machine learning models, including linear regression, gradient boosting
regression, and random forest regression, were employed for sensor calibration. In general, linear
regression models performed best for extrapolating data, whereas decision tree-based models were
generally more useful in handling non-linear datasets. Notably, a stack ensemble model combining
these techniques outperformed the individual models and significantly improved sensor accuracy by
approximately 65%. Overall, this study contributes to filling the gap in intercomparing CO2 sensors
across different price categories and underscores the potential of machine learning for enhancing
sensor accuracy, particularly in low-cost sensor applications.

1. Introduction
Carbon dioxide (CO2 ) is one of the major greenhouse gases (GHG) responsible for
contemporary climate change. Studies have shown that tropospheric CO2 levels often
exhibit significant spatial variation, which depends on land usage [1,2] and topography [3].
CO2 measurements can be used as a proxy to estimate carbon emissions. Monitoring these
fine-scale spatial variations of CO2 can help to identify emission hotspots, assess local
carbon cycling, track urbanization effects, and develop strategies to reduce overall carbon
emissions [1,3,4].
Historically, wide spatial coverage and resolution of CO2 measurements has been limited by the high cost of instrumentation. Low-cost CO2 sensors have become increasingly
popular over recent years owing to technological advancements in electronics and the Internet of Things (IoT). These sensors are generally small, portable, and low power. Usually,
these sensors either use a solid electrolyte or a non-dispersive infrared (NDIR) detector [5].
NDIR sensors are more stable, accurate, and consume less power compared to sensors
using solid electrolytes [6,7]. Furthermore, ease of operation and IoT capabilities make
them ideal for setting up a dense network of multiple sensors to measure the distribution

of CO2 concentrations at high spatial resolution. A dense network of reasonably accurate
low-cost CO2 sensors can provide vital information leading to a better understanding of
carbon fluxes and their sources [8]. However, obtaining accurate data from these low-cost
sensors is a major challenge. Many sensors suffer from inadequate quality control and
stability, leading to inconsistent performance across various conditions [9]. Over time,
sensor measurements tend to drift, compromising accuracy [10]. Moreover, conducting
in situ recalibration, especially within extensive sensor networks, is often impractical.
Additionally, environmental variables like temperature and humidity induce non-linear
responses, further complicating sensor usability [11]. Despite their cost-effectiveness, it is
imperative to address these shortcomings to ensure dependable environmental monitoring.
The United States Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) over the last few years has
focused on development and performance targets for particulate matter, ozone, nitrogen
dioxide, sulfur dioxide, and carbon monoxide sensors [12]. It published detailed guidelines
on testing protocols and target values for particulate matter and ozone sensors and is
currently participating in the American Society for Testing and Materials (ASTM) study
(ASTM WK74360) to develop methods for testing and evaluating CO2 sensors [12]. Studies
that evaluate the performance of low-cost sensors help in setting the performance targets
for the sensors. Past studies have evaluated low-cost CO2 sensors in controlled [8] and
uncontrolled environments [5,7,8]. These studies have also evaluated the dependence
of sensors on several factors, such as temperature, relative humidity (RH), and pressure.
Further, low-cost sensors vary significantly in cost, ranging from ~35 USD to ~3500 USD.
Past studies have evaluated low-cost CO2 sensors ranging from ~50–100 USD [13–17] to
~3500 USD [18]. However, the intercomparison of differences in the performance and
accuracy of low-cost sensors from different price categories has not been well studied in
the past, which is necessary to better understand the applicability of low-cost CO2 sensors.
This will also contribute to US EPA and ASTM efforts in setting performance targets for
CO2 sensors. Further, to make low-cost sensors an effective tool for research, it is required
to calibrate the sensors and ensure the data reported are accurate. Several past studies
have attempted to use statistical [8] and machine learning techniques [7,8,11,19] to improve
the performance of sensors. However, these studies do not compare the performance
differences of sensors from different price categories [20]. Our study aims to bridge this
gap. This comparison will help in selecting a sensor that balances accuracy and budget,
depending on the specific application.
We evaluated three different low-cost sensors, testing three replicates of each. The
low-cost sensors investigated in this study are as follows: (a) Sunrise AB by Senseair
(hereafter referred to as Sunrise), (b) K30 CO2 by Senseair (K30), and (c) GMP 343 by Vaisala
(Vaisala). The sensors’ performance evaluation is based on collocated measurements next
to a reference-grade instrument, a Los Gatos Research analyzer by ABB (model GLA 131;
hereafter referred to as LGR). The results from the study highlight the differences in the
performance of low-cost sensors from two different price categories: (a) Tier I, Vaisala
(~3500 USD) and (b) Tier II, Sunrise and K30 (~60 to 100 USD). One objective of this
study is to calibrate and improve the accuracy of low-cost sensors using machine learning.
Additionally, the study aims to evaluate the effectiveness of calibrating these sensors in
environmentally controlled chambers. To test this method, we operated three Sunrise
sensors alongside LGR in control chambers under varying conditions. The data collected
were used to calibrate the sensors with machine learning techniques and test the models’
performance using ambient air measurements. While previous studies have evaluated
sensor performance in controlled chambers [11,21] and indoor environments [22], to the
best of our knowledge, there are no studies that assess the performance of calibration
models developed in chamber settings when applied to ambient environmental data. This
evaluation is crucial for understanding the applicability of chamber-based calibration of
low-cost sensors.
